One Server, Three Languages#

Learn C, Go and Rust from scratch by building the same Redis-compatible server three times, and understand the power and the weakness of each.

Compiled bykodebot

October 2026 edition

C17 with clang 17 (notes on C23 and gcc) Go 1.27 Rust 1.99, edition 2024, tokio 1 (Part V also runs miri and loom on a nightly of 7 October 2026) redis-cli 8.10
Start with the preface Why these three languages Start building

21 chapters and 62 exercises. Reading time about 10 hours 15 minutes, measured by the build. Building time is yours. This copy was built on 24 October 2026.

NextPreface4 min

Preface#

You learn by building. So this book gives you one thing to build, and asks you to build it three times.

The thing is kv, a small server that speaks the Redis protocol. From chapter 4 on, the real redis-cli can talk to it. By the end it keeps keys and values in a hash table you wrote and serves many clients at once. It removes a key when its time limit runs out, survives a crash by replaying a log, and answers redis-benchmark at a respectable speed.

You build kv in C first, then in Go, then in Rust. The order is the order of history. C was made in 1972 to write an operating system. Go and Rust were both made, about forty years later, to fix the problems that forty years of C had shown. Go fixed them by making the language smaller and adding a garbage collector. Rust fixed them by making the compiler stricter. Building the same server in all three is the clearest way to feel the difference.

Who this book is for#

You wrote some C at university and have forgotten most of it. You used Go for a while and have forgotten that too. You have heard that Rust is good for systems programming and have never written any. You want to understand what each language is good at, what each one is bad at, and what the tools around each one are like. You do not want a long book.

No chapter assumes that you remember the chapter before. Each one restates the few facts it needs. Many readers read English as a second language, so every sentence holds one fact and no idiom.

How to read it#

Every teaching chapter has the same shape. A short lead says what the chapter is about. A table compares the concept across the three languages. Then you build the feature in C, in Go, and in Rust. Each build has an exercise. The exercise shows a design and partial code. You write the rest. If you are stuck, open the folded solution under the exercise. It holds the complete listing. The chapter closes with a verdict, a small scorecard of which language was strong, which was weak, and why.

Four kinds of box appear in the text. A history box says why a language is the way it is. A rough edge box warns about a mistake that many people make. A practice box names the convention professionals follow. A platforms box explains where macOS, Linux and Windows differ.

Code appears side by side on a wide screen and in tabs on a narrow one. Press 1, 2 or 3 to follow one language through the whole book, or use the Follow buttons in the sidebar. Press ⌘K to search.

Part V is optional#

Parts I to IV compare the three languages, and the verdict ends that comparison. Part V is for readers who chose Rust. In each of its five chapters you build one mechanism of the language yourself, inside kv. The mechanisms are a reply that borrows, a vtable, an executor, a reference count, a byte buffer and a derive macro. You check each one with tests, miri or loom, and then meet the version in the library. C and Go appear in Part V only in a table at the end of each chapter.

The code#

Every listing in this book is taken from a file in the code/ folder of the book's repository. There is one complete copy of kv for each chapter and each language, so code/rust/ch09 is exactly what chapter 9 ends with. The same test script drives all three versions through redis-cli and compares the replies. The build of the book reads the listings from those files, so the text and the code cannot disagree.

The book targets C17 with clang 17 (notes on C23 and gcc), Go 1.27 and Rust 1.99, edition 2024, tokio 1 (Part V also runs miri and loom on a nightly of 7 October 2026), with redis-cli 8.10 as the client. Version-sensitive facts were verified from 12 October 2026 onwards. The edition is October 2026.

This copy was built on 24 October 2026. Reading time is about 10 hours 15 minutes, measured by the build. Parts I to IV take about 7 hours 45 minutes, and Part V takes about 1 hour 35 minutes. The time you spend building is yours, and it is the point.

Fifty years, three answers#

Origins · Chapter 01· 13 min read

C was made in 1972 to write an operating system. Go and Rust were made about forty years later to fix what forty years of C had shown. Go made the language smaller and added a garbage collector. Rust made the compiler stricter. This chapter tells the three stories, because every design choice in this book has a reason in them.

One problem, three answers#

Every program in this book does the same job. It takes bytes from a network socket, keeps some of them in memory, and sends bytes back. That is systems programming. The hardware has not changed its nature since 1972. Memory is still a flat run of bytes. A socket is still a stream. What changed is how much a mistake costs.

The timeline below is the shape of the whole chapter. Read it once now and again at the end.

1969 to 1973: why C#

Bell Labs, 1969. Ken Thompson has a DEC PDP-7 that nobody else wants, a machine with little memory and almost no software. On it he has written the first Unix. He needs a language to write programs for it, and the languages he knows are too big for the machine. So he makes a small one and calls it B. B was BCPL, a language that Martin Richards had designed in the mid-1960s, "squeezed into 8K bytes of memory", in Dennis Ritchie's words. Ritchie also wrote that "B can be thought of as C without types".

B had one type. Every value was a machine word. On the PDP-7 that was fine, because the machine addressed memory in words. In 1970 the group got a PDP-11. The PDP-11 addressed memory in bytes. It also had no floating-point hardware at first. A language with one word-sized type did not fit a machine that worked in bytes. B was also slow, because its compiler produced code that an interpreter ran, not machine code.

So in 1971 Ritchie added a character type to B and made it produce PDP-11 machine code. During 1971 to 1973 he added more types and then structures. The result was C. In the summer of 1973 the Unix kernel was rewritten in C. An attempt in 1972 had failed. The attempt in 1973 succeeded because C now had structures, which the kernel needed to describe its own tables.

📜Why C has pointers and arrays the way it does

Ritchie called the rule that turns an array into a pointer "the crucial jump in the evolutionary chain between typeless BCPL and typed C". An array name in C is the address of its first element. That rule is why buf[3] and *(buf + 3) mean the same thing. It is also why C cannot check an array index at run time. The length is not part of the value.

Unix spread, and C spread with it. Brian Kernighan and Ritchie published The C Programming Language in 1978. In the same years the language was made portable. A compiler that could produce code for more than one machine was described in 1978, and Unix was moved to the Interdata 8/32. From then on, C was the language that operating systems were written in. In 1983 an ANSI committee began to write a standard. It finished at the end of 1989, and ISO adopted it in 1990. Newer standards followed in 1999, 2011, 2018 and 2024. The 2018 standard is called C17 and is the one this book uses. The 2024 standard is called C23.

In 1995, when it began the next revision, the committee wrote down what it wanted to keep. It called this the spirit of C, and listed it as five short rules. The first was "Trust the programmer". The second was "Don't prevent the programmer from doing what needs to be done". The fifth was "Make it fast, even if it is not guaranteed to be portable". Those rules explain almost everything about C that surprises a reader coming from another language. C does not check an array index. C does not know when to free memory. C lets you add one to a pointer and read whatever is there. The programmer is trusted to be right.

Ritchie's own summary of the language was "quirky, flawed, and an enormous success". Every word of that is true.

What forty years of C cost#

Trusting the programmer worked when one careful person wrote a kernel. It worked less well when thousands of people wrote browsers, and strangers on the internet sent those browsers input. The first stranger arrived in 1988.

📰The Morris worm, 1988

On the evening of 2 November 1988 a program began to copy itself from one Unix machine to the next, across the whole internet. Robert Tappan Morris, a graduate student at Cornell, released it from a machine at MIT. One of the ways it got in was a buffer overflow in the finger service. That service was a C program that read a request into a fixed array without checking the length. The worm sent a request longer than the array, and the bytes past the end became code that ran. About 6,000 machines were infected, by the figure most often reported. The case became the first felony conviction under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The bug was a C program trusting its input. Thirty years later it was still the most common kind.

In 2019 Microsoft reported that about 70 percent of the vulnerabilities it reported each year were memory safety bugs. The Chromium project reported the same figure for its own code. Around 70 percent of its serious security bugs, in a sample of 912 high and critical bugs since 2015, were memory safety problems. A memory safety bug is a read or write that the program should not have made. An index past the end of an array is one. Using memory after it was freed is another. C allows both, because of the rules above.

Memory was one cost. Build time was another. By 2007, Rob Pike wrote, a large C++ binary at Google took 45 minutes to build. The C++ language inherited the C way of sharing declarations, which is to copy a header file into every file that includes it. In one measurement, 4.2 megabytes of source expanded to more than 8 gigabytes of compiler input. That is about 2,000 bytes of work for every byte a programmer wrote. The problem was old. In 1984 a Unix build was found to include the same header file 37 times for one program.

The third cost was concurrency. By 2007 a computer had several processors, and a server had to use all of them. C gives you threads and locks and nothing else. A mistake with a lock is a data race, and a data race in C is undefined behaviour. The program may do anything.

The C committee has said this itself. The charter for the 2024 standard states that "Trust the programmer, as a goal, is outdated in respect to the security and safety programming communities". The committee kept the goal. A sixth rule, added for the 2011 standard, says "Make support for safety and security demonstrable". Two other groups of people did not wait for the committee. They made new languages.

2007 to 2012: why Go#

Google, 21 September 2007. A C++ build is running, and it will take 45 minutes. While it runs, Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson start to sketch a new language on a whiteboard. Thompson had made B in 1969. Now he was in the room again, 38 years later, to replace what B had become. Pike's own account says the idea came during one of those builds. The Go FAQ says the language "was born out of frustration with existing languages and environments". It names the frustrations. Large programs were too complex to build. Multiprocessor computers were "becoming universal but most languages offered little help to program them". And a programmer had to "choose either efficient compilation, efficient execution, or ease of programming".

The answers in Go are all answers to those frustrations. Each one is a thing C does not do.

  • A garbage collector. The FAQ says the lifetime of objects is "one of the biggest sources of bookkeeping in systems programs". Go frees memory for you. The collector pauses the program, but by now the pauses are "often to the sub-millisecond range".
  • Goroutines and channels. The concurrency comes from the idea of communicating sequential processes, which Tony Hoare described in 1978. Go took it through two earlier languages, Newsqueak and Limbo. A goroutine is cheap, and a channel sends a value from one to another.
  • Fast builds. A Go file names only the packages it imports, and never copies in a header. An import that is not used is a compile error. So the compiler reads each dependency once, and the build of a large program takes seconds.
  • No exceptions. The FAQ says the try-catch-finally idiom "results in convoluted code". A Go function returns its error as a second value, and the caller checks it. Go keeps panic for the cases that are truly exceptional.
  • One format. The tool gofmt decides how code looks. Pike wrote that this removed "an entire class of argument between programmers".

The syntax came from C. The packages and declarations came from the Pascal, Modula and Oberon family, which Griesemer knew from Niklaus Wirth. Go became an open source project on 10 November 2009. Go 1 was released on 28 March 2012 with a promise. A program written for Go 1 "will continue to compile and run correctly, unchanged, over the lifetime of that specification". The promise still holds. The version in this book is Go 1.27, from August 2026.

📜Why Go looks plain

Go was designed for a company with a very large code base and a very large number of programmers. A language that is small is a language that everyone on the team reads the same way. That is why Go has no classes, no generics until 2022, and one loop keyword. The plainness is the point. When Go feels limited in this book, remember who it was built for.

2006 to 2015: why Rust#

Mozilla, 2006. The company's product is a web browser written in C++, and a browser is the program that the 70 percent figure above describes. Every memory bug in it is a hole that a web page can reach. Graydon Hoare, an engineer there, starts a language of his own in his spare time and calls it Rust. He works on it alone for three years. From late 2009 Mozilla pays him to work on it, and in 2010 he presents it to the company. He hopes it will be "slightly less annoying" than the languages Mozilla uses. The two aims he gives are better memory safety and more concurrency.

Go answered the memory problem with a garbage collector. Mozilla did not want its engine to pause for a collector, or to pay for one in memory. So Rust needed a different answer. It found one in the compiler. Every value in Rust has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is freed. A value can be lent to another part of the program, but the compiler checks every loan. A loan may not outlive its owner. While one part of the program can change a value, no other part can read it. These rules are checked before the program runs, so they cost nothing at run time. The checker is called the borrow checker, and it is the part of Rust that new programmers argue with.

The same rules solve the concurrency problem. A data race needs two threads with access to one value, and at least one of them writing. The ownership rules do not allow that. A Rust program that compiles, and uses no unsafe, has no data races. The compiler proves it before the program runs. Go has a race detector, but the detector finds a race only when a test meets one.

Rust 1.0 was released on 15 May 2015. The announcement called it "the official beginning of our commitment to stability". It described the aim as "low-level control over performance with high-level convenience and safety guarantees", "without requiring a garbage collector or runtime". A new version has come out about every six weeks since then. The versions this book uses are 1.97 from July 2026, 1.98 from August and 1.99 from October. Larger changes to the language arrive as an edition, and a program chooses its edition. This book uses the 2024 edition, which shipped with Rust 1.85 in February 2025.

In February 2021 the Rust Foundation was created to own the language, with AWS, Google, Huawei, Microsoft and Mozilla as founding members. Mozilla, "the original home of the Rust project", gave it the trademarks and the package registry. The language no longer belongs to one company.

📜Why Rust is hard at first

C trusts you. Go checks a little, and a garbage collector handles the rest. Rust refuses to compile a program until it can prove that the memory rules hold. The proof is yours to supply, in the types you write. That is why a Rust program takes longer to write the first time and why the compiler's messages are so long. The compiler is doing the work that in C you do in your head, and in Go you leave to the collector.

Two answers to one question#

The question was what to do about the costs of trusting the programmer. Go and Rust gave different answers, and the table shows where they differ. The rest of the book is the long form of this table.

The costCGoRust
Memory that is freed too earlya crash or a security holeimpossible, the collector frees itdoes not compile, the owner frees it
Memory that is never freeda leakunreachable objects are always freed, but a kept reference is a leakfreed at the end of scope, but a reference cycle or mem::forget can leak
Two threads writing one valueundefined behavioura race the detector may finddoes not compile
A forgotten error checkthe error is lostthe error is lost, but a linter can warnthe compiler warns on an unused Result
A slow buildthe headers are copied into every filepackages are read once, builds take secondscrates are compiled once, but the checks take time
The cost you payyour attention, all the timememory and pauses for the collectorthe time to satisfy the compiler

No answer is free. Go pays with a collector and with some things it refuses to let you express. Rust pays with the time it takes to learn, and with code that spells out more than C or Go would ask for. C pays nothing in advance, and everything later. In each chapter of this book you will feel one of those costs directly, because you will build the same thing three times.

What this means for kv#

The server you will build, kv, is a small version of Redis. Redis itself is written in C, and is a well written C program. It was started by Salvatore Sanfilippo in 2009, the year Go was announced. It keeps every key in memory, serves many clients from one thread, and writes an append-only log to survive a crash. Each of those three ideas is a chapter in this book. In each one you see the C answer first, then what Go and Rust change.

Three languages, three toolchains, and one line of output each. Chapter 2 builds that line three times and ends with three files of very different sizes. Two of them are carrying something the third one left behind.

Toolchains and hello, three times#

Origins · Chapter 02· 20 min read· 148 lines of code
▶Scene

Three programs, one line of output each. Build all three and look at the files you got. On the author's Mac:

$ ./hello-c; ./hello-go; ./hello-rust
hello from C
hello from Go
hello from Rust
$ ls -l hello-c hello-go hello-rust | awk '{print $5, $9}'
8440 hello-c
2516816 hello-go
414728 hello-rust

The same line, three times. One file is 8 kilobytes, one is 2.5 megabytes, and one sits between them. What is in the big one that is not in the small one? Where did the small one leave it?

Install a C compiler, Go and Rust. Compile one small program in each. Then look at what the compiler made, because a binary is the thing all three languages exist to produce. The chapter also installs redis-cli, which the server will talk to from chapter 4.

kv does not exist yet. By the end of this chapter you have three programs that print a line. You also know what a compiler, a linker and a build tool each do. Every later chapter assumes those three tools are on your path.

The toolchainCGoRust
Compilercc (clang or gcc)gorustc, driven by cargo
Build toolMake, or CMake for large projectsgo build, with no build filecargo build, with Cargo.toml
Project filenone, a Makefile by conventiongo.modCargo.toml
Formatterclang-format, optionalgofmt, universalrustfmt, universal
Hello binary on macOS8 KB, links the C library2.5 MB, the runtime is inside415 KB, the standard library is inside
Where the standard library isa shared file the OS providescompiled into every binarycompiled into every binary

Install the three toolchains#

Each language has one official way to install it. For Go and Rust use that way, and not a package from a distribution, so that the version matches the baseline of this book. The commands are below for each platform.

🖥A C compiler on macOS, Linux and Windows

On macOS, run xcode-select --install. It installs Apple's clang, which answers to the name cc. On Debian and Ubuntu, run sudo apt install build-essential, which installs gcc, make and the C library headers. On Windows there are two choices. The Microsoft way is to download the Build Tools for Visual Studio and select the "Desktop development with C++" workload. The compiler is then cl.exe, and you run it from a Developer Command Prompt, because the tools need many environment variables set. The other way is to install WSL and use the Ubuntu line above. The C code in this book is written for POSIX, the Portable Operating System Interface that macOS and Linux share. So WSL is the simpler choice on Windows.

Go is installed from a package. On macOS the package installs into /usr/local/go and adds it to your path. On Linux, download the archive from go.dev/dl and extract it:

$ rm -rf /usr/local/go && tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
$ export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin
$ go version
go version go1.27.0 linux/amd64

On Windows, run the MSI installer and open a new command prompt. The check is the same, go version.

Rust is installed by rustup, which also manages versions later. On macOS, Linux and WSL the command is one line:

$ curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
$ rustc --version
rustc 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28)

On Windows, download and run rustup-init.exe. It may ask you to install the Visual Studio C++ Build Tools, because Rust uses the Microsoft linker there. Finally, install the Redis client. On macOS run brew install redis. On Debian and Ubuntu run sudo apt install redis-tools. Check with redis-cli --version.

⚠️Go downloads a newer Go when a module asks for one

The Go you run may not be the Go you installed. A go.mod file names a Go version. Since Go 1.21, when that version is newer than the installed one, the go command downloads the newer toolchain and uses it. The author's machine had Go 1.23 installed, and go version printed 1.27 inside this book's code. That is convenient, and it is also surprising. The environment variable GOTOOLCHAIN=local turns it off.

C: from source to binary in four steps#

The C program is six lines:

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("hello from C\n");
    return 0;
}
hello/c/hello.c · region hello

Compile and run it. The flags after -std=c17 turn on every useful warning and make each warning an error. Use them on every C file you ever compile:

$ cc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -o hello hello.c
$ ./hello
hello from C

The one command ran four tools, and it helps to see each one. The preprocessor copies stdio.h into the file, and expands macros. Those six lines become 571. The compiler turns C into assembly. The assembler turns assembly into an object file, which is machine code with holes where the addresses of other functions go. The linker fills the holes and joins the object file with the C library. You can stop after any step:

$ cc -std=c17 -E hello.c | wc -l        # preprocess only
     571
$ cc -std=c17 -S -O2 -o - hello.c       # compile to assembly, print it
_main:
        pushq   %rbp
        movq    %rsp, %rbp
        leaq    L_str(%rip), %rdi
        callq   _puts
        xorl    %eax, %eax
        popq    %rbp
        retq
$ cc -std=c17 -c -o hello.o hello.c     # assemble to an object file
$ nm hello.o                            # the names it defines (T) and needs (U)
0000000000000000 T _main
                 U _printf

Two details in that output matter for the rest of the book. The assembly calls _puts, not _printf. The compiler saw a format string with no arguments and chose the cheaper function. The compiler is allowed to do that, and much more, whenever the result is the same. The object file was built without -O2, so it lists _printf as undefined, marked U. The linker resolves it to the C library, which on macOS is the shared file libSystem.B.dylib. Your binary does not contain printf. It contains a note that says where to find it.

The -O2 is the optimisation level, and it is the reason for puts. At -O0, the default, the compiler translates each line as written, which is what you want under a debugger. At -O2 it may reorder, inline and replace, as long as the program behaves the same. At -O0 the hello program is 34 lines of assembly that call printf. At -O2 it is 29 that call puts. Every release build in this book uses -O2, and chapter 13 measures what it is worth.

📜Why C has header files

A C compiler reads one file at a time and knows nothing about the others. For a call to printf to compile, the file must have seen a declaration of printf first. Before header files, a declaration that several files needed was written again in each of them. A header file is that declaration written once and copied in by the preprocessor. The scheme was cheap on a PDP-11 and expensive. By 1984 one Unix program was found to include the same header 37 times. At Google in 2007 the same scheme turned 4.2 megabytes of source into 8 gigabytes of compiler input. Go and Rust both replaced headers with modules, which chapter 7 covers.

Exercise 02.1CWhat size is a word?

Add two lines to main. The first prints the size of an int, a long and a pointer. The second prints the compiler version. The operator sizeof gives a size in bytes, and the format %zu prints one. The macro __VERSION__ is a string that gcc and clang define. It is not part of the C standard, and cl.exe on Windows defines _MSC_VER instead. On the author's machine the output is int 4, long 8, pointer 8 bytes.

int main(void) {
    printf("hello from C\n");
    /* your two lines here */
    return 0;
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("hello from C\n");
    /* sizeof gives a size in bytes. The %zu format prints a size_t. */
    printf("int %zu, long %zu, pointer %zu bytes\n",
           sizeof(int), sizeof(long), sizeof(void *));
    printf("compiler " __VERSION__ "\n");
    return 0;
}
hello/c/hello.c
✅Compile with -Wall -Wextra -Werror from the first day C

The C compiler accepts a great many programs that are wrong. The warnings catch a large share of them, and -Werror stops you from ignoring one. Every C file in this book is compiled with those three flags, and with -std=c17 so that the compiler applies one known standard.

C: two files, one binary#

kv will not fit in one file for long. Split the hello program in two and the four steps above explain how C programs of any size are built. The second file holds the greeting. Its header declares the one function other files may call:

#ifndef GREET_H
#define GREET_H

/* Declared here, defined in greet.c. Every file that includes this header can call it. */
void greet(const char *who);

#endif
hello/c/greet.h · region header
#include <stdio.h>

#include "greet.h"

/* static: only this file can see the name. The linker never hears of it. */
static const char *prefix(void) {
    return "hello from";
}

/* No static: this name has external linkage. units.c calls it through greet.h. */
void greet(const char *who) {
    printf("%s %s\n", prefix(), who);
}
hello/c/greet.c · region unit

The first file includes the header and calls the function:

#include "greet.h"

int main(void) {
    greet("two files");
    return 0;
}
hello/c/units.c · region unit

Each .c file, with the headers pasted in, is a translation unit. The compiler reads one unit at a time and knows nothing about the others. So units.c compiles because greet.h promised that greet exists somewhere. The Makefile compiles each unit to an object file and links the two object files:

# Two translation units. Each .c is compiled alone into a .o, and the linker joins them.
units: units.o greet.o
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ units.o greet.o

units.o: units.c greet.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c units.c

greet.o: greet.c greet.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c greet.c
hello/c/Makefile · region units

nm shows what each object file defines and what it still needs. The letters are the linkage of each name. T is a function this file defines and other files may use. U is a name this file uses and someone else must define:

$ make units
$ nm units.o
                 U _greet
0000000000000000 T _main
$ nm greet.o
0000000000000000 T _greet
                 U _printf

prefix is missing from greet.o. It was declared static, so its name never leaves the file, and at -O2 the compiler pasted its body into greet. A function without static has external linkage, which means every file in the program shares its name. That is why every public name in kv starts with kv_, and why every private one is static. Leave an object file out and the linker says what is missing:

$ cc -o units units.o
Undefined symbols for architecture x86_64:
  "_greet", referenced from:
      _main in units.o
ld: symbol(s) not found for architecture x86_64

Hold on to that error. In chapter 7 the same mechanism holds the modules of kv together. In chapter 14 it is what linking a library means. In chapter 15 it is how Go and Rust call C at all.

Go: one command, one binary#

A Go program is a package. The file below is the whole of package main, and the function main is where the program starts:

package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	"unsafe"
)

func main() {
	fmt.Println("hello from Go")
}
hello/go/main.go · region hello

Go needs one more file, go.mod, which names the module and the Go version it is written for:

module hello

go 1.27
hello/go/go.mod

Then one command compiles and links. There is no Makefile, because the go tool finds every file in the folder itself:

$ go build -o hello .
$ ./hello
hello from Go
$ go run .                  # compile and run in one step, for development
hello from Go

The binary is 2.5 megabytes, three hundred times the C one. It contains the Go runtime, which is the garbage collector, the scheduler for goroutines, and the code that talks to the operating system. On Linux it has no dependency on the C library at all. On macOS it calls libSystem for system calls and nothing else. That is why a Go binary can be copied to another machine of the same kind and run there with nothing installed. Chapter 14 uses that fact.

Every variable starts at zero#

Look at the two declarations in the solution below, var i int and var p *int. The declarations give no value, and both variables are usable. In Go every variable begins as its zero value. A number is 0, a string is empty, a bool is false. A pointer, a slice, a map or a function is nil. A struct is the zero value of each field. There is no uninitialised memory to read by mistake, which in C is one of the ways a program is wrong without a warning. The rule shapes how Go code is written. A type is designed so that its zero value is ready to use, and most types need no constructor.

The documentation is in the source#

The comment above an exported name is its documentation, and go doc prints it. Ask about the function the hello program calls:

$ go doc fmt.Println
package fmt // import "fmt"

func Println(a ...any) (n int, err error)
    Println formats using the default formats for its operands and writes to

The same text is what pkg.go.dev shows for every public module. When you write a package in chapter 7, a sentence above each exported name is all the documentation needs.

Exercise 02.2GoWhat does the runtime know?

Add two lines to main. The first prints the size of an int and of a pointer, with unsafe.Sizeof, which works like sizeof in C. The second prints runtime.Version(), runtime.GOOS and runtime.GOARCH. Import the packages runtime and unsafe. An import you do not use is an error in Go, so add each import together with the line that uses it.

func main() {
	fmt.Println("hello from Go")
	// your two lines here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	"unsafe"
)

func main() {
	fmt.Println("hello from Go")
	// unsafe.Sizeof is a compile-time constant, like sizeof in C.
	var i int
	var p *int
	fmt.Printf("int %d, pointer %d bytes\n", unsafe.Sizeof(i), unsafe.Sizeof(p))
	fmt.Println("compiler", runtime.Version(), runtime.GOOS, runtime.GOARCH)
}
hello/go/main.go
✅Run gofmt and go vet before you commit Go

gofmt -l . lists the files whose layout is not the standard one, and gofmt -w . fixes them. go vet ./... finds mistakes the compiler accepts, such as a wrong format verb. Both tools come with Go, and every Go project runs them. There is no setting for the style, which is the point.

Rust: cargo owns the project#

In Rust you rarely run the compiler, rustc, yourself. The tool cargo creates the project, builds it, runs it, tests it and fetches its dependencies. cargo new hello makes a folder with two files. The first is the project file:

[package]
name = "hello"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
hello/rust/Cargo.toml

The edition line names the version of the language rules. There are four, 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2024, and a new one comes every three years. An edition may change what code means, such as which names are keywords, so a crate says which edition it is written for. Crates of different editions link together, so a dependency written in 2018 compiles unchanged in a 2024 project. That is how Rust changes the language without breaking the world. The 2024 edition is the current one and this book uses it. The second file is src/main.rs:

fn main() {
    println!("hello from Rust");
}
hello/rust/src/main.rs · region hello

The exclamation mark means that println! is a macro, not a function. A macro can check the format string at compile time, and this one does. A build has two modes. The default is a debug build, which compiles quickly. The release build is slower to compile and runs faster:

$ cargo build --release
   Compiling hello v0.1.0
    Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s)
$ ./target/release/hello
hello from Rust
$ cargo run --release       # build if needed, then run

Everything cargo makes goes under target/. cargo new already lists it in the project's .gitignore. The binary is 415 kilobytes. Like the Go one it contains its standard library. Like the C one it calls the C library of the operating system for a call such as write. Rust sits between C and Go.

Exercise 02.3RustWhat size is a usize?

Add two lines to main. The first prints the size of four types, with size_of::<T>(), which the compiler evaluates at compile time. The four types are i32, i64, usize and a reference. The second prints std::env::consts::OS and std::env::consts::ARCH. Then run cargo clippy and cargo fmt, and see whether either tool reports something.

fn main() {
    println!("hello from Rust");
    // your two lines here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
fn main() {
    println!("hello from Rust");
    // size_of is evaluated at compile time, like sizeof in C.
    println!(
        "i32 {}, i64 {}, usize {}, pointer {} bytes",
        size_of::<i32>(),
        size_of::<i64>(),
        size_of::<usize>(),
        size_of::<&i32>()
    );

hello/rust/src/main.rs
✅Run rustfmt and clippy before you commit Rust

cargo fmt formats the project. cargo clippy is a linter with more than 800 checks, from a needless clone to a loop that should be an iterator. Every Rust snapshot in this book passes cargo clippy -- -D warnings, which makes each warning an error, and cargo fmt --check.

The documentation is in the source, and it is tested#

A comment that starts with three slashes, ///, is a doc comment. cargo doc turns every doc comment in your crate and in every dependency into a website under target/doc, offline:

$ cargo doc
 Documenting hello v0.1.0
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s)
$ ls target/doc
crates.js  hello  help.html

A code block inside a doc comment is a test. cargo test compiles it and runs it, so an example in the documentation cannot go stale. Chapter 12 writes one.

What a binary is#

All three programs are files the operating system can load and run. On macOS the format is called Mach-O. On Linux it is called ELF, the Executable and Linkable Format. On Windows it is called PE, the Portable Executable. The file command names the format:

$ file hello
hello: Mach-O 64-bit executable x86_64

A binary holds machine code, the constant data such as the string to print, and a list of the shared libraries it needs. On macOS the list is printed by otool -L, on Linux by ldd, and on Windows by dumpbin /dependents. The three hello programs name the same library:

$ otool -L hello
hello:
        /usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib (compatibility version 1.0.0, current version 1356.0.0)

So the three binaries differ in what they carry, not in what they are. The C binary carries almost nothing and depends on the system for everything. The Go binary carries its own runtime. The Rust binary carries its standard library and depends on the system for the rest. The sizes in the table at the top of the chapter follow from that. The programs print the same word sizes too. An int is 4 bytes in C and 8 in Go. A pointer is 8 bytes in all three. A Rust usize is the size of a pointer. The pointer size comes from the machine. The size of int is a choice each language made, and C and Go chose differently.

🖥The same program on Linux and Windows

On Linux the C binary is an ELF file and links libc.so.6, the GNU C library. The Go binary links nothing at all, because Go makes its system calls directly on Linux. On Windows the C program links the Windows C runtime, and Rust links the system libraries it needs. Go loads kernel32.dll and a few other system libraries at start, because Windows has no stable system call interface. The chapter on shipping explains what that means for copying a binary from one machine to another.

Build tools, and the lack of one#

C has no build tool of its own. The convention is make, which Stuart Feldman wrote at Bell Labs in 1976. It reads a file called Makefile. The file lists each output, the inputs it depends on, and the command that makes it. The Makefile for the hello program is short:

CC     ?= cc
CFLAGS ?= -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2

hello: hello.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ hello.c

# Two translation units. Each .c is compiled alone into a .o, and the linker joins them.
units: units.o greet.o
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ units.o greet.o

units.o: units.c greet.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c units.c

greet.o: greet.c greet.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c greet.c

clean:
	rm -rf hello units *.o hello.dSYM units.dSYM

.PHONY: clean
hello/c/Makefile

The line hello: hello.c says that hello is made from hello.c, and the indented line below says how. make runs the command only when the input is newer than the output. The ?= sets a variable only when the environment has not set it, which is how the book's test script adds sanitizer flags later. Large C projects use CMake, which writes Makefiles for you from a description that works on every platform. The Redis source, by comparison, is plain Make.

⚠️A Makefile recipe begins with a tab C

Eight spaces are not a tab. The command line under a rule must start with a tab character, and an editor that converts tabs to spaces produces the error missing separator. Feldman has said the tab was a workaround in the first version, kept so as not to break the first users. Every C programmer since has met it.

Go and Rust each come with a build tool, and each tool is the only one anyone uses. For Go the description of the project is go.mod, and the build is go build. For Rust it is Cargo.toml and cargo build. Both tools also run tests, fetch dependencies, and format code. The difference from C is not that these tools are cleverer than Make. It is that there is one of them, so every project looks the same.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
InstallingOKStrongStrongA C compiler is one system command away on macOS and Linux. Go and Rust are one download each, on every platform.
BuildingWeakStrongStrongC has no build tool, only a convention. Go and Rust each have one tool that every project uses.
Seeing what you madeStrongOKOKC shows every step from preprocessor to linker. Go and Rust hide the steps, which is usually what you want.
Binary sizeStrongWeakOK8 KB for C, 2.5 MB for Go because the runtime is inside, 415 KB for Rust.
Running elsewhereWeakStrongOKThe C binary needs the right C library on the target, the Go binary needs nothing, and Rust is in between.
Carry forward
  • Translation unit. A C file with its headers pasted in, compiled alone, and joined to the others by the linker.
  • Zero value. A Go variable starts as zero, nil or empty, so a type is designed to be usable without a constructor.
  • Edition. A Rust crate names the version of the language rules it is written for, and crates of different editions link together.

Echo server#

Building kv · Chapter 03· 17 min read· 159 lines of code
▶Scene

You have a Redis client and no Redis. Ask it anyway:

$ redis-cli -p 6380 PING
Could not connect to Redis at 127.0.0.1:6380: Connection refused

Nothing is listening on the port. Every chapter from here on changes what the program on that port does. This one makes something listen.

A server that sends back what it receives. It is the smallest program that opens a port, accepts a client and moves bytes in both directions. Every later chapter adds to this one. The chapter teaches the socket calls that all three languages share, and how each language wraps them.

kv has to be reachable over the network. A client such as redis-cli connects to a port, sends bytes, and reads bytes back. Before kv can understand a command it must be able to hold that conversation at all. So the first version of kv is an echo server. Whatever the client sends, the server sends back, one client at a time.

The socket callsCGoRust
Open a portsocket, setsockopt, bind, listennet.Listen("tcp", ":6380")TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:6380")
Wait for a clientaccept, returns an intln.Accept(), returns a net.Connlistener.incoming(), yields a TcpStream
Read bytesread(fd, buf, n), returns a count or -1conn.Read(buf), returns a count and an errorstream.read(&mut buf), returns a Result
Copy in to outa loop you write, with a short-write loop insideio.Copy(conn, conn)io::copy(&mut reader, &mut writer)
Closeclose(fd), which you must rememberdefer conn.Close()dropped at the end of scope
An error-1 and a number in errnoa second return valuean Err you must handle or pass on

The four calls in the first row are all there is. A socket is a file descriptor that the operating system connects to the network instead of to a disk. To bind is to give the socket an address and a port. To listen is to tell the operating system that this socket accepts connections, and how many may wait. To accept is to block until a client connects, and to get a second socket that talks to that one client. The first socket keeps listening. The second one is read and written like a file, and closed like one.

📜Why every language has the same four calls

The calls come from 4.2BSD, the Berkeley version of Unix released in 1983, and are called the Berkeley sockets API. The operating system standard POSIX, the Portable Operating System Interface, adopted them. Windows copied them in 1992 under the name Winsock, with a few changes. Go and Rust do not replace these calls. They call them. Underneath, net.Listen and TcpListener::bind are the same four calls. So the C version of this chapter is also an explanation of the other two.

C: four calls, and a way to clean up#

The port comes from an environment variable, so the tests can pick one that is free. The C library function getenv returns a pointer to the value, or NULL when the variable is not set. The pointer belongs to the environment, not to you, so you do not free it:

/* The port comes from the environment, so the tests can pick a free one. */
static int kv_port(void) {
    const char *s = getenv("KV_PORT");
    if (s == NULL || *s == '\0') {
        return 6380;
    }
    return atoi(s);
}
c/ch03/kv.c · region port

Opening the port takes the four calls, and each of them can fail. The pattern below is the most common shape in C that does more than one thing that can fail. Each failure prints its reason and jumps to cleanup, which releases what was acquired so far:

/* Open a listening socket on every interface. Returns the socket, or -1 after
 * printing the reason. The caller owns the socket and must close() it. */
static int kv_listen(int port) {
    int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (fd < 0) {
        perror("socket");
        return -1;
    }
    /* Without this, a restart within a minute fails with "address in use". */
    int yes = 1;
    if (setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof yes) < 0) {
        perror("setsockopt");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    struct sockaddr_in addr;
    memset(&addr, 0, sizeof addr);
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY);
    addr.sin_port = htons((uint16_t)port);
    if (bind(fd, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof addr) < 0) {
        perror("bind");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    if (listen(fd, 16) < 0) {
        perror("listen");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    return fd;

cleanup:
    close(fd);
    return -1;
}
c/ch03/kv.c · region listen

Read the function from the bottom. There is one place where the socket is closed, and every failure after the socket exists reaches it. The goto is not a sign of bad code here. It is how C expresses "undo what I did" without exceptions and without destructors. perror prints the name you give it, a colon, and a message. The message is the text for the current value of errno. That is the global number which every failed system call sets.

✅One exit, through cleanup C

A function that acquires more than one resource has one label, cleanup, at the end. Each acquisition that fails jumps there. The cleanup code releases resources in the reverse order of acquisition. Each release must be safe to run when the resource was never acquired. For example, set a descriptor to -1 first, and skip close when it is still -1. The Linux kernel is written this way, and so is Redis.

⚠️Address already in use C

A server that you restart soon after it stopped fails to bind. When a connection over TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, closes, the operating system keeps its address in a waiting state for a while. The wait stops late packets from reaching a new program. The option SO_REUSEADDR says that your server may bind anyway. Every server sets it. Forget it and the second start of kv prints bind: Address already in use.

errno: the number a failed call leaves behind#

Every system call in kv_listen reports failure the same way. It returns -1 and puts a number in errno, a variable that errno.h declares. The number says what went wrong. EADDRINUSE is the port being taken, and EINTR is a signal arriving mid-call. strerror turns the number into words, and perror prints your label, a colon and those words, which is what perror("bind") did above. Three rules keep errno honest. Read it right after the call that failed, because the next call may overwrite it. Do not read it after a call that succeeded, because a library function may set it even then and never resets it to zero. And since C11 it is thread-local, so a thread in chapter 11 cannot see another thread's number. Go and Rust carry the same number inside their error values, and chapter 4 shows the three designs side by side.

Serving a client is a loop. read returns the number of bytes it put in the buffer, zero when the client closed the connection, or -1 on an error. Writing those bytes back needs a loop of its own, because write may send fewer bytes than you asked when the network is busy. Both calls can also be interrupted by a signal, in which case errno is EINTR and the right response is to try again.

Exercise 03.1CServe one client

Write kv_serve. Read into a 4 KB buffer until read returns zero or an error. After each read, write everything back, and keep writing until every byte is out. Treat EINTR as "try again" in both calls. The caller closes the client socket.

static void kv_serve(int client) {
    char buf[4096];
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = read(client, buf, sizeof buf);
        /* your code: handle n < 0 and n == 0, then write all n bytes back */
    }
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/* Copy everything the client sends back to it, until the client closes. */
static void kv_serve(int client) {
    char buf[4096];
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = read(client, buf, sizeof buf);
        if (n < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;
            }
            perror("read");
            return;
        }
        if (n == 0) {
            return; /* the client closed the connection */
        }
        /* write() may send fewer bytes than asked, so loop until all are out */
        ssize_t off = 0;
        while (off < n) {
            ssize_t w = write(client, buf + off, (size_t)(n - off));
            if (w < 0) {
                if (errno == EINTR) {
                    continue;
                }
                perror("write");
                return;
            }
            off += w;
        }
    }
}
c/ch03/kv.c · region serve

The main function ties the pieces together. It accepts one client, serves it to the end, closes it, and accepts the next. A second client waits in the operating system's queue until the first one is done. Chapter 9 removes that limit:

int main(void) {
    int port = kv_port();
    int fd = kv_listen(port);
    if (fd < 0) {
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(stderr, "kv listening on port %d\n", port);
    for (;;) {
        int client = accept(fd, NULL, NULL);
        if (client < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;
            }
            perror("accept");
            break;
        }
        kv_serve(client);
        close(client);
    }
    close(fd);
    return 1;
}
c/ch03/kv.c · region main

Build and run it with the Makefile from chapter 2, which has grown a SANITIZE variable for the tests:

CC      ?= cc
CFLAGS  ?= -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -g
SANITIZE ?=

kv: kv.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SANITIZE) -o $@ kv.c

clean:
	rm -rf kv kv.dSYM

.PHONY: clean
c/ch03/Makefile · region all

Then talk to it with nc, the netcat tool that comes with macOS and most Linux systems. Type a line and the server sends it back:

$ make
$ ./kv &
kv listening on port 6380
$ nc localhost 6380
hello
hello

Press Ctrl-C to stop nc, and kill %1 to stop the server.

Go: the loop you did not have to write#

The Go version has the same three parts. The port function reads the environment with os.Getenv, which returns the empty string when the variable is unset. There is no NULL to check, and nothing to free:

// The port comes from the environment, so the tests can pick a free one.
func port() string {
	if p := os.Getenv("KV_PORT"); p != "" {
		return p
	}
	return "6380"
}
go/ch03/main.go · region port

Serving a client is one call. io.Copy reads from its second argument and writes to its first until the reader returns end of file. Its signature is Copy(dst io.Writer, src io.Reader). An io.Reader is any type with a Read method. An io.Writer is any type with a Write method. A net.Conn has both, so copying a connection to itself is an echo. A file, a buffer and a compressed stream have them too, which is why one copy function serves them all. Chapter 7 names this mechanism. The short-write loop and the retry on interruption are inside io.Copy and the runtime:

Exercise 03.2GoServe one client with io.Copy

Write serve. It takes a net.Conn, closes it when the function returns, copies the connection to itself, and returns the error from the copy. Use defer for the close.

func serve(conn net.Conn) error {
	// your code here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
// serve copies everything the client sends back to it, until the client closes.
func serve(conn net.Conn) error {
	defer conn.Close()
	_, err := io.Copy(conn, conn)
	return err
}
go/ch03/main.go · region serve
✅defer the close on the line after the open Go

defer conn.Close() runs when the function returns, by whichever path. Write it on the line after the connection is created, so that no later return can forget it. This is the Go form of the C cleanup label, and it needs no label.

Two rules of defer#

defer has two rules that surprise everyone once. Deferred calls run in the reverse order of their defer lines, last in first out, which is the order a cleanup label releases things. And the arguments of a deferred call are evaluated at the defer line, not when the call runs. A closure that reads a variable sees the value at exit, while an argument carries the value at the defer. The test below is in the chapter's snapshot, and go test runs it:

// Two rules of defer, as a test you can run with go test: the deferred calls run last in
// first out, and each one's arguments are evaluated at the defer line, not at the exit.
func deferOrder(log *[]string) {
	n := 1
	defer func() { *log = append(*log, "third, closure sees n =", itoa(n)) }()
	defer func(v int) { *log = append(*log, "second, argument was", itoa(v)) }(n)
	n = 2
	*log = append(*log, "first, the body")
}

func TestDeferOrder(t *testing.T) {
	var log []string
	deferOrder(&log)
	want := []string{"first, the body", "second, argument was", "1", "third, closure sees n =", "2"}
	for i := range want {
		if i >= len(log) || log[i] != want[i] {
			t.Fatalf("log = %q, want %q", log, want)
		}
	}
}
go/ch03/defer_test.go · region defer

The main function listens and loops. net.Listen makes the four calls of the C version for you. It also sets SO_REUSEADDR, which you can see in the file net/sockopt_bsd.go of the Go source. An error from Accept is printed and the loop continues, because one bad connection must not stop the server:

func main() {
	ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", ":"+port())
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "kv listening on port", port())
	for {
		conn, err := ln.Accept()
		if err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "accept:", err)
			continue
		}
		if err := serve(conn); err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "client:", err)
		}
	}
}
go/ch03/main.go · region main
$ go run .
kv listening on port 6380
⚠️A missing error check is legal Go Go

Go lets you drop an error on the floor. serve(conn) on a line of its own compiles, and the error is lost. The compiler checks that a value you assign is used, but not that a value you never assign is looked at. go vet does not catch it either. A separate linter called errcheck does. This book does not add it, and writes every check out instead. In this chapter the check is written out, as if err := serve(conn); err != nil.

Rust: a Result at every step#

In Rust the environment variable is a Result. std::env::var returns Ok(value) or an error when the variable is unset or not valid text. unwrap_or_else turns the error case into the default:

/// The port comes from the environment, so the tests can pick a free one.
fn port() -> String {
    std::env::var("KV_PORT").unwrap_or_else(|_| "6380".to_string())
}
rust/ch03/src/main.rs · region port

Serving a client uses io::copy, which does the same as io.Copy in Go, with the arguments in the other order. There is one new idea. A TcpStream is one value, and the ownership rules allow one mutable use of it at a time. The simplest way to get two handles on it is to clone the stream. try_clone asks the operating system for a second descriptor to the same connection, and that can fail, so it returns a Result too:

Exercise 03.3RustServe one client with io::copy

Write serve. Clone the stream with try_clone, copy from the clone to the original with io::copy, and return Ok(()). Use ? after each call that returns a Result, so that an error returns from the function at once.

fn serve(stream: TcpStream) -> io::Result<()> {
    // your code here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/// Copy everything the client sends back to it, until the client closes.
fn serve(stream: TcpStream) -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut reader = stream.try_clone()?;
    let mut writer = stream;
    io::copy(&mut reader, &mut writer)?;
    Ok(())
}
rust/ch03/src/main.rs · region serve

A main that returns a Result#

The main function returns io::Result<()>, so ? works inside it and a failure to bind prints the error and exits with a non-zero status. The loop uses incoming(), which yields one Result per connection attempt. A match handles both arms, and the compiler would refuse the program if one arm were missing:

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let port = port();
    let listener = TcpListener::bind(format!("0.0.0.0:{port}"))?;
    eprintln!("kv listening on port {port}");
    for stream in listener.incoming() {
        match stream {
            Ok(stream) => {
                if let Err(e) = serve(stream) {
                    eprintln!("client: {e}");
                }
            }
            Err(e) => eprintln!("accept: {e}"),
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}
rust/ch03/src/main.rs · region main
$ cargo run --release
kv listening on port 6380

Nothing closes the stream, and nothing needs to. When serve returns, the TcpStream it owns goes out of scope, and Rust runs its destructor, which calls close. The clone is closed the same way. This is the third way to do what cleanup did in C and defer did in Go. It is the only one of the three that cannot be forgotten.

⚠️A Result you ignore is a warning, not an error Rust

The compiler warns about an unused Result and then compiles the program. serve(stream); on a line of its own produces warning: unused Result that must be used. The book's build turns warnings into errors with cargo clippy -- -D warnings, so in this book the line does not compile. Without that flag it does, and the error is lost as in Go. The difference from Go is that Rust told you.

?, expect and unwrap#

Three ways to take a value out of a Result appear in every Rust program, and each one is a decision. ? passes the error to the caller, and is the default. expect("the reason this cannot fail") stops the program with that message when it does fail. It is for a failure that would mean a bug, and the message says why you believed that. unwrap() is expect with no reason, and belongs in examples and tests. kv uses ? almost everywhere. In port above, unwrap_or_else is a fourth way, which gives a default instead of failing.

Errors, three ways#

The three versions of serve differ most in how they say that something went wrong, and the difference runs through the whole book. In C a function returns -1, and the reason is a number in the global errno. The caller must know to check, and must check before any other call overwrites the number. In Go a function returns the error as a second value, and nil means success. The caller must still choose to look. In Rust a function returns Result, which is either Ok(value) or Err(reason), and the value is inside. To use the value at all, the caller must take it out. The ways to take it out are match, ?, and unwrap. The last one crashes on an error and is for examples only. Chapter 4 builds a parser in all three styles, where the difference is larger.

🖥Sockets on Windows

Winsock has the same calls with the same names, with three differences that matter. A program must call WSAStartup before any of them. A socket is a handle of its own type, not an int, and it is closed with closesocket. And the option SO_REUSEADDR means something stronger on Windows, where it allows two programs to bind the same port. The C version of kv is written for POSIX and does not build on Windows without changes. The Go and Rust versions build there unchanged, because their standard libraries contain the differences.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
Opening a portWeakStrongStrongC needs four calls, a struct and an option. Go and Rust need one call that sets the option for you.
Closing it againWeakOKStrongC needs a cleanup label and Go needs a defer you must write, but Rust closes at the end of scope by itself.
The echo loopWeakStrongStrongC needs the short-write loop and the EINTR retry. Both standard libraries contain them.
A lost errorWeakWeakOKC and Go let a return value drop. Rust warns, and with the book's flags refuses.
Seeing what happensStrongOKOKThe C version shows every system call. The other two hide them, which is what you want on most days.
WindowsWeakStrongStrongThe C code needs Winsock changes. Go and Rust build unchanged.
What you must learn firstStrongOKWeakC is the calls themselves. Rust asks for Result, ?, ownership and try_clone before an echo works.
Carry forward
  • errno. A failed C call returns -1 and leaves a number you must read at once.
  • defer. Runs at function exit, last in first out, with its arguments taken at the defer line.
  • Result. The value is inside, and ?, expect and match are the ways out.
