Speaking RESP#

Building kv · Chapter 04· 33 min read· 545 lines of code
▶Scene

Start the chapter 3 server and point the real client at it:

$ redis-cli -p 6380 PING
1) "PING"
$ redis-cli -p 6380 SET a 1
1) "SET"
2) "a"
3) "1"

The client asked for PONG and got its own question back, as a list. The server echoed the bytes the client sent, and the client read them as a reply. Whatever those bytes are, kv has to understand them before it can answer.

Redis clients talk in a small wire format called RESP, the Redis serialization protocol. This chapter teaches kv to read it and write it. After this chapter the real redis-cli can say PING to your server and get PONG back. The chapter also compares how the three languages say "something went wrong", because a parser is where that question is asked most often.

The echo server sends bytes back. redis-cli does not want its bytes back. It wants an answer in the format it expects. When you type ECHO hi into redis-cli, it sends these 22 bytes to the server:

*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n

Written with one element per line, the request reads as follows. An array of 2 bulk strings. The first has 4 bytes, ECHO. The second has 2 bytes, hi. The server replies with a bulk string of its own, $2\r\nhi\r\n. Every message in RESP is built from five types, each marked by its first byte:

+OK\r\n                   a simple string, for short replies such as OK and PONG
-ERR unknown command\r\n  an error, which the client shows as an error
:42\r\n                   an integer
$5\r\nhello\r\n           a bulk string: the length, then exactly that many bytes
*2\r\n...                 an array: the count, then that many messages
$-1\r\n                   the null bulk string, which GET returns for a missing key

The parts are separated by \r\n, a carriage return and a line feed, which this chapter calls a line ending. A bulk string carries its length in front, so the bytes inside can be anything, including line endings. That one rule is what makes the format both readable and fast to parse. There is no quoting and no escaping.

📜Why RESP looks like this

The Redis protocol specification names its three aims as "Simple to implement. Fast to parse. Human readable." The length in front of a bulk string means the parser never scans the payload for special characters, as a JSON parser must. The second version of the protocol, RESP2, became the standard in Redis 2.0. A third version, RESP3, adds types such as maps and a null of its own. A client chooses it with the HELLO command. kv speaks RESP2, which every client still speaks. The specification also allows an inline command. That is a plain line of words, so that a person with only telnet can talk to a server. Those work in kv too, which is why nc still works after this chapter.

Reading a requestCGoRust
Where the bytes waita buffer you grow with realloca bufio.Readera BufReader
Reading a linememchr for the line feedr.ReadBytes('\n')r.read_until(b'\n', &mut line)
Reading n bytescheck the length, then take a pointerio.ReadFull(r, buf)r.read_exact(&mut buf)
The argumentspointers into the buffer, no copy[][]byte, one copyVec<Vec<u8>>, one copy
Not enough bytes yetthe status KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETEthe reader blocks until they arrivethe reader blocks until they arrive
Bytes that are not RESPthe status KV_PARSE_BADthe error value errProtocolan io::Error of kind InvalidData
The client went awayread returns 0io.EOFOk(None)

The table shows the first large difference between C and the other two. Go and Rust read from a buffered reader that blocks until the bytes arrive, so the parser can ask for a line and wait. C has stdio, a buffered reader built for text files, and kv does not use it. The event loop of chapter 9 needs to see the bytes that have arrived so far. The C parser works on whatever bytes have arrived so far, and says "incomplete" when the request is not all there. That design is more work now. In chapter 9 it is the design the C event loop needs.

C: a buffer, a parser and three answers#

C needs a place to keep bytes between reads, because one read may return half a request, or two and a half. The structure below is a growable byte buffer. The comment on data says who owns it. The book writes such a comment on every pointer in a structure, because nothing else in C will tell you:

/* A growable byte buffer. It owns data, and kv_buf_free releases it. */
typedef struct {
    char *data; /* owned; NULL until the first append */
    size_t len;
    size_t cap;
} kv_buf;

static bool kv_buf_reserve(kv_buf *b, size_t extra) {
    if (b->len + extra <= b->cap) {
        return true;
    }
    size_t cap = b->cap ? b->cap * 2 : 1024;
    while (cap < b->len + extra) {
        cap *= 2;
    }
    char *p = realloc(b->data, cap);
    if (p == NULL) {
        return false; /* the old block is still valid and still ours */
    }
    b->data = p;
    b->cap = cap;
    return true;
}

static bool kv_buf_append(kv_buf *b, const void *src, size_t n) {
    if (!kv_buf_reserve(b, n)) {
        return false;
    }
    memcpy(b->data + b->len, src, n);
    b->len += n;
    return true;
}

/* Drop the first n bytes. memmove allows the two ranges to overlap. */
static void kv_buf_consume(kv_buf *b, size_t n) {
    memmove(b->data, b->data + n, b->len - n);
    b->len -= n;
}

static void kv_buf_free(kv_buf *b) {
    free(b->data);
    b->data = NULL;
    b->len = b->cap = 0;
}
c/ch04/kv.c · region buf

Look at kv_buf_reserve. When realloc fails it returns NULL and leaves the old block alone, so the code must not write the result into b->data before checking it. Writing b->data = realloc(b->data, cap) is a common mistake that loses the buffer on failure. kv_buf_consume uses memmove, not memcpy, because the source and the destination overlap. memcpy on overlapping memory is undefined behaviour.

A parsed command is a small structure of pointers into the buffer. No bytes are copied. The cost of that choice is a rule. The pointers are valid only until the buffer changes, and the comment says so. The parser returns one of three statuses, and the names of the statuses are the whole design:

/* One parsed request. The arguments point into the request buffer, so they are valid
 * only until that buffer is consumed. A kv_cmd owns nothing. */
typedef struct {
    size_t argc;
    const char *argv[KV_MAX_ARGS];
    size_t arglen[KV_MAX_ARGS];
} kv_cmd;

typedef enum {
    KV_PARSE_OK,         /* cmd is filled in, and *used bytes were taken */
    KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE, /* read more bytes and try again */
    KV_PARSE_BAD         /* the bytes are not RESP: close the connection */
} kv_parse_status;
c/ch04/kv.c · region cmd

Two helpers find a line ending and read a number. The number reader refuses more than 18 digits, so that the multiplication cannot overflow a 64-bit long. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C, and a length field is exactly where an attacker would put a large number. A third helper splits an inline line into words:

/* The '\n' that ends the line starting at p, or NULL when it has not arrived yet. */
static const char *kv_find_eol(const char *p, const char *end) {
    return memchr(p, '\n', (size_t)(end - p));
}

/* A decimal number between p and the line end. False when the text is not a number. */
static bool kv_parse_number(const char *p, const char *eol, long *out) {
    const char *stop = eol;
    if (stop > p && stop[-1] == '\r') {
        stop--;
    }
    if (p == stop || stop - p > 18) {
        return false;
    }
    long v = 0;
    for (; p < stop; p++) {
        if (*p < '0' || *p > '9') {
            return false;
        }
        v = v * 10 + (*p - '0');
    }
    *out = v;
    return true;
}

/* An inline command: words separated by spaces, as typed into nc or telnet. */
static kv_parse_status kv_parse_inline(const char *data, const char *eol, kv_cmd *cmd,
                                       size_t *used) {
    const char *p = data;
    const char *stop = eol;
    if (stop > p && stop[-1] == '\r') {
        stop--;
    }
    while (p < stop) {
        while (p < stop && *p == ' ') {
            p++;
        }
        if (p == stop) {
            break;
        }
        const char *word = p;
        while (p < stop && *p != ' ') {
            p++;
        }
        if (cmd->argc == KV_MAX_ARGS) {
            return KV_PARSE_BAD;
        }
        cmd->argv[cmd->argc] = word;
        cmd->arglen[cmd->argc] = (size_t)(p - word);
        cmd->argc++;
    }
    *used = (size_t)(eol + 1 - data);
    return KV_PARSE_OK;
}
c/ch04/kv.c · region parse-helpers

kv.c sets three limits. KV_MAX_ARGS is 64 arguments and KV_MAX_BULK is 1 MB for one bulk string. KV_MAX_REQUEST is twice that. The Go and Rust files set the same two limits under the names maxBulk and MAX_BULK.

⚠️A length field is where an attacker writes

A header that says $999999999 asks the server to allocate a gigabyte before one byte of payload has arrived. A parser that trusts the number does it, and a few such connections empty the machine. All three parsers in this chapter refuse a length over the limit before they read anything. The protocol test 04-limits.test sends that header to each of them. Redis has the same limit, proto-max-bulk-len, set to 512 MB.

Exercise 04.1CParse the bulk strings

Write the loop in kv_parse that reads the n bulk strings after the array header. For each one, check that the next byte is $ and find its line ending. Read the length. Then check that the whole string and its line ending have arrived. Return KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE when bytes are missing and KV_PARSE_BAD when a byte is wrong. Store a pointer and a length in cmd, and set *used to the number of bytes the request took. Treat a length above KV_MAX_BULK as bad.

static kv_parse_status kv_parse(const char *data, size_t len, kv_cmd *cmd, size_t *used) {
    const char *end = data + len;
    const char *p = data;
    cmd->argc = 0;
    if (len == 0) return KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE;
    const char *eol = kv_find_eol(p, end);
    if (eol == NULL) return KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE;
    if (*p != '*') return kv_parse_inline(data, eol, cmd, used);
    long n;
    if (!kv_parse_number(p + 1, eol, &n) || n > KV_MAX_ARGS) return KV_PARSE_BAD;
    p = eol + 1;
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        /* your code here */
    }
    cmd->argc = (size_t)n;
    *used = (size_t)(p - data);
    return KV_PARSE_OK;
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/* Parse one request from data[0..len). The request is an array of bulk strings, such as
 * "*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n", or one inline line. */
static kv_parse_status kv_parse(const char *data, size_t len, kv_cmd *cmd, size_t *used) {
    const char *end = data + len;
    const char *p = data;
    cmd->argc = 0;
    if (len == 0) {
        return KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE;
    }
    const char *eol = kv_find_eol(p, end);
    if (eol == NULL) {
        return KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE;
    }
    /* The first byte says what the client sent. A client sends arrays. The other four
     * type bytes are replies, which only a server sends, so they are not a request. */
    switch (*p) {
    case '*':
        break;
    case '+':
    case '-':
    case ':':
    case '$':
        return KV_PARSE_BAD;
    default:
        return kv_parse_inline(data, eol, cmd, used);
    }
    long n;
    if (!kv_parse_number(p + 1, eol, &n) || n > KV_MAX_ARGS) {
        return KV_PARSE_BAD;
    }
    p = eol + 1;
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (p >= end) {
            return KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE;
        }
        if (*p != '$') {
            return KV_PARSE_BAD;
        }
        eol = kv_find_eol(p, end);
        if (eol == NULL) {
            return KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE;
        }
        long blen;
        if (!kv_parse_number(p + 1, eol, &blen) || blen > KV_MAX_BULK) {
            return KV_PARSE_BAD;
        }
        p = eol + 1;
        if (end - p < blen + 2) {
            return KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE;
        }
        if (p[blen] != '\r' || p[blen + 1] != '\n') {
            return KV_PARSE_BAD;
        }
        cmd->argv[i] = p;
        cmd->arglen[i] = (size_t)blen;
        p += blen + 2;
    }
    cmd->argc = (size_t)n;
    *used = (size_t)(p - data);
    return KV_PARSE_OK;
}
c/ch04/kv.c · region parse

switch, and the cases that run into each other#

Look at the top of the solution. The first byte of a request decides what it is, and the decision is a switch on that byte. A switch compares one integer against a list of constant cases and jumps to the one that matches. The four reply markers are stacked with no break between them. Any one of the four reaches the same return. That is fallthrough, and it is the feature of switch that bites. Forget a break after a case that has a body, and the next case runs too. The compiler says nothing, which is why every case in kv ends in a break, a return or a continue.

The serving loop has a second switch, on the parse status, and that one has no default on purpose. The status is an enum, a set of named integers. With -Wall, the compiler reports a switch on an enum that leaves a name out. Add a fourth status next year and every switch that forgot it fails to build. A default would hide that. The same trick does not work for a chain of if statements, which is why the loop changed shape in this chapter.

⚠️Pointers into a buffer that moves C

A pointer into a buffer dies when the buffer grows. realloc may move the block, and every pointer into the old block then points at freed memory. The kv_cmd holds such pointers. kv is safe because it runs the command and consumes the buffer before the next read appends to it. Move one line and it is not safe, and the compiler will not say a word. Chapter 12 shows AddressSanitizer catching exactly this.

Replies are appended to a second buffer. Each reply function returns false when memory runs out, and the callers pass that on:

static bool kv_reply_line(kv_buf *out, char first, const char *s) {
    return kv_buf_append(out, &first, 1) && kv_buf_append(out, s, strlen(s)) &&
           kv_buf_append(out, "\r\n", 2);
}

static bool kv_reply_simple(kv_buf *out, const char *s) { return kv_reply_line(out, '+', s); }
static bool kv_reply_error(kv_buf *out, const char *s) { return kv_reply_line(out, '-', s); }

static bool kv_reply_bulk(kv_buf *out, const char *s, size_t n) {
    char head[32];
    int h = snprintf(head, sizeof head, "$%zu\r\n", n);
    return kv_buf_append(out, head, (size_t)h) && kv_buf_append(out, s, n) &&
           kv_buf_append(out, "\r\n", 2);
}

static bool kv_reply_array(kv_buf *out, size_t n) {
    char head[32];
    int h = snprintf(head, sizeof head, "*%zu\r\n", n);
    return kv_buf_append(out, head, (size_t)h);
}
c/ch04/kv.c · region reply

A function that takes any number of arguments#

Two error messages need a value inside them, the command name in one and the unknown word in the other. printf solves this with a format and any number of arguments, and C lets you write such a function yourself. The ... in the parameter list is the variadic part. va_list from stdarg.h walks the arguments. va_start points it after the last named parameter. And vsnprintf is the snprintf that takes a va_list instead of the arguments themselves:

/* An error reply with a format, as printf would write it. The ... takes any arguments,
 * va_list walks them, and vsnprintf is the printf that accepts a va_list. */
static bool kv_reply_errorf(kv_buf *out, const char *fmt, ...) {
    char msg[128];
    va_list ap;
    va_start(ap, fmt);
    vsnprintf(msg, sizeof msg, fmt, ap);
    va_end(ap);
    return kv_reply_error(out, msg);
}
c/ch04/kv.c · region errorf

The compiler cannot check the arguments of a variadic function against the format, because the function's type says nothing about them. Both gcc and clang check printf itself by name. An attribute, __attribute__((format)), asks for the same check on yours. It is a compiler extension, not part of the standard, and kv does without it. Every format in kv is a literal in the call, so the mistake the check would catch cannot happen.

Running a command is a chain of comparisons on the first argument. Command names in Redis are case-insensitive, so the comparison uses strncasecmp from strings.h, with the length, because the argument is not a C string. It has no terminating zero byte. That is a theme of the next chapter:

/* True when argument i of the command is name, ignoring case. */
static bool kv_arg_is(const kv_cmd *c, size_t i, const char *name) {
    size_t n = strlen(name);
    return c->arglen[i] == n && strncasecmp(c->argv[i], name, n) == 0;
}

static bool kv_reply_arity(kv_buf *out, const char *name) {
    return kv_reply_errorf(out, "ERR wrong number of arguments for '%s' command", name);
}

/* Run one command and append its reply to out. */
static bool kv_exec(const kv_cmd *c, kv_buf *out) {
    if (c->argc == 0) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR empty command");
    }
    if (kv_arg_is(c, 0, "PING")) {
        if (c->argc == 1) {
            return kv_reply_simple(out, "PONG");
        }
        if (c->argc == 2) {
            return kv_reply_bulk(out, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
        }
        return kv_reply_arity(out, "ping");
    }
    if (kv_arg_is(c, 0, "ECHO")) {
        if (c->argc != 2) {
            return kv_reply_arity(out, "echo");
        }
        return kv_reply_bulk(out, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    }
    if (kv_arg_is(c, 0, "COMMAND")) {
        return kv_reply_array(out, 0); /* redis-cli asks on connect; an empty list is fine */
    }
    int n = c->arglen[0] < 40 ? (int)c->arglen[0] : 40;
    return kv_reply_errorf(out, "ERR unknown command '%.*s'", n, c->argv[0]);
}
c/ch04/kv.c · region exec

The serving loop ties it together. After each read it runs every complete request in the buffer, because a client may send several at once, which Redis calls a pipeline. Then it writes all the replies in one call. A request that grows past KV_MAX_REQUEST without ending is treated as bad, so that a client cannot make the server grow its buffer without limit. The write loop from chapter 3 becomes a function first:

/* write() may send fewer bytes than asked, so loop until all are out. */
static bool kv_write_all(int fd, const char *p, size_t n) {
    size_t off = 0;
    while (off < n) {
        ssize_t w = write(fd, p + off, n - off);
        if (w < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;
            }
            perror("write");
            return false;
        }
        off += (size_t)w;
    }
    return true;
}
c/ch04/kv.c · region write-all
/* Read requests, run them, send the replies, until the client closes. */
static void kv_serve(int client) {
    kv_buf in = {0};
    kv_buf out = {0};
    char tmp[4096];
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = read(client, tmp, sizeof tmp);
        if (n < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;
            }
            perror("read");
            break;
        }
        if (n == 0) {
            break; /* the client closed the connection */
        }
        if (!kv_buf_append(&in, tmp, (size_t)n)) {
            break;
        }
        /* A pipeline holds several requests in one read, so loop until one is incomplete. */
        bool bad = false;
        for (;;) {
            kv_cmd cmd;
            size_t used = 0;
            kv_parse_status st = kv_parse(in.data, in.len, &cmd, &used);
            /* No default: with -Wall the compiler reports a status this switch forgot. */
            switch (st) {
            case KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE:
                bad = in.len > KV_MAX_REQUEST; /* a request that never ends is not a request */
                break;
            case KV_PARSE_BAD:
                bad = true;
                break;
            case KV_PARSE_OK:
                if (!kv_exec(&cmd, &out)) {
                    bad = true;
                }
                kv_buf_consume(&in, used);
                continue;
            }
            break;
        }
        if (bad) {
            kv_reply_error(&out, "ERR Protocol error");
        }
        if (out.len > 0 && !kv_write_all(client, out.data, out.len)) {
            break;
        }
        out.len = 0;
        if (bad) {
            break;
        }
    }
    kv_buf_free(&in);
    kv_buf_free(&out);
}
c/ch04/kv.c · region serve

Build it, run it, and talk to it with the real client:

$ make && ./kv &
$ redis-cli -p 6380 PING
PONG
$ redis-cli -p 6380 ECHO "hello world"
"hello world"
$ redis-cli -p 6380 FOO
(error) ERR unknown command 'FOO'
✅Say who owns every pointer C

A pointer in C carries no information about who frees it or how long it stays valid. So the comment must. kv_buf says "owned". kv_cmd says "valid only until the buffer is consumed". A function that returns a pointer says whether the caller must free it. Redis does this, the Linux kernel does this, and so does every C codebase that has survived long enough to be read by strangers.

Go: a reader that waits, and an error that names itself#

Go has bufio.Reader, which reads ahead into its own buffer and gives you lines or exact counts of bytes. The parser becomes a set of calls that block until the bytes are there. The "incomplete" status disappears, because the reader waits instead. The first helper reads a line and removes its ending:

// readLine returns one line without its line ending. A bare LF is accepted as well as
// CRLF, so that a command typed into nc works. io.EOF means the client closed the
// connection cleanly between commands.
func readLine(r *bufio.Reader) ([]byte, error) {
	line, err := r.ReadBytes('\n')
	if err != nil {
		if err == io.EOF && len(line) > 0 {
			return nil, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF
		}
		return nil, err
	}
	line = bytes.TrimSuffix(line, []byte("\n"))
	return bytes.TrimSuffix(line, []byte("\r")), nil
}
go/ch04/resp.go · region read-line

Two errors from the standard library carry meaning here. io.EOF means the connection closed, and readLine returns it unchanged when it happens between requests, which is the normal way for a client to leave. io.ErrUnexpectedEOF means the connection closed in the middle of something, which is not normal. A third error, errProtocol, is this file's own. It is a package-level variable, and a caller tests for it with errors.Is. Such a value is called a sentinel error.

An error is any value with an Error method#

There is nothing special about an error in Go. error is an interface with one method, Error() string, and any type with that method is an error. A sentinel is the smallest one, a value with a fixed message. Sometimes a caller needs more than the fact of a failure, such as which byte was wrong. Then the error becomes a type of your own with fields:

// errProtocol means the bytes were not RESP. The connection is closed after it. A caller
// that only needs to know that much tests errors.Is(err, errProtocol).
var errProtocol = errors.New("protocol error")

// A ProtocolError says which byte was wrong. Unwrap returns the sentinel, so errors.Is still
// finds errProtocol in it, and errors.As gives a caller the byte.
type ProtocolError struct {
	Byte byte
}

func (e *ProtocolError) Error() string { return fmt.Sprintf("protocol error at byte %q", e.Byte) }
func (e *ProtocolError) Unwrap() error { return errProtocol }

func protoErr(b byte) error { return &ProtocolError{Byte: b} }
go/ch04/resp.go · region errors

Three things in that block are the whole of Go error handling. Error makes *ProtocolError an error. Unwrap says that a ProtocolError contains the sentinel, so errors.Is(err, errProtocol) is still true for one. And errors.Is and errors.As walk that chain of Unwrap calls. Is asks whether a given value is in the chain. As asks whether a value of a given type is, and gives it to you. In the reader, every error from the standard library is wrapped with what kv was doing. The wrapping is fmt.Errorf with the %w verb, which adds a message and keeps the cause in the chain.

Treat a size above maxBulk as bad. for range n runs the body n times, and is new in Go 1.22.

func readCommand(r *bufio.Reader) ([][]byte, error) {
	line, err := readLine(r)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	if len(line) == 0 || line[0] != '*' {
		return bytes.Fields(line), nil
	}
	n, err := strconv.Atoi(string(line[1:]))
	if err != nil || n < 0 || n > maxArgs {
		return nil, errProtocol
	}
	args := make([][]byte, 0, n)
	for range n {
		// your code here

Stuck?Show the full listing
// readCommand reads one request: an array of bulk strings such as
// "*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n", or one inline line of words. Every error from the
// reader is wrapped with what kv was doing, and the cause stays reachable with errors.Is.
func readCommand(r *bufio.Reader) ([][]byte, error) {
	line, err := readLine(r)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("read command: %w", err)
	}
	if len(line) == 0 || line[0] != '*' {
		return bytes.Fields(line), nil
	}
	n, err := strconv.Atoi(string(line[1:]))
	if err != nil || n < 0 || n > maxArgs {
		return nil, protoErr('*')
	}
	args := make([][]byte, 0, n)
	for range n {
		line, err := readLine(r)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("read argument: %w", unexpected(err))
		}
		if len(line) == 0 || line[0] != '$' {
			return nil, protoErr(first(line))
		}
		size, err := strconv.Atoi(string(line[1:]))
		if err != nil || size < 0 || size > maxBulk {
			return nil, protoErr('$')
		}
		buf := make([]byte, size+2)
		if _, err := io.ReadFull(r, buf); err != nil {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("read argument: %w", unexpected(err))
		}
		if buf[size] != '\r' || buf[size+1] != '\n' {
			return nil, protoErr(buf[size])
		}
		args = append(args, buf[:size])
	}
	return args, nil
}

// unexpected turns a clean EOF in the middle of a request into an error that says so.
func unexpected(err error) error {
	if err == io.EOF {
		return io.ErrUnexpectedEOF
	}
	return err
}

func first(line []byte) byte {
	if len(line) == 0 {
		return '\n'
	}
	return line[0]
}
go/ch04/resp.go · region read-command

Writing replies uses a bufio.Writer, which collects small writes and sends them in one system call when it is flushed:

func writeSimple(w *bufio.Writer, s string) error {
	_, err := w.WriteString("+" + s + "\r\n")
	return err
}

func writeError(w *bufio.Writer, s string) error {
	_, err := w.WriteString("-" + s + "\r\n")
	return err
}

func writeBulk(w *bufio.Writer, b []byte) error {
	if _, err := w.WriteString("$" + strconv.Itoa(len(b)) + "\r\n"); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := w.Write(b); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	_, err := w.WriteString("\r\n")
	return err
}

func writeArrayLen(w *bufio.Writer, n int) error {
	_, err := w.WriteString("*" + strconv.Itoa(n) + "\r\n")
	return err
}
go/ch04/resp.go · region write

The command switch is the C chain of comparisons, written as a switch on an upper-cased string. Go strings are immutable and can hold any bytes, so converting an argument to a string costs one copy and nothing else:

// execute runs one command and writes its reply.
func execute(args [][]byte, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	if len(args) == 0 {
		return writeError(w, "ERR empty command")
	}
	name := strings.ToUpper(string(args[0]))
	switch name {
	case "PING":
		switch len(args) {
		case 1:
			return writeSimple(w, "PONG")
		case 2:
			return writeBulk(w, args[1])
		}
		return writeArity(w, "ping")
	case "ECHO":
		if len(args) != 2 {
			return writeArity(w, "echo")
		}
		return writeBulk(w, args[1])
	case "COMMAND":
		return writeArrayLen(w, 0) // redis-cli asks on connect; an empty list is fine
	}
	shown := string(args[0])
	if len(shown) > 40 {
		shown = shown[:40]
	}
	return writeError(w, "ERR unknown command '"+shown+"'")
}

func writeArity(w *bufio.Writer, name string) error {
	return writeError(w, "ERR wrong number of arguments for '"+name+"' command")
}
go/ch04/exec.go · region exec

The serving loop reads a request, runs it, and flushes the writer when the reader has no bytes waiting. That last check is the Go form of the C pipeline loop. While a pipeline is still being read, replies collect in the writer, and go out together:

// serve reads requests, runs them and sends the replies, until the client closes.
func serve(conn net.Conn) error {
	defer conn.Close()
	r := bufio.NewReader(conn)
	w := bufio.NewWriter(conn)
	for {
		args, err := readCommand(r)
		// The error is wrapped, so == would miss io.EOF. errors.Is walks the chain.
		if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
			return nil
		}
		// errors.AsType finds the typed error in the chain and gives us its byte. Before
		// Go 1.26 the same check was errors.As(err, &pe) with a declared *ProtocolError.
		if pe, ok := errors.AsType[*ProtocolError](err); ok {
			writeError(w, "ERR Protocol error")
			w.Flush()
			return fmt.Errorf("closing client: %w", pe)
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := execute(args, w); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// A pipeline holds several requests; flush once the reader has nothing waiting.
		if r.Buffered() == 0 {
			if err := w.Flush(); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}
	}
}
go/ch04/main.go · region serve

The function returns nil on a clean close, and the error otherwise. On a protocol error it first tells the client why. The three tests on err are the Go way of handling three different failures, and the order matters. The specific checks come before the general err != nil. Two of them changed shape in this chapter. err == io.EOF became errors.Is(err, io.EOF), because the reader now wraps its errors, and a wrapped io.EOF is not equal to the bare one. And errors.AsType[*ProtocolError](err) pulls the typed error out of the chain so the log line can name the byte. AsType is new in Go 1.26. Before it the same check was errors.As(err, &pe) with a declared pe, and you will read that form in most code.

⚠️A wrapped error is not == its cause Go

The moment any function in the chain wraps with %w, every err == io.EOF above it becomes false. The comparison sees the outer value. errors.Is sees the chain. In this book every comparison with a sentinel is errors.Is, including the ones that would work today with ==. The function below may start wrapping tomorrow. The replay in chapter 11 is where that caught the author.

✅A sentinel for a condition, a type for its details Go

A caller that only needs to know that something went wrong tests err != nil. A caller that must tell one failure from another compares with errors.Is, so define a sentinel for that failure. A caller that needs the details, a byte, a path, a count, gets a type with fields and finds it with errors.As. Give the type an Unwrap that returns the sentinel, and both callers are served by one value. errors.Join combines several errors into one that Is and As search through, for the case where a loop collects failures.

Rust: an Option for the end, a Result for the rest#

The Rust reader is the BufRead trait, and read_until does the same as ReadBytes in Go. The line function returns io::Result<Option<Vec<u8>>>, which is a mouthful and exactly right. The outer Result is "did the read fail". The inner Option is "was there a line at all". A clean close is Ok(None), and nobody has to remember that a particular error value means "not really an error":

/// One line without its line ending. A bare LF is accepted as well as CRLF, so that a
/// command typed into nc works. `Ok(None)` means the client closed the connection
/// cleanly between commands.
fn read_line(r: &mut impl BufRead) -> Result<Option<Vec<u8>>> {
    let mut line = Vec::new();
    if r.read_until(b'\n', &mut line)? == 0 {
        return Ok(None);
    }
    if line.pop() != Some(b'\n') {
        return Err(io::Error::from(io::ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof).into());
    }
    if line.last() == Some(&b'\r') {
        line.pop();
    }
    Ok(Some(line))
}

fn parse_len(digits: &[u8], type_byte: u8) -> Result<usize> {
    std::str::from_utf8(digits)
        .ok()
        .and_then(|s| s.parse().ok())
        .ok_or(KvError::Protocol(type_byte))
}
rust/ch04/src/resp.rs · region read-line

The ? after read_until returns any read error at once, and it does one more thing, which the next section explains. parse_len turns the digits into a number in two steps. Each step returns an Option, and and_then chains them. The final ok_or turns a missing number into the protocol error, with the type byte that was being read.

One enum for everything that can go wrong#

Two kinds of failure can come out of the reader, a failed read and bytes that are not RESP, and they need different answers. In Rust the two become one enum, and each variant carries what its caller needs. Io holds the io::Error itself. Protocol holds the byte that was wrong. A match on the enum must handle both, and the compiler refuses the program if a third variant is added and one match forgets it:

/// Everything that can go wrong while reading a request. Each variant carries what the
/// caller needs to know: the io error itself, or the byte that was not RESP.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum KvError {
    Io(io::Error),
    Protocol(u8),
}

/// How the error prints, with `{}`. `to_string` and `eprintln!` use this.
impl fmt::Display for KvError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            KvError::Io(e) => write!(f, "io error: {e}"),
            KvError::Protocol(b) => write!(f, "protocol error at byte {:?}", *b as char),
        }
    }
}

/// Joining the standard error trait lets a `KvError` sit in a `Box<dyn Error>`.
impl std::error::Error for KvError {}

/// `?` calls this when an `io::Error` must become a `KvError`. Without it, every read in
/// this file would need `.map_err(KvError::Io)`.
impl From<io::Error> for KvError {
    fn from(e: io::Error) -> Self {
        KvError::Io(e)
    }
}

/// The other direction, so a function that returns `io::Result` can use `?` on ours.
impl From<KvError> for io::Error {
    fn from(e: KvError) -> Self {
        match e {
            KvError::Io(e) => e,
            KvError::Protocol(_) => io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData, e.to_string()),
        }
    }
}

pub type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, KvError>;
rust/ch04/src/resp.rs · region error

The four impl blocks are the standard shape of an error type, and every Rust error you meet has them. Display says how the error prints with {}. The empty Error block declares it an error, so it can live in a Box<dyn Error> with every other error. And From is the one that matters most. When ? meets an io::Error inside a function that returns our enum, it calls From::from to convert it. That is why no line in the reader says map_err. The second From goes the other way, so a function that still returns io::Result can use ? on ours. The last line gives the file its own Result, with the error type filled in, so the signatures below stay short.

pub fn read_command(r: &mut impl BufRead) -> io::Result<Option<Command>> {
    let Some(line) = read_line(r)? else {
        return Ok(None);
    };
    if line.first() != Some(&b'*') {
        let words = line.split(|b| *b == b' ').filter(|w| !w.is_empty());
        return Ok(Some(words.map(<[u8]>::to_vec).collect()));
    }
    let n = parse_len(&line[1..])?;
    if n > MAX_ARGS {
        return Err(protocol_error());
    }
    let mut args = Vec::with_capacity(n);
    for _ in 0..n {
        // your code here

Stuck?Show the full listing
/// One request: an array of bulk strings such as `*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n`,
/// or one inline line of words. `Ok(None)` means the client has gone.
pub fn read_command(r: &mut impl BufRead) -> Result<Option<Command>> {
    let Some(line) = read_line(r)? else {
        return Ok(None);
    };
    if line.first() != Some(&b'*') {
        let words = line.split(|b| *b == b' ').filter(|w| !w.is_empty());
        return Ok(Some(words.map(<[u8]>::to_vec).collect()));
    }
    let n = parse_len(&line[1..], b'*')?;
    if n > MAX_ARGS {
        return Err(KvError::Protocol(b'*'));
    }
    let mut args = Vec::with_capacity(n);
    for _ in 0..n {
        let line = read_line(r)?.ok_or(io::Error::from(io::ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof))?;
        if line.first() != Some(&b'$') {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(line.first().copied().unwrap_or(b'\n')));
        }
        let size = parse_len(&line[1..], b'$')?;
        if size > MAX_BULK {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(b'$'));
        }
        let mut buf = vec![0u8; size + 2];
        r.read_exact(&mut buf)?;
        if &buf[size..] != b"\r\n" {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(buf[size]));
        }
        buf.truncate(size);
        args.push(buf);
    }
    Ok(Some(args))
}
rust/ch04/src/resp.rs · region read-command

The reply functions take impl Write, which means any writer, and the write! macro formats straight into it:

pub fn write_simple(w: &mut impl Write, s: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    write!(w, "+{s}\r\n")
}

pub fn write_error(w: &mut impl Write, s: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    write!(w, "-{s}\r\n")
}

pub fn write_bulk(w: &mut impl Write, b: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
    write!(w, "${}\r\n", b.len())?;
    w.write_all(b)?;
    w.write_all(b"\r\n")
}

pub fn write_array_len(w: &mut impl Write, n: usize) -> io::Result<()> {
    write!(w, "*{n}\r\n")
}
rust/ch04/src/resp.rs · region write

Running a command is a match on the upper-cased name as bytes. The let ... else handles an empty request. A bulk string is Vec<u8> and not String, because a Rust String must be valid UTF-8 and a Redis value need not be. When the name must be shown in an error message, from_utf8_lossy replaces any invalid bytes with a marker:

/// Run one command and write its reply.
pub fn execute(args: &[Vec<u8>], w: &mut impl Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let Some(name) = args.first() else {
        return resp::write_error(w, "ERR empty command");
    };
    match name.to_ascii_uppercase().as_slice() {
        b"PING" => match args.len() {
            1 => resp::write_simple(w, "PONG"),
            2 => resp::write_bulk(w, &args[1]),
            _ => write_arity(w, "ping"),
        },
        b"ECHO" => match args.len() {
            2 => resp::write_bulk(w, &args[1]),
            _ => write_arity(w, "echo"),
        },
        // redis-cli asks on connect; an empty list is fine
        b"COMMAND" => resp::write_array_len(w, 0),
        _ => {
            let shown = String::from_utf8_lossy(&name[..name.len().min(40)]);
            resp::write_error(w, &format!("ERR unknown command '{shown}'"))
        }
    }
}

fn write_arity(w: &mut impl Write, name: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
    resp::write_error(
        w,
        &format!("ERR wrong number of arguments for '{name}' command"),
    )
}
rust/ch04/src/cmd.rs · region exec

The serving loop matches on the three outcomes of read_command. The arm Err(e @ KvError::Protocol(_)) matches one variant and, with @, also binds the whole error to e so it can be returned. That is the Rust form of errors.As, checked by the compiler rather than searched at run time. The compiler also checks that the four arms cover every case:

/// Read requests, run them and send the replies, until the client closes. The function
/// returns a `KvError`, so `?` converts every `io::Error` on the way with `From`.
fn serve(stream: TcpStream) -> resp::Result<()> {
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream.try_clone()?);
    let mut writer = BufWriter::new(stream);
    loop {
        match resp::read_command(&mut reader) {
            Ok(Some(args)) => cmd::execute(&args, &mut writer)?,
            Ok(None) => return Ok(()),
            Err(e @ KvError::Protocol(_)) => {
                resp::write_error(&mut writer, "ERR Protocol error")?;
                writer.flush()?;
                return Err(e);
            }
            Err(e) => return Err(e),
        }
        // A pipeline holds several requests; flush once the reader has nothing waiting.
        if reader.buffer().is_empty() {
            writer.flush()?;
        }
    }
}
rust/ch04/src/main.rs · region serve
⚠️A String is not a byte string Rust

String::from_utf8(bytes) fails on a value that is not text. Redis keys and values are bytes, and a client may store an image under a key. A parser that converts every argument to String rejects such a client with an error that looks like a bug in the client. Keep arguments as Vec<u8> and convert only for display, with from_utf8_lossy, or for commands that need text, such as a number.

Three ways to say what went wrong#

Each version of the parser had to express four different outcomes. The request is complete. The bytes are not RESP. The client closed the connection cleanly. The client closed it in the middle of a request. The table shows the three vocabularies.

The outcomeCGoRust
A value, or a failurea return code and an out-parametertwo return values, (v, err)one value, Result<T, E>
The reason for a failurethe global errno, or an enum of your ownan error value, found with errors.Is or errors.Asthe Err payload, an enum matched on its variant
Passing a failure upif (x < 0) return -1; on every callif err != nil { return err } on every callone character, ?
Ignoring a failurewrite nothing, and nothing warnswrite nothing, and nothing warnsthe compiler warns about an unused Result
"Not an error, but nothing"a special return value, such as 0 from reada special error value, io.EOFOption, which is not an error at all
Adding a reasona format string into a fixed arrayfmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)a variant of your enum, and From so that ? converts

C has one mechanism, the return value, and uses it for everything. The design works, and the whole of Unix is built on it, but it has two costs that the book will keep meeting. The first is that the check is optional and silent when missing. The second is that the value and the error share one channel. A function that returns a pointer uses NULL for failure. A function that returns a count uses -1. The caller must know which.

Go separates the value from the error, which fixes the second cost, and leaves the first in place by choice. The Go FAQ says the designers found try-catch-finally produced "convoluted code". The price is the three lines of if err != nil after every call, and a Go file of any size has many such checks. Rust puts the value inside the Result, so that the caller cannot reach the value without facing the failure. The ? operator makes the common case one character. The price is a type system that the programmer must learn before any of it makes sense. There is also a long error message from the compiler when a ? is used where the error types do not match.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
Reading bytesWeakStrongStrongC has stdio, which blocks, so kv grows its own buffer. Both standard libraries have one.
Holding the argumentsStrongOKOKThe C parser copies nothing. Go and Rust copy each argument once, which is simpler and almost never matters.
Saying "not RESP"OKOKStrongC and Go use a value by convention. Rust uses a kind the compiler knows about and a match the compiler checks.
Saying "the client left"OKWeakStrongGo reuses an error value for a non-error. Rust has Option for exactly this.
Passing an error upWeakWeakStrongC and Go repeat the check at every call. Rust writes one character.
Binary valuesStrongStrongOKC and Go treat all bytes alike. Rust makes you choose between String and Vec<u8>, and the wrong choice rejects real data.
An error with detailsWeakOKStrongC has an enum and a fixed buffer, and Go has a type found by searching a chain. Rust has an enum variant the compiler matches.
Carry forward
  • switch. One integer against constant cases. A case with no break continues into the next, and an enum switch with no default is checked by the compiler.
  • Error chain. A Go error wraps its cause with %w. The functions errors.Is and errors.As search the chain, and == cannot.
  • From and ?. A Rust error enum with a From impl lets ? convert every lower error into yours.

GET and SET#

Building kv · Chapter 05· 38 min read· 693 lines of code
▶Scene

Start the chapter 4 server and ask it to remember something:

$ redis-cli -p 6380 SET name kv
(error) ERR unknown command 'SET'
$ redis-cli -p 6380 GET name
(error) ERR unknown command 'GET'

It speaks the protocol and has nothing to say. Every command it will ever learn is a name, a number of arguments and a function. This chapter gives it a place to keep that list, and the first five entries.

kv starts to remember. SET stores a value under a key and GET returns it. Two commands take several keys, DEL and EXISTS. INCR treats a value as a number. The chapter is about strings and bytes, because a key and a value are bytes, and the three languages disagree about what a string is.

A Redis value is a sequence of bytes. It may be the text hello, the digits 42, or the first kilobyte of a JPEG. A Redis key is the same. The server must keep a copy of both and find a key again later. It must compare two keys for equality. For INCR it must read a value as an integer and write one back. Each of those steps asks the question "what is a string?", and each language answers it differently.

A stringCGoRust
What it isa pointer to bytes that end with a zero bytean immutable sequence of bytesa sequence of bytes that must be valid UTF-8
Bytes with a lengtha pointer and a size_t, by convention[]byteVec<u8>, or a borrowed &[u8]
Lengthstrlen walks to the zero, or you carry the lengthlen(s), stored with the valuev.len(), stored with the value
Equalitymemcmp with the lengths== on strings, bytes.Equal on slices== on both
As a map keya hash you write, in chapter 6string, because a slice cannot be a keyVec<u8>, because it is hashable
To an integeryou parse the digits, watching for overflowstrconv.ParseIntstr::parse::<i64>() after a UTF-8 check
Who owns the byteswhoever the comment saysthe garbage collectorexactly one binding, checked by the compiler
A command, as dataa function pointer in a table, built by a macroa map from the name to a funca fn pointer in a const table, built by a macro
📜Why a C string ends with a zero byte

In BCPL, the language before B, a string began with its length in one byte. B dropped the count and ended a string with a marker character instead, and C kept that rule with the zero byte as the marker. Ritchie gave two reasons. The one-byte count limited a string to 255 characters, and "maintaining the count seemed, in our experience, less convenient than using a terminator". Fifty years later, that marker is why a C string cannot hold a zero byte. It is also why every C string function walks the whole string to find its end. Go and Rust store the length with the bytes, as BCPL did.

C: bytes, a length and an owner#

The arguments that the parser produces are not C strings. They are pointers into the request buffer with a length beside them, and no zero byte ends them. Every function in kv that touches a key or a value takes a pointer and a length. The C string library is never called on them. The first helpers copy, compare and parse such bytes:

/* A copy of n bytes that the caller owns and must free. Never NULL on success, even
 * for n == 0, because malloc(0) may return NULL and that would look like failure. */
static char *kv_bytes_dup(const char *src, size_t n) {
    char *p = malloc(n ? n : 1);
    if (p == NULL) {
        return NULL;
    }
    memcpy(p, src, n);
    return p;
}

static bool kv_bytes_eq(const char *a, size_t alen, const char *b, size_t blen) {
    return alen == blen && memcmp(a, b, alen) == 0;
}

/* Parse a signed decimal integer from bytes that have no terminating zero. Strict, as
 * Redis is: no spaces, no plus sign, no leading zeros, and no overflow. */
static bool kv_parse_int(const char *s, size_t n, long long *out) {
    size_t i = 0;
    bool neg = false;
    if (n == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    if (s[0] == '-') {
        neg = true;
        i = 1;
        if (n == 1) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    if (s[i] == '0' && n - i > 1) {
        return false;
    }
    unsigned long long v = 0;
    for (; i < n; i++) {
        if (s[i] < '0' || s[i] > '9') {
            return false;
        }
        unsigned d = (unsigned)(s[i] - '0');
        if (v > (ULLONG_MAX - d) / 10) {
            return false;
        }
        v = v * 10 + d;
    }
    if (!neg && v > (unsigned long long)LLONG_MAX) {
        return false;
    }
    if (neg && v > (unsigned long long)LLONG_MAX + 1) {
        return false;
    }
    *out = neg ? -(long long)(v - 1) - 1 : (long long)v;
    return true;
}
c/ch05/kv.c · region bytes

Three details deserve a look. kv_bytes_dup asks for at least one byte. The reason is that malloc(0) is allowed to return NULL, which would look like an out-of-memory failure. The integer parser works in unsigned arithmetic and checks before every multiplication, because overflow of a signed integer is undefined behaviour in C. The last line turns the unsigned result into a negative number. It avoids computing -v when v is one more than the largest positive value. That value is exactly the smallest negative one, and the obvious expression would overflow on the way there.

⚠️strlen on bytes that are not a C string C

Calling a string function on a key reads past the key. The key hello in a request is followed by \r\n and the rest of the buffer, not by a zero byte. strlen walks on until it finds a zero somewhere, and strcmp compares bytes that belong to another argument. Most of the time there is no crash. Both are undefined behaviour, and AddressSanitizer, which chapter 12 introduces, reports such a read. The rule in kv is simple. A key or a value is always a pointer and a length, and string.h is for messages the program writes itself.

📰Heartbleed, 2014

In April 2014 anyone on the internet could read 64 kilobytes of a web server's memory by sending it one message. The TLS heartbeat extension of OpenSSL, a C library, let a client send a payload and its length, and the server sent the payload back. The code allocated the reply "based on the length field in the requesting message, without regard to the actual size of that message's payload". A length of 65,535 and a payload of one byte returned that byte and whatever lay after it. Passwords, keys, other people's sessions. The bug is CVE-2014-0160 in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, and it had been in the library since the end of 2011. About 17 percent of the secure web servers on the internet were believed to be open to it on the day it was disclosed. It is the trusted length of chapter 4 and the pointer without a length of this chapter, in one line of C.

The store in this chapter is a list of entries. A lookup walks the list and compares each key, which is slow once there are thousands of keys. Chapter 6 replaces the list with a hash table. The entry owns copies of its key and value, and the comments say so:

/* One key and its value. Both are owned copies, freed with the entry. */
typedef struct {
    char *key;
    size_t klen;
    char *val;
    size_t vlen;
} kv_entry;

/* Every entry, in a list. A lookup walks the whole list, which chapter 6 fixes. */
typedef struct {
    kv_entry *items; /* owned */
    size_t len;
    size_t cap;
} kv_store;

static kv_entry *kv_store_find(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < s->len; i++) {
        if (kv_bytes_eq(s->items[i].key, s->items[i].klen, key, klen)) {
            return &s->items[i];
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

Exercise 05.1CStore a copy

Write kv_store_set. Copy the value first, because that can fail. If the key exists, free its old value and keep the new one. If not, grow the list when it is full, copy the key, and append an entry. On any failure, free what you copied and return false, leaving the store as it was.

static bool kv_store_set(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen, const char *val,
                         size_t vlen) {

    if (v == NULL) return false;

Stuck?Show the full listing
/* Store a copy of val under a copy of key, replacing any old value. */
static bool kv_store_set(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen, const char *val,
                         size_t vlen) {
    char *v = kv_bytes_dup(val, vlen);
    if (v == NULL) {
        return false;
    }
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, key, klen);
    if (e != NULL) {
        free(e->val); /* the old value, which nothing else points to */
        e->val = v;
        e->vlen = vlen;
        return true;
    }
    if (s->len == s->cap) {
        size_t cap = s->cap ? s->cap * 2 : 16;
        kv_entry *items = realloc(s->items, cap * sizeof *items);
        if (items == NULL) {
            free(v);
            return false;
        }
        s->items = items;
        s->cap = cap;
    }
    char *k = kv_bytes_dup(key, klen);
    if (k == NULL) {
        free(v);
        return false;
    }
    s->items[s->len++] = (kv_entry){k, klen, v, vlen};
    return true;
}

/* Remove a key. The last entry moves into the hole, so the order is not kept. */
static bool kv_store_del(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, key, klen);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return false;
    }
    free(e->key);
    free(e->val);
    *e = s->items[--s->len];
    return true;
}

static void kv_store_free(kv_store *s) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < s->len; i++) {
        free(s->items[i].key);
        free(s->items[i].val);
    }
    free(s->items);
    s->items = NULL;
    s->len = s->cap = 0;
}
c/ch05/kv.c · region store-ops

kv_store_del moves the last entry into the hole that the deleted one leaves. That keeps the list packed without moving everything after it, at the cost of order, which a store does not promise. A value is freed in three places. kv_store_set frees the old one on replacement, kv_store_del frees it, and at exit kv_store_free walks the list once. Every malloc in this file has one free that matches it, and a reader can find the pair.

INCR is where bytes and numbers meet. The stored value is bytes. The command parses them, adds one, and stores bytes again. The error messages are the ones Redis uses, so that a client written for Redis understands kv. The check against LLONG_MAX comes before the add, and the section on integers at the end of the chapter says why it must:

/* INCR: the value is bytes that must parse as an integer, and the new value is bytes too.
 * The check against LLONG_MAX comes before the add, because overflowing a signed integer
 * is undefined behaviour, and the compiler may assume it never happens. */
static bool kv_cmd_incr(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    long long n = 0;
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    if (e != NULL && !kv_parse_int(e->val, e->vlen, &n)) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
    }
    if (n == LLONG_MAX) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR increment or decrement would overflow");
    }
    n++;
    char text[32];
    int len = snprintf(text, sizeof text, "%lld", n);
    if (!kv_store_set(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], text, (size_t)len)) {
        return false;
    }
    return kv_reply_int(out, n);
}
c/ch05/kv.c · region incr

A table of functions#

Chapter 4 ran a command through a chain of if statements, one per name. Five more commands make the chain long, and the arity check is repeated in every link. The shape underneath is the same each time. A name, how many arguments it takes, and what to do. That is a row of a table, and C can hold the "what to do" in a function pointer. A function pointer is the address of a function, with the signature it expects spelled out, so the compiler knows how to call through it. Every command becomes a function of one shape:

/* Each command is a function of this one shape, so a table can hold them all. */
typedef bool (*kv_cmd_fn)(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out);

static bool kv_cmd_ping(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    (void)s;
    if (c->argc == 1) {
        return kv_reply_simple(out, "PONG");
    }
    if (c->argc == 2) {
        return kv_reply_bulk(out, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    }
    return kv_reply_arity(out, "ping");
}

static bool kv_cmd_echo(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    (void)s;
    return kv_reply_bulk(out, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
}

static bool kv_cmd_set(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    if (!kv_store_set(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], c->argv[2], c->arglen[2])) {
        return false;
    }
    return kv_reply_simple(out, "OK");
}

static bool kv_cmd_get(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    return e ? kv_reply_bulk(out, e->val, e->vlen) : kv_reply_nil(out);
}

static bool kv_cmd_del(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    long long n = 0;
    for (size_t i = 1; i < c->argc; i++) {
        n += kv_store_del(s, c->argv[i], c->arglen[i]);
    }
    return kv_reply_int(out, n);
}

static bool kv_cmd_exists(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    long long n = 0;
    for (size_t i = 1; i < c->argc; i++) {
        n += kv_store_find(s, c->argv[i], c->arglen[i]) != NULL;
    }
    return kv_reply_int(out, n);
}

static bool kv_cmd_command(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    (void)c;
    (void)s;
    return kv_reply_array(out, 0); /* redis-cli asks on connect; an empty list is fine */
}
c/ch05/kv.c · region commands

The table is the list of rows. It is written once, as a macro that calls another macro, X, on each row. Each place that needs the list defines X to say what to make of a row, uses the list, and undefines X again. The first use builds the array of rows. The second counts them, by turning each row into +1. This is called an X-macro, and it is how C keeps one list in one place when several things have to agree with it:

/* The command list, written once. Each use of KV_COMMANDS defines X to say what to make
 * of a row. The first use below builds the table, the second counts it. A name is spelled
 * as the arity error must show it, and arity is counted as Redis counts it: a positive
 * number is the exact argc, name included, and a negative one is a minimum. */
#define KV_COMMANDS                     \
    X(ping, kv_cmd_ping, -1)            \
    X(echo, kv_cmd_echo, 2)             \
    X(set, kv_cmd_set, 3)               \
    X(get, kv_cmd_get, 2)               \
    X(del, kv_cmd_del, -2)              \
    X(exists, kv_cmd_exists, -2)        \
    X(incr, kv_cmd_incr, 2)             \
    X(append, kv_cmd_append, 3)         \
    X(strlen, kv_cmd_strlen, 2)         \
    X(getrange, kv_cmd_getrange, 4)     \
    X(command, kv_cmd_command, -1)

typedef struct {
    const char *name;
    kv_cmd_fn fn;
    int arity;
} kv_command;

static const kv_command kv_commands[] = {
#define X(name, fn, arity) {#name, fn, arity},
    KV_COMMANDS
#undef X
};

enum {
#define X(name, fn, arity) +1
    KV_COMMAND_COUNT = 0 KV_COMMANDS
#undef X
};
c/ch05/kv.c · region table

Running a command is now a walk down the table. The arity check happens once, in the loop, and the function is called through its pointer with the same arguments the chain used to pass:

/* Run one command against the store and append its reply to out: find the row, check
 * the arity, call the function through its pointer. */
static bool kv_exec(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    if (c->argc == 0) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR empty command");
    }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < KV_COMMAND_COUNT; i++) {
        const kv_command *cmd = &kv_commands[i];
        if (!kv_arg_is(c, 0, cmd->name)) {
            continue;
        }
        int argc = (int)c->argc;
        bool ok = cmd->arity < 0 ? argc >= -cmd->arity : argc == cmd->arity;
        if (!ok) {
            return kv_reply_arity(out, cmd->name);
        }
        return cmd->fn(c, s, out);
    }
    int n = c->arglen[0] < 40 ? (int)c->arglen[0] : 40;
    return kv_reply_errorf(out, "ERR unknown command '%.*s'", n, c->argv[0]);
}
c/ch05/kv.c · region exec
✅Behaviour in a table, not in a chain C

When several things of one shape are chosen by name, put them in a table of structs. Each struct holds a function pointer, and the code walks the table. Redis does this with its command table, and every interpreter, driver model and plugin system in C does the same. A chain of if grows with every feature, and a table grows by one row.

Growing, measuring and slicing bytes#

Three more commands work on the bytes of a value. APPEND makes a value longer, STRLEN measures it, and GETRANGE cuts a piece out by offset. Each one is a few lines, and each one meets a rule of C bytes:

/* APPEND key value: grow the stored bytes in place. A missing key starts empty. */
static bool kv_cmd_append(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    if (e == NULL) {
        if (!kv_store_set(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], c->argv[2], c->arglen[2])) {
            return false;
        }
        return kv_reply_int(out, (long long)c->arglen[2]);
    }
    char *v = realloc(e->val, e->vlen + c->arglen[2] + 1);
    if (v == NULL) {
        return false; /* e->val is still valid: realloc leaves it alone on failure */
    }
    memcpy(v + e->vlen, c->argv[2], c->arglen[2]);
    e->val = v;
    e->vlen += c->arglen[2];
    return kv_reply_int(out, (long long)e->vlen);
}

/* STRLEN key: the length in bytes, which is the only length the store knows. */
static bool kv_cmd_strlen(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    return kv_reply_int(out, e ? (long long)e->vlen : 0);
}

/* GETRANGE key start end: a slice by byte offsets, both inclusive. A negative offset
 * counts from the end, and an offset past either end is clamped, as Redis does. */
static bool kv_cmd_getrange(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    long long start, end;
    if (!kv_parse_int(c->argv[2], c->arglen[2], &start) ||
        !kv_parse_int(c->argv[3], c->arglen[3], &end)) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
    }
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    long long len = e ? (long long)e->vlen : 0;
    if (start < 0) {
        start += len;
    }
    if (end < 0) {
        end += len;
    }
    if (start < 0) {
        start = 0;
    }
    if (end >= len) {
        end = len - 1;
    }
    if (len == 0 || start > end) {
        return kv_reply_bulk(out, "", 0);
    }
    return kv_reply_bulk(out, e->val + start, (size_t)(end - start + 1));
}
c/ch05/kv.c · region strings

APPEND asks realloc to grow the block the value lives in. When the block cannot grow in place, realloc moves it, copies the bytes and frees the old one. So the pointer in the entry must be replaced. On failure it returns NULL and the old block is untouched, which is why the result goes into a new variable first. STRLEN answers in bytes, because the store knows no other length. GETRANGE is arithmetic on offsets, with four clamps, and then a pointer plus a length into the value. No byte is copied until the reply is written. The one function from the C string library in this chapter is snprintf, which turns the number in INCR into digits. It takes the size of its buffer, writes at most that many bytes with a terminator, and returns how many it wanted to write. Its older cousin sprintf takes no size and is how buffers overflow.

Run it, and the first real session with the real client works:

$ make && ./kv &
$ redis-cli -p 6380
127.0.0.1:6380> SET name kv
OK
127.0.0.1:6380> GET name
"kv"
127.0.0.1:6380> INCR visits
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6380> INCR name
(error) ERR value is not an integer or out of range
127.0.0.1:6380> DEL name visits
(integer) 2
✅A pointer and a length travel together C

Any function that takes bytes takes two parameters, the pointer and the length, in that order. A structure that holds bytes holds both fields side by side. The habit is older than kv. The read and write calls of POSIX, the Portable Operating System Interface, take a pointer and a length. Redis keeps a length in front of every string it stores. A C string is only for text the program itself writes, such as an error message, where the zero byte is guaranteed.

Go: two kinds of string, and a copy between them#

Go has both answers to the question. A string is immutable bytes with a length. A []byte is mutable bytes with a length. Converting one to the other copies the bytes, because the string must not change when the slice does. The store uses a string for the key, because a map key must support ==, and a slice does not. The value stays a slice:

// store keeps every key and its value. The parser allocated each slice, so the store can
// keep them without copying: nothing else holds them.
type store struct {
	m map[string][]byte
}

func newStore() *store {
	return &store{m: make(map[string][]byte)}
}

func (s *store) get(key []byte) ([]byte, bool) {
	v, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	return v, ok
}

func (s *store) set(key, val []byte) {
	s.m[string(key)] = val
}

func (s *store) del(key []byte) bool {
	_, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	delete(s.m, string(key))
	return ok
}

func (s *store) has(key []byte) bool {
	_, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	return ok
}
go/ch05/store.go · region store

The value is not copied on set. The key is converted to a string, which copies it once, because a map key must be comparable. The parser allocated a fresh slice for every argument, and nothing else holds it. The garbage collector keeps it alive for as long as the map refers to it. The question that took a paragraph of comments in C does not arise. The cost is in the collector, which must find out, from time to time, which slices are still referred to.

// The two ways INCR fails. Their text is what the client sees.
var (
	errNotInteger = errors.New("ERR value is not an integer or out of range")
	errOverflow   = errors.New("ERR increment or decrement would overflow")
)

Write the incr method. Read the current value if there is one, parse it with strconv.ParseInt, and return errNotInteger when parsing fails. Return errOverflow when the value is already math.MaxInt64. Otherwise store the new value, formatted with strconv.FormatInt, and return it.
