Stuck?Show the full listing
// incr adds one to the integer stored under key, which counts as 0 when absent.
func (s *store) incr(key []byte) (int64, error) {
	var n int64
	if cur, ok := s.get(key); ok {
		var err error
		n, err = strconv.ParseInt(string(cur), 10, 64)
		if err != nil {
			return 0, errNotInteger
		}
	}
	if n == math.MaxInt64 {
		return 0, errOverflow
	}
	n++
	s.set(key, []byte(strconv.FormatInt(n, 10)))
	return n, nil
}
go/ch05/store.go · region incr

The two errors are package-level values with the exact text the client should see. The command code does not look inside them. It writes err.Error() as the reply, which keeps the knowledge of what can go wrong next to the code that knows it.

A map of functions#

In Go a function is a value like any other. It can sit in a variable, in a struct field or in a map, and a func type names its shape. The command table is a map from the upper-cased name to a struct that holds the function and its arity:

// A handler is any function of this shape. The table maps the upper-cased name to one,
// with the arity as Redis counts it: a positive number is the exact argc, name included,
// and a negative one is a minimum.
type handler func(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error

type command struct {
	run   handler
	arity int
}

var commands = map[string]command{
	"PING":     {ping, -1},
	"ECHO":     {echo, 2},
	"SET":      {set, 3},
	"GET":      {get, 2},
	"DEL":      {del, -2},
	"EXISTS":   {exists, -2},
	"INCR":     {incr, 2},
	"APPEND":   {appendCmd, 3},
	"STRLEN":   {strlenCmd, 2},
	"GETRANGE": {getrange, 4},
	"COMMAND":  {commandCmd, -1},
}
go/ch05/exec.go · region table

Running a command is a map lookup, an arity check, and a call. The chain of cases is gone, and adding a command is one line in the map and one function:

// execute runs one command against the store and writes its reply: look the name up,
// check the arity, call the function the table holds.
func execute(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	if len(args) == 0 {
		return writeError(w, "ERR empty command")
	}
	name := strings.ToUpper(string(args[0]))
	cmd, ok := commands[name]
	if !ok {
		shown := string(args[0])
		if len(shown) > 40 {
			shown = shown[:40]
		}
		return writeError(w, "ERR unknown command '"+shown+"'")
	}
	if n := len(args); (cmd.arity < 0 && n < -cmd.arity) || (cmd.arity > 0 && n != cmd.arity) {
		return writeArity(w, strings.ToLower(name))
	}
	return cmd.run(args, s, w)
}

func writeArity(w *bufio.Writer, name string) error {
	return writeError(w, "ERR wrong number of arguments for '"+name+"' command")
}
go/ch05/exec.go · region exec

Two of the handlers show what a function value can be. countKeys takes a function from a key to a bool and counts the keys for which it is true. DEL passes s.del, which is a method value. It is the method with its receiver already bound, so it can be called later with the key alone. EXISTS passes a closure, a function literal that captures s from the surrounding function and calls get on it. A closure captures by reference. It sees the variable as it is when the closure runs, not as it was when the closure was made. The defer test of chapter 3 showed the same rule:

func ping(args [][]byte, _ *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	switch len(args) {
	case 1:
		return writeSimple(w, "PONG")
	case 2:
		return writeBulk(w, args[1])
	}
	return writeArity(w, "ping")
}

func echo(args [][]byte, _ *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	return writeBulk(w, args[1])
}

func set(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	s.set(args[1], args[2])
	return writeSimple(w, "OK")
}

func get(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	if v, ok := s.get(args[1]); ok {
		return writeBulk(w, v)
	}
	return writeNil(w)
}

// countKeys counts the keys for which hit returns true. DEL and EXISTS differ only in
// which method they pass: s.del removes as it counts, s.has only looks.
func countKeys(keys [][]byte, hit func([]byte) bool) int64 {
	var n int64
	for _, key := range keys {
		if hit(key) {
			n++
		}
	}
	return n
}

func del(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	return writeInt(w, countKeys(args[1:], s.del))
}

func exists(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	return writeInt(w, countKeys(args[1:], s.has))
}

func incr(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	n, err := s.incr(args[1])
	if err != nil {
		return writeError(w, err.Error())
	}
	return writeInt(w, n)
}

func commandCmd(_ [][]byte, _ *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	return writeArrayLen(w, 0) // redis-cli asks on connect; an empty list is fine
}
go/ch05/exec.go · region commands

Bytes, runes and a builder#

Three more commands work on the bytes of a value. APPEND uses the built-in append. It may write into the spare capacity of the old slice or allocate a new array, and the map keeps whichever slice comes back. STRLEN replies with len, which counts bytes. The character count of a string is a different question in Go. A string is bytes in UTF-8, and a character outside ASCII takes more than one byte. A rune is one character as an int32, range over a string walks runes, and utf8.RuneCount counts them. GETRANGE slices by byte offset, which is what Redis does and what may cut a rune in half. The test below is in the chapter's snapshot. It shows the three facts and strings.Builder, which grows a string without copying it at every step:

// A string is bytes. len counts them, and a character outside ASCII takes more than one.
func TestBytesAndRunes(t *testing.T) {
	s := "héllo"
	if len(s) != 6 || utf8.RuneCountInString(s) != 5 {
		t.Fatalf("len %d, runes %d", len(s), utf8.RuneCountInString(s))
	}
	// range walks runes, not bytes: the index jumps from 1 to 3 over the two bytes of é
	var idx []int
	for i := range s {
		idx = append(idx, i)
	}
	if idx[2] != 3 {
		t.Fatalf("indexes %v", idx)
	}
	// s[1:2] is one byte, half of é, and not a valid string on its own
	if utf8.ValidString(s[1:2]) {
		t.Fatal("half a rune should not be valid")
	}
	// strings.Builder grows a string without copying it at every step
	var b strings.Builder
	for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
		b.WriteString("ab")
	}
	if b.String() != "ababab" {
		t.Fatal(b.String())
	}
}
go/ch05/strings_test.go · region runes
// appendCmd grows the stored bytes. append may reuse the old slice's spare capacity or
// allocate a new array; either way the map is updated with the slice it returns.
func appendCmd(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	old, _ := s.get(args[1])
	v := append(old, args[2]...)
	s.set(args[1], v)
	return writeInt(w, int64(len(v)))
}

// strlenCmd replies with the length in bytes. len counts bytes, and so does Redis; the
// number of characters is a different question, which utf8.RuneCount answers.
func strlenCmd(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	v, _ := s.get(args[1])
	_ = utf8.RuneCount(v) // the count a user would expect for text, which STRLEN is not
	return writeInt(w, int64(len(v)))
}

// getrange slices by byte offsets, both inclusive. A negative offset counts from the end,
// and an offset past either end is clamped, as Redis does.
func getrange(args [][]byte, s *store, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	start, err1 := strconv.ParseInt(string(args[2]), 10, 64)
	end, err2 := strconv.ParseInt(string(args[3]), 10, 64)
	if err1 != nil || err2 != nil {
		return writeError(w, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range")
	}
	v, _ := s.get(args[1])
	n := int64(len(v))
	if start < 0 {
		start += n
	}
	if end < 0 {
		end += n
	}
	start = max(start, 0)
	end = min(end, n-1)
	if n == 0 || start > end {
		return writeBulk(w, nil)
	}
	return writeBulk(w, v[start:end+1])
}
go/ch05/exec.go · region strings
⚠️ParseInt is more generous than Redis Go

strconv.ParseInt accepts +5 and 007. Redis stores both and then refuses to INCR them, and the C version of kv does the same. The Go version accepts them, and so does the Rust version, because both standard libraries parse numbers the same generous way. The book leaves the difference in and tells you about it, because that is what happens in real ports. A strict parser in Go is a short function, and the C version shows what it must check.

Rust: a value has one owner#

Rust has the same two kinds as Go, String for text and Vec<u8> for bytes, with one more rule. A String must be valid UTF-8, and the compiler will not let you build one from bytes without a check. A Redis key is bytes, so the store is a map from Vec<u8> to Vec<u8>. A Vec can be a key because it supports hashing and equality:

/// Every key and its value. The store owns both: a key or value that is put in is moved,
/// not copied, and is freed when it is replaced, deleted or the store is dropped.
#[derive(Default)]
pub struct Store {
    map: HashMap<Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>>,
}

impl Store {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self::default()
    }

    /// A borrowed view of the value, which lives as long as the borrow of the store.
    pub fn get(&self, key: &[u8]) -> Option<&[u8]> {
        self.map.get(key).map(Vec::as_slice)
    }

    pub fn set(&mut self, key: Vec<u8>, val: Vec<u8>) {
        self.map.insert(key, val);
    }

    pub fn del(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> bool {
        self.map.remove(key).is_some()
    }

    /// Append to the value under key, which starts empty, and return the new length. The
    /// entry API finds or inserts in one lookup, and `extend_from_slice` grows the `Vec`
    /// in place when it has room.
    pub fn append(&mut self, key: Vec<u8>, val: Vec<u8>) -> usize {
        let v = self.map.entry(key).or_default();
        v.extend_from_slice(&val);
        v.len()
    }
}
rust/ch05/src/store.rs · region store

Two signatures carry the whole ownership story. get takes &self and returns Option<&[u8]>, a borrowed view that lives only as long as the borrow of the store. set takes Vec<u8> by value, which means the caller gives the bytes away. Nothing is copied, and nothing can be used twice.

The command function takes its arguments by value for the same reason. For SET, mem::take moves the key and the value out of the argument list and leaves empty vectors behind. The store receives them without a copy.

A table of fn pointers, built by a macro#

Rust has function pointers too, with the type fn(...) -> ..., and a const array of structs can hold them. The signature has one new thing in it. The writer is &mut dyn Write, which means any writer, chosen at run time. The helpers in resp take impl Write, which means any writer chosen at compile time. The compiler makes a copy of each helper per writer type. A table of pointers cannot hold a copy per type, so the handlers take the run-time form. Chapter 7 returns to the difference. The table itself is written through a macro_rules! macro, which turns each name => function, arity line into an Entry:

/// Every command is a function of this one shape, so a table can hold them. The writer is
/// `dyn Write`, any writer decided at run time, because a table cannot hold one function
/// per writer type. Chapter 7 explains `dyn`.
type Handler = fn(&mut Command, &mut Store, &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()>;

/// A row of the table: the name as the client spells it, the function, and the arity as
/// Redis counts it. Positive is the exact argc, name included; negative is a minimum.
struct Entry {
    name: &'static [u8],
    run: Handler,
    arity: i32,
}

/// The table, written once. The macro turns each `name => function, arity` line into an
/// `Entry`, so the list reads like a list and not like a struct literal eleven times.
macro_rules! commands {
    ($($name:literal => $run:ident, $arity:expr;)*) => {
        const COMMANDS: &[Entry] = &[$(Entry { name: $name, run: $run, arity: $arity }),*];
    };
}

commands! {
    b"PING" => ping, -1;
    b"ECHO" => echo, 2;
    b"SET" => set, 3;
    b"GET" => get, 2;
    b"DEL" => del, -2;
    b"EXISTS" => exists, -2;
    b"INCR" => incr, 2;
    b"APPEND" => append, 3;
    b"STRLEN" => strlen, 2;
    b"GETRANGE" => getrange, 4;
    b"COMMAND" => command, -1;
}
rust/ch05/src/cmd.rs · region table

A macro_rules! macro matches the tokens between its brackets against a pattern and writes code from a template. $name:literal captures a literal and $run:ident a name. $arity:expr captures an expression, and $( ... ;)* repeats for every line. The macro runs before type checking, so what it writes is checked as if you had typed it. The lookup is then a search of the array, and the call goes through the pointer:

/// Run one command against the store and write its reply: find the row, check the arity,
/// call the function. The command is taken by value, so that SET can move the key and
/// the value into the store instead of copying them.
pub fn execute(mut args: Command, store: &mut Store, w: &mut impl Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let Some(name) = args.first() else {
        return resp::write_error(w, "ERR empty command");
    };
    let name = name.to_ascii_uppercase();
    let Some(entry) = COMMANDS.iter().find(|e| e.name == name.as_slice()) else {
        let shown = String::from_utf8_lossy(&args[0][..args[0].len().min(40)]);
        return resp::write_error(w, &format!("ERR unknown command '{shown}'"));
    };
    let argc = args.len() as i32;
    let ok = if entry.arity < 0 {
        argc >= -entry.arity
    } else {
        argc == entry.arity
    };
    if !ok {
        return write_arity(w, entry.name);
    }
    (entry.run)(&mut args, store, w)
}

fn write_arity(w: &mut dyn Write, name: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
    let name = String::from_utf8_lossy(name).to_ascii_lowercase();
    resp::write_error(
        w,
        &format!("ERR wrong number of arguments for '{name}' command"),
    )
}
rust/ch05/src/cmd.rs · region exec
fn ping(args: &mut Command, _: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    match args.as_slice() {
        [_] => resp::write_simple(w, "PONG"),
        [_, msg] => resp::write_bulk(w, msg),
        _ => write_arity(w, b"ping"),
    }
}

fn echo(args: &mut Command, _: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    resp::write_bulk(w, &args[1])
}

fn set(args: &mut Command, store: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let [_, key, val] = args.as_mut_slice() else {
        unreachable!("arity checked")
    };
    store.set(mem::take(key), mem::take(val));
    resp::write_simple(w, "OK")
}

fn get(args: &mut Command, store: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    match store.get(&args[1]) {
        Some(val) => resp::write_bulk(w, val),
        None => resp::write_nil(w),
    }
}

fn del(args: &mut Command, store: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let n = args[1..].iter().filter(|k| store.del(k)).count();
    resp::write_int(w, n as i64)
}

fn exists(args: &mut Command, store: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let n = args[1..].iter().filter(|k| store.get(k).is_some()).count();
    resp::write_int(w, n as i64)
}

fn incr(args: &mut Command, store: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    match store.incr(&args[1]) {
        Ok(n) => resp::write_int(w, n),
        Err(e) => resp::write_error(w, e.message()),
    }
}

fn command(_: &mut Command, _: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    resp::write_array_len(w, 0) // redis-cli asks on connect; an empty list is fine
}
rust/ch05/src/cmd.rs · region commands

Each handler is a match on the argument slice. One arm can say "PING with nothing", the next "PING with one message". A let ... else with a slice pattern takes the key and the value out of SET. The unreachable! says that the arity check above makes the other case impossible.

str, String, char and a slice of bytes#

Three more commands work on the bytes of a value. APPEND uses the map's entry API to find or insert in one lookup and extends the Vec in place. STRLEN is len, in bytes. GETRANGE slices the Vec by byte offset. None of them can be written on a String. A String is a Vec<u8> with a promise, that its bytes are valid UTF-8. A slice at a byte offset can break the promise. The test below is in the chapter's snapshot. A str has a length in bytes and a count of char, which are different. A slice of a str must land on a character boundary, and one that does not is a panic. The same bytes as a &[u8] can be cut anywhere, which is why kv stores values as bytes:

/// A `str` is bytes that are valid UTF-8. `len` counts the bytes, `chars` the
/// characters, and a slice must land on a character boundary.
#[test]
fn bytes_and_chars() {
    let s = "héllo";
    assert_eq!(s.len(), 6);
    assert_eq!(s.chars().count(), 5);
    assert_eq!(&s[0..1], "h");
    assert_eq!(&s[1..3], "é");
    assert!(s.is_char_boundary(3));
    assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(2));
    // the same bytes as a slice can be cut anywhere, which is what GETRANGE needs
    assert_eq!(&s.as_bytes()[1..2], &[0xC3]);
}

/// Slicing a `str` in the middle of a character is a panic, not a corrupt string.
#[test]
#[should_panic(expected = "byte index 2 is not a char boundary")]
fn half_a_char_panics() {
    let s = "héllo";
    let _ = &s[0..2];
}
rust/ch05/src/store.rs · region text
/// APPEND key value: grow the stored bytes. The value is moved in when the key is new.
fn append(args: &mut Command, store: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let [_, key, val] = args.as_mut_slice() else {
        unreachable!("arity checked")
    };
    let n = store.append(mem::take(key), mem::take(val));
    resp::write_int(w, n as i64)
}

/// STRLEN key: the length in bytes. `len` on a `Vec<u8>` counts bytes, and so does Redis.
/// The number of characters is a different question, which `chars().count()` answers on
/// a `str`, and which the store cannot ask, because a value need not be text.
fn strlen(args: &mut Command, store: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let n = store.get(&args[1]).map_or(0, <[u8]>::len);
    resp::write_int(w, n as i64)
}

/// GETRANGE key start end: a slice by byte offsets, both inclusive. A negative offset
/// counts from the end, and an offset past either end is clamped, as Redis does.
fn getrange(args: &mut Command, store: &mut Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let (Some(start), Some(end)) = (parse_int(&args[2]), parse_int(&args[3])) else {
        return resp::write_error(w, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
    };
    let val = store.get(&args[1]).unwrap_or(b"");
    let len = val.len() as i64;
    let start = if start < 0 { start + len } else { start }.max(0);
    let end = if end < 0 { end + len } else { end }.min(len - 1);
    if len == 0 || start > end {
        return resp::write_bulk(w, b"");
    }
    resp::write_bulk(w, &val[start as usize..=end as usize])
}

/// Why INCR could not add one.
pub enum IncrError {
    NotInteger,
    Overflow,
}

impl IncrError {
    pub fn message(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::NotInteger => "ERR value is not an integer or out of range",
            Self::Overflow => "ERR increment or decrement would overflow",
        }
    }
}
/// The bytes as a signed 64-bit integer, if that is what they are.
pub fn parse_int(bytes: &[u8]) -> Option<i64> {
    std::str::from_utf8(bytes).ok()?.parse().ok()
}

Stuck?Show the full listing
impl Store {
    /// Add one to the integer stored under key, which counts as 0 when absent.
    pub fn incr(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> Result<i64, IncrError> {
        let n = match self.get(key) {
            None => 0,
            Some(bytes) => parse_int(bytes).ok_or(IncrError::NotInteger)?,
        };
        let n = n.checked_add(1).ok_or(IncrError::Overflow)?;
        self.set(key.to_vec(), n.to_string().into_bytes());
        Ok(n)
    }
}
rust/ch05/src/store.rs · region incr

IncrError is an enum with two cases, and the command code matches on it to write the reply. This is the Rust form of the two Go sentinel values. The difference is that a match on an enum must handle every case. So a third kind of failure, added later, is a compile error at every place that forgot it.

⚠️You cannot keep a value and change the store Rust

A borrowed value blocks every write to the store until it is dropped. The following three lines do not compile, and the compiler says why:

let old = store.get(b"a");
store.set(b"a".to_vec(), b"2".to_vec());
println!("{:?}", old);
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `store` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
   |     let old = store.get(b"a");
   |               ----- immutable borrow occurs here
   |     store.set(b"a".to_vec(), b"2".to_vec());
   |     ^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
   |     println!("{:?}", old);
   |                      --- immutable borrow later used here

In C the same three lines compile, and old points at freed memory after the set. The Rust error is the C bug, caught before the program runs. When you need the old value after a write, copy it first with to_vec(). That is what the C code did with kv_bytes_dup, and it is what the compiler is asking for.

Three answers to the largest integer plus one#

Start any of the three servers and run SET big 9223372036854775807, then INCR big. All three reply with the Redis error, because each one checks before it adds. Remove the check and the three languages give three different answers, and that is the lesson of this section.

In C, adding one to LLONG_MAX is undefined behaviour. The standard does not say what happens, so the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, and it does. A check written after the add, such as if (n + 1 < n), is removed by the optimiser as impossible. The check must come before, as kv_cmd_incr writes it. The parser of chapter 5 had the same rule and refused more than 18 digits for the same reason. Unsigned arithmetic is the exception. It wraps around by definition, which is why a hash function in chapter 6 is written with unsigned types.

In Go, integers wrap. The largest int64 plus one is the smallest, with no error, no panic and no flag. The test in the chapter's snapshot shows it:

// Go integers wrap. The largest int64 plus one is the smallest, with no error and no panic,
// which is why incr checks against math.MaxInt64 before it adds.
func TestOverflowWraps(t *testing.T) {
	n := int64(math.MaxInt64)
	n++
	if n != math.MinInt64 {
		t.Fatalf("got %d", n)
	}
}
go/ch05/strings_test.go · region overflow

In Rust, the answer depends on the build. A debug build panics on the overflow, with the message attempt to add with overflow. A release build wraps, as Go does. Three methods say what you want in their names, checked_add, wrapping_add and saturating_add. They behave the same in both builds. kv uses checked_add, which returns None on overflow, and turns that into the Redis error:

/// Three ways to add one to the largest integer: a debug build panics on plain `+`,
/// a release build wraps, and `checked_add` returns `None` in both. kv uses the last.
#[test]
fn overflow_three_ways() {
    let n = i64::MAX;
    assert_eq!(n.checked_add(1), None);
    assert_eq!(n.wrapping_add(1), i64::MIN);
    assert_eq!(n.saturating_add(1), i64::MAX);
}

#[test]
#[cfg(debug_assertions)]
#[should_panic(expected = "attempt to add with overflow")]
fn plain_add_panics_in_debug() {
    let n = std::hint::black_box(i64::MAX);
    let _ = n + 1;
}
rust/ch05/src/store.rs · region overflow
⚠️The compiler believes you C

A test for signed overflow that runs after the arithmetic may be deleted by the compiler. Because the overflow cannot happen in a correct program, a branch that only runs when it did happen is dead code to the optimiser. The same reasoning removes a NULL check after a pointer has already been used. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, in chapter 12, reports the overflow at run time, and -ftrapv turns it into a crash. Both are off in a release build.

Who owns the bytes#

Every version of SET had to answer one question. The bytes arrived in a request buffer. Who keeps them, and who frees them? C answered with a copy and a comment. The store makes its own copy with kv_bytes_dup and frees it on replacement. The comment on the field is the only record of the rule. Go answered with the collector. The store keeps the parser's slice. The collector frees it when nothing refers to it any more, at a time the program does not choose. Rust answered with a move. The store takes the bytes from the argument list, which is left empty. The compiler refuses any later use of what was moved.

All three answers work. The C answer costs a copy and a rule the compiler does not know. The Go answer costs memory until the next collection and a pause when it runs. The Rust answer costs nothing at run time. It costs a type signature that says Vec<u8> in place of the char * of C. Chapter 6 makes the costs larger, because the store becomes a structure that must free and move things itself.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
A key is bytesOKStrongOKC carries a length beside every pointer, Go has []byte and string, and Rust makes you pick Vec<u8> because String rejects binary data.
Copying and owningWeakStrongStrongC copies and comments, Go lets the collector own everything, and Rust moves and checks.
Parsing a numberWeakOKOKC needs a careful parser to avoid undefined behaviour. The other two accept forms Redis rejects.
OverflowWeakOKStrongC must check before it adds and Go checks against a constant, while Rust has checked_add built in.
A missing caseWeakWeakStrongAn enum match in Rust must be complete. In C and Go, a new error kind can be forgotten at a call site.
Reading the codeOKStrongOKThe Go store is the shortest. The Rust signatures say more and take longer to read.
A table of commandsOKStrongOKC needs an X-macro and a function pointer type, and Go has a map of funcs. Rust needs dyn Write and a macro for the rows.
Text against bytesWeakOKStrongC has no text type at all, and Go has rune helpers. Rust makes a str keep its promise and a Vec<u8> make none.
Carry forward
  • Function pointer. A function is a value with an address, and a table of them replaces a chain of ifs in all three languages.
  • Bytes against text. A length in bytes is not a count of characters, and a slice at a byte offset can cut a character in half.
  • Signed overflow. Undefined in C, a silent wrap in Go, a panic in a Rust debug build, and a checked add in kv.
Next

The store is a list, and a lookup walks it. Fill it with twenty thousand keys, and a GET from one client takes a sixth of a millisecond, twenty times longer than Redis takes.

Your own hash table#

Building kv · Chapter 06· 36 min read· 606 lines of code
▶Scene

Start the chapter 5 server and fill it with twenty thousand keys. Then let the Redis benchmark tool ask for them, one client, one request at a time:

$ redis-cli -p 6380 --pipe < twenty-thousand-sets.txt
errors: 0, replies: 20000
$ redis-benchmark -p 6380 -c 1 -n 5000 -r 20000 -t get -q
GET: 6257.82 requests per second, p50=0.151 msec

Six thousand a second, from a program that does nothing but compare bytes. Real Redis answers the same question from one client about twenty times faster. Every GET is walking the list from chapter 5, and the list has twenty thousand entries.

The list from chapter 5 gets slower with every key. This chapter replaces it with a hash table that you write yourself, in all three languages. In C the table becomes the store. In Go and Rust the standard map stays, and your table stands beside it. The chapter is about memory, because a hash table must allocate, move and free its own parts.

With 20,000 keys in the store, the C server from chapter 5 answers about 6,300 GET requests a second from one client. Each lookup walks half the list on average. The same server with the hash table from this chapter answers about 17,700, and the median request takes 39 microseconds instead of 151. That is the measurement on the author's machine, and chapter 13 shows how to take it yourself. The difference grows with the number of keys, because the list takes time in proportion to the keys and the table does not.

A hash table turns a key into a number, called its hash. The low bits of that number are an index into an array of buckets. Two keys may land in the same bucket, so each bucket holds a chain of entries, and a lookup walks that short chain. When the table holds more entries than buckets, the array doubles and every entry moves to its new bucket. The chapter also adds two commands that ask about the whole table, DBSIZE and KEYS.

The tableCGoRust
A bucketa pointer to the first entry of a chaina slice of entriesa Vec of entries
A chain linka next pointer the entry ownsthe next element of the slicethe next element of the Vec
Growingcalloc a bigger array, relink every entrymake a bigger slice, append every entrydrain every chain into a bigger Vec

📜Why Redis rehashes a little at a time

Doubling the array is the simplest way to grow a table, and it is what this chapter does. It has a cost. The move of every entry takes a time proportional to the table, and a Redis server with ten million keys cannot stop for that long. So the Redis dictionary keeps two arrays during a resize and moves a few buckets on every operation. The function is dictRehash(dict *d, int n) in dict.c, and a field named rehashidx records how far the move has gone. The built-in map of Go also grows incrementally. It splits a large map into several small tables that grow one at a time. The server kv needs no such trick, and the simple version is easier to see.

C: an array of chains, and every pointer accounted for#

The hash is FNV-1a, a few lines that multiply and exclusive-or. It is fast and spreads keys well, and it is not safe against an attacker who chooses keys that collide. The Rust section says why that matters:

/* FNV-1a: a small, fast hash of bytes. Not safe against an attacker who chooses keys
 * to collide, which Redis guards against with a secret seed. Chapter 12 returns to it. */
static uint64_t kv_hash(const char *s, size_t n) {
    uint64_t h = 14695981039346656037ULL;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        h ^= (unsigned char)s[i];
        h *= 1099511628211ULL;
    }
    return h;
}
c/ch06/kv.c · region hash

Two details of the hash are rules of C integers. The multiply overflows on almost every step, and that is fine, because uint64_t is unsigned and unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition. A signed type here would be undefined behaviour. And each byte is cast to unsigned char before it is mixed in. A plain char may be signed or unsigned, by platform. On this machine it is signed, so the byte 0xC3 of an é is the value -61. Mixing -61 into a 64-bit hash sets the top 56 bits. The cast makes it 195 on every platform, and the hash the same everywhere. The same cast belongs in front of every ctype.h call, for the same reason.

An entry now has a next pointer, and the comment says that the entry owns it. That one word decides who frees a chain. The table is an array of chain heads. The count of buckets is always a power of two, so that the index is the hash masked with cap - 1 instead of a division:

/* One key and its value, in a chain of entries that share a bucket. The key and the
 * value are owned copies. The next pointer is owned too: freeing an entry frees its
 * chain. */
typedef struct kv_entry {
    char *key;
    size_t klen;
    char *val;
    size_t vlen;
    struct kv_entry *next;
} kv_entry;

/* A hash table with separate chaining. buckets[i] is the head of a chain, or NULL. The
 * table grows when it holds more entries than buckets, so a chain stays short. */
typedef struct {
    kv_entry **buckets; /* owned array of cap pointers */
    size_t cap;         /* a power of two, or 0 before the first insert */
    size_t len;         /* how many entries, over all chains */
} kv_store;

static kv_entry *kv_store_find(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen) {
    if (s->cap == 0) {
        return NULL;
    }
    size_t i = kv_hash(key, klen) & (s->cap - 1);
    for (kv_entry *e = s->buckets[i]; e != NULL; e = e->next) {
        if (kv_bytes_eq(e->key, e->klen, key, klen)) {
            return e;
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}
/* The command list, written once. Each use of KV_COMMANDS defines X to say what to make
 * of a row. The first use builds the table, the second counts it. A positive arity is
 * the exact argc, name included, and a negative one is a minimum, as Redis counts. */
#define KV_COMMANDS                     \
    X(ping, kv_cmd_ping, -1)            \
    X(echo, kv_cmd_echo, 2)             \
    X(set, kv_cmd_set, 3)               \
    X(get, kv_cmd_get, 2)               \
    X(del, kv_cmd_del, -2)              \
    X(exists, kv_cmd_exists, -2)        \
    X(incr, kv_cmd_incr, 2)             \
    X(append, kv_cmd_append, 3)         \
    X(strlen, kv_cmd_strlen, 2)         \
    X(getrange, kv_cmd_getrange, 4)     \
    X(dbsize, kv_cmd_dbsize, 1)         \
    X(keys, kv_cmd_keys, 2)             \
    X(command, kv_cmd_command, -1)

typedef struct {
    const char *name;
    kv_cmd_fn fn;
    int arity;
} kv_command;

static const kv_command kv_commands[] = {
#define X(name, fn, arity) {#name, fn, arity},
    KV_COMMANDS
#undef X
};

enum {
#define X(name, fn, arity) +1
    KV_COMMAND_COUNT = 0 KV_COMMANDS
#undef X
};
c/ch06/kv.c · region table

Growing allocates a new array with calloc, which returns memory set to zero, so every new bucket starts as an empty chain. Then it walks every old chain and pushes each entry onto the front of its new one. No key or value is copied. Only the next pointers change, which is the point of keeping entries as separate allocations:

/* Double the bucket array and move every entry to its new chain. No entry is copied or
 * freed: only the next pointers change. */
static bool kv_store_grow(kv_store *s) {
    size_t cap = s->cap ? s->cap * 2 : 16;
    kv_entry **buckets = calloc(cap, sizeof *buckets);
    if (buckets == NULL) {
        return false;
    }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < s->cap; i++) {
        kv_entry *e = s->buckets[i];
        while (e != NULL) {
            kv_entry *next = e->next; /* read it before the chain is changed */
            size_t j = kv_hash(e->key, e->klen) & (cap - 1);
            e->next = buckets[j];
            buckets[j] = e;
            e = next;
        }
    }
    free(s->buckets);
    s->buckets = buckets;
    s->cap = cap;
    return true;
}
c/ch06/kv.c · region grow
⚠️Read next before you change it C

The line kv_entry *next = e->next must come first. The loop sets e->next to the head of the new chain, and after that the old chain is gone. Swap the two lines and the loop follows the new chain instead of the old one. It loses every entry after the first, and ends in a cycle or a crash. The compiler accepts both orders. Nothing but your reading of the code tells them apart.

Inserting has three allocations that can each fail, and the cleanup must free exactly the ones that succeeded. The code calls free on every pointer, because free(NULL) does nothing. That rule makes the failure path three lines instead of a tree of conditions:

/* Store a copy of val under a copy of key, replacing any old value. */
static bool kv_store_set(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen, const char *val,
                         size_t vlen) {
    char *v = kv_bytes_dup(val, vlen);
    if (v == NULL) {
        return false;
    }
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, key, klen);
    if (e != NULL) {
        free(e->val);
        e->val = v;
        e->vlen = vlen;
        return true;
    }
    if (s->len >= s->cap && !kv_store_grow(s)) {
        free(v);
        return false;
    }
    e = malloc(sizeof *e);
    char *k = kv_bytes_dup(key, klen);
    if (e == NULL || k == NULL) {
        free(e);
        free(k);
        free(v);
        return false;
    }
    size_t i = kv_hash(key, klen) & (s->cap - 1);
    *e = (kv_entry){k, klen, v, vlen, s->buckets[i]};
    s->buckets[i] = e;
    s->len++;
    return true;
}

Write kv_store_del. Walk the chain with a pointer to a pointer. Then removing the first entry of a chain and removing a middle one are the same operation. When the key matches, make the previous link skip the entry, free its key, its value and the entry itself, and reduce the count.

Stuck?Show the full listing
/* Remove a key. The chain is walked with a pointer to the pointer that leads to each
 * entry, so that the head of the chain and the middle of it are the same case. */
static bool kv_store_del(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen) {
    if (s->cap == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    size_t i = kv_hash(key, klen) & (s->cap - 1);
    for (kv_entry **link = &s->buckets[i]; *link != NULL; link = &(*link)->next) {
        kv_entry *e = *link;
        if (kv_bytes_eq(e->key, e->klen, key, klen)) {
            *link = e->next;
            free(e->key);
            free(e->val);
            free(e);
            s->len--;
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}

static void kv_store_free(kv_store *s) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < s->cap; i++) {
        kv_entry *e = s->buckets[i];
        while (e != NULL) {
            kv_entry *next = e->next;
            free(e->key);
            free(e->val);
            free(e);
            e = next;
        }
    }
    free(s->buckets);
    s->buckets = NULL;
    s->cap = s->len = 0;
}
c/ch06/kv.c · region del

The pointer-to-pointer walk is an old C idiom, and it is worth a moment. link points at whichever pointer currently leads to e. At the head of the chain that is the bucket itself. In the middle it is the next field of the entry before. Writing *link = e->next removes e in both cases without a special case for the head. Linus Torvalds has said that code which special-cases the head tells him "this person doesn't understand pointers". The version without the special case is also harder to read the first time.

KEYS walks every bucket and every chain. It needs a pattern matcher, and the one here supports * and ?. The Go and Rust files hold the same function in their glob regions. The reply is an array whose length is known only after the walk, so the keys are collected in a second buffer first:

/* KEYS pattern: every matching key, as an array. The count is known only after the
 * walk, so the keys are collected first and the header is written in front of them. */
static bool kv_cmd_keys(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_buf keys = {0};
    size_t n = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < s->cap; i++) {
        for (kv_entry *e = s->buckets[i]; e != NULL; e = e->next) {
            if (kv_glob(c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], e->key, e->klen)) {
                if (!kv_reply_bulk(&keys, e->key, e->klen)) {
                    kv_buf_free(&keys);
                    return false;
                }
                n++;
            }
        }
    }
    bool ok = kv_reply_array(out, n) && kv_buf_append(out, keys.data, keys.len);
    kv_buf_free(&keys);
    return ok;
}

✅Every malloc has one free you can point to C

Open kv.c and find each malloc and calloc. For each one, find the free that releases it. The value of an entry is freed in kv_store_set on replacement. The key and the value are freed in kv_store_del and in kv_store_free. The bucket array is freed in kv_store_grow and in kv_store_free. If you cannot find the pair for an allocation, that is a leak, and chapter 12 shows how Valgrind finds it for you.

Where a value lives, and for how long#

Every object in C has a storage duration, and the table uses all three. A local variable such as i in kv_store_grow has automatic duration. It lives on the stack from its declaration to the end of its block, and its address must not be kept after that. A static variable, and anything declared outside a function, lives for the whole run, in memory the loader set up before main. And everything malloc returns has allocated duration. It lives on the heap until free, whatever block or function ends in between. The entries must outlive the function that made them, so they are allocated. The bucket index is needed for a few lines, so it is a local. Returning the address of a local is the mistake the three durations make possible, and the compiler warns about the plain form of it.

What C does instead of generics#

The table stores bytes under bytes, and nothing else. A table of integers under strings would be a second copy of the file with the types changed. Go and Rust write the table once with a type parameter, as the next two sections show. C has three ways to avoid the copy, each with a cost, and the file generic.c in the chapter's snapshot runs all three. make test builds it, and every claim in it is an assert. The first way is a void * and an element size. The function moves bytes without knowing what they are, and the caller casts them back:

/* 1. A void pointer and an element size. The caller says how big one element is, and the
 * function moves bytes without knowing what they are. qsort and bsearch work this way.
 * The compiler checks nothing: pass the wrong size and the sort is silently wrong. */
static int cmp_u32(const void *a, const void *b) {
    uint32_t x = *(const uint32_t *)a;
    uint32_t y = *(const uint32_t *)b;
    return (x > y) - (x < y);
}

static void sort_demo(void) {
    uint32_t xs[] = {30, 10, 20};
    qsort(xs, 3, sizeof xs[0], cmp_u32);
    assert(xs[0] == 10 && xs[1] == 20 && xs[2] == 30);
}
c/ch06/generic.c · region void

The cast (const uint32_t *)a is a claim the compiler cannot check. Pass qsort a size of 2 and it sorts garbage in silence. The second way is a macro that writes the typed code for each type. The macro is the template, and each use is a copy with T filled in. ## pastes two tokens into one name, so name##_push becomes vec_u32_push:

/* 2. A macro that writes a typed container for each element type. The macro is the
 * template, and each use is a copy with T filled in. A Rust generic compiles the same
 * way, one copy per type, with the difference that Rust checks the template once. */
#define DEFINE_VEC(name, T)                                                           \
    typedef struct {                                                                  \
        T *data; /* owned */                                                          \
        size_t len, cap;                                                              \
    } name;                                                                           \
    static bool name##_push(name *v, T x) {                                           \
        if (v->len == v->cap) {                                                       \
            size_t cap = v->cap ? v->cap * 2 : 8;                                     \
            T *p = realloc(v->data, cap * sizeof *p);                                 \
            if (p == NULL) {                                                          \
                return false;                                                         \
            }                                                                         \
            v->data = p;                                                              \
            v->cap = cap;                                                             \
        }                                                                             \
        v->data[v->len++] = x;                                                        \
        return true;                                                                  \
    }

DEFINE_VEC(vec_u32, uint32_t)
DEFINE_VEC(vec_str, const char *)

static void vec_demo(void) {
    vec_u32 nums = {0};
    vec_str words = {0};
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
        assert(vec_u32_push(&nums, i * i));
    }
    assert(vec_str_push(&words, "hello") && vec_str_push(&words, "world"));
    assert(nums.len == 100 && nums.data[9] == 81);
    assert(strcmp(words.data[1], "world") == 0);
    free(nums.data);
    free(words.data);
}
c/ch06/generic.c · region macro

That is also how a Rust generic is compiled, one copy per type. The difference is that Rust checks the template once. A C macro is checked only when it is used, in error messages that point at the use. The third way is _Generic, a compile-time switch on the type of an expression, which lets one name reach several functions:

/* 3. _Generic: a compile-time switch on the type of an expression. It is how C11 gives
 * one name to several functions, which is as close as C gets to overloading. */
static const char *name_u32(uint32_t x) {
    (void)x;
    return "uint32_t";
}

static const char *name_str(const char *s) {
    (void)s;
    return "const char *";
}

#define type_name(x) _Generic((x), uint32_t: name_u32, const char *: name_str, char *: name_str)(x)

static void generic_demo(void) {
    uint32_t n = 7;
    const char *s = "seven";
    assert(strcmp(type_name(n), "uint32_t") == 0);
    assert(strcmp(type_name(s), "const char *") == 0);
}

Redis uses the first way and the second. Its dictionary stores void * keys and values, with a table of function pointers that say how to hash, compare and free them. Chapter 7 returns to that table, because it is also how C does an interface.

What a struct is made of, and an arena#

A kv_entry is 40 bytes on this machine, five fields of 8. Change the order of fields in a struct, or mix sizes, and the compiler inserts padding. Every type has an alignment, and a member must start at a multiple of its own. offsetof reads where a member starts, and alignof reads the alignment. _Static_assert checks a claim about either when the file is compiled, so a wrong one never runs:

/* What a struct is made of. Every type has an alignment, and the compiler inserts padding
 * so that each member starts at a multiple of its own alignment. One byte of tag before
 * an eight-byte number costs seven bytes of padding, and reordering the members saves it.
 * offsetof reads the layout, and _Static_assert checks it when the program is compiled. */
typedef struct {
    uint8_t tag;
    uint64_t n;
    uint8_t flag;
} loose;

typedef struct {
    uint64_t n;
    uint8_t tag;
    uint8_t flag;
} tight;

_Static_assert(sizeof(loose) == 24, "two bytes of tags cost 14 bytes of padding");
_Static_assert(sizeof(tight) == 16, "the same members, reordered, need 6");
_Static_assert(offsetof(loose, n) == 8, "n starts at the next multiple of 8");
_Static_assert(alignof(uint64_t) == 8, "a 64-bit integer is aligned to 8 bytes");

static void layout_demo(void) {
    printf("loose %zu bytes, tight %zu bytes, char is %s\n", sizeof(loose), sizeof(tight),
           CHAR_MIN < 0 ? "signed" : "unsigned");
}
c/ch06/generic.c · region layout

Chapter 15 needs these numbers, because a struct that crosses into Go or Rust must have the same layout on both sides. The last demonstration is an arena, the other way to own memory in C. One block is given out from the front, each piece rounded up to the largest alignment, and the whole block is freed at once. A parser that builds a tree for one request frees a thousand things with one call. So does a game that throws away a frame, and no piece leaks:

/* An arena: one block, handed out from the front, freed all at once. Each piece starts
 * at a multiple of the largest alignment, so any type may live in it. A parser that
 * builds a tree per request, or a game that frees everything per frame, uses one. */
typedef struct {
    char *base; /* owned */
    size_t used;
    size_t cap;
} arena;

static void *arena_alloc(arena *a, size_t n) {
    size_t align = alignof(max_align_t);
    size_t start = (a->used + align - 1) / align * align; /* round up */
    if (start + n > a->cap) {
        return NULL;
    }
    a->used = start + n;
    return a->base + start;
}

static void arena_demo(void) {
    arena a = {malloc(4096), 0, 4096};
    assert(a.base != NULL);
    char *name = arena_alloc(&a, 5);
    uint64_t *count = arena_alloc(&a, sizeof *count);
    memcpy(name, "kv!!", 5);
    *count = 42;
    assert((uintptr_t)count % alignof(uint64_t) == 0); /* padded past the 5 bytes */
    assert(a.used == 16 + sizeof *count);
    free(a.base); /* one free for every piece */
}

Go: the same table, with nothing to free#

The Go version keeps the shape of the C one and drops the bookkeeping. A chain is a slice, so there is no next pointer. The entry has two fields, and the types of both are type parameters. K comparable says the key may be any type that supports ==, which is what a lookup needs. V any says the value may be anything at all. The table is written once, and the compiler produces the code for each pair of types a program uses. The hash comes from the caller as a function, because comparable promises equality and nothing about bytes:

// fnv1a hashes bytes the way kv does in C, so the two tables spread keys the same way.
func fnv1a(b []byte) uint64 {
	h := uint64(14695981039346656037)
	for _, c := range b {
		h ^= uint64(c)
		h *= 1099511628211
	}
	return h
}
go/ch06/table.go · region hash
// entry is one key and its value in a chain. There is no next pointer: a chain is a
// slice, and the garbage collector owns everything. K and V are type parameters: the
// table is written once, for any key that supports == and any value at all.
type entry[K comparable, V any] struct {
	key K
	val V
}

// Table is a hash table with separate chaining. It grows when it holds more entries
// than buckets, so a chain stays short. The hash function comes from the caller, because
// the constraint comparable promises == and nothing else.
type Table[K comparable, V any] struct {
	hash    func(K) uint64
	buckets [][]entry[K, V]
	n       int
}

func NewTable[K comparable, V any](hash func(K) uint64) *Table[K, V] {
	return &Table[K, V]{hash: hash}
}

func (t *Table[K, V]) Get(key K) (V, bool) {
	if len(t.buckets) == 0 {
		var zero V
		return zero, false
	}
	chain := t.buckets[t.hash(key)&uint64(len(t.buckets)-1)]
	for i := range chain {
		if chain[i].key == key {
			return chain[i].val, true
		}
	}
	var zero V
	return zero, false
}
go/ch06/table.go · region table

A constraint is an interface used as a bound. comparable and any are built in. cmp.Ordered covers the types with a less-than, and a union such as ~int | ~string names a set of types. Go had no generics until version 1.18 in 2022, thirteen years into its life, and the design kept them small on purpose. There are no generic methods, and a type parameter cannot be used as a receiver. The question of when to use them has a short answer. A container or an algorithm over several types, such as this table, is a generic. A function that takes behaviour is an interface, which chapter 7 covers.

Exercise 06.2GoGrow the table

Write the grow method. Make a slice of buckets twice as long. Walk every old chain, and append each entry to its new chain. Use fnv1a and the new length to find the index. Then replace t.buckets. Nothing is freed, because nothing in Go is freed by you.

func (t *table) grow() {
	buckets := make([][]entry, 2*len(t.buckets))
	// your code here
	t.buckets = buckets
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
func (t *Table[K, V]) Set(key K, val V) {
	if len(t.buckets) == 0 {
		t.buckets = make([][]entry[K, V], 16)
	}
	i := t.hash(key) & uint64(len(t.buckets)-1)
	chain := t.buckets[i]
	for j := range chain {
		if chain[j].key == key {
			chain[j].val = val
			return
		}
	}
	if t.n >= len(t.buckets) {
		t.grow()
		i = t.hash(key) & uint64(len(t.buckets)-1)
	}
	t.buckets[i] = append(t.buckets[i], entry[K, V]{key, val})
	t.n++
}

// grow doubles the bucket slice and moves every entry to its new chain. The old slices
// become garbage, and the collector frees them.
func (t *Table[K, V]) grow() {
	buckets := make([][]entry[K, V], 2*len(t.buckets))
	for _, chain := range t.buckets {
		for _, e := range chain {
			i := t.hash(e.key) & uint64(len(buckets)-1)
			buckets[i] = append(buckets[i], e)
		}
	}
	t.buckets = buckets
}
go/ch06/table.go · region set

The old slices become garbage when t.buckets is replaced, and the collector frees them at some later moment. Deleting moves the last entry of a chain into the hole, as the C list did in chapter 5. The removed entry is garbage too:

func (t *Table[K, V]) Del(key K) bool {
	if len(t.buckets) == 0 {
		return false
	}
	i := t.hash(key) & uint64(len(t.buckets)-1)
	chain := t.buckets[i]
	for j := range chain {
		if chain[j].key == key {
			// move the last entry into the hole, then shorten the chain by one
			chain[j] = chain[len(chain)-1]
			t.buckets[i] = chain[:len(chain)-1]
			t.n--
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

// Len is the number of entries, and Keys is every key in no particular order.
func (t *Table[K, V]) Len() int { return t.n }

func (t *Table[K, V]) Keys() []K {
	keys := make([]K, 0, t.n)
	for _, chain := range t.buckets {
		for _, e := range chain {
			keys = append(keys, e.key)
		}
	}
	return keys
}

The table is never used by the server. It is checked by a test, which runs five thousand random operations against a built-in map and stops at the first disagreement. The test is in table_test.go, and go test finds it by the file name and the function name:

// TestTableAgainstMap runs random operations on the table and on a map, and checks
// after each one that the table agrees with the map. The table is instantiated with
// string keys and string values; the compiler writes that version of the code.
func TestTableAgainstMap(t *testing.T) {
	tb := NewTable[string, string](hashString)
	ref := map[string]string{}
	r := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2))
	for step := range 5000 {
		key := fmt.Sprintf("k%d", r.IntN(200))
		switch r.IntN(3) {
		case 0:
			val := fmt.Sprintf("v%d", step)
			tb.Set(key, val)
			ref[key] = val
		case 1:
			_, want := ref[key]
			if got := tb.Del(key); got != want {
				t.Fatalf("step %d: del %q = %v, want %v", step, key, got, want)
			}
			delete(ref, key)
		case 2:
			want, ok := ref[key]
			got, found := tb.Get(key)
			if found != ok || got != want {
				t.Fatalf("step %d: get %q = %q,%v, want %q,%v", step, key, got, found, want, ok)
			}
		}
		if tb.Len() != len(ref) {
			t.Fatalf("step %d: table has %d entries, map has %d", step, tb.Len(), len(ref))
		}
	}
	// the generic slices and maps packages: collect the map's keys, sort both, compare
	want := slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(ref))
	got := tb.Keys()
	slices.Sort(got)
	if !slices.Equal(got, want) {
		t.Fatalf("keys differ: %v vs %v", got, want)
	}
}

// TestTableWithIntKeys is the same table with another key type. Nothing in table.go
// changed; the compiler made a second copy for int keys.
func TestTableWithIntKeys(t *testing.T) {
	tb := NewTable[int, []byte](func(k int) uint64 { return uint64(k) * 11400714819323198485 })
	for i := range 100 {
		tb.Set(i, []byte{byte(i)})
	}
	if v, ok := tb.Get(42); !ok || v[0] != 42 {
		t.Fatalf("get 42 = %v, %v", v, ok)
	}
	if tb.Del(42) != true || tb.Len() != 99 {
		t.Fatal("del")
	}
}

The test ends with the generic standard packages. maps.Keys walks the reference map, and slices.Sorted orders it. slices.Sort orders the table's list and slices.Equal compares both lists. Before 1.18 each of those was a loop you wrote. The second command runs the two benchmarks at the bottom of the test file. On the author's machine the hand-written table answers a lookup in 17 nanoseconds and the built-in map in 20. That is not a reason to use your own. The built-in map grows without a pause, and is what every Go programmer reads without thinking. The store keeps the map, and adds the two new commands:

// store keeps every key and its value in a map. The hand-written table in table.go
// would work too, and the tests show it does, but the map is faster and nobody would
// use anything else in Go.
type store struct {
	m map[string][]byte
}

func newStore() *store {
	return &store{m: make(map[string][]byte)}
}

func (s *store) get(key []byte) ([]byte, bool) {
	v, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	return v, ok
}

func (s *store) set(key, val []byte) {
	s.m[string(key)] = val
}

func (s *store) del(key []byte) bool {
	_, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	delete(s.m, string(key))
	return ok
}

func (s *store) size() int {
	return len(s.m)
}

// keys returns every key that matches the pattern, in no particular order.
func (s *store) keys(pattern []byte) [][]byte {
	var out [][]byte
	for k := range s.m {
		if glob(pattern, []byte(k)) {
			out = append(out, []byte(k))
		}
	}
	return out
}
go/ch06/store.go · region store

Where the compiler puts a value#

Nothing in the Go table says stack or heap, and the compiler decides. A value that no pointer outlives stays on the stack of its function, which is free. A value that a pointer could reach after the function returns moves to the heap, where the collector must find it later. The decision is called escape analysis, and the compiler will show it:

$ go build -gcflags=-m . 2>&1 | grep -E 'table.go|store.go' | head -4
./table.go:8:6: can inline fnv1a
./table.go:8:12: b does not escape
./store.go:30:21: key does not escape
./store.go:31:22: string(key) does not escape

b does not escape means the slice passed to fnv1a never leaves it, so no copy is made. string(key) does not escape in del is the compiler noticing something. The string made from the key is only used to look in the map, so it is built on the stack and never allocated. In set the same conversion escapes, because the map keeps it. This is the tool to open when a Go program allocates more than you expect, and chapter 13 does.

⚠️A chain slice may share memory with its old self Go

append may or may not allocate. When a chain has room, the new entry goes into the existing array, and any other slice that pointed at that array sees it. In del, the shortened slice chain[:len(chain)-1] still points at the same array as before. The slot past the new end still holds a copy of the entry that was moved. Its key and value stay reachable until the next append writes over them. None of this is a bug here. It is the reason that a Go programmer must know what a slice is. A slice is a pointer, a length and a capacity, and not an array.

Rust: the table that drops itself#

In Rust the chain is a Vec<Entry>, and the entry owns its key and value. Dropping the table drops the outer Vec, which drops every chain, which drops every entry, which frees every byte. No function in table.rs frees anything, and nothing leaks. The table is generic too, in two type parameters. The where clause on the impl block is the bound. It says what the table needs from a key, a view of it as bytes to hash and equality to find it. AsRef<[u8]> and PartialEq are traits, which chapter 7 explains. A key type that has both compiles. One that lacks either is refused at the impl, not deep inside a method:

/// FNV-1a, the same hash the C version of kv uses.
fn fnv1a(bytes: &[u8]) -> u64 {
    bytes.iter().fold(0xcbf2_9ce4_8422_2325, |h, &b| {
        (h ^ u64::from(b)).wrapping_mul(0x0100_0000_01b3)
    })
}
rust/ch06/src/table.rs · region hash
/// One key and its value in a chain. The chain is a Vec, which owns its entries, and
/// the entries own their bytes. Dropping the table drops all of it. `K` and `V` are type
/// parameters: the table is written once for any key that can be seen as bytes and
/// compared, and any value at all.
struct Entry<K, V> {
    key: K,
    val: V,
}

/// A hash table with separate chaining. It grows when it holds more entries than
/// buckets, so a chain stays short.
pub struct Table<K, V> {
    buckets: Vec<Vec<Entry<K, V>>>,
    len: usize,
}

/// An empty table, for every `K` and `V`. `derive(Default)` would also demand that `K`
/// and `V` have defaults, which an empty table does not need, so this is written out.
impl<K, V> Default for Table<K, V> {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            buckets: Vec::new(),
            len: 0,
        }
    }
}

/// The bounds say what the table needs from a key: a view of it as bytes, to hash, and
/// equality, to find it. A key type with more is fine; one with less does not compile.
impl<K, V> Table<K, V>
where
    K: AsRef<[u8]> + PartialEq,
{
    fn index(&self, key: &K) -> usize {
        (fnv1a(key.as_ref()) & (self.buckets.len() as u64 - 1)) as usize
    }

    pub fn get(&self, key: &K) -> Option<&V> {
        if self.buckets.is_empty() {
            return None;
        }
        let chain = &self.buckets[self.index(key)];
        chain.iter().find(|e| e.key == *key).map(|e| &e.val)
    }
rust/ch06/src/table.rs · region table

Two shapes in this file have appeared since chapter 4 without a name. The hash is a fold, an iterator method that walks the bytes and carries a value along. get is iter().find(...).map(...), a chain where each call wraps the one before and nothing runs until the end asks for a value. And the |e| e.key == *key inside find is a closure, a function written in place that captures key from the method around it. The C loop with an index, the Go for range and this chain do the same work. Chapter 8 gives iterators and closures a section of their own, because SCAN needs both.

The compiler produces one copy of every method for each pair of types a program uses, which is called monomorphisation. The copy for byte keys and the copy for &str keys share no code at run time. So a generic costs nothing to call and something to compile. The Default block is written out rather than derived. The derive would also demand a default for the key and the value types, which an empty table does not need.

Exercise 06.3RustInsert, and grow when full

Write set. If the buckets are empty, create sixteen. Find the chain by index. If an entry with the key exists, replace its value. Otherwise grow when the table is full, compute the index again, because the length changed, and push a new entry. The compiler will tell you if you hold a borrow of a chain across the call to grow.

pub fn set(&mut self, key: Vec<u8>, val: Vec<u8>) {
    if self.buckets.is_empty() {
        self.buckets.resize_with(16, Vec::new);
    }
    // your code here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
pub fn set(&mut self, key: K, val: V) {
    if self.buckets.is_empty() {
        self.buckets.resize_with(16, Vec::new);
    }
    let i = self.index(&key);
    if let Some(e) = self.buckets[i].iter_mut().find(|e| e.key == key) {
        e.val = val;
        return;
    }
    if self.len >= self.buckets.len() {
        self.grow();
    }
    let i = self.index(&key);
    self.buckets[i].push(Entry { key, val });
    self.len += 1;
}

/// Double the buckets and move every entry to its new chain. The entries are moved,
/// not copied: `drain` takes them out of the old chains.
fn grow(&mut self) {
    let mut buckets: Vec<Vec<Entry<K, V>>> = Vec::new();
    buckets.resize_with(self.buckets.len() * 2, Vec::new);
    let mask = buckets.len() as u64 - 1;
    for chain in &mut self.buckets {
        for e in chain.drain(..) {
            let i = (fnv1a(e.key.as_ref()) & mask) as usize;
            buckets[i].push(e);
        }
    }
    self.buckets = buckets;
}
rust/ch06/src/table.rs · region set

Look at grow. The call chain.drain(..) moves every entry out of the old chain and into the new one. There is no copy of a key or a value, as in C, and the old chains are empty when the loop ends. The last line replaces self.buckets, and the old outer Vec is dropped at that moment, not later. Deleting uses swap_remove, which does what the Go version did and drops the removed entry on the same line:

    pub fn del(&mut self, key: &K) -> bool {
        if self.buckets.is_empty() {
            return false;
        }
        let i = self.index(key);
        let chain = &mut self.buckets[i];
        match chain.iter().position(|e| e.key == *key) {
            Some(j) => {
                // move the last entry into the hole; the removed entry is dropped here
                chain.swap_remove(j);
                self.len -= 1;
                true
            }
            None => false,
        }
    }

    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.len
    }

    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.len == 0
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::Table;
    use std::collections::HashMap;

    /// A small deterministic random number generator, so the test is the same every run.
    fn next(state: &mut u64) -> u64 {
        *state ^= *state << 13;
        *state ^= *state >> 7;
        *state ^= *state << 17;
        *state
    }

    #[test]
    fn agrees_with_hashmap() {
        let mut table: Table<Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>> = Table::default();
        let mut reference: HashMap<Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>> = HashMap::new();
        let mut rng = 0x2545_f491_4f6c_dd1d_u64;
        for step in 0..5000 {
            let key = format!("k{}", next(&mut rng) % 200).into_bytes();
            match next(&mut rng) % 3 {
                0 => {
                    let val = format!("v{step}").into_bytes();
                    table.set(key.clone(), val.clone());
                    reference.insert(key, val);
                }
                1 => {
                    assert_eq!(
                        table.del(&key),
                        reference.remove(&key).is_some(),
                        "step {step}"
                    );
                }
                _ => {
                    assert_eq!(table.get(&key), reference.get(&key));
                }
            }
            assert_eq!(table.len(), reference.len());
        }
    }

    /// The same table with another key type. `&str` is bytes with `as_ref`, and a
    /// `u32` value needs nothing. The compiler made a second copy of every method.
    #[test]
    fn works_with_str_keys_and_integer_values() {
        let mut table: Table<&str, u32> = Table::default();
        for (i, word) in ["one", "two", "three"].iter().enumerate() {
            table.set(word, i as u32);
        }
        assert_eq!(table.get(&"two"), Some(&1));
        assert!(table.del(&"two"));
        assert_eq!(table.len(), 2);
    }

Two owners of one table#

Every value in Rust has one owner, and the table so far has had one. A program sometimes needs two parts to hold one thing, and no part is the owner. The standard library has two types for that in one thread. Rc is a reference count. Cloning an Rc makes a second owner and adds one to the count, and the value is dropped when the count reaches zero. RefCell moves the borrow rules from compile time to run time. borrow and borrow_mut give a shared or a mutable reference, and a second mutable borrow while one is live is a panic. The rule did not go away. It moved to where the compiler could not see it. This is called interior mutability. Cell is the same idea for a small copyable value, with a getter and a setter instead of references. The third test shows all three:

/// Two owners of one table, in one thread. `Rc` counts the owners and frees the table
/// when the last one goes; `RefCell` moves the borrow rules to run time, so each
/// owner can borrow it mutably in turn. A second mutable borrow at the same moment
/// is a panic, not a compile error: the check moved, it did not go away.
#[test]
fn two_owners_with_rc_and_refcell() {
    use std::cell::{Cell, RefCell};
    use std::rc::Rc;

    let shared: Rc<RefCell<Table<&str, u32>>> = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Table::default()));
    let writer = Rc::clone(&shared);
    let reader = Rc::clone(&shared);
    assert_eq!(Rc::strong_count(&shared), 3);

    writer.borrow_mut().set("hits", 1);
    assert_eq!(reader.borrow().get(&"hits"), Some(&1));
    drop(writer);
    assert_eq!(Rc::strong_count(&shared), 2);

    // Cell is the same idea for a Copy value: change it through a shared reference
    let counter = Cell::new(0);
    let bump = |c: &Cell<u32>| c.set(c.get() + 1);
    bump(&counter);
    bump(&counter);
    assert_eq!(counter.get(), 2);

    // the run-time check: a borrow_mut while a borrow is live
    let guard = shared.borrow();
    assert!(shared.try_borrow_mut().is_err());
    drop(guard);
    assert!(shared.try_borrow_mut().is_ok());
}
rust/ch06/src/table.rs · region shared

Both types refuse to cross a thread. Chapter 9 replaces them with Arc and Mutex, which are the same two ideas with a lock. A chain written as a linked list, the way the C table does it, would need one more type, Box. A struct cannot contain itself without a pointer, and chapter 8 writes one.

As in Go, the server keeps the standard HashMap. The standard map uses a hash called SipHash 1-3, which the documentation describes as "selected to provide resistance against HashDoS attacks". An attacker who knows the hash function can send thousands of keys that land in one bucket. Every lookup of such a key then walks that one chain, which holds every key the attacker sent. FNV-1a has no defence against that. Redis uses SipHash too, and seeds it with random bytes at startup, for the same reason.

📰Hash flooding, 2011

On 28 December 2011 one HTTP request could hold a web server at full CPU for hours. Alexander Klink and Julian Wälde showed where the hole was. Nearly every web platform kept its form parameters in a hash table with a known hash and no secret. A POST with tens of thousands of parameter names chosen to collide turned every insert into a walk of one long chain. The advisory listed Java, PHP, Python, Ruby, the V8 JavaScript engine and the servers built on them. The fix across the industry was a hash with a secret seed, and SipHash was designed in 2012 for that purpose. Your FNV-1a table has exactly this hole. The standard maps of Go and Rust, and Redis, do not.

⚠️The dead code warning is a feature Rust

A module nobody calls produces a warning for every function in it. The binary never calls Table, so the compiler reports each method as dead code, and the book's clippy -D warnings turns that into an error. The file opens with #![allow(dead_code)] and a comment that says why. In C, an unused function that is not static compiles in silence, because the compiler cannot know whether another file calls it. A static one gets a warning under -Wall, which the book's -Werror turns into an error.

Memory, three ways#

The chapter touched memory in every function. The table shows what each language asked of you.

The questionCGoRust
Who frees an entryyou, in three places that must agreethe collector, when nothing refers to itthe owner, at the end of its scope
Forgetting to freea leak that grows until the process diesimpossible for unreachable memoryimpossible, the compiler inserts the drop
Freeing twiceundefined behaviour, often a security holeimpossibledoes not compile
Using after freeundefined behaviour, often a security holeimpossible, the reference keeps it alivedoes not compile
Keeping a pointer across a moveyour responsibility, and grow relies on itsafe, the entry is reachable from the new slicechecked, and set recomputes the index after grow
The costyour attentionmemory held until the next collection, and a pausethe time to satisfy the borrow checker

The C table is about 140 lines, and about a third of them exist to allocate, check and free. The Go table is 75 lines with none of that. The price is a collector that runs in the background and holds freed memory until it does. The Rust table is also 75 lines, and it frees memory at the moment the C one does. The price is a compiler that refused several early drafts of set. Each table is the right answer for its language, and the differences between them are the differences between the languages.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
Writing the tableWeakStrongOKC needs an owner comment on every pointer and three cleanup paths, Go is the shortest, and Rust argues about borrows in set.
Freeing memoryWeakStrongStrongC must free in three places that agree. Go and Rust free for you, in different ways.
Freeing on timeStrongWeakStrongC and Rust free on the line that removes an entry. Go frees at the next collection.
Testing itWeakStrongStrongC has no test runner in the box. go test and cargo test are built in.
Shipping unused codeWeakOKStrongC warns only for static functions and Go ignores unused functions, while Rust reports each one.
Needing to write oneStrongWeakWeakIn C the table is the store. In Go and Rust it is an exercise, because the map is built in.
Writing it once for any typeWeakOKStrongC has void pointers, macros and _Generic, each with a hole. Go has type parameters since 2022, and Rust has bounds the compiler checks at the impl.
Seeing where a value livesStrongOKStrongC says it in every line, and Rust says it in the types. Go decides for you and shows its decision with a flag.
Carry forward
  • Storage duration. A C value lives on the stack to the end of its block, in static memory for the run, or on the heap until freed.
  • Type parameter. A table written once for any key and value, with a bound that says what the type must support.
  • Rc and RefCell. Two owners of one value in one thread, with the borrow rules checked at run time instead of compile time.

Modules, packages and dependencies#

Building kv · Chapter 07· 33 min read· 500 lines of code
▶Scene

The chapter 6 file is 868 lines. Cut it the obvious way, by moving the hash table into store.c as it stands, and compile the two files together:

$ wc -l kv.c

$ cc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -o kv kv.c store.c
kv.c:357:44: error: unknown type name 'kv_store'

Twenty-five errors. Every function that uses the store has lost the word kv_store. The file that defines it is now a different file, and C compiles one file at a time. The cut needs a third file, which says what the second one offers.

kv is nearly nine hundred lines in one file, and the next chapters double it. This chapter splits the server into parts, in each language's own way. C gets header files and a Makefile that knows about them. Go gets packages under internal. Rust gets a library crate with a thin binary. It also covers dependencies, and the tools that keep code in one style.

The server does not change in this chapter. Every test from chapter 6 still passes, and no command is added. What changes is where the code lives, how one part sees another, and how a reader finds anything. That sounds like housekeeping. It is also where the three languages differ most in their daily feel. A module system is what you touch every time you open a file.

The unitCGoRust

📜Why Go has a compatibility promise and Rust has editions

A module system is a promise about what stays the same. Go 1 was released in 2012 with a written promise. Programs written to the Go 1 specification "will continue to compile and run correctly, unchanged, over the lifetime of that specification". Fourteen years later the promise holds, and a Go package from 2012 is meant to still build. Rust made a different promise. The language can change in ways that would break old code, but only in a new edition. A crate names its edition in Cargo.toml. The 2024 edition shipped with Rust 1.85 in February 2025. A crate on the 2015 edition still builds with today's compiler, next to one on the 2024 edition, in the same program. C made no promise at all, and relies on the fact that no compiler vendor dares to break the code that already exists.

C: headers, static, and a Makefile that knows about both#

C has no modules. It has files, and a convention. A module is a .c file that holds the code and a .h file that holds the declarations other files may use. The buffer from chapter 4 becomes two files. The header is the public part:

#ifndef KV_BUF_H
#define KV_BUF_H

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>

/* A growable byte buffer. It owns data, and kv_buf_free releases it. Start one with
 * kv_buf b = {0}. */
typedef struct {
    char *data; /* owned; NULL until the first append */
    size_t len;
    size_t cap;
} kv_buf;

bool kv_buf_append(kv_buf *b, const void *src, size_t n);
void kv_buf_consume(kv_buf *b, size_t n);
void kv_buf_free(kv_buf *b);

#endif
c/ch07/src/buf.h

Three conventions are at work. The first lines and the last line are a header guard. The preprocessor copies a header into every file that includes it. A file that includes buf.h twice, once directly and once through resp.h, would see the typedef twice. The guard makes the second copy empty. The second convention is the prefix. C has one namespace for the whole program. So every public name in kv begins with kv_, and a name from another library cannot collide with it. The third is that the header says what the caller must do, in comments, because nothing else will. The .c file holds the rest, and marks the one function that only it uses as static:

/* Private: only this file calls it, so it is static and not in the header. */
static bool kv_buf_reserve(kv_buf *b, size_t extra) {
    if (b->len + extra <= b->cap) {
        return true;
    }
    size_t cap = b->cap ? b->cap * 2 : 1024;
    while (cap < b->len + extra) {
        cap *= 2;
    }
    char *p = realloc(b->data, cap);
    if (p == NULL) {
        return false; /* the old block is still valid and still ours */
    }
    b->data = p;
    b->cap = cap;
    return true;
}
c/ch07/src/buf.c · region static

A static function is invisible outside its file. That is the whole of information hiding in C. There is no private keyword and no module boundary, only a function the linker never hears about. Every file in src/ follows the same shape. The header of the store is the most useful one to read. It says who owns every pointer, and how long a pointer from kv_store_find stays valid:

#include <stdint.h>

/* The keys and values, in a hash table with separate chaining. */

/* One key and its value, in a chain of entries that share a bucket. The key, the value
 * and the next entry are owned. */
typedef struct kv_entry {
    char *key;
    size_t klen;
    char *val;
    size_t vlen;
    struct kv_entry *next;
} kv_entry;

/* How the table treats a key: a struct of function pointers, which is how C describes
 * behaviour a caller may choose. A store is made with one of the types below, and every
 * hash and comparison inside it goes through that type. Redis calls the same thing a
 * dictType. */
typedef struct {
    const char *name;
    uint64_t (*hash)(const char *key, size_t klen, uint64_t seed);
    bool (*eq)(const char *a, size_t alen, const char *b, size_t blen);
    bool seeded; /* kv_store_new draws a random seed, so keys cannot be chosen to collide */
} kv_store_type;

extern const kv_store_type kv_fnv_type;    /* FNV-1a, the same hash on every run */
extern const kv_store_type kv_seeded_type; /* FNV-1a mixed with a seed drawn at start */

/* The store itself is opaque: this header says it exists, store.c says what is in it.
 * Other files hold a pointer and call the functions below, and cannot reach inside. */
typedef struct kv_store kv_store;

/* A new, empty store of the given type, or NULL when out of memory. Free it with
 * kv_store_free, which also frees every entry. */
kv_store *kv_store_new(const kv_store_type *type);
void kv_store_free(kv_store *s);

size_t kv_store_len(const kv_store *s);

/* The entry for key, or NULL. The pointer is valid until the next set or del. */
kv_entry *kv_store_find(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen);

/* Store a copy of val under a copy of key, replacing any old value. */
bool kv_store_set(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen, const char *val, size_t vlen);
bool kv_store_del(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen);

/* Call fn once for every entry, with ctx passed through, until fn returns false. The
 * callback must not set or del: the chain it is walking would move under it. */
void kv_store_each(kv_store *s, bool (*fn)(kv_entry *e, void *ctx), void *ctx);

#endif
