An opaque type, and a struct of functions#

The header above still shows the fields of kv_store. So any file that includes it can reach inside and walk the buckets, as KEYS did in chapter 6. The second half of the header takes that away. It declares the struct without defining it, and store.c holds the definition. Every other file has a pointer to something it cannot look inside. That is called an opaque type, and it is the strongest form of hiding C has. FILE from stdio.h is the one you have used all along:

/* The store itself is opaque: this header says it exists, store.c says what is in it.
 * Other files hold a pointer and call the functions below, and cannot reach inside. */
typedef struct kv_store kv_store;

/* A new, empty store of the given type, or NULL when out of memory. Free it with
 * kv_store_free, which also frees every entry. */
kv_store *kv_store_new(const kv_store_type *type);
void kv_store_free(kv_store *s);

size_t kv_store_len(const kv_store *s);

/* The entry for key, or NULL. The pointer is valid until the next set or del. */
kv_entry *kv_store_find(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen);

/* Store a copy of val under a copy of key, replacing any old value. */
bool kv_store_set(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen, const char *val, size_t vlen);
bool kv_store_del(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen);

/* Call fn once for every entry, with ctx passed through, until fn returns false. The
 * callback must not set or del: the chain it is walking would move under it. */
void kv_store_each(kv_store *s, bool (*fn)(kv_entry *e, void *ctx), void *ctx);
c/ch07/src/store.h · region opaque

Because nobody outside can walk the table, the table walks itself. kv_store_each takes a function pointer and a void *, and calls the function once per entry with that pointer passed back. The void * is the context, whatever the caller needs the callback to see. The callback casts it back to the real type on its first line. This pair, a function pointer and a context pointer, is how C passes a closure, and KEYS now uses it:

void kv_store_each(kv_store *s, bool (*fn)(kv_entry *e, void *ctx), void *ctx) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < s->cap; i++) {
        for (kv_entry *e = s->buckets[i]; e != NULL; e = e->next) {
            if (!fn(e, ctx)) {
                return;
            }
        }
    }
}
c/ch07/src/store.c · region each
/* What the KEYS walk needs to know, passed to the callback through a void pointer. */
typedef struct {
    const char *pat;
    size_t plen;
    kv_buf keys; /* the matching keys, as replies, collected before the count is known */
    size_t n;
    bool ok;
} kv_keys_ctx;

/* Called once per entry by kv_store_each. The context comes back as a void pointer, and
 * the first line turns it into the real type again. */
static bool kv_keys_visit(kv_entry *e, void *ctx) {
    kv_keys_ctx *k = ctx;
    if (!kv_glob(k->pat, k->plen, e->key, e->klen)) {
        return true;
    }
    if (!kv_reply_bulk(&k->keys, e->key, e->klen)) {
        k->ok = false;
        return false; /* stop the walk */
    }
    k->n++;
    return true;
}

/* KEYS pattern: every matching key, as an array. The walk is the store's; this file only
 * supplies what to do with each entry. */
static bool kv_cmd_keys(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_keys_ctx k = {c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], {0}, 0, true};
    kv_store_each(s, kv_keys_visit, &k);
    bool ok = k.ok && kv_reply_array(out, k.n) && kv_buf_append(out, k.keys.data, k.keys.len);
    kv_buf_free(&k.keys);
    return ok;
}
c/ch07/src/cmd.c · region keys

The header also lets a caller choose how the table treats a key. A kv_store_type is a struct whose fields are function pointers, one for the hash and one for equality, and a store is made with one. Inside store.c every hash is s->type->hash(...), a call through a pointer, so the table never names a hash function. This is the C form of an interface, and Redis builds its dictionary on exactly this struct, which it calls dictType:

/* How the table treats a key: a struct of function pointers, which is how C describes
 * behaviour a caller may choose. A store is made with one of the types below, and every
 * hash and comparison inside it goes through that type. Redis calls the same thing a
 * dictType. */
typedef struct {
    const char *name;
    uint64_t (*hash)(const char *key, size_t klen, uint64_t seed);
    bool (*eq)(const char *a, size_t alen, const char *b, size_t blen);
    bool seeded; /* kv_store_new draws a random seed, so keys cannot be chosen to collide */
} kv_store_type;

extern const kv_store_type kv_fnv_type;    /* FNV-1a, the same hash on every run */
extern const kv_store_type kv_seeded_type; /* FNV-1a mixed with a seed drawn at start */
c/ch07/src/store.h · region type
/* FNV-1a: a small, fast hash of bytes. The seed is mixed into the starting value, so a
 * seeded store hashes the same key differently on every run. */
static uint64_t kv_fnv1a(const char *s, size_t n, uint64_t seed) {
    uint64_t h = 14695981039346656037ULL ^ seed;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        h ^= (unsigned char)s[i];
        h *= 1099511628211ULL;
    }
    return h;
}

const kv_store_type kv_fnv_type = {"fnv", kv_fnv1a, kv_bytes_eq, false};
const kv_store_type kv_seeded_type = {"seeded", kv_fnv1a, kv_bytes_eq, true};

/* Eight random bytes from the operating system, or the clock when that fails. */
static uint64_t kv_random_seed(void) {
    uint64_t seed = 0;
    FILE *f = fopen("/dev/urandom", "rb");
    if (f != NULL) {
        size_t got = fread(&seed, sizeof seed, 1, f);
        fclose(f);
        if (got == 1) {
            return seed;
        }
    }
    return (uint64_t)(uintptr_t)&seed * 2654435761ULL;
}
c/ch07/src/store.c · region types

The two types here differ in one field. The seeded one mixes eight random bytes into the hash when the store is made. So the chain an attacker's keys land in cannot be predicted. That is the fix for the hash flooding of chapter 6, and the server uses it by default. KV_HASH=fnv picks the plain one, for a run that must be repeatable. kv_store_new is where the choice is applied:

kv_store *kv_store_new(const kv_store_type *type) {
    kv_store *s = calloc(1, sizeof *s);
    if (s == NULL) {
        return NULL;
    }
    s->type = type;
    s->seed = type->seeded ? kv_random_seed() : 0;
    return s;
}

size_t kv_store_len(const kv_store *s) {
    return s->len;
}

 * seeds the hash, so that nobody can choose keys that all land in one chain. */

const kv_store_type *type = hash && strcmp(hash, "fnv") == 0 ? &kv_fnv_type : &kv_seeded_type;

With six source files, the Makefile from chapter 2 is not enough. The one below finds every .c file, compiles each into an object file under build/, and links them. The -MMD flag asks the compiler to write a small file beside each object that lists the headers it included. make reads those files, so a change to store.h rebuilds exactly the files that include it:

CC       ?= cc
CFLAGS   ?= -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -g
SANITIZE ?=

# every .c under src/ becomes a .o under build/, and kv is linked from all of them
SRC := $(wildcard src/*.c)
OBJ := $(SRC:src/%.c=build/%.o)

kv: $(OBJ)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SANITIZE) -o $@ $(OBJ)

# -MMD writes a .d file beside each .o that lists the headers it included, so that a
# change to a header rebuilds exactly the files that use it
build/%.o: src/%.c | build
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SANITIZE) -MMD -c -o $@ $<

build:
	mkdir -p build

-include $(OBJ:.o=.d)

clean:
	rm -rf kv kv.dSYM build

.PHONY: clean
c/ch07/Makefile
⚠️A header without a guard C

Include a header twice and the compiler reports a redefinition. main.c includes buf.h directly and again through cmd.h. Without the guard the second copy defines kv_buf a second time, and the error names the header, not the file that included it twice. Every header gets a guard on the day it is created. Many compilers accept #pragma once as a shorter form, and it is not in the standard.

✅Include your own header first C

A .c file includes its own header before any other, as buf.c does. Suppose the header forgot an include it needs, such as stddef.h for size_t. The mistake then shows in the file that owns the header. It does not hide in another file that included things in a luckier order.

Dependencies in C: the package manager that is not there#

C has no package manager, and that sentence has to be said carefully, because it has several. The operating system has one. A C program that needs a library usually says apt install libssl-dev or brew install openssl. Then it asks a tool called pkg-config where the headers went. The second way is to copy the source into your own tree, which is called vendoring. Redis does this. Its deps/ folder holds its own copies of the libraries it needs, and they build with the rest. The third way is a package manager that is not part of the language, such as vcpkg. Microsoft describes vcpkg as "a free and open-source C/C++ package manager maintained by Microsoft and the C++ community". Conan is another. It works with CMake, Make and MSBuild. Both are used. There is no default.

Each way has a cost. A system package is whatever version the operating system has. A vendored copy must be updated yourself. A third-party manager is one more thing to install before the build works. The server kv has no dependency. That is not unusual for a C program, and it is one reason C programs so often write things themselves.

Go: a folder is a package, and a capital letter is an export#

A Go package is a folder. Every file in the folder begins with the same package line and sees everything in the other files. Another package sees only the names that begin with a capital letter. The spec puts it in one sentence. An identifier is exported if "the first character of the identifier's name is a Unicode uppercase letter". There is no keyword. The protocol code moves to internal/resp, and readCommand becomes ReadCommand:

// ReadCommand reads one request: an array of bulk strings, or one inline line of words.
// It returns io.EOF when the client closed the connection between commands.
func ReadCommand(r *bufio.Reader) ([][]byte, error) {
	line, err := readLine(r)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("read command: %w", err)
	}
	if len(line) == 0 || line[0] != '*' {
		return bytes.Fields(line), nil
	}
	n, err := strconv.Atoi(string(line[1:]))
	if err != nil || n < 0 || n > maxArgs {
		return nil, protoErr('*')
	}
	args := make([][]byte, 0, n)
	for range n {
		line, err := readLine(r)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("read argument: %w", unexpected(err))
		}
		if len(line) == 0 || line[0] != '$' {
			return nil, protoErr(first(line))
		}
		size, err := strconv.Atoi(string(line[1:]))
		if err != nil || size < 0 || size > maxBulk {
			return nil, protoErr('$')
		}
		buf := make([]byte, size+2)
		if _, err := io.ReadFull(r, buf); err != nil {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("read argument: %w", unexpected(err))
		}
		if buf[size] != '\r' || buf[size+1] != '\n' {
			return nil, protoErr(buf[size])
		}
		args = append(args, buf[:size])
	}
	return args, nil
}
go/ch07/internal/resp/resp.go · region exported

The folder is named internal on purpose. The Go 1.4 release notes state the rule. A package with internal in its path "can be imported only by code in the directory tree rooted at" the parent of that folder. So kv/internal/store can be used by kv/cmd/kv and by nobody outside the module. The rule is in the go tool, not in the language, and it is how a Go program says "this is not an API". The import path begins with the module path from go.mod:

// above are this module's own packages: kv is the module path from go.mod.
func Execute(args [][]byte, s Storer, w *bufio.Writer) error {
go/ch07/internal/cmd/cmd.go · region imports

The store exports a type and its methods, and keeps the map itself private, so that no other package can reach into it:

// Store keeps every key and its value in a map. Exported, so that package cmd can use
// it; its field is not, so that only this package can touch the map.
type Store struct {
	m map[string][]byte
}

func New() *Store {
	return &Store{m: make(map[string][]byte)}
}

func (s *Store) Get(key []byte) ([]byte, bool) {
	v, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	return v, ok
}

func (s *Store) Set(key, val []byte) {
	s.m[string(key)] = val
}

func (s *Store) Del(key []byte) bool {
	_, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	delete(s.m, string(key))
	return ok
}

func (s *Store) Len() int {
	return len(s.m)
}

// Keys returns every key that matches the pattern, in no particular order.
func (s *Store) Keys(pattern []byte) [][]byte {
	var out [][]byte
	for k := range s.m {
		if glob(pattern, []byte(k)) {
			out = append(out, []byte(k))
		}
	}
	return out
}
go/ch07/internal/store/store.go · region exported

An interface is a set of methods#

The commands do not need the map. They need six methods, and an interface is a type that lists methods and nothing else. Any type that has those methods satisfies the interface, with no declaration that says so. The interface lives in the cmd package, next to the code that calls it. Go puts an interface on the side that uses it. The package that implements it never hears of it:

// A Storer is whatever the commands need from a store: these six methods, and nothing
// about how they are done. Any type with these methods is a Storer, without saying so.
// The interface lives here, with the code that uses it, which is where Go puts one.
type Storer interface {
	Get(key []byte) ([]byte, bool)
	Set(key, val []byte)
	Del(key []byte) bool
	Len() int
	Keys(pattern []byte) [][]byte
	Incr(key []byte) (int64, error)
}
go/ch07/internal/cmd/cmd.go · region storer

Two types satisfy it. *store.Store is the map. *store.ByteTable is the table from chapter 6, wrapped so that its methods have the right shapes. Nothing in the file names cmd.Storer, and it could not, because store is imported by cmd and a Go import cannot go both ways:

// ByteTable is the hand-written table from chapter 6, used as a store. It has the same
// methods as Store, so it satisfies the cmd.Storer interface without naming it. Nothing
// here says "implements": the methods are the whole of the contract.
type ByteTable struct {
	t *Table[string, []byte]
}

func NewByteTable() *ByteTable {
	return &ByteTable{t: NewTable[string, []byte](func(s string) uint64 { return fnv1a([]byte(s)) })}
}

func (b *ByteTable) Get(key []byte) ([]byte, bool) { return b.t.Get(string(key)) }
func (b *ByteTable) Set(key, val []byte)           { b.t.Set(string(key), val) }
func (b *ByteTable) Del(key []byte) bool           { return b.t.Del(string(key)) }
func (b *ByteTable) Len() int                      { return b.t.Len() }

func (b *ByteTable) Keys(pattern []byte) [][]byte {
	var out [][]byte
	for _, k := range b.t.Keys() {
		if glob(pattern, []byte(k)) {
			out = append(out, []byte(k))
		}
	}
	return out
}

func (b *ByteTable) Incr(key []byte) (int64, error) {
	var n int64
	if cur, ok := b.Get(key); ok {
		var err error
		n, err = strconv.ParseInt(string(cur), 10, 64)
		if err != nil {
			return 0, ErrNotInteger
		}
	}
	if n == math.MaxInt64 {
		return 0, ErrOverflow
	}
	n++
	b.Set(key, []byte(strconv.FormatInt(n, 10)))
	return n, nil
}

// value inside it is whichever the environment asked for.
var s cmd.Storer = store.New()
if os.Getenv("KV_STORE") == "table" {

This is why io.Copy in chapter 3 could copy a socket, a file or a buffer with one function. It is why error in chapter 4 was a type with one method. The small interfaces of the standard library are the ones most code accepts, such as io.Reader, io.Writer and error. A type that has a Read method joins them without asking.

Embedding, and the nil that is not nil#

A struct may hold a field with no name, only a type, which is called embedding. The methods of the embedded type are promoted to the outer struct, so a wrapper can replace one method and inherit the rest. The test below wraps any Storer and counts the writes:

// counting wraps any Storer and counts the writes. The embedded field lends the wrapped
// store's methods to counting, so only Set is written here: the rest are promoted.
type counting struct {
	Storer
	sets int
}

func (c *counting) Set(key, val []byte) {
	c.sets++
	c.Storer.Set(key, val)
}

func TestEmbeddedStorerPromotesMethods(t *testing.T) {
	c := &counting{Storer: store.New()}
	var buf bytes.Buffer
	w := bufio.NewWriter(&buf)
	for _, line := range [][]string{{"SET", "a", "1"}, {"SET", "b", "2"}, {"GET", "a"}} {
		var args [][]byte
		for _, s := range line {
			args = append(args, []byte(s))
		}
		if err := Execute(args, c, w); err != nil {
			t.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
	w.Flush()
	if c.sets != 2 || c.Len() != 2 || !bytes.Contains(buf.Bytes(), []byte("$1\r\n1\r\n")) {
		t.Fatalf("sets %d, len %d, out %q", c.sets, c.Len(), buf.String())
	}
}
go/ch07/internal/cmd/cmd_test.go · region embed

An interface value is two words, a type and a pointer. That shape has a trap, and the second test walks into it on purpose:

// A nil pointer inside an interface is not a nil interface. The interface holds a type
// and a pointer; the type is set, so the interface is not nil, and a method call reaches
// the pointer receiver with nil. This is the trap every Go programmer meets once.
func TestNilPointerInInterfaceIsNotNil(t *testing.T) {
	var p *store.Store // nil
	var s Storer = p   // a Storer holding (*store.Store, nil)
	if s == nil {
		t.Fatal("an interface holding a typed nil compares unequal to nil")
	}
	var none Storer // no type, no value
	if none != nil {
		t.Fatal("an interface with no type is nil")
	}
}
go/ch07/internal/cmd/cmd_test.go · region nil
⚠️A typed nil in an interface is not nil Go

A function that returns an interface, and returns a nil pointer of a concrete type, returns something that is not nil. The caller's if err != nil is true, and the method call inside it runs on a nil receiver. The rule is to return the literal nil, never a nil pointer, from a function whose result type is an interface. The test above is the whole explanation, and most Go programmers learn it from a crash.

✅Accept interfaces, return structs, and define one late Go

A function that takes an argument asks for the smallest interface that has what it needs. That is why io.Copy takes a Reader and not a file. A function that returns a value returns the concrete type, so the caller has every method. And an interface is defined when the second implementation exists, not before. One implementation is a struct.

Stuck?Show the full listing
func TestGlob(t *testing.T) {
	cases := []struct {
		pat, key string
		want     bool
	}{
		{"*", "", true},
		{"*", "anything", true},
		{"user:*", "user:1", true},
		{"user:*", "order:1", false},
		{"us?r:1", "user:1", true},
		{"us?r:1", "usr:1", false},
		{"*:2", "user:2", true},
		{"a*b*c", "aXXbYYc", true},
		{"a*b*c", "aXXbYY", false},
	}
	for _, c := range cases {
		if got := glob([]byte(c.pat), []byte(c.key)); got != c.want {
			t.Errorf("glob(%q, %q) = %v, want %v", c.pat, c.key, got, c.want)
		}
	}
}

$ go build -o kv ./cmd/kv
$ go test ./...
?   	kv/cmd/kv	[no test files]
?   	kv/internal/cmd	[no test files]
?   	kv/internal/resp	[no test files]
ok  	kv/internal/store	0.020s

kv still has no dependency, and Go makes that a normal state. The standard library has the network, the buffered reader, the map and the test runner, and most Go programs of this size use nothing else. When a dependency is needed, go get adds a line to go.mod and a hash to go.sum. The hash is checked on every later download, against the file and against a public log that Google runs. So a changed upload cannot replace what you tested. There is no central registry. A module path is a URL, and the go tool fetches through a proxy that caches every version it has seen.

⚠️An import you do not use is an error Go

Delete the last use of a package and the build fails. The error is "strings" imported and not used. Go does this on purpose, so that a dependency graph never holds a package that nothing needs, and the build stays fast. Editors remove the line for you, and new Go programmers curse it for a week.

Rust: a module is a file you must announce#

kv already had modules in Rust. Chapter 4 wrote mod resp; and mod cmd;, and each line told the compiler to read a file of that name. The new step is to put the modules in a library. Then a test or a benchmark can use the parser and the store without starting a server. A crate with both src/lib.rs and src/main.rs builds a library and a binary of the same name:

pub mod cmd;
pub mod resp;
pub mod store;
pub mod table;
rust/ch07/src/lib.rs · region mods

The pub on each mod line makes the module visible outside the library, and the pub on each function inside makes the function visible. Without either, the item is private to the file. The binary uses the library through its name:

use kv::store::{MapStore, Store};
use kv::table::Table;

A trait is a promise of methods#

The Rust store is now a trait, a set of methods a type promises, and two types keep the promise. Unlike a Go interface, the promise is written down. A type says impl Store for MapStore and lists the methods, and the compiler checks that none is missing and none has the wrong shape:

/// What the commands need from a store. A trait is a set of methods a type promises, and
/// any type that writes an `impl Store for` block with these methods is a store. The
/// server is written against the trait, so the type behind it can change.
pub trait Store {
    /// A borrowed view of the value, which lives as long as the borrow of the store.
    fn get(&self, key: &[u8]) -> Option<&[u8]>;
    fn set(&mut self, key: Vec<u8>, val: Vec<u8>);
    fn del(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> bool;
    fn len(&self) -> usize;
    /// Every key that matches the pattern, in no particular order.
    fn keys(&self, pattern: &[u8]) -> Vec<&[u8]>;

    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.len() == 0
    }

    /// Add one to the integer stored under key, which counts as 0 when absent. A default
    /// method: written once here, in terms of `get` and `set`, and shared by every
    /// implementation unless one replaces it.
    fn incr(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> Result<i64, IncrError> {
        let n = match self.get(key) {
            None => 0,
            Some(bytes) => parse_int(bytes).ok_or(IncrError::NotInteger)?,
        };
        let n = n.checked_add(1).ok_or(IncrError::Overflow)?;
        self.set(key.to_vec(), n.to_string().into_bytes());
        Ok(n)
    }
}
rust/ch07/src/store.rs · region trait

Two of the methods have bodies in the trait. is_empty and incr are default methods, written once in terms of the others and shared by every implementation unless one replaces them. The map store implements the five that remain:

/// The store the server uses: the standard HashMap. The hand-written table in table.rs
/// implements the same trait, and `KV_STORE=table` runs the server on it.
#[derive(Default)]
pub struct MapStore {
    map: HashMap<Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>>,
}

impl MapStore {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self::default()
    }
}

impl Store for MapStore {
    fn get(&self, key: &[u8]) -> Option<&[u8]> {
        self.map.get(key).map(Vec::as_slice)
    }

    fn set(&mut self, key: Vec<u8>, val: Vec<u8>) {
        self.map.insert(key, val);
    }

    fn del(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> bool {
        self.map.remove(key).is_some()
    }

    fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.map.len()
    }

    fn keys(&self, pattern: &[u8]) -> Vec<&[u8]> {
        self.map
            .keys()
            .map(Vec::as_slice)
            .filter(|k| glob(pattern, k))
            .collect()
    }
}
rust/ch07/src/store.rs · region store

The table from chapter 6 implements the same five. The block lives in table.rs, next to the type. It could as well live next to the trait, because Rust allows an impl wherever the crate owns the trait or the type. That is the orphan rule. A crate may implement its own trait for any type, or any trait for its own type. It may never implement a foreign trait for a foreign type, so two crates cannot disagree about what Display means for Vec:

/// The hand-written table as a store: the same trait as MapStore, so the server can run
/// on either. The methods are those of the trait; the body of each is one line.
impl crate::store::Store for Table<Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>> {
    fn get(&self, key: &[u8]) -> Option<&[u8]> {
        Table::get(self, &key.to_vec()).map(Vec::as_slice)
    }

    fn set(&mut self, key: Vec<u8>, val: Vec<u8>) {
        Table::set(self, key, val);
    }

    fn del(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> bool {
        Table::del(self, &key.to_vec())
    }

    fn len(&self) -> usize {
        Table::len(self)
    }

    fn keys(&self, pattern: &[u8]) -> Vec<&[u8]> {
        self.buckets
            .iter()
            .flatten()
            .map(|e| e.key.as_slice())
            .filter(|k| crate::store::glob(pattern, k))
            .collect()
    }
}
rust/ch07/src/table.rs · region impl-store

Static and dynamic dispatch#

There are two ways to call a method of a trait, and kv uses both. The main function builds a Box<dyn Store>, a box holding whichever type the environment asked for. dyn Store is a trait object. A pointer to one carries a second pointer to a table of the type's methods. Every call looks the method up in that table at run time:

// Either type implements Store. A Box<dyn Store> holds whichever one the environment
// asked for, and every call through it is decided at run time.
let mut store: Box<dyn Store> = match std::env::var("KV_STORE").as_deref() {
    Ok("table") => Box::new(Table::default()),
    _ => Box::new(MapStore::new()),
};
rust/ch07/src/main.rs · region choose

The test in store.rs takes the other road. fn behaves_like_a_store<S: Store> is generic with a bound, and the compiler writes one copy of it per type it is called with. Each copy calls the methods directly, which is static dispatch, the same mechanism as the generic table of chapter 6. impl Store in an argument position is the short spelling of the same bound:

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::{MapStore, Store};
    use crate::table::Table;

    /// One test for every store. `S: Store` is a bound, and the compiler writes a copy of
    /// this function for each type it is called with: static dispatch, no trait object.
    fn behaves_like_a_store<S: Store>(mut store: S) {
        assert!(store.is_empty());
        store.set(b"a".to_vec(), b"1".to_vec());
        assert_eq!(store.get(b"a"), Some(&b"1"[..]));
        assert_eq!(store.incr(b"a"), Ok(2));
        assert_eq!(store.keys(b"*").len(), 1);
        assert!(store.del(b"a"));
        assert!(store.get(b"a").is_none());
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_map_store_is_a_store() {
        behaves_like_a_store(MapStore::new());
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_table_is_a_store() {
        behaves_like_a_store(Table::<Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>>::default());
    }
}
rust/ch07/src/store.rs · region test

The handlers of chapter 5 took &mut dyn Write for the reason that appears again here. A table of function pointers holds one function, so the function must work for any writer at run time. The helpers in resp take impl Write + ?Sized, which is the generic form. The ?Sized is a note that the type may be a trait object, whose size the compiler does not know. One rule limits which traits can be objects. A trait with a generic method cannot be a dyn. The same holds for a method that returns Self. The method table could not hold either. Store has no such method, so it can.

One more word of visibility appeared in this chapter. parse_int is pub(crate), which every module in the crate may use and no user of the library can see. Between private and pub, it is the one that most helpers want.

A dependency in Rust is a line in Cargo.toml, which cargo add writes for you, and a crate on crates.io, which is the one registry. The Cargo book draws the line between the two files in one sentence each. "Cargo.toml is about describing your dependencies in a broad sense, and is written by you." "Cargo.lock contains exact information about your dependencies. It is maintained by Cargo and should not be manually edited." The first dependency of kv arrives in chapter 9. That is when the lock file appears. Two more Cargo words will come up before then. A feature is a named switch in Cargo.toml that turns part of a crate on. The code behind it is marked with a cfg attribute that names the feature. tokio in chapter 9 is built from features. Few programs need all of it. A workspace is a folder of crates that share one Cargo.lock and one target directory, for a project with a library and several binaries. Go has the same two ideas under other names. A build tag is a feature, and a go.work file is a workspace. Chapter 14 uses a workspace when a module must build with a local copy of another.

⚠️A file is not a module until something declares it Rust

Add src/glob.rs and nothing happens. The compiler reads only the files that a mod line names, starting from lib.rs or main.rs. A forgotten mod line produces an error about an unresolved name somewhere else, and the file that holds the name is never mentioned. Go reads every file in the folder. C reads only what the Makefile lists. Rust reads what the tree of mod declarations reaches.

Three answers to "where does code come from"#

Set the three languages side by side and the pattern of the book repeats. C has a convention where the other two have a tool, and the convention has several competing forms. Go has one tool with no registry, which fits a company that hosts its own code. Rust has one tool with one registry, which fits a community that shares small crates. The number of dependencies a program of this size has in practice follows from that. A C program has few, because each one is work. A Go program has few, because the standard library is wide. A Rust program often has dozens, because adding one is a single command, and that is the weakness of the strongest answer. Chapter 14 shows what every dependency costs at the border, and chapter 15 what a C one costs.

One style, enforced by a tool#

All three languages now have a formatter, and the difference is who decides the style. clang-format takes a configuration file, and the one for kv is four settings:

# The layout every C file in kv keeps. clang-format -i src/*.c src/*.h applies it.
BasedOnStyle: LLVM
IndentWidth: 4
ColumnLimit: 100
AllowShortFunctionsOnASingleLine: Inline
c/ch07/.clang-format

It comes with clang, so it is installed on macOS with Xcode and on Linux as a package. A project that uses it must agree on the configuration first. gofmt has no configuration. The Go team decided the style when the language was released. The result is that every Go file anyone has ever read looks the same. rustfmt is between clang-format and gofmt. It has a configuration file, rustfmt.toml, and almost nobody writes one. The book runs all three formatters in make verify. A file that is not formatted fails the build.

Beside each formatter is a linter that finds mistakes the compiler allows. clang-tidy for C must be installed and configured. go vet comes with Go and runs in make verify, and staticcheck adds more. cargo clippy comes with Rust, has more than 800 checks, and is the tool that asked for is_empty above. The verdict for this chapter is mostly about these tools, because the day-to-day experience of a language is the experience of its tools.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
Splitting codeWeakStrongOKC needs guards, prefixes and a Makefile that tracks headers, while Go needs a folder and Rust a mod line that is easy to forget.
Hiding a nameOKStrongStrongC has static, for functions only. Go and Rust hide by default or by a letter.
Adding a dependencyWeakOKStrongC has three competing ways and no default, while Go and Rust each have one command, and Rust also has one registry.
Having too manyStrongStrongWeakC and Go programs stay small by cost and by a wide standard library. Rust programs grow dozens of crates.
Keeping one styleOKStrongStrongclang-format needs a config everyone agrees on. gofmt and rustfmt need nothing.
Finding mistakesWeakOKStrongclang-tidy must be installed. go vet is built in. clippy is built in and has 800 checks.
Swapping an implementationOKStrongStrongC has a struct of function pointers that nobody checks. Go has implicit interfaces, and Rust has checked traits with two kinds of dispatch.
Hiding a structStrongStrongStrongC has the opaque type, and Go and Rust have unexported fields. All three keep the map out of reach.
Carry forward
  • Opaque type. A C header declares a struct it does not define, so other files hold a pointer and nothing more.
  • Interface. A Go type satisfies an interface by having its methods, and a nil pointer inside one is not nil.
  • Trait object. A dyn Store is dispatched at run time through a method table, and a generic bound is dispatched at compile time.

Data types#

Building kv · Chapter 08· 32 min read· 706 lines of code
▶Scene

Fill the chapter 7 server with a million keys. Then, from one terminal, ask for all of them, and fifty milliseconds later, from another, ask for one:

$ redis-cli -p 6380 --pipe < million-sets.txt
errors: 0, replies: 1000000
$ time redis-cli -p 6380 KEYS '*' > /dev/null         # terminal one
real    0m0.75s
$ time redis-cli -p 6380 GET user:1                     # terminal two, 50 ms later
"v"
real    0m0.68s

A GET takes no measurable time on its own. This one took most of a second, because it waited for another client's KEYS to finish walking a million entries. One question, and everyone waits. Redis answers it with a command that walks the table a page at a time, and with values that are more than strings.

A key can hold more than a string. This chapter gives kv lists, hashes and sets, and a TYPE command that says which. It adds SCAN, which walks the keys a page at a time. The chapter is about sum types, which each language builds in its own way, and about iteration.

Redis is not a map from strings to strings. Its documentation calls it a data structure server. The value under a key may be a string, a list, a hash of fields or a set of members. There are several more, and kv takes the first four. Each needs the same three things from the store. A value must say which kind it is. A command must take the value apart as that kind, and refuse any other kind with the error Redis uses, WRONGTYPE. And a command such as HGETALL or SMEMBERS must walk whatever is inside. The first need is a sum type, a value that is one of several shapes. The third is iteration. The three languages answer both, and the answers are the chapter.

One value, four kindsCGoRust
The valuea struct with a tag and a unionan any, holding one of four concrete typesan enum with data in each variant
Asking whichswitch (v->kind)a type switch, switch v := x.(type)match, which must cover every variant
Taking one kindread the union member the tag names, and nothing checksa type assertion, v.(*List), with an oka pattern, Value::List(l), in a match or let else
Adding a fifth kindthe compiler warns at each switch with no defaultnothing warns; a missed case falls to defaultthe compiler refuses every match that forgot it
A listan array of byte strings, shifted along for LPUSHa slice of byte slicesa VecDeque, with both ends cheap
A hash and a seta nested store, the set with empty valuesa map, and a generic Set[T]a HashMap and a HashSet
Walking a collectiona callback with a void * contextan iterator function that range callsan Iterator, with map, filter and collect
📜Why Redis has lists and sets, and not only strings

Salvatore Sanfilippo began Redis in 2009 while trying to improve the scalability of his startup, a real-time web log analyser. He had met "significant problems in scaling some types of workloads using traditional database systems". A log analyser keeps lists of recent events and sets of visitors. A list in a string store is a string the client must rewrite on every push. A list in the server is one command. The documentation calls Redis "a data structure server", and the name Remote Dictionary Server undersells it. The value is where the work is.

C: a tag and a union#

A C value that may be one of four things is a struct of two parts. The first is a tag, an enum that says which shape is live. The second is a union, a type whose members share the same bytes. So a value holds one string, or one list, or one table, and never more than one at a time. The pair is called a tagged union, and C checks nothing about it. Read the list member of a value whose tag says string and you read the string's pointer as an array length:

/* Which of the four shapes a value has. The number is the tag of the union below. */
typedef enum { KV_STRING, KV_LIST, KV_HASH, KV_SET } kv_kind;

/* A tagged union: the tag says which member of the union is live, and reading another
 * member is a bug the compiler will not catch. A hash and a set are each a nested store,
 * whose entries hold strings; a set keeps its values empty and uses only the keys. */
typedef struct {
    kv_kind kind;
    union {
        kv_bytes str;
        kv_list list;
        kv_store *table; /* owned, for KV_HASH and KV_SET */
    } u;
} kv_value;

const char *kv_kind_name(kv_kind kind); /* "string", "list", "hash" or "set" */
void kv_value_free(kv_value *v);
c/ch08/src/store.h · region value

A hash and a set are each a nested store. The store of chapter 7 is opaque, holds values under byte keys, and can be made with the same type as its parent. So a hash is a store whose values are strings. A set is a store whose values are empty. Nothing new was written for either. The list is new. It is an array of byte strings, and LPUSH shifts the whole array along by one, which costs the length of the list. Redis uses a linked structure there. kv keeps the array, because the chapter is about the union, and says what it costs:

/* A list: an array of owned byte strings. RPUSH appends; LPUSH shifts the array along by
 * one, which costs the length of the list. Redis keeps a linked structure instead, and
 * pays for that in other ways. */
typedef struct {
    kv_bytes *items; /* owned array of owned strings */
    size_t len;
    size_t cap;
} kv_list;
c/ch08/src/store.h · region list

Freeing a value is a switch on the tag with a case per kind and no default. The compiler reports a kind this switch forgot. That is the only check C gives a tagged union, and the reason the switch is written that way:

const char *kv_kind_name(kv_kind kind) {
    switch (kind) {
    case KV_STRING:
        return "string";
    case KV_LIST:
        return "list";
    case KV_HASH:
        return "hash";
    case KV_SET:
        return "set";
    }
    return "none";
}

bool kv_bytes_set(kv_bytes *b, const char *src, size_t n) {
    char *copy = kv_bytes_dup(src, n);
    if (copy == NULL) {
        return false;
    }
    free(b->p);
    b->p = copy;
    b->len = n;
    return true;
}

static void kv_list_free(kv_list *l) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < l->len; i++) {
        free(l->items[i].p);
    }
    free(l->items);
}

bool kv_list_push(kv_list *l, const char *src, size_t n, bool front) {
    char *copy = kv_bytes_dup(src, n);
    if (copy == NULL) {
        return false;
    }
    if (l->len == l->cap) {
        size_t cap = l->cap ? l->cap * 2 : 4;
        kv_bytes *items = realloc(l->items, cap * sizeof *items);
        if (items == NULL) {
            free(copy);
            return false;
        }
        l->items = items;
        l->cap = cap;
    }
    if (front) {
        memmove(l->items + 1, l->items, l->len * sizeof *l->items);
        l->items[0] = (kv_bytes){copy, n};
    } else {
        l->items[l->len] = (kv_bytes){copy, n};
    }
    l->len++;
    return true;
}

/* Free whatever the tag says is live. The switch has no default, so a fifth kind would
 * be reported by the compiler here, with -Wall, until it is handled. */
void kv_value_free(kv_value *v) {
    switch (v->kind) {
    case KV_STRING:
        free(v->u.str.p);
        break;
    case KV_LIST:
        kv_list_free(&v->u.list);
        break;
    case KV_HASH:
    case KV_SET:
        kv_store_free(v->u.table);
        break;
    }
    *v = (kv_value){KV_STRING, {{NULL, 0}}};
}
c/ch08/src/store.c · region value-fns

Every command that takes a value apart starts in one of two helpers. The first returns the string of an entry, or writes the WRONGTYPE error and returns NULL. The second returns an entry as a given kind, making an empty one when the key is new. Each is the tag check written once:

#define KV_WRONGTYPE "WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value"

/* The string of an entry, or NULL after writing the WRONGTYPE error. Every string
 * command starts here, so the check against the tag is in one place. */
static kv_bytes *kv_string_of(kv_entry *e, kv_buf *out) {
    if (e->val.kind != KV_STRING) {
        kv_reply_error(out, KV_WRONGTYPE);
        return NULL;
    }
    return &e->val.u.str;
}

/* The entry for key as the given kind, made empty when the key is new, or NULL after
 * writing the WRONGTYPE error when it holds another kind. */
static kv_entry *kv_entry_as(kv_store *s, const kv_cmd *c, kv_kind kind, kv_buf *out, bool *oom) {
    bool created;
    *oom = false;
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_insert(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], &created);
    if (e == NULL) {
        *oom = true;
        return NULL;
    }
    if (created) {
        e->val.kind = kind;
        if (kind == KV_HASH || kind == KV_SET) {
            e->val.u.table = kv_store_new(kv_store_type_of(s));
            if (e->val.u.table == NULL) {
                kv_store_del(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
                *oom = true;
                return NULL;
            }
        }
    } else if (e->val.kind != kind) {
        kv_reply_error(out, KV_WRONGTYPE);
        return NULL;
    }
    return e;
}
c/ch08/src/cmd.c · region wrongtype

The string commands of chapter 5 change by one line each, the call to kv_string_of. GETRANGE and LRANGE share a clamp, because a list is sliced by position exactly as a string is sliced by byte:

/* LPUSH and RPUSH: the same function, told which end by the table. */
static bool kv_push(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out, bool front) {
    bool oom;
    kv_entry *e = kv_entry_as(s, c, KV_LIST, out, &oom);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return !oom;
    }
    for (size_t i = 2; i < c->argc; i++) {
        if (!kv_list_push(&e->val.u.list, c->argv[i], c->arglen[i], front)) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return kv_reply_int(out, (long long)e->val.u.list.len);
}

static bool kv_cmd_lpush(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    return kv_push(c, s, out, true);
}

static bool kv_cmd_rpush(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    return kv_push(c, s, out, false);
}

/* The list of an entry, or NULL after the WRONGTYPE error. */
static kv_list *kv_list_of(kv_entry *e, kv_buf *out) {
    if (e->val.kind != KV_LIST) {
        kv_reply_error(out, KV_WRONGTYPE);
        return NULL;
    }
    return &e->val.u.list;
}

static bool kv_cmd_llen(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return kv_reply_int(out, 0);
    }
    kv_list *l = kv_list_of(e, out);
    return l == NULL || kv_reply_int(out, (long long)l->len);
}

static bool kv_cmd_lrange(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    long long start, end;
    if (!kv_parse_int(c->argv[2], c->arglen[2], &start) ||
        !kv_parse_int(c->argv[3], c->arglen[3], &end)) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
    }
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return kv_reply_array(out, 0);
    }
    kv_list *l = kv_list_of(e, out);
    if (l == NULL) {
        return true;
    }
    size_t from, to;
    if (!kv_clamp(start, end, (long long)l->len, &from, &to)) {
        return kv_reply_array(out, 0);
    }
    if (!kv_reply_array(out, to - from + 1)) {
        return false;
    }
    for (size_t i = from; i <= to; i++) {
        if (!kv_reply_bulk(out, l->items[i].p, l->items[i].len)) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

Stuck?Show the full listing
static bool kv_cmd_sadd(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    bool oom;
    kv_entry *e = kv_entry_as(s, c, KV_SET, out, &oom);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return !oom;
    }
    long long added = 0;
    for (size_t i = 2; i < c->argc; i++) {
        bool created;
        if (kv_store_insert(e->val.u.table, c->argv[i], c->arglen[i], &created) == NULL) {
            return false;
        }
        added += created;
    }
    return kv_reply_int(out, added);
}

static bool kv_cmd_sismember(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return kv_reply_int(out, 0);
    }
    kv_store *set = kv_table_of(e, KV_SET, out);
    return set == NULL || kv_reply_int(out, kv_store_find(set, c->argv[2], c->arglen[2]) != NULL);
}

static bool kv_cmd_smembers(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return kv_reply_array(out, 0);
    }
    kv_store *set = kv_table_of(e, KV_SET, out);
    if (set == NULL) {
        return true;
    }
    if (!kv_reply_array(out, kv_store_len(set))) {
        return false;
    }
    kv_members_ctx m = {out, false, true};
    kv_store_each(set, kv_members_visit, &m);
    return m.ok;
}
c/ch08/src/cmd.c · region sets

HGETALL and SMEMBERS walk the nested store with the callback of chapter 7. One callback serves both, told by its context whether to write the values as well as the keys:

/* HSET key field value [field value ...]: the fields go into the nested store. */
static bool kv_cmd_hset(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    if (c->argc % 2 != 0) {
        return kv_reply_arity(out, "hset");
    }
    bool oom;
    kv_entry *e = kv_entry_as(s, c, KV_HASH, out, &oom);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return !oom;
    }
    long long added = 0;
    for (size_t i = 2; i + 1 < c->argc; i += 2) {
        added += kv_store_find(e->val.u.table, c->argv[i], c->arglen[i]) == NULL;
        if (!kv_store_set(e->val.u.table, c->argv[i], c->arglen[i], c->argv[i + 1], c->arglen[i + 1])) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return kv_reply_int(out, added);
}

/* The nested table of an entry, or NULL after the WRONGTYPE error. */
static kv_store *kv_table_of(kv_entry *e, kv_kind kind, kv_buf *out) {
    if (e->val.kind != kind) {
        kv_reply_error(out, KV_WRONGTYPE);
        return NULL;
    }
    return e->val.u.table;
}

static bool kv_cmd_hget(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return kv_reply_nil(out);
    }
    kv_store *h = kv_table_of(e, KV_HASH, out);
    if (h == NULL) {
        return true;
    }
    kv_entry *f = kv_store_find(h, c->argv[2], c->arglen[2]);
    return f ? kv_reply_bulk(out, f->val.u.str.p, f->val.u.str.len) : kv_reply_nil(out);
}

/* The context of the HGETALL and SMEMBERS walks: the reply so far, and whether a
 * reply failed to append. */
typedef struct {
    kv_buf *out;
    bool with_values;
    bool ok;
} kv_members_ctx;

static bool kv_members_visit(kv_entry *e, void *ctx) {
    kv_members_ctx *m = ctx;
    m->ok = kv_reply_bulk(m->out, e->key, e->klen) &&
            (!m->with_values || kv_reply_bulk(m->out, e->val.u.str.p, e->val.u.str.len));
    return m->ok;
}

static bool kv_cmd_hgetall(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return kv_reply_array(out, 0);
    }
    kv_store *h = kv_table_of(e, KV_HASH, out);
    if (h == NULL) {
        return true;
    }
    if (!kv_reply_array(out, kv_store_len(h) * 2)) {
        return false;
    }
    kv_members_ctx m = {out, true, true};
    kv_store_each(h, kv_members_visit, &m);
    return m.ok;
}
c/ch08/src/cmd.c · region hashes

SCAN costs C the least. The store's buckets are an array, and a cursor is an index into it. The walk starts at the cursor's bucket and visits whole buckets until it has seen enough entries. Then it returns the next bucket as the new cursor, or 0 at the end. A client that calls SCAN with each returned cursor sees every key that was there throughout, without the server ever holding the whole list:

size_t kv_store_scan(kv_store *s, size_t cursor, size_t count,
                     bool (*fn)(kv_entry *e, void *ctx), void *ctx) {
    size_t seen = 0;
    while (cursor < s->cap) {
        for (kv_entry *e = s->buckets[cursor]; e != NULL; e = e->next) {
            seen++;
            if (!fn(e, ctx)) {
                return 0;
            }
        }
        cursor++;
        if (seen >= count) {
            break;
        }
    }
    return cursor < s->cap ? cursor : 0;
}
c/ch08/src/store.c · region scan
static bool kv_cmd_type(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    return kv_reply_simple(out, e ? kv_kind_name(e->val.kind) : "none");
}

/* The context of a SCAN walk: the pattern, and the matching keys collected so far. */
typedef struct {
    const char *pat;
    size_t plen;
    kv_buf keys;
    size_t n;
    bool ok;
} kv_scan_ctx;

static bool kv_scan_visit(kv_entry *e, void *ctx) {
    kv_scan_ctx *k = ctx;
    if (k->pat != NULL && !kv_glob(k->pat, k->plen, e->key, e->klen)) {
        return true;
    }
    if (!kv_reply_bulk(&k->keys, e->key, e->klen)) {
        k->ok = false;
        return false;
    }
    k->n++;
    return true;
}

/* SCAN cursor [MATCH pattern] [COUNT n]: a page of keys and the cursor for the next page.
 * The reply is an array of two things, the cursor as a string and the array of keys. */
static bool kv_cmd_scan(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out) {
    long long cursor;
    if (!kv_parse_int(c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], &cursor) || cursor < 0) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR invalid cursor");
    }
    kv_scan_ctx k = {NULL, 0, {0}, 0, true};
    long long count = 10;
    for (size_t i = 2; i + 1 < c->argc; i += 2) {
        if (kv_arg_is(c, i, "MATCH")) {
            k.pat = c->argv[i + 1];
            k.plen = c->arglen[i + 1];
        } else if (kv_arg_is(c, i, "COUNT")) {
            if (!kv_parse_int(c->argv[i + 1], c->arglen[i + 1], &count) || count < 1) {
                return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
            }
        } else {
            return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR syntax error");
        }
    }
    if (c->argc % 2 != 0) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR syntax error");
    }
    size_t next = kv_store_scan(s, (size_t)cursor, (size_t)count, kv_scan_visit, &k);
    char text[32];
    int len = snprintf(text, sizeof text, "%zu", next);
    bool ok = k.ok && kv_reply_array(out, 2) && kv_reply_bulk(out, text, (size_t)len) &&
              kv_reply_array(out, k.n) && kv_buf_append(out, k.keys.data, k.keys.len);
    kv_buf_free(&k.keys);
    return ok;
}

⚠️The union member the tag does not name C

Reading a union member that is not the live one is undefined behaviour in the general case, and the compiler will not say a word. The only defence is the habit the helpers above enforce. Check the tag, then read the member, and never pass a union member around without the tag beside it. A switch on the tag with no default keeps the check honest when a kind is added.

Go: any, and a switch on the type#

Go has no union. It has any, the interface with no methods, which every value satisfies. The store holds an any under each key, and the four kinds are four concrete types inside it. A type switch asks which. It is a switch whose cases are types, and Kind is one. The 'a in its name says that the reference it holds borrows the store, which chapter 10 explains:

// A value is one of four things, and the store holds it as `any`: an interface with no
// methods, which any value satisfies. The four concrete types are the cases, and a type
// switch takes the value apart. ErrWrongType is what a command replies when the case is
// not the one it needs.
var ErrWrongType = errors.New("WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value")

// Kind names the case, as TYPE reports it. The switch has no default on purpose: a
// value of a fifth type would reach "none", and the tests would say so.
func Kind(v any) string {
	switch v.(type) {
	case []byte:
		return "string"
	case *List:
		return "list"
	case Hash:
		return "hash"
	case *Set[string]:
		return "set"
	}
	return "none"
}
go/ch08/internal/store/value.go · region kinds

A type assertion asks for one type and gets a second result that says whether the value had it. With that ok an assertion never panics. Without it, one that fails stops the program, which is the form to avoid on data from a client. The string commands start in stringOf, and the three collection kinds start in as, which is generic over the kind it returns:

// stringOf is the value as bytes, or ErrWrongType. The assertion v.([]byte) asks whether
// the value inside the interface has that type; the second result says. Every string
// command starts here, so the check is in one place.
func stringOf(v any) ([]byte, error) {
	b, ok := v.([]byte)
	if !ok {
		return nil, store.ErrWrongType
	}
	return b, nil
}

// as returns the value under key as T, making one with mk when the key is new. A key
// that holds another kind is ErrWrongType. T is a type parameter, so one function
// serves *store.List, store.Hash and *store.Set[string].
func as[T any](s Storer, key []byte, mk func() T) (T, error) {
	if v, ok := s.Get(key); ok {
		t, isT := v.(T)
		if !isT {
			var zero T
			return zero, store.ErrWrongType
		}
		return t, nil
	}
	t := mk()
	s.Set(key, t)
	return t, nil
}
go/ch08/internal/cmd/cmd.go · region as

Nothing warns when a type switch forgets a case. A fifth kind added to the store falls to the default of every switch that did not know it, and TYPE would answer none. That is the cost of a sum type built from an interface, and the tests are what catch it. The list, the hash and the set are three types of their own. The set is generic, because nothing in it depends on what the members are:

// A Hash is a map from field to value, with nothing to add: a map already does it all.
type Hash map[string][]byte

// A Set is a map with no values. It is generic, because nothing about it depends on
// what the members are, only that they can be compared.
type Set[T comparable] struct {
	m map[T]struct{}
}

func NewSet[T comparable]() *Set[T] { return &Set[T]{m: make(map[T]struct{})} }

// Add reports whether the member was new.
func (s *Set[T]) Add(v T) bool {
	_, had := s.m[v]
	s.m[v] = struct{}{}
	return !had
}

func (s *Set[T]) Has(v T) bool { _, ok := s.m[v]; return ok }
func (s *Set[T]) Len() int     { return len(s.m) }

// All yields every member, in no particular order.
func (s *Set[T]) All() iter.Seq[T] {
	return func(yield func(T) bool) {
		for v := range s.m {
			if !yield(v) {
				return
			}
		}
	}
}
go/ch08/internal/store/value.go · region hash-set

A function that range can call#

Since Go 1.23, range can loop over a function. The function takes the loop body, called yield, and calls it once per item until it returns false. The type iter.Seq[T] names that shape. The list's Range is one, and LRANGE loops over it without ever seeing the slice inside:

// A List is a slice of byte strings. PushBack appends; PushFront makes room at the
// start by copying the slice along, which costs the length of the list.
type List struct {
	items [][]byte
}

func (l *List) PushBack(v []byte)  { l.items = append(l.items, v) }
func (l *List) PushFront(v []byte) { l.items = append([][]byte{v}, l.items...) }
func (l *List) Len() int           { return len(l.items) }

// Range yields the items from start to end, both inclusive, with negative offsets
// counted from the end and out-of-range offsets clamped. It is an iterator: a function
// that takes the loop body, and range calls it. The caller never sees the slice.
func (l *List) Range(start, end int64) iter.Seq[[]byte] {
	return func(yield func([]byte) bool) {
		n := int64(len(l.items))
		if start < 0 {
			start += n
		}
		if end < 0 {
			end += n
		}
		start = max(start, 0)
		end = min(end, n-1)
		for i := start; i <= end; i++ {
			if !yield(l.items[i]) {
				return
			}
		}
	}
}

Stuck?Show the full listing
func push(args [][]byte, s Storer, w *bufio.Writer, front bool) error {
	l, err := as(s, args[1], func() *store.List { return &store.List{} })
	if err != nil {
		return resp.WriteError(w, err.Error())
	}
	for _, v := range args[2:] {
		if front {
			l.PushFront(v)
		} else {
			l.PushBack(v)
		}
	}
	return resp.WriteInt(w, int64(l.Len()))
}

func lpush(args [][]byte, s Storer, w *bufio.Writer) error { return push(args, s, w, true) }
func rpush(args [][]byte, s Storer, w *bufio.Writer) error { return push(args, s, w, false) }

// listOf is the list under key, an empty one when the key is missing, or an error.
func listOf(s Storer, key []byte) (*store.List, error) {
	v, ok := s.Get(key)
	if !ok {
		return &store.List{}, nil
	}
	l, isList := v.(*store.List)
	if !isList {
		return nil, store.ErrWrongType
	}
	return l, nil
}

func llen(args [][]byte, s Storer, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	l, err := listOf(s, args[1])
	if err != nil {
		return resp.WriteError(w, err.Error())
	}
	return resp.WriteInt(w, int64(l.Len()))
}

// lrange collects the page with range over the list's iterator. The count is needed
// before the items, so the iterator is drained into a slice first.
func lrange(args [][]byte, s Storer, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	start, err1 := strconv.ParseInt(string(args[2]), 10, 64)
	end, err2 := strconv.ParseInt(string(args[3]), 10, 64)
	if err1 != nil || err2 != nil {
		return resp.WriteError(w, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range")
	}
	l, err := listOf(s, args[1])
	if err != nil {
		return resp.WriteError(w, err.Error())
	}
	var page [][]byte
	for item := range l.Range(start, end) {
		page = append(page, item)
	}
	return writeBulks(w, page)
}
go/ch08/internal/cmd/cmd.go · region lists

A Go map cannot be scanned from a position. Each range over a map starts in a new random order, by design, so that no program comes to depend on the order. The map store sorts its keys and uses the cursor as an index into the sorted list, which costs a sort per page. The table from chapter 6 owns its buckets and scans them as the C store does, in one walk. That difference is the reason Redis owns its table, and the one place in the book where the hand-written table is the better store:

// Scan returns a page of keys from the cursor on, and the cursor for the next page, or
// 0 when the walk is done. A Go map cannot be walked from a position: each range starts
// in a new random order. So the keys are sorted and the cursor is an index into that
// order, which costs a sort per page. The hand-written table scans by bucket instead.
func (s *Store) Scan(cursor uint64, count int) (uint64, [][]byte) {
	sorted := slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(s.m))
	if cursor >= uint64(len(sorted)) {
		return 0, nil
	}
	end := min(int(cursor)+count, len(sorted))
	var page [][]byte
	for _, k := range sorted[cursor:end] {
		page = append(page, []byte(k))
	}
	if end == len(sorted) {
		return 0, page
	}
	return uint64(end), page
}
go/ch08/internal/store/store.go · region scan
// Scan walks the buckets from cursor, collecting keys until at least count have been
// seen or the buckets end. The returned cursor is the next bucket, or 0 at the end: a
// cursor is a bucket index, which is why the walk can resume.
func (t *Table[K, V]) Scan(cursor uint64, count int) (uint64, []K) {
	var page []K
	for cursor < uint64(len(t.buckets)) {
		for _, e := range t.buckets[cursor] {
			page = append(page, e.key)
		}
		cursor++
		if len(page) >= count {
			break
		}
	}
	if cursor >= uint64(len(t.buckets)) {
		return 0, page
	}
	return cursor, page
}

⚠️A type assertion without the ok panics Go

v.(*List) on a value that is not a *List stops the program with interface conversion. On a value that came from a client, that is a crash any client can cause. The two-result form, l, ok := v.(*List), never panics, and every assertion in kv has the ok. A type switch has the same safety with no extra code, because an unmatched type takes the default branch.

Rust: an enum with data in each variant#

A Rust enum is the tagged union with the check the C version lacks. Each variant carries its own data, and the compiler knows which variant is live. The only way to read the data is a pattern that names the variant. A match must cover every variant, so a fifth kind added next year is a compile error at every match that forgot it:

/// The four kinds of value, as one enum. Each variant carries its own data, and a match
/// must handle every variant, so a fifth kind added later is a compile error at every
/// place that forgot it. This is the sum type that C builds by hand with a tag and a
/// union, and Go builds with an interface and a type switch.
pub enum Value {
    Str(Vec<u8>),
    List(VecDeque<Vec<u8>>),
    Hash(HashMap<Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>>),
    Set(HashSet<Vec<u8>>),
}

impl Value {
    /// The name TYPE reports.
    pub fn kind(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Value::Str(_) => "string",
            Value::List(_) => "list",
            Value::Hash(_) => "hash",
            Value::Set(_) => "set",
        }
    }
}

/// The error a command replies when the value is not the kind it needs.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct WrongType;

impl WrongType {
    pub const MESSAGE: &'static str =
        "WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value";
}
rust/ch08/src/store.rs · region value

The trait gains five methods that work on a value of any kind, and the string commands become default methods on top of them. get returns a Result of an Option, because a string command has three outcomes, the string, no key, and a key of another kind. incr uses ? on that result. A From turns the wrong-type error into the IncrError it returns:

/// What the commands need from a store. Five methods work on values of any kind, and the
/// string commands are default methods written on top of them.
pub trait Store {
    fn value(&self, key: &[u8]) -> Option<&Value>;
    fn value_mut(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> Option<&mut Value>;
    /// The value under key, made with `make` when the key is new.
    fn value_or_insert(&mut self, key: Vec<u8>, make: fn() -> Value) -> &mut Value;
    /// Store a value of any kind, replacing whatever kind was there.
    fn insert(&mut self, key: Vec<u8>, val: Value);
    fn del(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> bool;
    fn len(&self) -> usize;
    /// Every key that matches the pattern, in no particular order.
    fn keys(&self, pattern: &[u8]) -> Vec<&[u8]>;
    /// A page of up to `count` keys from `cursor` on, and the cursor of the next page,
    /// or 0 when the walk is complete.
    fn scan(&self, cursor: usize, count: usize) -> (usize, Vec<&[u8]>);

    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.len() == 0
    }

    /// The string under key: `None` for a missing key, an error for another kind.
    fn get(&self, key: &[u8]) -> Result<Option<&[u8]>, WrongType> {
        match self.value(key) {
            None => Ok(None),
            Some(Value::Str(s)) => Ok(Some(s)),
            Some(_) => Err(WrongType),
        }
    }

    fn set(&mut self, key: Vec<u8>, val: Vec<u8>) {
        self.insert(key, Value::Str(val));
    }

    /// Add one to the integer stored under key, which counts as 0 when absent.
    fn incr(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> Result<i64, IncrError> {
        let n = match self.get(key)? {
            None => 0,
            Some(bytes) => parse_int(bytes).ok_or(IncrError::NotInteger)?,
        };
        let n = n.checked_add(1).ok_or(IncrError::Overflow)?;
        self.set(key.to_vec(), n.to_string().into_bytes());
        Ok(n)
    }
}
rust/ch08/src/store.rs · region trait

The commands take a value apart with let ... else, which matches one variant and leaves the function when the value is another. The list is a VecDeque, which pushes at either end in constant time. The arguments are moved into it with drain, so no byte of a pushed item is copied:

/// LPUSH and RPUSH: the same function, told which end by a flag. A `VecDeque` pushes at
/// either end in constant time, which is why the list is one and not a `Vec`.
fn push(
    args: &mut Command,
    store: &mut dyn Store,
    w: &mut dyn Write,
    front: bool,
) -> io::Result<()> {
    let key = mem::take(&mut args[1]);
    let Value::List(list) = store.value_or_insert(key, || Value::List(VecDeque::new())) else {
        return write_wrongtype(w);
    };
    for item in args.drain(2..) {
        if front {
            list.push_front(item);
        } else {
            list.push_back(item);
        }
    }
    resp::write_int(w, list.len() as i64)
}

fn lpush(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    push(args, store, w, true)
}

fn rpush(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    push(args, store, w, false)
}

/// The value under key as the kind the command needs: `None` for a missing key, an
/// error for another kind. `Kind<'a, T>` is a name for the shape all three helpers return.
type Kind<'a, T> = Result<Option<&'a T>, WrongType>;

/// The list under key, an empty one when the key is missing, or the wrong kind.
fn list_of<'a>(store: &'a dyn Store, key: &[u8]) -> Kind<'a, VecDeque<Vec<u8>>> {
    match store.value(key) {
        None => Ok(None),
        Some(Value::List(l)) => Ok(Some(l)),
        Some(_) => Err(WrongType),
    }
}

fn llen(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    match list_of(store, &args[1]) {
        Ok(l) => resp::write_int(w, l.map_or(0, VecDeque::len) as i64),
        Err(WrongType) => write_wrongtype(w),
    }
}

/// LRANGE key start end: a slice of the list by position. `range` on a `VecDeque` is
/// an iterator over the items in that range, and `write_bulks` drains it.
fn lrange(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let (Some(start), Some(end)) = (parse_int(&args[2]), parse_int(&args[3])) else {
        return resp::write_error(w, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
    };
    let list = match list_of(store, &args[1]) {
        Ok(Some(l)) => l,
        Ok(None) => return resp::write_array_len(w, 0),
        Err(WrongType) => return write_wrongtype(w),
    };
    match clamp(start, end, list.len()) {
        Some(range) => write_bulks(w, list.range(range).map(Vec::as_slice)),
        None => resp::write_array_len(w, 0),
    }
}

Closures and iterators, named at last#

Rust has written iterators since chapter 4 without naming them. An iterator is any value with a next method that gives the next item or None. Every adaptor comes with that one method. map changes each item and filter keeps some. skip and take cut a range. flat_map turns each item into several, and collect builds a collection from what is left. Each adaptor wraps the one before and does nothing until something at the end asks for an item. That is laziness, and the scan below depends on it. skip(cursor) and take(count) describe a page of a million keys without touching the other keys:

/// A HashMap walks in one fixed order while it is not changed, so the cursor is a
/// count of keys already seen. `skip` and `take` are lazy: nothing runs until
/// `collect` asks, and the map is never copied. One more `next` tells whether a
/// page follows.
fn scan(&self, cursor: usize, count: usize) -> (usize, Vec<&[u8]>) {
    let mut rest = self.map.keys().skip(cursor);
    let page: Vec<&[u8]> = rest.by_ref().take(count).map(Vec::as_slice).collect();
    let next = if rest.next().is_some() {
        cursor + page.len()
    } else {
        0
    };
    (next, page)
}
rust/ch08/src/store.rs · region scan

The |k| glob(p, k) inside a filter is a closure, a function written where it is used, which can capture the variables around it. A closure has one of three traits, by what it does with what it captured. Fn only reads, FnMut changes something, and FnOnce consumes it and can run once. filter asks for an FnMut, so a closure that counts as it filters is allowed. sadd uses that to count the members that were new:

fn sadd(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let key = mem::take(&mut args[1]);
    let Value::Set(set) = store.value_or_insert(key, || Value::Set(HashSet::new())) else {
        return write_wrongtype(w);
    };
    let added = args.drain(2..).filter(|m| set.insert(m.clone())).count();
    resp::write_int(w, added as i64)
}

fn set_of<'a>(store: &'a dyn Store, key: &[u8]) -> Kind<'a, HashSet<Vec<u8>>> {
    match store.value(key) {
        None => Ok(None),
        Some(Value::Set(s)) => Ok(Some(s)),
        Some(_) => Err(WrongType),
    }
}

fn sismember(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    match set_of(store, &args[1]) {
        Ok(s) => resp::write_int(w, i64::from(s.is_some_and(|s| s.contains(&args[2])))),
        Err(WrongType) => write_wrongtype(w),
    }
}

fn smembers(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    match set_of(store, &args[1]) {
        Ok(Some(s)) => write_bulks(w, s.iter().map(Vec::as_slice)),
        Ok(None) => resp::write_array_len(w, 0),
        Err(WrongType) => write_wrongtype(w),
    }
}

Stuck?Show the full listing
fn hset(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    if !args.len().is_multiple_of(2) {
        return write_arity(w, b"hset");
    }
    let key = mem::take(&mut args[1]);
    let Value::Hash(hash) = store.value_or_insert(key, || Value::Hash(HashMap::new())) else {
        return write_wrongtype(w);
    };
    let mut added = 0;
    let mut pairs = args.drain(2..);
    while let (Some(field), Some(val)) = (pairs.next(), pairs.next()) {
        added += usize::from(hash.insert(field, val).is_none());
    }
    resp::write_int(w, added as i64)
}

fn hash_of<'a>(store: &'a dyn Store, key: &[u8]) -> Kind<'a, HashMap<Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>>> {
    match store.value(key) {
        None => Ok(None),
        Some(Value::Hash(h)) => Ok(Some(h)),
        Some(_) => Err(WrongType),
    }
}

fn hget(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    match hash_of(store, &args[1]) {
        Ok(h) => match h.and_then(|h| h.get(&args[2])) {
            Some(v) => resp::write_bulk(w, v),
            None => resp::write_nil(w),
        },
        Err(WrongType) => write_wrongtype(w),
    }
}

/// HGETALL: every field and value, as one flat array. `flat_map` turns each pair into
/// two items, and the count is twice the number of fields.
fn hgetall(args: &mut Command, store: &mut dyn Store, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    let hash = match hash_of(store, &args[1]) {
        Ok(Some(h)) => h,
        Ok(None) => return resp::write_array_len(w, 0),
        Err(WrongType) => return write_wrongtype(w),
    };
    let flat: Vec<&[u8]> = hash
        .iter()
        .flat_map(|(f, v)| [f.as_slice(), v.as_slice()])
        .collect();
    write_bulks(w, flat.into_iter())
}

Writing an iterator of your own is one method. The file chain.rs in the snapshot is the C chain of chapter 6 in Rust, kept for two lessons the server did not need. A type that contains itself must do so through a Box, a pointer to the heap that owns what it points to. The compiler must know the size of a value, and a Chain inside a Chain has none. And a type becomes an iterator by implementing next. Every adaptor then works on it, and so does for:

/// A recursive enum. Without the `Box`, a `Chain` would contain a `Chain` directly, and
/// the compiler could not say how large one is. `Box` puts the next link on the heap,
/// which makes the size one pointer, and it owns that link, so dropping the head drops
/// the whole chain.
pub enum Chain {
    Link(Vec<u8>, Box<Chain>),
    End,
}

impl Chain {
    pub fn push(self, item: Vec<u8>) -> Chain {
        Chain::Link(item, Box::new(self))
    }
}

/// An iterator over a chain: a value with one method, `next`, which gives the next item
/// or `None`. Everything else, `map`, `filter`, `count` and the `for` loop, comes with
/// the trait. The iterator takes the chain apart as it goes, so it owns it.
pub struct IntoIter(Chain);

impl Iterator for IntoIter {
    type Item = Vec<u8>;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
        match std::mem::replace(&mut self.0, Chain::End) {
            Chain::Link(item, rest) => {
                self.0 = *rest;
                Some(item)
            }
            Chain::End => None,
        }
    }
}

impl IntoIterator for Chain {
    type Item = Vec<u8>;
    type IntoIter = IntoIter;

    fn into_iter(self) -> IntoIter {
        IntoIter(self)
    }
}
rust/ch08/src/chain.rs · region chain

Three methods give three kinds of iterator over a collection. iter borrows each item, iter_mut borrows each mutably, and into_iter takes the collection apart and gives the items away. The chain only has the last, because its next consumes a link.

⚠️An iterator that nobody consumes does nothing Rust

keys.iter().map(|k| store.del(k)); deletes nothing. The adaptor builds a value that would delete on each next, and no one calls next. The compiler warns that the iterator is unused, and the book's build makes the warning an error. A side effect wants a for loop, or a call such as count() at the end, as del in this chapter writes it.

Iteration, three ways#

Every collection in this chapter is walked three times, once per language, and the three walks are the three answers to one question. Who holds the loop?

Walking a collectionCGoRust
Who holds the loopthe collection, which calls backthe collection, which calls yieldthe caller, which calls next
What the caller suppliesa function pointer and a void * contextthe loop body, through rangenothing, and adaptors between
Stopping earlythe callback returns falsethe body returns, and yield returns falsethe caller stops calling next
Composing two walksby hand, with a second callbackby hand, or with the iter packagefilter on map on skip, for free
Where the state livesin the context structin the closure the collection madein the iterator value
The cost of a stepan indirect callan indirect call, which the compiler often inlinesnothing: the chain compiles to a loop

The C and Go answers are the same shape, a collection that runs the loop and hands each item to a function. The Rust answer inverts it. The caller runs the loop, and the collection only knows how to give the next item. That inversion is why Rust iterators compose. A filter does not need to know what it filters, only how to ask for the next item and whether to pass it on. The slices and maps packages of Go now take and return an iterator function, a decade after Rust. C never will.

Carry forward
  • Sum type. One value that is one of several shapes, with a tag that says which. C checks nothing, Go checks at a type switch, and Rust checks at compile time.
  • Cursor. A number the client sends back so the server can continue a walk where it stopped, without holding the whole list.
  • Iterator. A value with a next method, which every adaptor wraps and nothing runs until something asks.
