Many clients#

Building kv · Chapter 09· 47 min read· 760 lines of code
▶Scene

Start the chapter 8 server and point redis-benchmark at it with its default fifty connections. Then, from a second terminal, ask it one question:

$ redis-benchmark -p 6380 -c 50 -n 1000 -t ping -q
PING_INLINE: rps=0.0 (overall: 262.2) avg_msec=0.000 (overall: 0.043)
$ redis-cli -p 6380 PING                              # terminal two
Could not connect to Redis at 127.0.0.1:6380: Operation timed out

The benchmark answered a few hundred requests in its first moment and then nothing. It never finishes. The second terminal waited fifteen seconds and could not even connect. One client is being served. Forty-nine are waiting, and the server does not know they exist.

kv serves one client at a time. This chapter makes it serve thousands. C gets an event loop on one thread, with the kernel's own list of ready sockets. Go gets a goroutine for each client and a load generator built from channels. Rust gets a thread for each client, the same tool built from scoped threads, and then the server on tokio.

The scene has a precise shape. The chapter 8 server accepts one connection and serves it until it closes. The benchmark keeps every connection open until the whole run ends, so the first client is never done. Behind it, the kernel keeps a queue of connections that are complete but not yet accepted. The server chose its length with listen(fd, 16) in chapter 3, so sixteen clients sit in that queue. The other thirty-three sent their first packet and got no answer at all. The kernel drops a connection it cannot queue, and the client tries again a second later, and again. That is the fifteen seconds.

There are two ways out, and the three languages take both. The first is to keep one thread and never block it. The thread asks the operating system which sockets have bytes waiting, reads from those, and asks again. That is an event loop, and it is what Redis does. The second is to give each client its own thread of control and let it block. The operating system or a runtime then switches between them. Go does that with goroutines. Rust does it with threads first, and then with tasks on an asynchronous runtime. That runtime is an event loop written as if each client had its own thread.

ConcurrencyCGoRust
One client isa heap struct the poller hands backa goroutinea thread, then a task
Who waitsone call, for all clients at onceeach goroutine, on its own readeach thread on its read, then the tokio runtime
Which sockets are readypoll, kqueue or epoll, chosen by #ifdefthe runtime asks, you never see itthe runtime asks, you never see it
Platform code lives ina file per system, under #ifdefa file per system, with a //go:build lineone function per system, with #[cfg]
Memory for a clienttwo buffers you sizea stack of a few kilobytes that growsa 2 MiB stack, then a task of a few kilobytes, mostly its buffers
The store is shared bynobody, there is one threada sync.RWMutexan Arc<Mutex<Store>>
Forgetting the locknot possiblea data race, which go test -race may finddoes not compile
Fifty workers talk throughnothing: C has no load generator herechannels and a WaitGroupan mpsc channel and a scope
Using all the coresnoyes, the runtime spreads goroutinesyes, with threads or with tokio
📜Readiness and completion: two shapes of the same question

The question "which socket can I use now?" got different answers on different systems, and every language has to hide the difference. Unix from Berkeley, the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD), answered first with select. poll came later and takes an array instead of a fixed-size set of bits. FreeBSD 4.1 added kqueue, which is what macOS uses. Linux added epoll in October 2002. All of those report readiness. They say "this socket has bytes", and the program then reads. Windows NT 3.5 took the other shape with I/O completion ports. A program hands the operating system a buffer and a read request, and the port reports completion. It says "this read has finished, and the bytes are in your buffer". The Go runtime and tokio both contain a layer that makes the two shapes look the same. That is why the Go and Rust versions of kv run on Windows unchanged, and the C one does not.

C: one thread, and a poller to say who is ready#

The loop keeps a structure for each client, holding the socket, the bytes read so far, and the replies not yet written. The buffers are the ones from chapter 4. The clients live on the heap, one allocation each, and the loop keeps an array of pointers to them. The poller in the next section stores a pointer to each client, so a client must never move:

/* One client: its socket, the bytes read so far, and the replies not yet written. */
typedef struct {
    int fd;
    kv_buf in;
    kv_buf out;
    bool writing; /* the poller is watching for room to write */
    bool closing; /* after a protocol error: close once out is written */
    bool dead;    /* gone; removed once the batch of events it was part of is done */
} kv_conn;

/* Every client, beside the poller that watches their sockets. The array holds
 * pointers, so a client stays where it is in memory when another one is removed, and
 * the tag the poller hands back stays valid. */
typedef struct {
    kv_conn **conns;
    size_t len;
    size_t cap;
    kv_poller *poller;
} kv_clients;
c/ch09/src/server.c · region conn

Every socket in the loop is non-blocking. A blocking read on a socket with no bytes would stop the one thread, and every other client with it. A non-blocking one returns -1 with errno set to EAGAIN, which means "nothing right now", and the loop moves on:

/* A non-blocking socket returns EAGAIN instead of waiting, which the loop relies on. */
static bool kv_set_nonblocking(int fd) {
    int flags = fcntl(fd, F_GETFL, 0);
    return flags >= 0 && fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK) >= 0;
}
c/ch09/src/server.c · region nonblock

Accepting clients follows the same rule. When the poller says the listening socket is ready, there may be several connections waiting, so the loop accepts until accept itself says EAGAIN:

/* Accept every waiting client. The listening socket is non-blocking, so accept()
 * returns EAGAIN when the queue is empty. */
static void kv_accept_all(int listen_fd, kv_clients *cs) {
    for (;;) {
        int fd = accept(listen_fd, NULL, NULL);
        if (fd < 0) {
            if (errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK || errno == EINTR) {
                return;
            }
            perror("accept");
            return;
        }
        if (!kv_set_nonblocking(fd) || !kv_clients_add(cs, fd)) {
            close(fd);
        }
    }
}
c/ch09/src/server.c · region accept

Reading from a ready client follows the pattern once more. Read until the socket is empty, then run every complete request in the buffer and queue the replies in the output buffer. The parser from chapter 4 was written for exactly this moment. Its KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE status looked like extra work in a one-client server. Here it lets the loop stop in the middle of a request and come back later:

/* Read what has arrived, run every complete request, and queue the replies. Returns
 * false when the client has gone or must be dropped. */
static bool kv_conn_input(kv_conn *c, kv_store *store) {
    char tmp[4096];
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = read(c->fd, tmp, sizeof tmp);
        if (n < 0) {
            if (errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK) {
                break; /* nothing more for now */
            }
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;
            }
            return false;
        }
        if (n == 0) {
            return false; /* the client closed */
        }
        if (!kv_buf_append(&c->in, tmp, (size_t)n)) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    for (;;) {
        kv_cmd cmd;
        size_t used = 0;
        kv_parse_status st = kv_parse(c->in.data, c->in.len, &cmd, &used);
        if (st == KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE && c->in.len > KV_MAX_REQUEST) {
            st = KV_PARSE_BAD; /* a request that never ends is not a request */
        }
        /* No default: with -Wall the compiler reports a status this switch forgot. */
        switch (st) {
        case KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE:
            return true; /* the poller says when more bytes arrive */
        case KV_PARSE_BAD:
            kv_reply_error(&c->out, "ERR Protocol error");
            c->closing = true;
            return true;
        case KV_PARSE_OK:
            if (!kv_exec(&cmd, store, &c->out)) {
                return false;
            }
            kv_buf_consume(&c->in, used);
            break;
        }
    }
}

When it returns EAGAIN, return true and stop, because the socket is full and the poller will say when it has room. Retry on EINTR. Return false on any other error.

Stuck?Show the full listing
/* Write as much of the queued reply as the socket will take right now. */
static bool kv_conn_output(kv_conn *c) {
    while (c->out.len > 0) {
        ssize_t w = write(c->fd, c->out.data, c->out.len);
        if (w < 0) {
            if (errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK) {
                return true; /* the socket is full: the poller will say when to continue */
            }
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;
            }
            return false;
        }
        kv_buf_consume(&c->out, (size_t)w);
    }
    return true;
}
c/ch09/src/server.c · region output

One function serves a client that the poller reported. It reads if there is input and writes if a reply is queued. Then it does two things that every event loop has to get right. It asks to be told about room to write only while a reply is waiting, because a socket is almost always writable. And it does not free a finished client. It marks it dead, because the batch of events may hold a second event for the same client:

/* One client had an event. Read if there is input, write if there is room or a reply is
 * queued, then ask to be told about room only while a reply is waiting. A socket is
 * almost always writable, so asking every time would make every wait return at once. */
static void kv_conn_ready(kv_clients *cs, kv_conn *c, const kv_event *ev, kv_store *store) {
    bool alive = true;
    if (ev->readable || ev->hangup) {
        alive = kv_conn_input(c, store);
    }
    if (alive && (ev->writable || c->out.len > 0)) {
        alive = kv_conn_output(c);
    }
    if (!alive || (c->closing && c->out.len == 0)) {
        c->dead = true; /* not freed yet: this batch may hold another event for it */
        return;
    }
    bool want = c->out.len > 0;
    if (want != c->writing && kv_poller_want_write(cs->poller, c->fd, c, want)) {
        c->writing = want;
    }
}
c/ch09/src/server.c · region ready

The loop itself is short. Wait, walk the batch, accept when the listening socket is ready and serve the client otherwise, then remove the dead. The removal walks backwards, so that moving the last client into a hole does not skip anyone:

int kv_server_run(int listen_fd, kv_store *store) {
    kv_clients cs = {0};
    cs.poller = kv_poller_new();
    /* the listening socket is watched too, with a null tag to tell it from a client */
    if (cs.poller == NULL || !kv_set_nonblocking(listen_fd) ||
        !kv_poller_add(cs.poller, listen_fd, NULL)) {
        kv_poller_free(cs.poller);
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(stderr, "kv waits with %s\n", kv_poller_name());
    kv_event events[64];
    for (;;) {
        int n = kv_poller_wait(cs.poller, events, 64, -1);
        if (n < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;
            }
            perror("wait");
            break;
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            kv_conn *c = events[i].tag;
            if (c == NULL) {
                kv_accept_all(listen_fd, &cs);
            } else if (!c->dead) {
                kv_conn_ready(&cs, c, &events[i], store);
            }
        }
        /* walk backwards, because removing a client moves the last one into its slot */
        for (size_t i = cs.len; i-- > 0;) {
            if (cs.conns[i]->dead) {
                kv_clients_remove(&cs, i);
            }
        }
    }
    for (size_t i = cs.len; i-- > 0;) {
        kv_clients_remove(&cs, i);
    }
    free(cs.conns);
    kv_poller_free(cs.poller);
    return 1;
}
c/ch09/src/server.c · region loop

About two hundred lines of new code, and the server now serves fifty clients from one thread. It also uses one core, which is the limit of this design, and the one Redis still lives with for running commands. The main function shrinks to a call, with one addition. Every client is an open file, and a process starts with a soft limit on those, often 256 on macOS and 1,024 on Linux. The server raises its limit to the hard one, as Redis does, and says how many clients that leaves room for:

/* Every client is an open file, and a process starts with a soft limit on those, often
 * 256 on macOS and 1024 on Linux. Raise it to the hard limit, as Redis does, and say
 * how many clients that leaves room for. */
static void kv_raise_fd_limit(void) {
    struct rlimit lim;
    if (getrlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE, &lim) < 0) {
        return;
    }
    if (lim.rlim_cur < lim.rlim_max && setrlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE, &(struct rlimit){lim.rlim_max, lim.rlim_max}) == 0) {
        lim.rlim_cur = lim.rlim_max;
    }
    if (lim.rlim_cur == RLIM_INFINITY) {
        fprintf(stderr, "kv has no limit on open files\n");
    } else {
        /* the listener, the poller, stdio and some spare take the rest */
        fprintf(stderr, "kv can hold %llu clients\n", (unsigned long long)lim.rlim_cur - 32);
    }
}
c/ch09/src/main.c · region fdlimit
⚠️One blocking call stops every client C

Forget O_NONBLOCK on one socket and a slow client stops the server. The poller says the socket is readable, and the loop calls read. A client that sent half a request and went away keeps the one thread waiting for the other half. The other forty-nine clients see a server that has stopped answering. Nothing crashes and nothing is reported, which makes it one of the harder bugs to find in a C server. That is one reason the kv_set_nonblocking call is the first thing done with every new socket.

C again: poll, kqueue and epoll behind one header#

The loop above never names poll. It talks to a poller, which is six functions in a header, and the header decides which of three files provides them. The preprocessor decides, from macros the compiler defines for the target. There is no runtime check and no configuration file. The files that do not match compile to nothing, because everything in them sits under an #ifdef:

/* One of poller_poll.c, poller_kqueue.c and poller_epoll.c holds the code; the other two
 * compile to nothing. The compiler predefines a macro for the target: __linux__ on
 * Linux, __APPLE__ on macOS, __FreeBSD__ on FreeBSD. KV_POLL on the command line, as in
 * `make kv KV_POLL=1`, forces the portable poll() version on any system. */
#if defined(KV_POLL)
#define KV_POLLER_POLL 1
#elif defined(__linux__)
#define KV_POLLER_EPOLL 1
#elif defined(__APPLE__) || defined(__FreeBSD__)
#define KV_POLLER_KQUEUE 1
#else
#define KV_POLLER_POLL 1
#endif
c/ch09/src/poller.h · region choose

The six functions are the smallest shape the three system calls have in common. A socket is added with a tag, which comes back in every event for that socket, and the tag is the client pointer. A wait fills an array of events and says how many:

typedef struct kv_poller kv_poller;

/* What a wait reports for one socket: the tag given when it was added, and which of
 * the three things happened to it. */
typedef struct {
    void *tag;
    bool readable;
    bool writable;
    bool hangup;
} kv_event;

kv_poller *kv_poller_new(void);
void kv_poller_free(kv_poller *p);

/* Watch fd for input. The tag comes back in every event for fd. */
bool kv_poller_add(kv_poller *p, int fd, void *tag);

/* Also watch fd for room to write, or stop watching for it. */
bool kv_poller_want_write(kv_poller *p, int fd, void *tag, bool want);

/* Stop watching fd. Call it before close(). */
void kv_poller_remove(kv_poller *p, int fd);

/* Block until a socket is ready or timeout_ms passes, where -1 means wait for ever.
 * Fills up to max events and returns how many, 0 on timeout, or -1 with errno set. */
int kv_poller_wait(kv_poller *p, kv_event *events, int max, int timeout_ms);

/* "poll", "kqueue" or "epoll", for the startup line. */
const char *kv_poller_name(void);
c/ch09/src/poller.h · region api

poll is in POSIX, the Portable Operating System Interface, so its file builds anywhere, and make kv KV_POLL=1 asks for it on any system. Its cost is that every call gives the kernel the whole array to walk. So one wait costs more with every client. kqueue on macOS and epoll on Linux keep the list in the kernel. Adding a socket is one call. A wait sends nothing and gets back only the sockets that changed. The Linux file is the shorter one, and its state is one descriptor:

/* The whole state is one descriptor: the kernel holds the list. */
struct kv_poller {
    int ep;
};

kv_poller *kv_poller_new(void) {
    kv_poller *p = malloc(sizeof *p);
    if (p == NULL) {
        return NULL;
    }
    p->ep = epoll_create1(0);
    if (p->ep < 0) {
        free(p);
        return NULL;
    }
    return p;
}

void kv_poller_free(kv_poller *p) {
    if (p != NULL) {
        close(p->ep);
        free(p);
    }
}

/* One socket has one entry with one mask of events, so a change replaces the mask. */
static bool kv_ep_ctl(kv_poller *p, int op, int fd, uint32_t mask, void *tag) {
    struct epoll_event change = {.events = mask, .data.ptr = tag};
    return epoll_ctl(p->ep, op, fd, &change) == 0;
}

bool kv_poller_add(kv_poller *p, int fd, void *tag) {
    return kv_ep_ctl(p, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd, EPOLLIN, tag);
}

bool kv_poller_want_write(kv_poller *p, int fd, void *tag, bool want) {
    return kv_ep_ctl(p, EPOLL_CTL_MOD, fd, EPOLLIN | (want ? EPOLLOUT : 0), tag);
}

/* close() drops a socket from the list by itself, unless another descriptor refers to
 * the same socket, which is why the explicit call is the safe habit. */
void kv_poller_remove(kv_poller *p, int fd) {
    epoll_ctl(p->ep, EPOLL_CTL_DEL, fd, NULL);
}

int kv_poller_wait(kv_poller *p, kv_event *events, int max, int timeout_ms) {
    struct epoll_event ready[64];
    if (max > 64) {
        max = 64;
    }
    int n = epoll_wait(p->ep, ready, max, timeout_ms);
    if (n <= 0) {
        return n;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        uint32_t mask = ready[i].events;
        events[i] = (kv_event){
            .tag = ready[i].data.ptr,
            .readable = (mask & EPOLLIN) != 0,
            .writable = (mask & EPOLLOUT) != 0,
            .hangup = (mask & (EPOLLHUP | EPOLLERR)) != 0,
        };
    }
    return n;
}

const char *kv_poller_name(void) {
    return "epoll";
}
c/ch09/src/poller_epoll.c · region epoll

The designated initialisers, .events = mask and .data.ptr = tag, name the fields they set and leave the rest zero. They are the C way to build a struct without remembering the order of its fields. Redis has the same three files and a fourth for select, and picks one the same way.

Exercise 09.2CWrite the kqueue poller

Write poller_kqueue.c for macOS and FreeBSD. The whole state is one descriptor from kqueue(). One call, kevent, both changes the list and waits on it. So write a helper that makes one change with EV_SET and asks for no results. A filter is one kind of event on one socket. Watching a socket for reading and for writing is two entries, and a wait can report the socket twice. The loop in the previous section already copes with that. Treat EV_DELETE of a filter that was never added as success.

struct kv_poller {
    int kq;
};

static bool kv_kq_change(kv_poller *p, int fd, int16_t filter, uint16_t flags, void *tag) {
    /* your code here: EV_SET, then kevent with one change and no results */
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/* The whole state is one descriptor: the kernel holds the list. */
struct kv_poller {
    int kq;
};

kv_poller *kv_poller_new(void) {
    kv_poller *p = malloc(sizeof *p);
    if (p == NULL) {
        return NULL;
    }
    p->kq = kqueue();
    if (p->kq < 0) {
        free(p);
        return NULL;
    }
    return p;
}

void kv_poller_free(kv_poller *p) {
    if (p != NULL) {
        close(p->kq);
        free(p);
    }
}

/* kevent() both changes the list and waits on it. This call only changes it: one
 * entry, no room for results, no timeout. A filter is one kind of event on one socket,
 * so a socket watched for reading and for writing is two entries. */
static bool kv_kq_change(kv_poller *p, int fd, int16_t filter, uint16_t flags, void *tag) {
    struct kevent change;
    EV_SET(&change, (uintptr_t)fd, filter, flags, 0, 0, tag);
    if (kevent(p->kq, &change, 1, NULL, 0, NULL) < 0) {
        /* deleting a filter that was never added is not an error worth stopping for */
        return (flags & EV_DELETE) && errno == ENOENT;
    }
    return true;
}

bool kv_poller_add(kv_poller *p, int fd, void *tag) {
    return kv_kq_change(p, fd, EVFILT_READ, EV_ADD, tag);
}

bool kv_poller_want_write(kv_poller *p, int fd, void *tag, bool want) {
    return kv_kq_change(p, fd, EVFILT_WRITE, want ? EV_ADD : EV_DELETE, tag);
}

/* close() drops a socket from every kqueue by itself; this only makes it explicit. */
void kv_poller_remove(kv_poller *p, int fd) {
    kv_kq_change(p, fd, EVFILT_READ, EV_DELETE, NULL);
    kv_kq_change(p, fd, EVFILT_WRITE, EV_DELETE, NULL);
}

int kv_poller_wait(kv_poller *p, kv_event *events, int max, int timeout_ms) {
    struct kevent ready[64];
    if (max > 64) {
        max = 64;
    }
    struct timespec ts = {timeout_ms / 1000, (timeout_ms % 1000) * 1000000L};
    int n = kevent(p->kq, NULL, 0, ready, max, timeout_ms < 0 ? NULL : &ts);
    if (n <= 0) {
        return n;
    }
    /* A socket ready for both reading and writing is two entries, with the same tag.
     * The loop that gets them copes with that, so they are passed on as they are. */
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        events[i] = (kv_event){
            .tag = ready[i].udata,
            .readable = ready[i].filter == EVFILT_READ,
            .writable = ready[i].filter == EVFILT_WRITE,
            .hangup = (ready[i].flags & (EV_EOF | EV_ERROR)) != 0,
        };
    }
    return n;
}

const char *kv_poller_name(void) {
    return "kqueue";
}
c/ch09/src/poller_kqueue.c · region kqueue

Build the server both ways, and the startup line names the poller. At fifty clients they run at the same speed, because fifty sockets are not enough for the cost of poll to show:

$ make kv && ./kv
kv waits with kqueue
$ make clean && make kv KV_POLL=1 && ./kv
kv waits with poll
🖥Windows, and the loop turned inside out

The three pollers all report readiness, so one loop fits all of them. Windows reports completion, so a fourth file would not be enough. The loop itself would change, and chapter 14 comes back to what that means for porting the C version.

Go: one word, and one lock#

The Go change in main is the keyword go. The call serve(conn, s) runs on a new goroutine, and the loop goes straight back to Accept. The serving function is unchanged. It still blocks on its reads, which is fine, because it blocks only its own goroutine, and the runtime runs another:

func main() {
	ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", ":"+port())
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "kv listening on port", port())
	if n, ok := sys.OpenFiles(); ok {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "kv can hold", n-32, "clients")
	}
	s := store.New()
	for {
		conn, err := ln.Accept()
		if err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "accept:", err)
			continue
		}
		// the one word that changes: the client is served on its own goroutine, and
		// the loop goes straight back to accept
		go func() {
			if err := serve(conn, s); err != nil {
				fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "client:", err)
			}
		}()
	}
}
go/ch09/cmd/kv/main.go · region main

A goroutine is not a thread. The Go FAQ says one costs "little overhead beyond the memory for the stack", which is a few kilobytes. It also says it "is practical to create hundreds of thousands of goroutines in the same address space". The event loop that C needed is inside the runtime, and it talks to kqueue or epoll or a completion port on your behalf.

The runtime in one paragraph#

As many threads run Go code as GOMAXPROCS allows, which by default is the number of CPUs the process may use. Each thread takes a goroutine from a queue and runs it until it blocks, or for ten milliseconds. A goroutine that blocks on a socket is parked, and the runtime's poller queues it again when the socket is ready. One that blocks in a system call keeps its thread, and the runtime starts another. None of this appears in the code, and all of it appears in the numbers at the end of the chapter.

The price appears in the store. Fifty goroutines now call Set and Get at the same time, and a Go map is not safe for that. The language FAQ says that a mutex on every map operation "would slow down most programs and add safety to few". So the store adds its own, a read-write lock. Readers take RLock and may hold it together. Writers take Lock and hold it alone:

// Store keeps every key and its value in a map, behind a lock. Many goroutines read and
// write the store at once, and a Go map is not safe for that without one. The value is
// any of the four kinds in value.go.
type Store struct {
	mu sync.RWMutex
	m  map[string]any
}

func New() *Store {
	return &Store{m: make(map[string]any)}
}

// Get takes the read lock, which any number of readers may hold together.
func (s *Store) Get(key []byte) (any, bool) {
	s.mu.RLock()
	defer s.mu.RUnlock()
	v, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	return v, ok
}

// Set takes the write lock, which excludes every other reader and writer.
func (s *Store) Set(key []byte, val any) {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	s.m[string(key)] = val
}

func (s *Store) Del(key []byte) bool {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	_, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	delete(s.m, string(key))
	return ok
}

func (s *Store) Len() int {
	s.mu.RLock()
	defer s.mu.RUnlock()
	return len(s.m)
}

// Keys returns every key that matches the pattern, in no particular order.
func (s *Store) Keys(pattern []byte) [][]byte {
	s.mu.RLock()
	defer s.mu.RUnlock()
	var out [][]byte
	for k := range s.m {
		if glob(pattern, []byte(k)) {
			out = append(out, []byte(k))
		}
	}
	return out
}

// Scan returns a page of keys from the cursor on, in sorted order, and the cursor for
// the next page, or 0 when the walk is done.
func (s *Store) Scan(cursor uint64, count int) (uint64, [][]byte) {
	s.mu.RLock()
	defer s.mu.RUnlock()
	sorted := slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(s.m))
	if cursor >= uint64(len(sorted)) {
		return 0, nil
	}
	end := min(int(cursor)+count, len(sorted))
	var page [][]byte
	for _, k := range sorted[cursor:end] {
		page = append(page, []byte(k))
	}
	if end == len(sorted) {
		return 0, page
	}
	return uint64(end), page
}

Exercise 09.3GoMake INCR atomic

Rewrite Incr so that it holds the write lock from the moment it reads the old value to the moment it writes the new one. Do not call Get and Set inside it. Each of those takes the lock again, and a Go lock cannot be taken twice by the same goroutine. Read and write the map directly.

func (s *Store) Incr(key []byte) (int64, error) {
	// your code here: lock, read s.m, parse, add, write s.m, unlock
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
// Incr holds the write lock from the read to the write, so that two clients that
// increment the same key at the same moment cannot both read the same old value.
func (s *Store) Incr(key []byte) (int64, error) {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	var n int64
	if cur, ok := s.m[string(key)]; ok {
		b, isStr := cur.([]byte)
		if !isStr {
			return 0, ErrWrongType
		}
		var err error
		n, err = strconv.ParseInt(string(b), 10, 64)
		if err != nil {
			return 0, ErrNotInteger
		}
	}
	if n == math.MaxInt64 {
		return 0, ErrOverflow
	}
	n++
	s.m[string(key)] = []byte(strconv.FormatInt(n, 10))
	return n, nil
}
go/ch09/internal/store/store.go · region incr

Without the single lock, two clients can both read 41, both write 42, and one increment is lost. The test below adds one to the same key from fifty goroutines, two hundred times each, and expects exactly ten thousand. The WaitGroup counts the goroutines, and its Go method, new in Go 1.25, starts one and counts it in one call. Wait blocks until every one of them has returned:

// TestIncrFromManyGoroutines adds one to the same key from 50 goroutines, 200 times
// each. With the lock the result is 10000. Without it, go test -race reports the data
// race, and the count comes out short.
func TestIncrFromManyGoroutines(t *testing.T) {
	s := New()
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	for range 50 {
		wg.Go(func() {
			for range 200 {
				if _, err := s.Incr([]byte("n")); err != nil {
					t.Error(err)
				}
			}
		})
	}
	wg.Wait()
	got, _ := s.Get([]byte("n"))
	if b, _ := got.([]byte); string(b) != "10000" {
		t.Fatalf("n = %s, want 10000", got)
	}
}
go/ch09/internal/store/store_test.go · region test
$ go test -race ./...
ok  	kv/internal/store	1.514s

The -race flag turns on the race detector. It watches every memory access during the test, and reports two goroutines that touch the same byte without a lock between them. Remove the lock from Incr and the test fails twice. The count comes out short, and the detector prints both stack traces. Keep the flag on in every test run, which the book's make verify does.

⚠️The race detector finds races that happen, not races that exist Go

A race the test never provokes is a race the detector never reports. The detector watches real accesses, so a missing lock on a path the test does not run stays hidden until production runs it. It is a tool for finding races, not a proof that there are none. The Rust compiler makes the other kind of claim later in this chapter.

Go again: fifty workers and three channels#

The scene said that one client was served and forty-nine waited. A tool that counts who got answered can prove it, and it is the best place to meet the rest of Go's concurrency. kvload is a worker pool. One goroutine for each connection, a channel of jobs they all take from, and channels of answers they all send to:

// answer is one round trip: which connection made it and how long it took.
type answer struct {
	worker int
	took   time.Duration
}

// worker owns one connection. It takes job after job from the channel until the channel
// is closed and empty, and reports each round trip on answers, or its first error on
// errs, after which it gives up.
func worker(id int, addr string, jobs <-chan int, answers chan<- answer, errs chan<- error) {
	conn, err := net.Dial("tcp", addr)
	if err != nil {
		errs <- fmt.Errorf("worker %d: %w", id, err)
		return
	}
	defer conn.Close()
	r := bufio.NewReader(conn)
	for range jobs {
		start := time.Now()
		if _, err := conn.Write([]byte("PING\r\n")); err != nil {
			errs <- fmt.Errorf("worker %d: %w", id, err)
			return
		}
		if _, err := r.ReadString('\n'); err != nil {
			errs <- fmt.Errorf("worker %d: %w", id, err)
			return
		}
		answers <- answer{id, time.Since(start)}
	}
}
go/ch09/cmd/kvload/main.go · region worker

The for range jobs loop receives from the channel until the channel is closed and empty, and then ends. The channel types in the signature say which way each one flows, and the compiler holds the worker to that. The main function fills the jobs channel, starts the workers, and then waits on three things at once:

func main() {
	addr := flag.String("addr", "127.0.0.1:6380", "the server")
	clients := flag.Int("c", 50, "connections")
	n := flag.Int("n", 10000, "requests in total")
	timeout := flag.Duration("timeout", 5*time.Second, "give up after this long")
	flag.Parse()

	// A buffered channel holds every job up front. Closing it tells the workers that
	// nothing more is coming: their range loops end once the buffer is empty.
	jobs := make(chan int, *n)
	for i := range *n {
		jobs <- i
	}
	close(jobs)

	answers := make(chan answer, *n)
	errs := make(chan error, *clients)
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	for id := range *clients {
		wg.Go(func() { worker(id, *addr, jobs, answers, errs) })
	}
	// Only the sender may close a channel, and here there are many senders, so a
	// goroutine of its own waits for all of them and closes both channels after.
	go func() {
		wg.Wait()
		close(answers)
		close(errs)
	}()

	start := time.Now()
	var took []time.Duration
	byWorker := map[int]int{}
	failed := 0
	deadline := time.After(*timeout)
	// select waits on three channels at once. A closed channel is set to nil, and a nil
	// channel never fires, which takes its case out of the select until the loop ends.
	for answers != nil || errs != nil {
		select {
		case a, ok := <-answers:
			if !ok {
				answers = nil
				continue
			}
			took = append(took, a.took)
			byWorker[a.worker]++
		case err, ok := <-errs:
			if !ok {
				errs = nil
				continue
			}
			failed++
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		case <-deadline:
			// the workers still blocked on a read are left behind: the process is
			// about to exit, so their goroutines go with it
			fmt.Printf("gave up after %v\n", *timeout)
			answers, errs = nil, nil
		}
	}
	report(took, byWorker, *clients, failed, time.Since(start))
}
go/ch09/cmd/kvload/main.go · region main

Four rules of channels are in that function. A channel with a buffer holds that many values without a receiver, so jobs can be filled before any worker exists. Closing a channel is how a sender says "no more". The language specification says that "sending to or closing a closed channel causes a run-time panic". So only the side that sends may close, and only once. That is why a goroutine of its own waits for every worker and then closes the two result channels. A select waits on several channels and takes the first that is ready, and with a default case it does not wait at all. And a nil channel "is never ready for communication", which sounds useless until a case must be switched off. Setting a closed channel to nil is the idiom, and the loop ends when both are nil.

The deadline case is the one to study. time.After returns a channel that delivers once, after the duration. When it fires, the workers still blocked on a read are abandoned, and the program exits with them still there. That is a goroutine leak, the Go bug that replaces the C memory leak. A goroutine that waits for a reply that never comes lives until the process ends, with its stack. Here the process ends at once. In a server that runs for a year it matters, and the cure is a timeout or a context, which chapter 10 adds. Run the tool against the chapter 8 server and then against this one:

$ go run ./cmd/kvload                        # the chapter 8 server, one client at a time
10000 answered by 17 of 50 connections, 9984 of them by one, 0 failed, 2.07 s in all
p50 0.045 ms, max 539.894 ms
$ go run ./cmd/kvload                        # the chapter 9 server
10000 answered by 50 of 50 connections, 232 of them by one, 0 failed, 0.11 s in all
p50 0.525 ms, max 1.861 ms

Seventeen is one plus sixteen. One connection was served and took nearly every job. Sixteen sat in the kernel's queue with their first PING already sent, and were answered once each when the first one closed. The other thirty-three connected after the jobs were gone. The second run is the chapter. Every connection was served, in a tenth of a second.

The rest of the sync package#

The rest of the sync package is short, and kv needs none of it yet. Once "will perform exactly one action", however many goroutines call it. Pool is a cache of temporary objects, such as buffers, that relieves "pressure on the garbage collector". sync/atomic gives a counter or a flag that many goroutines may change without a lock. Its own documentation says most code should use channels or a mutex instead. The Go proverb behind all of it says to share memory by communicating, and not to communicate by sharing memory. The channels in kvload are that proverb, and the lock in the store is its exception.

Go's platform files: a line at the top#

C chose its poller with #ifdef. Go has no preprocessor, so it chooses files. A comment on the first line, before the package clause, says which systems a file belongs to, and the compiler ignores the file everywhere else. The one place kv needs it is the open-file limit. Since Go 1.19, programs that import the os package "automatically increase the open file limit (RLIMIT_NOFILE) to the maximum allowed value". Reading it back is a system call that Windows does not have, so there are two files. One for every Unix:

// OpenFiles reports how many files, and so how many clients, the process may hold open.
// The Go runtime has already raised the soft limit to the hard one at startup.
func OpenFiles() (uint64, bool) {
	var lim syscall.Rlimit
	if err := syscall.Getrlimit(syscall.RLIMIT_NOFILE, &lim); err != nil {
		return 0, false
	}
	return lim.Cur, true
}
go/ch09/internal/sys/limit_unix.go · region unix

And one for everything else, with the opposite constraint, so that exactly one of them is ever in the build:

// OpenFiles reports false where the system has no such limit to ask about.
func OpenFiles() (uint64, bool) {
	return 0, false
}
go/ch09/internal/sys/limit_other.go · region other

A file name ending in _linux.go is the same constraint without the comment. GOOS=windows go vet ./... checks the other file without a Windows machine.

Rust: a thread for each client, and a compiler that checks the sharing#

The thread version is the Go version with the sharing made explicit. The store is wrapped in two types. An Arc counts how many owners the store has. A Mutex lets one thread at a time use it. Each new thread gets a clone of the Arc, which is a new owner of the same store:

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let port = port();
    let listener = TcpListener::bind(format!("0.0.0.0:{port}"))?;
    eprintln!("kv listening on port {port}");
    if let Some(n) = kv::sys::open_files() {
        eprintln!("kv can hold {} clients", n - 32);
    }
    let store = Arc::new(Mutex::new(MapStore::new()));
    for stream in listener.incoming() {
        match stream {
            Ok(stream) => {
                // a clone of the Arc is a new owner of the same store, moved into the thread
                let store = Arc::clone(&store);
                thread::spawn(move || {
                    if let Err(e) = serve(stream, store) {
                        eprintln!("client: {e}");
                    }
                });
            }
            Err(e) => eprintln!("accept: {e}"),
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}
rust/ch09/src/main.rs · region main

Inside the serving function, the lock is taken for one command. It is released at the end of the line, when the guard goes out of scope. The unwrap_or_else handles a poisoned lock, which is what a mutex becomes when a thread panics while holding it. The store is still usable, so the server takes it anyway:

/// The store is shared: an Arc counts the owners, and a Mutex lets one thread at a
/// time use it. The lock is taken for one command and released at the end of the line.
fn serve(stream: TcpStream, store: Arc<Mutex<MapStore>>) -> resp::Result<()> {
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream.try_clone()?);
    let mut writer = BufWriter::new(stream);
    loop {
        match resp::read_command(&mut reader) {
            Ok(Some(args)) => {
                let mut store = store.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
                cmd::execute(args, &mut *store, &mut writer)?;
            }
            Ok(None) => return Ok(()),
            Err(e @ resp::KvError::Protocol(_)) => {
                resp::write_error(&mut writer, "ERR Protocol error")?;
                writer.flush()?;
                return Err(e);
            }
            Err(e) => return Err(e),
        }
        if reader.buffer().is_empty() {
            writer.flush()?;
        }
    }
}
rust/ch09/src/main.rs · region serve

What happens without the Arc and the Mutex? The compiler refuses. Try to move one Store into two threads and it says error[E0382]: use of moved value: store. Try to share a reference instead and the compiler refuses that too, because the thread may outlive main. The only way through is a type that is safe to share, and Arc<Mutex<T>> is the simplest one. The rule is the one the borrow checker applied in chapter 5. A value can have many readers or one writer, never both, and a thread is only another reader or writer. A data race in a Rust program that compiles without unsafe is not possible. The race detector that Go runs at test time is work the Rust compiler does at compile time.

Send and Sync#

The check has a name, and you met the single-threaded half of it in chapter 6. Replace the Arc with an Rc. Replace the Mutex with a RefCell, which shares and mutates a value as well on one thread. The compiler says:

error[E0277]: `Rc<RefCell<MapStore>>` cannot be sent between threads safely
   --> src/main.rs:57:31
    |
 57 |                 thread::spawn(move || {
    |                 ------------- ^------
    = help: within `{closure@src/main.rs:57:31: 57:38}`, the trait `Send` is not implemented
            for `Rc<RefCell<MapStore>>`
note: required by a bound in `spawn`
    |
128 |     F: Send + 'static,

Send and Sync are two marker traits with no methods. Send means a value may move to another thread. Sync means a reference to it may be shared between threads. The compiler derives both for every type from its parts. A type that holds an Rc loses Send. The reason is that Rc counts its owners without atomic operations, and two threads updating that count at once "is undefined behavior". The spawn function demands Send of its closure, as the note says. So thread safety in Rust is two traits, derived by the compiler and demanded where a value crosses between threads. There is nothing to remember, and no way to forget.

Rust again: the load generator with scoped threads#

The Rust kvload has the shape of the Go one, with each Go idea replaced by the Rust one. A worker owns one connection. The jobs are a counter, an AtomicUsize, rather than a channel. Its fetch_add returns the old value, so every job number is given out once without a lock. The answers go back on an mpsc channel, which has many senders and one receiver, as its name says. The timeout is on the socket, for a reason that comes in a moment:

/// One connection. It takes job numbers from the shared counter until they run out and
/// sends each round trip on the channel. An error ends the worker, and the caller
/// reports it. The read timeout is what lets a worker give up on a server that never
/// answers, because a scoped thread must finish before the scope ends.
fn worker(
    id: usize,
    addr: SocketAddr,
    jobs: &AtomicUsize,
    total: usize,
    timeout: Duration,
    answers: &mpsc::Sender<Answer>,
) -> io::Result<()> {
    let mut stream = TcpStream::connect_timeout(&addr, timeout)?;
    stream.set_read_timeout(Some(timeout))?;
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream.try_clone()?);
    let mut line = String::new();
    // fetch_add returns the old value, so every job number is handed out exactly once
    while jobs.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed) < total {
        let start = Instant::now();
        stream.write_all(b"PING\r\n")?;
        line.clear();
        if reader.read_line(&mut line)? == 0 {
            return Err(io::ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof.into());
        }
        // send fails only when main has stopped listening, and then there is nothing to do
        let _ = answers.send(Answer {
            worker: id,
            took: start.elapsed(),
        });
    }
    Ok(())
}
rust/ch09/src/bin/kvload.rs · region worker

The main function is the interesting half. The workers borrow the counter and the sender from main's own stack frame, with no Arc and no cloning of anything but the sender. That is what thread::scope is for. The standard library says that "the scope guarantees all threads will be joined at the end of the scope". No thread outlives the data it borrows, so the borrow checker allows it:

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let (addr, clients, total, timeout) = args();
    let jobs = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
    let failed = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    let start = Instant::now();
    // The scope borrows jobs, failed and tx from this stack frame, and the threads it
    // spawns can use them without an Arc, because the scope joins every thread before
    // it returns. No thread outlives the data.
    let mut took: Vec<Duration> = thread::scope(|s| {
        for id in 0..clients {
            let tx = tx.clone();
            let (jobs, failed) = (&jobs, &failed);
            s.spawn(move || {
                if let Err(e) = worker(id, addr, jobs, total, timeout, &tx) {
                    failed.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                    eprintln!("worker {id}: {e}");
                }
            });
        }
        // Each worker holds a clone of the sender. Once main drops its own, the receiver
        // ends when the last worker drops the last clone, which ends the for loop.
        drop(tx);
        let mut took = Vec::new();
        let mut by_worker = vec![0usize; clients];
        for answer in rx {
            took.push(answer.took);
            by_worker[answer.worker] += 1;
        }
        let answered = by_worker.iter().filter(|n| **n > 0).count();
        let most = by_worker.iter().max().copied().unwrap_or(0);
        println!(
            "{} answered by {answered} of {clients} connections, {most} of them by one, {} failed, {:.2} s in all",
            took.len(),
            failed.load(Ordering::Relaxed),
            start.elapsed().as_secs_f64()
        );
        took
    });
    if !took.is_empty() {
        took.sort();
        let ms = |d: Duration| d.as_secs_f64() * 1e3;
        println!(
            "p50 {:.3} ms, max {:.3} ms",
            ms(took[took.len() / 2]),
            ms(took[took.len() - 1])
        );
    }
    Ok(())
}
rust/ch09/src/bin/kvload.rs · region main

The channel ends the loop. Each worker holds a clone of the sender. When the last worker drops the last clone, the receiver reports that the channel is disconnected, and the for loop ends. The main thread has to drop its own sender first, or the loop would wait for ever. That replaces the WaitGroup, the closing goroutine and the nil channels of the Go version. The scope replaces the leak. A scoped thread must finish before the scope returns, so a stuck worker cannot be abandoned the way the Go version abandons it. The read timeout on the socket is what lets it give up and report an error. The result against the chapter 8 server is the same seventeen:

$ cargo run --release --bin kvload           # the chapter 8 server
10000 answered by 17 of 50 connections, 9984 of them by one, 0 failed, 2.06 s in all
p50 0.033 ms, max 410.443 ms
$ cargo run --release --bin kvload           # the chapter 9 server
10000 answered by 50 of 50 connections, 221 of them by one, 0 failed, 0.12 s in all
p50 0.540 ms, max 2.066 ms

Atomics#

An atomic is an integer that many threads may change without a lock, because the processor does each operation in one step. Every operation takes an Ordering, which says what else it promises about memory. Relaxed promises nothing beyond the counter itself, which is enough here and not enough for publishing data to another thread. A mutex or a channel promises that. Both are built from atomics, and so is Arc, which is why it may cross threads and Rc may not.

RwLock#

Go's store took a read-write lock, and Rust has the same type. A RwLock "allows a number of readers or at most one writer at any point in time". The server does not use it yet, because every command takes the store mutably. Chapter 13 makes the commands say which of them only read, and measures what the read lock gives.

📰Mars Pathfinder, 1997

A few days after it landed on Mars in July 1997, the Pathfinder lander began resetting itself. Its software ran on VxWorks, with tasks at fixed priorities and a shared area of memory behind a mutex. A low-priority task that published weather data took the mutex. A medium-priority communications task then preempted it and ran for a long time. The high-priority task that managed the shared memory waited for the mutex, behind a task that could not run. A watchdog noticed that the high-priority task had not run and reset the whole system. The engineers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory reproduced it on the replica in their lab, with tracing on, and saw a classic priority inversion. The mutex had been created with priority inheritance turned off. They uploaded a short C program that changed the flag from FALSE to TRUE, and the resets stopped. A lock is a promise about memory, which Go checks at test time and Rust at compile time. It is also a promise about time, who holds it and for how long, and no language checks that one. Taking the lock for one command and dropping it at the end of the line is the answer kv has.

Rust's platform code: an attribute on the item#

Rust answers the platform question with an attribute, not a file. #[cfg(unix)] on a function, a module or a statement keeps it out of the build on every other system. #[cfg(target_os = "linux")] names one system. The open-file limit is the one place kv needs it, and the standard library has no call for it. So the function asks the C library, through the libc crate, which tokio already depends on. That call is the first unsafe block in the book. The word marks a promise the compiler cannot check, and chapter 15 is about it:

/// How many files, and so how many clients, the process may hold open. The standard
/// library has no call for it, so this asks the C library, which chapter 15 explains.
#[cfg(unix)]
pub fn open_files() -> Option<u64> {
    let mut lim = libc::rlimit {
        rlim_cur: 0,
        rlim_max: 0,
    };
    // SAFETY: getrlimit writes one struct through a valid pointer and reads nothing.
    let rc = unsafe { libc::getrlimit(libc::RLIMIT_NOFILE, &mut lim) };
    (rc == 0 && lim.rlim_cur != libc::RLIM_INFINITY).then_some(lim.rlim_cur)
}
rust/ch09/src/sys.rs · region unix

The other version carries the opposite condition, so that exactly one of them is compiled:

/// Where the system has no such limit to ask about, the answer is None.
#[cfg(not(unix))]
pub fn open_files() -> Option<u64> {
    None
}

Rust once more: tasks on tokio#

A thread for each client works for fifty clients and for five thousand. Each thread has a 2 MiB stack, on every main platform. So fifty thousand threads would reserve a hundred gigabytes of stack. The operating system limits how many threads a process may create long before that. The answer is the C answer, an event loop, with the Go answer on top of it. That is a cheap unit of concurrency that looks like a thread. In Rust that is an async task, and the runtime that schedules tasks is a library, not part of the language. The one almost everyone uses is tokio, and it becomes the first line in the [dependencies] section of Cargo.toml:

$ cargo add tokio@1 --features rt-multi-thread,net,io-util,macros
      Adding tokio v1.53.2 to dependencies

That command also writes Cargo.lock, with the exact version of tokio and of the fourteen crates it depends on. Every later build uses those versions until you ask for new ones, which is what the lock file is for. The server is a second binary in the same crate, src/bin/kv_async.rs. Its serving function looks like the thread version with one word added after every read and write:

/// The replies are written into a Vec first, with the ordinary synchronous command
/// code from the library, and then sent with one awaited write. The lock is never held
/// across an await, so a plain std Mutex is the right one.
async fn serve(stream: TcpStream, store: Arc<Mutex<MapStore>>) -> resp::Result<()> {
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream);
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    loop {
        match read_command(&mut reader).await {
            Ok(Some(args)) => {
                let mut store = store.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
                cmd::execute(args, &mut *store, &mut out)?;
            }
            Ok(None) => return Ok(()),
            Err(e @ KvError::Protocol(_)) => {
                resp::write_error(&mut out, "ERR Protocol error")?;
                reader.get_mut().write_all(&out).await?;
                return Err(e);
            }
            Err(e) => return Err(e),
        }
        if reader.buffer().is_empty() {
            reader.get_mut().write_all(&out).await?;
            out.clear();
        }
    }
}
rust/ch09/src/bin/kv_async.rs · region serve

What a future is#

An async fn does not run when it is called. It returns a future, which the standard library defines as "a value that might not have finished computing yet". A future has one method, poll. It "attempts to resolve the future into a final value" and returns either Ready with the value or Pending. "Futures alone are inert", the documentation says. Nothing happens until a runtime polls them. A waker, a handle the future stores and the socket wakes, tells the runtime when to poll again. Each .await in the function above is a point where the task may return Pending and let another task use the thread. That is the C event loop with the bookkeeping done by the compiler. It turns the function into a state machine with one state per await.

Pin in one paragraph#

That state machine is why Pin appears in every async signature. Between two awaits, the function's local variables live inside the future, and one may be a reference to another. A value that points into itself must never move, or the pointer would point at the old address. Pin is a wrapper that promises a value will "remain located at the same place in memory" until it is dropped. You write the word only when you implement a future yourself, which this book never does.

The parser from chapter 4 has to be written again with .await after each read. A function that blocks must not be called from a task, because it stops the thread and every task on it:

/// The parser from chapter 4 again, with `.await` after every read. A blocking read
/// would stop the whole thread; an awaited one lets the thread run another task.
async fn read_line(r: &mut BufReader<TcpStream>) -> resp::Result<Option<Vec<u8>>> {
    let mut line = Vec::new();
    if r.read_until(b'\n', &mut line).await? == 0 {
        return Ok(None);
    }
    if line.pop() != Some(b'\n') {
        return Err(io::Error::from(io::ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof).into());
    }
    if line.last() == Some(&b'\r') {
        line.pop();
    }
    Ok(Some(line))
}

fn parse_len(digits: &[u8], type_byte: u8) -> resp::Result<usize> {
    std::str::from_utf8(digits)
        .ok()
        .and_then(|s| s.parse().ok())
        .ok_or(KvError::Protocol(type_byte))
}

async fn read_command(r: &mut BufReader<TcpStream>) -> resp::Result<Option<Command>> {
    let Some(line) = read_line(r).await? else {
        return Ok(None);
    };
    if line.first() != Some(&b'*') {
        let words = line.split(|b| *b == b' ').filter(|w| !w.is_empty());
        return Ok(Some(words.map(<[u8]>::to_vec).collect()));
    }
    let n = parse_len(&line[1..], b'*')?;
    if n > MAX_ARGS {
        return Err(KvError::Protocol(b'*'));
    }
    let mut args = Vec::with_capacity(n);
    for _ in 0..n {
        let line = read_line(r)
            .await?
            .ok_or(io::Error::from(io::ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof))?;
        if line.first() != Some(&b'$') {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(line.first().copied().unwrap_or(b'\n')));
        }
        let size = parse_len(&line[1..], b'$')?;
        if size > MAX_BULK {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(b'$'));
        }
        let mut buf = vec![0u8; size + 2];
        r.read_exact(&mut buf).await?;
        if &buf[size..] != b"\r\n" {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(buf[size]));
        }
        buf.truncate(size);
        args.push(buf);
    }
    Ok(Some(args))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    let port = port();
    let listener = TcpListener::bind(format!("0.0.0.0:{port}")).await?;
    eprintln!("kv (tokio) listening on port {port}");
    let store = Arc::new(Mutex::new(MapStore::new()));
    loop {
        let (stream, _) = listener.accept().await?;
        let store = Arc::clone(&store);
        // a task, not a thread: it costs a few hundred bytes and no kernel resources
        tokio::spawn(async move {
            if let Err(e) = serve(stream, store).await {
                eprintln!("client: {e}");
            }
        });
    }
}

select!, cancellation and blocking#

Two more pieces of tokio appear in the next chapters. tokio::select! is the select of Go, for futures. It "waits on multiple concurrent branches, returning when the first branch completes, cancelling the remaining branches". Cancelling means dropping, and that is the whole of cancellation in Rust. A dropped future stops, because a future that is not polled does nothing. Chapter 10 uses it to wait for a client and for a shutdown signal at once. The other piece is the rule about blocking. A blocking call inside a task stops the thread from advancing every other task on it. The cure is spawn_blocking, which "runs the provided closure on a thread dedicated to blocking operations", and chapter 11 uses it for fsync.

⚠️A lock held across an await Rust

Hold a std::sync::Mutex guard across .await and the task will not compile. The error is future cannot be sent between threads safely. The note says that MutexGuard is not Send, and that "await occurs here, with mut guard maybe used later". It is the same Send check as the thread version, on the future this time. A task may resume on another thread after an await, and a mutex must be unlocked by the thread that locked it. The serving function above takes the lock, runs the command into a buffer, and drops the guard before the write is awaited. The tokio crate has its own mutex for the cases where a lock must be held across an await. It is slower, which is why the code avoids needing it.

✅Keep the blocking code and call it from the task Rust

The command code in the library did not change for tokio. It writes replies into any Write, and a Vec<u8> is one. The task fills a vector with the synchronous code and sends the vector with one awaited write. That keeps the async surface of a program small, which makes the compiler's messages shorter and the code easier to test without a runtime.

What the four servers measure#

Each server was given fifty connections and two hundred thousand requests by redis-benchmark, driven from four threads, on a machine with twelve cores. The numbers are requests a second, and chapter 13 explains how to take and read such numbers properly.

C, kqueue, one thread    SET  72,700   GET  79,900
Go, goroutines           SET  88,700   GET  79,800
Rust, threads            SET  99,900   GET  88,800
Rust, tokio              SET  99,800   GET  88,800

Three things in the table are worth more than the numbers. The C server uses one core and is within a third of the others, which is why Redis stayed single-threaded for so long. The Go and Rust servers use every core. A lock on one store stops them from using the cores well. Chapter 13 returns to that. And the tokio version is no faster than the thread version at fifty clients, because fifty threads are cheap. Its advantage starts where threads run out, at tens of thousands of connections.

TopicCGoRustWhy

Using every coreWeakStrongStrongThe C loop is one thread by design. Go and Rust spread clients over every core.

Carry forward
  • Event loop. One thread asks the kernel which sockets are ready and serves those. poll walks an array every time. The other two keep a list in the kernel.
  • Unit of concurrency. A C client is a struct. A Go client is a goroutine of a few kilobytes. A Rust client is a 2 MiB thread or a small tokio task.
  • Who checks the lock. Nobody in C, the race detector at test time in Go, and the Send and Sync traits at compile time in Rust. None of them checks how long you hold it.

Expiry#

Building kv · Chapter 10· 39 min read· 635 lines of code
▶Scene

Give the chapter 9 C server a value of a million bytes. Then be a bad client. Ask for it eight times, read sixteen bytes of the eight megabytes, and hang up. Do it in a loop:

$ redis-cli -p 6380 -x SET big < million-x.txt
OK
$ for i in 1 2 3; do
>   (exec 3<>/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/6380; for _ in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do printf 'GET big\r\n'; done >&3
>    head -c 16 <&3 >/dev/null)
>   kill -0 $pid && echo "hang-up $i: the server is still here" || { wait $pid; echo "hang-up $i: gone, status $?"; break; }
> done
hang-up 1: the server is still here
hang-up 2: gone, status 141

Status 141 is 128 plus 13, and signal 13 is SIGPIPE. One client that did not want its reply has killed the server for every other client, and nothing was logged.

A cache forgets. This chapter gives kv keys that die on time, with two options on SET and the commands EXPIRE and TTL. It also teaches the server about signals, so that a hang-up no longer kills it and a kill stops it cleanly. And the Rust parser stops copying, which is where lifetimes come in.

Redis is used as a cache more than as anything else, and a cache entry is only useful with a lifetime. A session that lasts an hour is a key with a deadline. So is a rate limit that resets each minute, and a lock that must not outlive a crashed holder. After the deadline the key must behave as if it had been deleted, whether or not anybody asks for it.

That last clause is where the work is. A key that is read after its deadline is the simple case. The read notices and deletes it. A key that nobody reads again must still go, or the server fills with dead entries. So there are two mechanisms. Lazy expiry checks the deadline on every access. Active expiry runs on a timer and removes dead keys that nobody has touched. Redis does both, and so does kv.

Time, signals and background workCGoRust
A deadlinean int64_t of milliseconds, 0 for nonea time.Time, zero for nonean Option<Instant>
Reading the clockclock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)time.Now(), which carries both clocksInstant::now()
Lazy expirykv_store_find unlinks a dead entryGet reports it absent, the sweep removes itget filters it out, the sweep removes it
The sweep runsin the event loop, between waitson a goroutine with a tickeron a thread with a sleep, then a tokio task with an interval
A hang-up mid-replySIGPIPE, ignored since this chapteran EPIPE error, by defaultan EPIPE error, by default
Ctrl-C or killa handler writes to a pipe the loop waits ona context that the signal cancelsa thread that waits for the signal, then a scope that waits for the threads
Stopping the clientsthe loop returnsAfterFunc closes each connectionthe socket is shut, or the task is dropped
The arguments of a requestpointers into the buffer, by conventioncopies, with the capacity cappedslices of the buffer, by lifetime

The whole chapter rests on one question, "is this entry dead yet?", and each language answers it in its own shape. The C entry stores a deadline as a number and treats zero as never. Go stores a time.Time and treats the zero time as never. Rust stores an Option, so "never" is a case the compiler makes every reader handle:

C
/* 0 means the key never expires */
typedef struct kv_entry {
    /* ... key, value ... */
    int64_t expires_at;
    struct kv_entry *next;
} kv_entry;

static bool kv_expired(const kv_entry *e, int64_t now) {
    return e->expires_at != 0 && e->expires_at <= now;
}
Go
// the zero time means the key never expires
type entry struct {
	val     []byte
	expires time.Time
}

func (e entry) expired(now time.Time) bool {
	return !e.expires.IsZero() && !now.Before(e.expires)
}
Rust
// None means the key never expires
struct Entry {
    val: Vec<u8>,
    expires: Option<Instant>,
}

impl Entry {
    fn expired(&self, now: Instant) -> bool {
        self.expires.is_some_and(|at| at <= now)
    }
}
📜Two clocks, and why a deadline uses the boring one

Every operating system offers two clocks. The wall clock says what time it is, and it can jump, when an administrator sets it or when the network corrects it. The monotonic clock says how much time has passed since some moment, and it only moves forward. A deadline measured on the wall clock expires at once when the clock jumps ahead an hour, and never when it jumps back. Redis stores expiry times as Unix timestamps, on the wall clock, because it must write them to disk and read them back on another machine. Its documentation warns that setting the computer time forward expires keys at once. The server kv keeps everything in memory, so it uses the monotonic clock. A deadline is then a reading of a clock that only moves forward, and the number means nothing to another process.

C: a deadline on the entry, and a sweep with a cursor#

The clock is one function, in a file of its own because chapter 11 will need it too. CLOCK_MONOTONIC is POSIX, the Portable Operating System Interface, and the call is clock_gettime:

/* Milliseconds on the monotonic clock, which only moves forward. It is not the time of
 * day: that clock jumps when the system time is set, and a deadline must not. */
int64_t kv_now_ms(void);
c/ch10/src/clock.h · region clock

An entry gains a field. The comment says what zero means, which matters because every check in the file depends on it:

/* One key and its value. expires_at is a deadline in milliseconds on the monotonic
 * clock, or 0 for a key that never expires. The key, the value and the next entry are
 * owned. */
typedef struct kv_entry {
    char *key;
    size_t klen;
    kv_value val;
    int64_t expires_at;
    struct kv_entry *next;
} kv_entry;
c/ch10/src/store.h · region entry

Lazy expiry goes into kv_store_find, which now takes the current time. An entry past its deadline is unlinked on the spot, which is why the walk uses the pointer-to-pointer form from chapter 6 again. The special value now = 0 turns the check off, for the callers that have already decided the key is alive:

static bool kv_expired(const kv_entry *e, int64_t now) {
    return e->expires_at != 0 && e->expires_at <= now;
}

/* Unlink and free the entry that *link points to. */
static void kv_unlink(kv_store *s, kv_entry **link) {
    kv_entry *e = *link;
    *link = e->next;
    kv_entry_free(e);
    s->len--;
}

kv_entry *kv_store_find(kv_store *s, const char *key, size_t klen, int64_t now) {
    if (s->cap == 0) {
        return NULL;
    }
    size_t i = kv_index(s, key, klen, s->cap);
    for (kv_entry **link = &s->buckets[i]; *link != NULL; link = &(*link)->next) {
        kv_entry *e = *link;
        if (s->type->eq(e->key, e->klen, key, klen)) {
            if (kv_expired(e, now)) {
                kv_unlink(s, link); /* lazy expiry: the key dies when it is touched */
                return NULL;
            }
            return e;
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

Stuck?Show the full listing
size_t kv_store_sweep(kv_store *s, int64_t now, size_t budget) {
    size_t removed = 0;
    size_t seen = 0;
    for (size_t n = 0; n < s->cap && seen < budget; n++) {
        kv_entry **link = &s->buckets[s->cursor];
        while (*link != NULL && seen < budget) {
            seen++;
            if (kv_expired(*link, now)) {
                kv_unlink(s, link); /* *link now points at the next entry */
                removed++;
            } else {
                link = &(*link)->next;
            }
        }
        s->cursor = (s->cursor + 1) & (s->cap - 1);
    }
    return removed;
}
c/ch10/src/store.c · region sweep

The budget matters because the sweep runs on the one thread that serves every client. A sweep that walks ten million keys stops the server for the time that takes. The cursor makes a long walk into many short ones. Redis uses a different bound, a random sample, but the purpose is the same. The sweep is called from the event loop. The loop now waits at most a tenth of a second, so that keys expire on time even when no client is talking:

/* Wait at most 100 ms, so that keys expire even when no client is talking. */
int n = kv_poller_wait(cs.poller, events, 64, 100);
if (n < 0) {
    if (errno == EINTR) {
        continue;
    }
    perror("wait");
    break;
}
kv_store_sweep(store, kv_now_ms(), 200);
c/ch10/src/server.c · region tick

The SET command grows two options, and a plain SET removes any deadline, because that is what Redis does and what clients expect. A number that is not a number, and a lifetime of zero, get the two error texts Redis uses:

/* SET key value [EX seconds | PX milliseconds]. A plain SET removes any deadline, as
 * Redis does; a SET with EX or PX sets a new one. */
static bool kv_cmd_set(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out, int64_t now) {
    if (c->argc != 3 && c->argc != 5) {
        return kv_reply_arity(out, "set");
    }
    int64_t ttl_ms = 0;
    if (c->argc == 5) {
        long long n;
        bool ex = kv_arg_is(c, 3, "EX");
        if (!ex && !kv_arg_is(c, 3, "PX")) {
            return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR syntax error");
        }
        if (!kv_parse_int(c->argv[4], c->arglen[4], &n)) {
            return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
        }
        if (n <= 0 || n > INT64_MAX / 1000) {
            return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR invalid expire time in 'set' command");
        }
        ttl_ms = ex ? n * 1000 : n;
    }
    if (!kv_store_set(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], c->argv[2], c->arglen[2])) {
        return false;
    }
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], 0);
    e->expires_at = ttl_ms ? now + ttl_ms : 0;
    return kv_reply_simple(out, "OK");
}
c/ch10/src/cmd.c · region set

EXPIRE and TTL are short. The one surprise is that EXPIRE with zero or a negative number deletes the key at once. The Redis documentation says a non-positive timeout results in the key "being deleted rather than expired", and the test file checks for it:

/* EXPIRE key seconds: 1 if the key exists and got a deadline, 0 if it does not exist. */
static bool kv_cmd_expire(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out, int64_t now) {
    long long secs;
    if (!kv_parse_int(c->argv[2], c->arglen[2], &secs)) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
    }
    if (secs > INT64_MAX / 1000) { /* now + secs * 1000 must not overflow */
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR invalid expire time in 'expire' command");
    }
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], now);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return kv_reply_int(out, 0);
    }
    if (secs <= 0) {
        kv_store_del(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]); /* a deadline in the past is a DEL */
    } else {
        e->expires_at = now + secs * 1000;
    }
    return kv_reply_int(out, 1);
}

/* TTL key: the seconds left, -1 for a key with no deadline, -2 for a missing key. */
static bool kv_cmd_ttl(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out, int64_t now) {
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], now);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return kv_reply_int(out, -2);
    }
    if (e->expires_at == 0) {
        return kv_reply_int(out, -1);
    }
    return kv_reply_int(out, (e->expires_at - now + 500) / 1000); /* nearest, as Redis */
}

⚠️A find that deletes C

kv_store_find can now free the entry it is asked about. Any pointer to that entry held across the call is a pointer to freed memory. Inside kv_exec_incr the code finds the entry and reads its deadline. Then it calls kv_store_set and finds the entry again. The first pointer must not be trusted after a call that can change the table. This rule was true in chapter 6. It became easier to break in this chapter, because a function named find no longer sounds like one that writes.

Go: a ticker, and a clock the test can hold still#

A Go time.Time carries both clocks. The documentation says a value from time.Now "contains both a wall clock reading and a monotonic clock reading". Sub and Before use the monotonic one. So a deadline is a plain time.Time, and a zero value means none:

// entry is a value of any kind and its deadline. A zero time means the key never
// expires. The deadline is a time.Time, which carries a monotonic reading, so a change
// to the system clock does not move it.
type entry struct {
	val     any
	expires time.Time
}

func (e entry) expired(now time.Time) bool {
	return !e.expires.IsZero() && !now.Before(e.expires)
}
go/ch10/internal/store/store.go · region entry

Every method takes now as a parameter instead of calling time.Now itself. That is a small decision with a large effect. The command code reads the clock once per command. So every check inside one command, such as the expiry test and the deadline it sets, sees the same moment. And a test can pass any time it likes, which is how the expiry test runs in a millisecond without sleeping:

// TestExpiry uses a clock the test controls, so it never sleeps.
func TestExpiry(t *testing.T) {
	s := New()
	t0 := time.Now()
	s.Set([]byte("k"), []byte("v"))
	s.SetExpiry([]byte("k"), t0.Add(time.Second), t0)
	if _, ok := s.Get([]byte("k"), t0.Add(999*time.Millisecond)); !ok {
		t.Fatal("key died early")
	}
	if _, ok := s.Get([]byte("k"), t0.Add(time.Second)); ok {
		t.Fatal("key outlived its deadline")
	}
	if n := s.Sweep(t0.Add(time.Second), 100); n != 1 {
		t.Fatalf("sweep removed %d keys, want 1", n)
	}
	if s.Len() != 0 {
		t.Fatalf("store holds %d keys after the sweep, want 0", s.Len())
	}
}
go/ch10/internal/store/store_test.go · region expiry-test

Get holds the read lock, and a dead key cannot be removed under a read lock. So Get reports the key absent and leaves the removal to the sweep. The sweep takes the write lock, walks the map, and stops after a budget. Go promises no order for a map walk, and the runtime starts each walk at a different place. That gives the sweep a fresh sample without any cursor:

// SetExpiry gives a live key a deadline. It reports whether the key was there.
func (s *Store) SetExpiry(key []byte, at time.Time, now time.Time) bool {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	e, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	if !ok || e.expired(now) {
		return false
	}
	e.expires = at
	s.m[string(key)] = e
	return true
}

// TTL returns the time left, and a status: -2 for a missing key, -1 for a key with
// no deadline, 0 for a key with one.
func (s *Store) TTL(key []byte, now time.Time) (time.Duration, int) {
	s.mu.RLock()
	defer s.mu.RUnlock()
	e, ok := s.m[string(key)]
	if !ok || e.expired(now) {
		return 0, -2
	}
	if e.expires.IsZero() {
		return 0, -1
	}
	return e.expires.Sub(now), 0
}

// Sweep removes keys past their deadline, looking at no more than budget of them. The
// map iterates in a different order each time, so each call sees a fresh sample.
func (s *Store) Sweep(now time.Time, budget int) int {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	removed := 0
	for k, e := range s.m {
		if budget == 0 {
			break
		}
		budget--
		if e.expired(now) {
			delete(s.m, k)
			removed++
		}
	}
	return removed
}

// sweep removes keys past their deadline ten times a second, so that a key nobody reads
// still dies on time. It takes the store's lock like any other goroutine. The select
// waits on the ticker and on the context at once, and returns when the server stops.
func sweep(ctx context.Context, s *store.Store) {
	tick := time.NewTicker(100 * time.Millisecond)
	defer tick.Stop()
	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return
		case now := <-tick.C:
			s.Sweep(now, 200)
		}
	}
}
