✅Pass the clock in Go

A function that calls time.Now can only be tested with real time, which means tests that sleep and tests that fail on a slow machine. A function that takes now can be tested with any time at all. The store does the second. The command layer reads the clock once and passes it down. The same shape works in Rust and in C, and the C version of kv does it too, in kv_exec, though without the test.

Rust: an Option for the deadline, a thread and then a task for the sweep#

Rust separates the clocks into two types. SystemTime is the wall clock. Instant is the monotonic one, and its documentation says it "will never go backwards". A deadline is Option<Instant>, so the "none" case is a case the compiler makes you handle rather than a zero you must remember:

/// A value and its deadline. `None` means the key never expires. An `Instant` is a
/// reading of the monotonic clock, so a change to the system time cannot move it.
struct Entry {
    val: Value,
    expires: Option<Instant>,
}

impl Entry {
    fn expired(&self, now: Instant) -> bool {
        self.expires.is_some_and(|at| at <= now)
    }
}
rust/ch10/src/store.rs · region entry

get borrows the store immutably, so it filters a dead key out and leaves it for the sweep, as the Go version does. TTL has three answers, and the enum Ttl gives each a name. The command code then matches on three names instead of on -2, -1 and a number:

fn set_expiry(&mut self, key: &[u8], at: Instant, now: Instant) -> bool {
    match self.map.get_mut(key) {
        Some(e) if !e.expired(now) => {
            e.expires = Some(at);
            true
        }
        _ => false,
    }
}

fn ttl(&self, key: &[u8], now: Instant) -> Ttl {
    match self.map.get(key) {
        None => Ttl::Missing,
        Some(e) if e.expired(now) => Ttl::Missing,
        Some(Entry { expires: None, .. }) => Ttl::Never,
        Some(Entry {
            expires: Some(at), ..
        }) => Ttl::Left(*at - now),
    }
}

/// `retain` walks the whole map, which is fine for a store of this size; Redis
/// samples instead, to bound the time.
fn sweep(&mut self, now: Instant) -> usize {
    let before = self.map.len();
    self.map.retain(|_, e| !e.expired(now));
    before - self.map.len()
}
rust/ch10/src/store.rs · region expire

The SET options are a second match arm with five elements. The inner match on the unit and the parsed number has one arm for each error text. The compiler checks that the arms are complete:

/// SET key value [EX seconds | PX milliseconds]. A plain SET removes any deadline, as
/// Redis does; a SET with EX or PX sets a new one.
fn set(args: &Command, store: &mut dyn Store, now: Instant, w: &mut dyn Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    match args.as_slice() {
        [_, key, val] => {
            // the one copy: the store must own its key and value, the buffer does not
            store.set(key.to_vec(), val.to_vec());
            resp::write_simple(w, "OK")
        }
        [_, key, val, unit, n] => {
            let ttl = match (unit.to_ascii_uppercase().as_slice(), parse_int(n)) {
                (b"EX" | b"PX", None) => {
                    return resp::write_error(w, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
                }
                (b"EX", Some(n)) if n > 0 && n <= i64::MAX / 1000 => Duration::from_secs(n as u64),
                (b"PX", Some(n)) if n > 0 => Duration::from_millis(n as u64),
                (b"EX" | b"PX", Some(_)) => {
                    return resp::write_error(w, "ERR invalid expire time in 'set' command");
                }
                _ => return resp::write_error(w, "ERR syntax error"),
            };
            let Some(at) = now.checked_add(ttl) else {
                return resp::write_error(w, "ERR invalid expire time in 'set' command");
            };
            store.set(key.to_vec(), val.to_vec());
            store.set_expiry(key, at, now);
            resp::write_simple(w, "OK")
        }
        _ => write_arity(w, b"set"),
    }
}

// The sweep is a task like the clients. The await on the interval costs no thread,
// and select! ends the task when the stop arrives.
let sweeper = Arc::clone(&store);
let mut stop_rx = stop.subscribe();
tokio::spawn(async move {
    let mut tick = tokio::time::interval(Duration::from_millis(100));
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            _ = tick.tick() => {
                let mut store = sweeper.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
                store.sweep(Instant::now());
            }
            _ = stop_rx.recv() => return,
        }
    }
});
rust/ch10/src/bin/kv_async.rs · region sweeper

The two sweepers differ in one way that matters. The thread version occupies a thread that spends almost all its time asleep, which is cheap at one sweeper and wasteful at a thousand timers. The task version occupies nothing while it waits. The await on the interval hands the thread back to the runtime, and the runtime wakes the task when the tick arrives. That is the same trade as chapter 9, seen from the other side.

⚠️retain walks the whole map Rust

The Rust sweep has no budget. retain visits every entry under the lock, which is fine at ten thousand keys and a pause at ten million. The C version has a cursor, and the Go version has a budget on an iteration that starts at a random place. A Rust HashMap iterates in a fixed order for a given state, so taking the first 200 entries would sweep the same 200 every time. A bounded sweep in Rust needs its own cursor, or a random sample, as Redis takes. The book leaves it unbounded and says so, which is the honest version of a difference between the three standard libraries.

C: a signal, a flag and a pipe#

Back to the scene. A write to a socket whose other end has gone raises SIGPIPE, and the default action for SIGPIPE is to end the process. The kernel does not ask. That default is from the days when a pipeline such as cat file | head was the only pipe. A writer with nobody left to read should end, without a message. A server is the opposite case. One line in main changes the default to ignoring the signal. The write then fails with EPIPE instead, and the loop closes that one client:

/* A write to a client that has gone raises SIGPIPE, which kills the process by
 * default. Ignore it, and write() reports EPIPE instead, which closes that client.
 * Linux can ask for the same with MSG_NOSIGNAL on send(), and macOS with the
 * SO_NOSIGPIPE socket option. Ignoring the signal covers both. */
signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);
/* Ctrl-C and kill send SIGINT and SIGTERM, which also end the process by default.
 * From here on they end the event loop instead, through a pipe it waits on. */
int stop_fd = kv_stop_fd();
if (stop_fd < 0) {
    perror("kv_stop_fd");
    return 1;
}
c/ch10/src/main.c · region signals

The same line adds the second signal story. Ctrl-C sends SIGINT and kill sends SIGTERM, and both end the process at once by default, in the middle of whatever it was doing. A server would rather finish the command it is running, and in chapter 11 write the last bytes of its log. So the two signals get a handler. A handler is a function the kernel calls between any two instructions of the program, even in the middle of malloc. It may only do two things safely. It may set a flag of the one type made for that. And it may call the functions on the async-signal-safe list, which holds write and not printf:

/* Which signal asked the server to stop, or 0. sig_atomic_t is the one integer type
 * that a signal handler may write while the program reads it, without a torn value, and
 * volatile tells the compiler the value can change behind its back. */
extern volatile sig_atomic_t kv_stop_signal;
c/ch10/src/stop.h · region flag
/* A signal handler runs between any two instructions of the program, even in the middle
 * of malloc or printf. So it may only do what is safe at any moment: set the flag, and
 * call functions on the async-signal-safe list. write() is on the list. The byte wakes
 * the loop, which is otherwise asleep in its wait and would not look at the flag. */
static void kv_on_stop(int sig) {
    int saved = errno; /* write() may change errno, and the interrupted code needs it */
    kv_stop_signal = sig;
    if (write(kv_stop_write, "s", 1) < 0) {
        /* the pipe is full or closed: the loop is already awake, or already gone */
    }
    errno = saved;
}
c/ch10/src/stop.c · region handler

The flag alone is not enough, and the reason is a race. The loop is asleep in its wait when the signal arrives, and it checks the flag only when it wakes. A signal that arrives a moment before the wait is missed until the next event, which may be an hour away. The answer is the self-pipe trick, which Daniel Bernstein described in 1991. The handler writes one byte into a pipe, and the loop watches the pipe's other end like a socket. A signal is then an event, delivered through the same wait as everything else:

int kv_stop_fd(void) {
    int fds[2];
    if (pipe(fds) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    /* non-blocking, so that a handler can never wait on a full pipe */
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        int flags = fcntl(fds[i], F_GETFL, 0);
        if (flags < 0 || fcntl(fds[i], F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK) < 0) {
            return -1;
        }
    }
    kv_stop_write = fds[1];
    /* sigaction, not signal(): it says exactly what happens, on every Unix. SA_RESTART
     * lets a read or accept that the signal interrupted carry on, because the pipe,
     * not the interruption, is what tells the loop to stop. */
    struct sigaction sa = {0};
    sa.sa_handler = kv_on_stop;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = SA_RESTART;
    if (sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL) < 0 || sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    return fds[0];
}
c/ch10/src/stop.c · region install

sigaction is the call to install a handler. The older signal is for SIG_IGN only, because what it does to an interrupted call differs between systems. The flag SA_RESTART says that a read or an accept the signal interrupted should carry on as if nothing happened. The pipe, not the interruption, is what tells the loop to stop. In the loop, the byte is an event with a tag of its own:

/* A byte on the pipe is the signal, delivered to the loop as an event like
 * any other. Nothing was interrupted in the middle, so there is nothing to
 * repair: the loop ends, and main closes everything in order. */
if (c == (kv_conn *)&stop_tag) {
    rc = 0;
    break;
}
c/ch10/src/server.c · region stop

Nothing was interrupted in the middle, so nothing needs repair. The loop returns zero, and main frees the store and closes the socket in order, as it would have after any other return. The protocol tests gain a line, terminate, which sends SIGTERM and expects exit status 0 within two seconds. From this chapter on, every server in the book passes it.

⚠️A handler that does too much C

A signal handler that calls printf, malloc or free can deadlock or corrupt the heap. Those functions take locks and keep state, and the handler may run while the main program is inside them. The symptom is a server that hangs once a month, on a signal that arrived at the wrong instruction. The rule is short. A handler sets a sig_atomic_t, writes a byte, or calls _exit, and everything else happens in the loop. The volatile on the flag is the other half. Without it the compiler may read the flag once and keep the value in a register for ever.

Go: a context that a signal cancels#

Go's runtime handles SIGPIPE on a socket by itself. The os/signal package says a write to a broken pipe on any descriptor but 1 and 2 "will fail with a syscall.EPIPE error". So the Go server survived the scene without a line of code. For SIGINT and SIGTERM, the same package offers a channel, and a context. One call turns the signal into a cancelled context, and every part of the server that holds the context can see it:

// Ctrl-C and kill send SIGINT and SIGTERM, which end a Go program at once by default.
// NotifyContext changes that: the signal cancels a context instead, and every part of
// the server that holds the context sees it. A second signal, after stop() has run,
// ends the program the default way, for a server that will not finish.
ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
defer stop()
go/ch10/cmd/kv/main.go · region signals

context in one paragraph#

A Context "carries deadlines, cancellation signals, and other request-scoped values" down a chain of calls, as the first parameter of every function in the chain. WithCancel gives a child that a function call cancels. WithTimeout and WithDeadline give one that time cancels. Done is a channel that closes when the context is cancelled, which is what a select waits on, and Err says why. Values ride along with WithValue, for request-scoped data such as a trace identifier. The documentation warns against using them to pass ordinary parameters. kv needs only the cancel. The sweeper's select waits on the ticker and on ctx.Done() at once, and returns when the server stops.

A clean stop has three parts, and each is a few lines. Closing the listener makes a blocked Accept "unblocked and return errors", which ends the loop. context.AfterFunc runs a function when the context is cancelled, and the function closes a connection, which ends that client's serve. The WaitGroup from chapter 9 waits for every serve to return:

// Three parts to a clean stop. Closing the listener makes Accept return an error,
// which ends the loop. AfterFunc closes each client when the context is cancelled,
// which ends its serve. The WaitGroup waits for every serve to return.
var clients sync.WaitGroup
context.AfterFunc(ctx, func() { ln.Close() })
for {
	conn, err := ln.Accept()
	if err != nil {
		if ctx.Err() != nil {
			break
		}
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "accept:", err)
		continue
	}
	clients.Go(func() {
		defer context.AfterFunc(ctx, func() { conn.Close() })()
		if err := serve(conn, s); err != nil && ctx.Err() == nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "client:", err)
		}
	})
}
fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "kv stopping:", context.Cause(ctx))
clients.Wait()
go/ch10/cmd/kv/main.go · region shutdown

panic and recover#

One more defence goes into serve, and it is against the book's own bugs. A panic "stops the ordinary flow of control", unwinds the goroutine's stack running every deferred call, and then ends the whole process. An index out of range in one command handler would take down every client. recover "regains control of a panicking goroutine", and the specification says it works only when called directly by a deferred function. So the deferred function below catches the panic, turns it into an error for this one connection, and the connection closes. The bug is logged and is still a bug. The result is named, err, because a deferred function can set a named result and nothing else:

// A panic in one command would end the whole process, and every other client with
// it. recover, which only works inside a deferred function, turns it into an error
// for this one connection, which closes. The bug is still logged, and still a bug.
defer func() {
	if r := recover(); r != nil {
		err = fmt.Errorf("panic: %v", r)
	}
}()
go/ch10/cmd/kv/main.go · region recover

That is the Go rule for the two kinds of failure. An error is a value for the caller, returned and checked, as every err in this book has been. A panic is a bug in the program. recover is for the one place that must survive bugs in code below it, which is a server's per-connection loop. A library that panics at a caller's mistake is thought badly of. A library that returns an error for its own bugs hides them.

Rust: a thread that waits for the signal, then a scope that waits for the threads#

The Rust standard library ignores SIGPIPE before main runs, so the thread server of chapter 9 logged client: Broken pipe (os error 32) in the scene and went on. It has no signal handling of its own, so the stop goes through the C library again, with the pattern that fits threads best. The signals are blocked in main before any thread exists, so every thread inherits the block. One thread then asks for them with sigwait, which "suspends execution of the calling thread until one of the signals" arrives. No handler ever runs between two instructions. An ordinary thread gets the signal as a return value and may do anything:

/// Block SIGINT and SIGTERM in the calling thread. Every thread spawned afterwards
/// inherits the mask, so the one thread that calls `wait_for_stop` is the only one that
/// ever sees them, and no handler runs in the middle of anything.
#[cfg(unix)]
pub fn block_stop_signals() {
    // SAFETY: the set is initialised by sigemptyset before any use, and the mask call
    // reads it and writes nothing else.
    unsafe {
        let mut set = std::mem::zeroed::<libc::sigset_t>();
        libc::sigemptyset(&mut set);
        libc::sigaddset(&mut set, libc::SIGINT);
        libc::sigaddset(&mut set, libc::SIGTERM);
        libc::pthread_sigmask(libc::SIG_BLOCK, &set, std::ptr::null_mut());
    }
}

/// Wait until SIGINT or SIGTERM arrives, and say which. sigwait takes the signal off
/// the pending list and returns it to an ordinary thread, which may then do anything.
#[cfg(unix)]
pub fn wait_for_stop() -> i32 {
    // SAFETY: as above, and sigwait writes one int through a valid pointer.
    unsafe {
        let mut set = std::mem::zeroed::<libc::sigset_t>();
        libc::sigemptyset(&mut set);
        libc::sigaddset(&mut set, libc::SIGINT);
        libc::sigaddset(&mut set, libc::SIGTERM);
        let mut sig = 0;
        libc::sigwait(&set, &mut sig);
        sig
    }
}

/// Elsewhere there is nothing to block, and nothing to wait for: Ctrl-C ends the
/// process the default way.
#[cfg(not(unix))]
pub fn block_stop_signals() {}

#[cfg(not(unix))]
pub fn wait_for_stop() -> i32 {
    loop {
        std::thread::park();
    }
}
rust/ch10/src/sys.rs · region signals

With that, the whole server fits in one thread::scope. The store, the stop flag and the list of clients are locals of main, lent to every thread. The Arc from chapter 9 is gone. The sweeper and the signal thread run inside the scope. Each client runs inside it. And the scope ends only when all of them have returned, which is the waiting part of a clean stop, done by the type system:

// One thread waits for the signal. It raises the flag and then wakes the accept
// loop the only way a plain listener can be woken: by connecting to it.
s.spawn(|| {
    let sig = sys::wait_for_stop();
    eprintln!("kv stopping on signal {sig}");
    stopping.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed);
    let _ = TcpStream::connect(("127.0.0.1", port.parse().unwrap_or(6380)));
});
rust/ch10/src/main.rs · region stopper
// Shutting a socket makes its read return 0, and that client's serve returns.
// The scope then joins every thread, so nothing is still running when main ends.
for c in clients.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner()).iter() {
    let _ = c.shutdown(Shutdown::Both);
}
rust/ch10/src/main.rs · region drain

Two details are unusual, and both are honest. A plain listener can only be woken by a connection. So the signal thread connects to its own server, and the accept loop sees the flag and breaks. And a client blocked in read is woken by shutting its socket from outside, through a second handle. After that, "all currently blocked and future reads will return Ok(0)". The tokio version has no such problem, because tokio owns the event loop:

/// Completes when Ctrl-C or kill asks the process to stop. Asking tokio for the signal
/// is what turns off the default, which would end the process at once.
async fn stop_signal() {
    #[cfg(unix)]
    {
        use tokio::signal::unix::{SignalKind, signal};
        let mut term = signal(SignalKind::terminate()).expect("SIGTERM handler");
        tokio::select! {
            _ = tokio::signal::ctrl_c() => {}
            _ = term.recv() => {}
        }
    }
    #[cfg(not(unix))]
    {
        let _ = tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await;
    }
}
rust/ch10/src/bin/kv_async.rs · region signal

Asking tokio for a signal is what turns off the default. From then on the accept loop waits on two futures with select!, the next connection and the stop. The stop reaches the tasks through the two channels from chapter 9's last section. A broadcast channel, where "each sent value is seen by all consumers", tells every task. An mpsc channel, where every task holds a sender it never uses, lets main wait until the last sender is dropped:

// Two channels for a clean stop. The broadcast channel tells: every task holds a
// receiver, and one send reaches all of them. The mpsc channel waits: every task
// holds a sender it never uses, and recv() returns None once the last one is dropped.
let (stop, _) = broadcast::channel::<()>(1);
let (done, mut all_done) = mpsc::channel::<()>(1);
rust/ch10/src/bin/kv_async.rs · region channels
loop {
    let stream = tokio::select! {
        accepted = listener.accept() => accepted?.0,
        _ = stop_signal() => break,
    };
    let store = Arc::clone(&store);
    let mut stop_rx = stop.subscribe();
    let done = done.clone();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        // A task waits on its client and on the stop at once. When the stop wins,
        // the serve future is dropped where it stands, between two awaits, and that
        // is the whole of cancellation: nothing to flag, nothing to catch.
        tokio::select! {
            res = serve(stream, store) => {
                if let Err(e) = res {
                    eprintln!("client: {e}");
                }
            }
            _ = stop_rx.recv() => {}
        }
        drop(done);
    });
}
eprintln!("kv (tokio) stopping");
let _ = stop.send(());
drop(done);
all_done.recv().await; // None, once every task has dropped its sender
rust/ch10/src/bin/kv_async.rs · region accept

The line to look at is the select! inside the task. When the stop wins, the serve future is dropped where it stands, at whichever await it was parked on. That is cancellation in Rust, all of it. The lock is never held across an await, so a command is never cut in half. The socket closes when the future's locals are dropped. Go needed an AfterFunc and a closed connection to get the same effect, because a goroutine cannot be dropped, only persuaded.

The parser stops copying#

Every parser so far has copied each argument out of the buffer the bytes arrived in. Redis does not, and from this chapter the Rust version of kv does not either. A SET copies its key and value when it stores them, and only then. A GET copies nothing at all. The change is one type, and the type is a lifetime:

/// A parsed request: the command name and its arguments, as slices of the buffer the
/// request arrived in. Nothing is copied. The lifetime `'a` is the buffer's, and it says
/// that a `Command` cannot outlive the bytes it points into. A command that needs to
/// keep an argument, as SET keeps its value, copies it then, and only then.
pub type Command<'a> = Vec<&'a [u8]>;

/// What `parse` found in the bytes so far.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum Parsed<'a> {
    /// A whole request, and how many bytes of the buffer it used.
    Done(Command<'a>, usize),
    /// Not a whole request yet: read more bytes and call again.
    Incomplete,
}
rust/ch10/src/resp.rs · region command

Lifetimes, in the one place kv needs them#

A struct or a type alias that holds a reference must say what the reference borrows from, and 'a is that name. The Rust book puts it in one sentence. An instance "can't outlive the reference it holds". So a Command<'a> cannot be kept after the buffer it points into is changed or freed, and the compiler refuses a program that tries. The annotation changes nothing about how long anything lives. It only gives the compiler a name to check against, where it cannot infer one. In a function it usually can. The elision rules say that one reference in means the reference out borrows from it. So parse below writes '_, and the compiler fills in the rest:

/// One request from the front of `buf`: an array of bulk strings such as
/// `*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n`, or one inline line of words. The returned
/// `Command` borrows `buf`, which the signature says with the elided lifetime: one
/// reference in, so the one reference out lives as long as it.
pub fn parse(buf: &[u8]) -> Result<Parsed<'_>> {
    let Some((line, mut used)) = take_line(buf, 0) else {
        return Ok(Parsed::Incomplete);
    };
    if line.first() != Some(&b'*') {
        let words = line.split(|b| *b == b' ').filter(|w| !w.is_empty());
        return Ok(Parsed::Done(words.collect(), used));
    }
    let n = parse_len(&line[1..], b'*')?;
    if n > MAX_ARGS {
        return Err(KvError::Protocol(b'*'));
    }
    let mut args = Vec::with_capacity(n);
    for _ in 0..n {
        let Some((line, start)) = take_line(buf, used) else {
            return Ok(Parsed::Incomplete);
        };
        if line.first() != Some(&b'$') {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(line.first().copied().unwrap_or(b'\n')));
        }
        let size = parse_len(&line[1..], b'$')?;
        if size > MAX_BULK {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(b'$'));
        }
        let end = start + size;
        if buf.len() < end + 2 {
            return Ok(Parsed::Incomplete);
        }
        if &buf[end..end + 2] != b"\r\n" {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(buf[end]));
        }
        args.push(&buf[start..end]);
        used = end + 2;
    }
    Ok(Parsed::Done(args, used))
}

/// The line that starts at `from`, without its ending, and where the next line starts.
/// A bare LF is accepted as well as CRLF, so that a command typed into nc works.
fn take_line(buf: &[u8], from: usize) -> Option<(&[u8], usize)> {
    let rest = &buf[from..];
    let nl = rest.iter().position(|b| *b == b'\n')?;
    let line = rest[..nl].strip_suffix(b"\r").unwrap_or(&rest[..nl]);
    Some((line, from + nl + 1))
}

fn parse_len(digits: &[u8], type_byte: u8) -> Result<usize> {
    std::str::from_utf8(digits)
        .ok()
        .and_then(|s| s.parse().ok())
        .ok_or(KvError::Protocol(type_byte))
}
rust/ch10/src/resp.rs · region parse

The serving loop is where the borrow is felt. It reads into a Vec, parses a command out of it, runs it, and then removes the used bytes with drain. The drain changes the vector, and a Command that still pointed into it would be a bug. The compiler allows the call because the borrow ended at the last use of args, not at the end of the block. That is the non-lexical rule from Rust 2018, and without it this loop would need an extra scope:

/// Bytes are read into a buffer and whole requests are parsed out of it without a
/// copy. The store is shared: the Mutex lets one thread at a time use it, and the scope
/// in main lends it to every client, so no Arc is needed.
fn serve(mut stream: TcpStream, store: &Mutex<MapStore>) -> resp::Result<()> {
    let mut writer = BufWriter::new(stream.try_clone()?);
    let mut buf: Vec<u8> = Vec::with_capacity(4096);
    let mut chunk = [0u8; 4096];
    loop {
        let n = stream.read(&mut chunk)?;
        if n == 0 {
            return Ok(()); // the client closed, or the server shut the socket
        }
        buf.extend_from_slice(&chunk[..n]);
        let mut used = 0;
        loop {
            match resp::parse(&buf[used..]) {
                Ok(Parsed::Done(args, n)) => {
                    let mut store = store.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
                    cmd::execute(&args, &mut *store, &mut writer)?;
                    used += n;
                }
                Ok(Parsed::Incomplete) => break,
                Err(e @ resp::KvError::Protocol(_)) => {
                    resp::write_error(&mut writer, "ERR Protocol error")?;
                    writer.flush()?;
                    return Err(e);
                }
                Err(e) => return Err(e),
            }
        }
        // the arguments borrowed the buffer, and they are gone, so the buffer may change
        buf.drain(..used);
        if buf.len() > resp::MAX_REQUEST {
            return Err(resp::KvError::Protocol(b'*')); // a request that never ends
        }
        writer.flush()?;
    }
}
rust/ch10/src/main.rs · region serve

Three smaller things fall out of the same change. A &[u8] is Copy, so a handler can use an argument twice without a clone, where a Vec would have moved. The unknown-command reply uses String::from_utf8_lossy, which returns a Cow, "a clone-on-write smart pointer". It borrows when the bytes are valid text and allocates only when it must replace a byte. And thread::spawn demands 'static of its closure, as chapter 9's error message showed, which means "owns everything it holds". A Command can never be sent to a spawned thread, and a scoped thread may borrow it. The tokio server gained the most. Its second copy of the parser, with an await after every read, is gone. A parser that works on bytes already in memory has nothing to wait for.

Go cannot say any of this in a type, and so it chose to copy. What it can say is how much an argument may grow in place. Each argument is a slice of a buffer with two bytes of line ending after it. append "re-uses the underlying array" when there is room. So an append to such an argument would write over the line ending, or over whatever a later parser keeps there. The next command would see it. The full slice expression buf[:size:size] sets the capacity to the length, so an append must copy:

// buf[:size] would share its spare two bytes with the line ending. The full slice
// expression caps the capacity at the length, so an append to the argument copies.
args = append(args, buf[:size:size])
go/ch10/internal/resp/resp.go · region alias
// Every argument is a slice into a buffer the parser allocated, with two bytes of line
// ending after it. The full slice expression buf[:size:size] sets the capacity to the
// length, so that an append to an argument must copy instead of writing over the line
// ending, or over whatever a later version of the parser keeps there.
func TestArgumentsDoNotShareSpareCapacity(t *testing.T) {
	r := bufio.NewReader(strings.NewReader("*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$1\r\nk\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n"))
	args, err := ReadCommand(r)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	val := args[2]
	if cap(val) != len(val) {
		t.Fatalf("cap %d, len %d: an append would write into the parser's buffer", cap(val), len(val))
	}
	grown := append(val, '!')
	if &grown[0] == &val[0] {
		t.Fatal("append reused the argument's memory")
	}
	if string(val) != "hi" || string(grown) != "hi!" {
		t.Fatalf("val %q, grown %q", val, grown)
	}
}
go/ch10/internal/resp/resp_test.go · region alias

C has had the borrowed parser since chapter 4, and the rule since then has been one comment. The const on each argument is the part of it the compiler can check. It is a promise not to write through the pointer, carried through every call that takes one:

/* One parsed request. The arguments point into the request buffer, so they are valid
 * only until that buffer is consumed. A kv_cmd owns nothing: the comment is the whole
 * of the rule, and const is the part of it the compiler can check. */
typedef struct {
    size_t argc;
    const char *argv[KV_MAX_ARGS];
    size_t arglen[KV_MAX_ARGS];
} kv_cmd;
c/ch10/src/resp.h · region cmd
📰Cloudbleed, 2017

On 18 February 2017 a security researcher found other people's cookies and passwords in pages served by Cloudflare. Cloudflare's edge servers rewrote HTML with a parser generated by Ragel, and the generated C checked for the end of the buffer with if (++p == pe). A pointer that had already stepped past the end never equalled it. The parser read on, into memory that held fragments of other customers' requests. The company's report says that "had the check been done using >= instead of == jumping over the buffer end would have been caught". About one request in three million leaked, over five months, and search engines had cached some of the leaked pages. A parser that returns pointers into a buffer is the fastest kind and the most dangerous kind. The C rule is a comment and a habit. The Rust rule is the lifetime on Command<'a>, and the compiler would have refused the bug.

Background work, three ways#

The sweep is the first work in kv that no client asked for. Each language had a natural place to put it. In C it went into the loop that already existed, with a timeout on the wait, and the loop does the sweep between clients. There is no second thread and no lock. In Go it went into a goroutine with a ticker, and the lock on the store made that safe without a thought. In Rust it went into a thread, and then into a task, and the compiler checked that the store was shared correctly both times.

Each placement reflects the chapter before. The C loop is one thread, so the sweep must share it and must be short, which is why it has a budget. The Go and Rust servers have many threads of control, so the sweep can be one more. The cost is a lock that every client also pays. Chapter 11 adds the second kind of background work, writing to disk, where the cost of sharing is higher and the three answers differ more.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
A deadlineOKStrongStrongC uses zero to mean none, which the comments must say. Go's zero Time and Rust's Option say it in the type.
The clockOKStrongStrongC picks the clock by name, while Go carries both in one value and Rust gives each a type.
Lazy expiryStrongOKOKC deletes on find. Go and Rust must leave it to the sweep because of the read lock or the borrow.
The sweepStrongStrongWeakC has a cursor and Go a random sample. Rust's retain walks the whole map.
A client that hangs upWeakStrongStrongC dies unless one line ignores SIGPIPE. Both runtimes turn it into an error.
Stopping cleanlyOKStrongOKC needs a handler, a pipe and a rule about what a handler may do. Go needs a context, and Rust the C library or tokio.
A bug in one commandWeakStrongOKC corrupts or crashes, and Go recovers per connection. Rust panics per thread, and the scope reports it.
The parser's argumentsOKOKStrongC borrows by comment, Go copies and caps the capacity, Rust borrows by lifetime and the compiler checks it.
Testing timeWeakStrongStrongGo and Rust tests pass a clock in. The C store has no test runner yet.
Carry forward
  • Two expiries. Lazy expiry checks the deadline on every access. Active expiry sweeps on a timer, with a budget, so that a key nobody reads still dies.
  • A signal is an event. The C handler writes a byte into a pipe the loop waits on. Go turns it into a cancelled context. Rust gives it to one thread, or to a select! in tokio.
  • A lifetime is a name. Command<'a> says the arguments borrow the buffer and cannot outlive it. The annotation changes nothing about how long anything lives.

Persistence#

Building kv · Chapter 11· 32 min read· 534 lines of code
▶Scene

Start this chapter's C server with a log file, pour a million writes into it, and pull the plug a second and a half in. Then start it again:

$ KV_AOF=kv.aof ./kv &
$ redis-benchmark -p 6380 -t set -n 1000000 -r 100000 -q &
$ kill -9 $pid                        # no signal handler runs for this one
$ ls -l kv.aof
-rw-r--r--  1 you  staff  2686230 Oct 12 kv.aof
$ KV_AOF=kv.aof ./kv
kv replayed 59694 commands from kv.aof
$ redis-cli -p 6380 DBSIZE
45076

Fifty-nine thousand commands came back from a file the server never had time to force to disk. Now set KV_FSYNC=always and run the benchmark again. It manages 43 commands a second. The chapter is about the space between those two numbers.

Stop kv and every key is gone. This chapter gives it an append-only file, a log of every write in the bytes the client sent. A restart replays the log through the parser, and the store comes back. The chapter is about files and fsync, about the thread that waits for the disk, and about what a crash takes.

A cache may forget, but a store that forgets on every restart is not much use. The simplest way to remember is to write down every command that changed something, in order. At startup, run them all again. Redis calls this the append-only file, and its documentation says the commands "are logged using the same format as the Redis protocol itself". That one decision means the parser you already have is also the loader, and a text editor can read the file.

Two details make it work. The first is expiry. A command such as SET k v EX 60 means "sixty seconds from now", and "now" is gone by the time the file is replayed. So the file stores a deadline on the wall clock instead, as PEXPIREAT k 1760000000000, which is a Redis command too. The second is fsync. A write call hands bytes to the kernel, which keeps them in memory and writes them to the disk when it likes. fsync waits until they are on the disk. The first survives a crash of the process, which is what the scene showed. Only the second survives a crash of the machine, and it is slow.

📜Why the log is in RESP, and why Redis rewrites it

The append-only file arrived in Redis 1.1, and it has kept the protocol format since. The persistence documentation gives the reason in practical terms. The file is "an easy to understand and parse format". If you flush the database by mistake, "you can still save your data set just by stopping the server, removing the latest command, and restarting". The cost is size. A counter incremented a hundred times is one key in memory and a hundred records on disk. Redis solves that by rewriting the file in the background, as "the minimal set of operations needed to create the current data set". The server kv does not rewrite, and the chapter says where that leaves it.

C: a file descriptor, a write, and a thread for the fsync#

The file is opened once, with O_APPEND, which makes every write go to the end of the file whatever else has happened to it. The policy is one of three, and they are the three that Redis offers under the names always, everysec and no:

/* How often the file is forced to disk. Redis has the same three settings. */
typedef enum {
    KV_FSYNC_ALWAYS,   /* after every command: slow and safe */
    KV_FSYNC_EVERYSEC, /* once a second: lose at most a second of writes */
    KV_FSYNC_NO        /* never: the operating system decides */
} kv_fsync_policy;

typedef struct {
    int fd; /* -1 when persistence is off */
    kv_fsync_policy policy;
    bool dirty;           /* bytes written since the last fsync was asked for */
    int64_t last_request; /* monotonic ms of the last request to the syncer */
    kv_syncer syncer;     /* the thread that waits for the disk */
} kv_aof;
c/ch11/src/aof.h · region policy
bool kv_aof_open(kv_aof *a, const char *path, kv_fsync_policy policy) {
    /* O_APPEND: every write goes to the end, even if another process appends too */
    int fd = open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_APPEND, 0644);
    if (fd < 0) {
        perror(path);
        return false;
    }
    *a = (kv_aof){.fd = fd, .policy = policy, .last_request = kv_now_ms()};
    if (!kv_syncer_start(&a->syncer, fd)) {
        perror("kv_syncer_start");
        close(fd);
        a->fd = -1;
        return false;
    }
    return true;
}
c/ch11/src/aof.c · region open

Recording a command means encoding it as an array of bulk strings, which is the format the client sent and the format kv_parse reads. The one rewrite turns a relative expiry into an absolute one, with the wall clock from a second function in clock.c. The record goes to the kernel with write at once. That is the system call, not fwrite, which would put a buffer of the C library's own in front of the kernel's. The Go gotcha below is what such a buffer does to a log. With the always policy it goes to the disk before the reply, on the one thread, and that is the 43 a second:

static bool kv_write_all(int fd, const char *p, size_t n) {
    size_t off = 0;
    while (off < n) {
        ssize_t w = write(fd, p + off, n - off);
        if (w < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) {
                continue;
            }
            perror("aof write");
            return false;
        }
        off += (size_t)w;
    }
    return true;
}

/* PEXPIREAT key <ms since 1970>, as the absolute form of EX, PX and EXPIRE. */
static bool kv_encode_pexpireat(kv_buf *out, const char *key, size_t klen, int64_t at) {
    char digits[32];
    int n = snprintf(digits, sizeof digits, "%lld", (long long)at);
    const char *argv[3] = {"PEXPIREAT", key, digits};
    size_t arglen[3] = {9, klen, (size_t)n};
    return kv_aof_encode(out, 3, argv, arglen);
}

bool kv_aof_record(kv_aof *a, const kv_cmd *c, int64_t wall_now) {
    if (a->fd < 0) {
        return true;
    }
    kv_buf out = {0};
    bool ok;
    long long n;
    if (kv_arg_is(c, 0, "SET") && c->argc == 5 && kv_parse_int(c->argv[4], c->arglen[4], &n) &&
        n > 0) {
        /* SET key value EX|PX n becomes SET key value, then PEXPIREAT key <absolute> */
        int64_t at = wall_now + (kv_arg_is(c, 3, "EX") ? n * 1000 : n);
        ok = kv_aof_encode(&out, 3, c->argv, c->arglen) &&
             kv_encode_pexpireat(&out, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], at);
    } else if (kv_arg_is(c, 0, "EXPIRE") && c->argc == 3 &&
               kv_parse_int(c->argv[2], c->arglen[2], &n)) {
        if (n <= 0) {
            const char *argv[2] = {"DEL", c->argv[1]};
            size_t arglen[2] = {3, c->arglen[1]};
            ok = kv_aof_encode(&out, 2, argv, arglen);
        } else {
            ok = kv_encode_pexpireat(&out, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], wall_now + n * 1000);
        }
    } else {
        ok = kv_aof_encode(&out, c->argc, c->argv, c->arglen);
    }
    ok = ok && kv_write_all(a->fd, out.data, out.len);
    kv_buf_free(&out);
    if (!ok) {
        return false;
    }
    a->dirty = true;
    if (a->policy == KV_FSYNC_ALWAYS) {
        /* always: wait for the disk here, before the reply, on the one thread */
        if (!kv_fsync(a->fd)) {
            perror("fsync");
        }
        a->dirty = false;
    }
    return true;
}

In the input function, a write command is recorded after it runs and before its reply is sent. So a client never sees OK for a write the file does not have:

/* The command ran; now it goes to the file, before the reply goes to the client. */
if (kv_cmd_is_write(&cmd) && !kv_aof_record(aof, &cmd, kv_wall_ms())) {
    return false;
}
c/ch11/src/server.c · region log

C again: the second thread#

With everysec, the fsync happens once a second, and the question is who waits for it. On this machine one takes 23 milliseconds, and the event loop cannot stop for 23 milliseconds without every client noticing. So the fsync gets a thread of its own, the first second thread in the C version of kv. The thread tools come from POSIX, the Portable Operating System Interface. A thread is started with pthread_create from a function and one void *, and waited for with pthread_join. The two threads share a struct, and the struct says which rule guards each field:

typedef struct {
    pthread_t thread;
    pthread_mutex_t mu; /* guards wanted and stop */
    pthread_cond_t cv;  /* signalled when either changes */
    bool wanted;        /* an fsync has been asked for */
    bool stop;          /* the thread should return */
    int fd;
    /* when the last fsync finished, in monotonic ms; written by the thread and read by
     * the loop without the lock, which is what an atomic is for */
    _Atomic int64_t last_sync;
} kv_syncer;
c/ch11/src/syncer.h · region struct

Three fields are guarded by a mutex, which one thread at a time may hold. A thread that reads or writes them without holding it has a data race. C says a data race is undefined behaviour, as chapter 6 said of an overrun. Nothing stops you forgetting the lock. The thread itself spends its life asleep on a condition variable, which is a place to wait until another thread says something has changed. The wait "atomically release[s] mutex and cause[s] the calling thread to block", and the mutex is held again when it returns:

/* The thread. It sleeps on the condition variable until the loop asks for an fsync or
 * for it to stop, and it never holds the mutex while it waits for the disk. */
static void *kv_syncer_run(void *arg) {
    kv_syncer *s = arg;
    pthread_mutex_lock(&s->mu);
    for (;;) {
        /* a while, not an if: a wait may return early, and the loop may change its mind */
        while (!s->wanted && !s->stop) {
            pthread_cond_wait(&s->cv, &s->mu); /* releases mu while asleep, takes it back after */
        }
        if (s->stop) {
            break;
        }
        s->wanted = false;
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&s->mu);
        if (!kv_fsync(s->fd)) {
            perror("fsync");
        }
        /* release: every write the fsync made visible is published with the time */
        atomic_store_explicit(&s->last_sync, kv_now_ms(), memory_order_release);
        pthread_mutex_lock(&s->mu);
    }
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&s->mu);
    return NULL;
}
c/ch11/src/syncer.c · region run

The wait is inside a while, never an if, and the manual says why. "Spurious wakeups from the pthread_cond_timedwait() or pthread_cond_wait() functions may occur", so the condition must be checked again on every return. The fourth field is an atomic. The thread writes the time the fsync finished. The loop reads it without taking the lock, to know whether the last request is still running. An atomic operation is one no other thread can see half done, and the memory order on it says what else it promises. The release on the store and the acquire on the load pair up. Everything the thread wrote before the store is visible to the loop after the load. The loop's side is three short functions:

bool kv_syncer_start(kv_syncer *s, int fd) {
    *s = (kv_syncer){.fd = fd};
    atomic_init(&s->last_sync, kv_now_ms());
    if (pthread_mutex_init(&s->mu, NULL) != 0 || pthread_cond_init(&s->cv, NULL) != 0) {
        return false;
    }
    /* A signal is delivered to any thread that does not block it. The stop handler must
     * run on the event loop's thread, so this thread is created with every signal
     * blocked, which it inherits, and the loop's mask is put back afterwards. */
    sigset_t all, before;
    sigfillset(&all);
    pthread_sigmask(SIG_BLOCK, &all, &before);
    int rc = pthread_create(&s->thread, NULL, kv_syncer_run, s);
    pthread_sigmask(SIG_SETMASK, &before, NULL);
    return rc == 0;
}

void kv_syncer_request(kv_syncer *s) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&s->mu);
    s->wanted = true;
    pthread_cond_signal(&s->cv);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&s->mu);
}

int64_t kv_syncer_last(const kv_syncer *s) {
    /* acquire: pairs with the release in the thread, so the reader sees the fsync */
    return atomic_load_explicit(&s->last_sync, memory_order_acquire);
}

void kv_syncer_stop(kv_syncer *s) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&s->mu);
    s->stop = true;
    pthread_cond_signal(&s->cv);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&s->mu);
    pthread_join(s->thread, NULL);
    pthread_cond_destroy(&s->cv);
    pthread_mutex_destroy(&s->mu);
}
c/ch11/src/syncer.c · region api

The event loop has woken ten times a second since chapter 10, for the sweep, and the request joins it. Once a second, when there is something to force and the last fsync has finished, the loop asks and goes straight back to its clients:

void kv_aof_tick(kv_aof *a, int64_t now) {
    if (a->fd < 0 || !a->dirty || a->policy != KV_FSYNC_EVERYSEC) {
        return;
    }
    if (now - a->last_request < 1000) {
        return; /* not yet a second since the last request */
    }
    if (kv_syncer_last(&a->syncer) < a->last_request) {
        return; /* the last fsync is still running: a slow disk gets one at a time */
    }
    a->dirty = false;
    a->last_request = now;
    kv_syncer_request(&a->syncer); /* returns at once; the thread waits for the disk */
}
c/ch11/src/aof.c · region tick

One line in the start function is about signals, and it answers a question chapter 10 left open. A signal is delivered to any thread that does not block it. The stop handler must run on the loop's thread, whose wait it is meant to interrupt. So the fsync thread is created with every signal blocked, a mask it inherits from the thread that created it. The loop's own mask is put back at once. ThreadSanitizer found the need for that line, in a way. Under it, a signal that landed on the sleeping thread was never acted on, and the server did not stop.

The thread is where the macOS surprise lives. On macOS, fsync only passes the bytes to the drive. The manual says that "the drive may not physically write the data to the platters for quite some time". The call that reaches the disk is fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC). The Go and Rust standard libraries both make it when you ask for a sync on macOS. So the C version makes it too, behind an #ifdef:

bool kv_fsync(int fd) {
#ifdef __APPLE__
    /* On macOS fsync() only hands the bytes to the drive, which may hold them in its own
     * cache. F_FULLFSYNC asks the drive to write them, and is what Go and Rust call. */
    return fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC) >= 0;
#else
    return fsync(fd) >= 0;
#endif
}
c/ch11/src/syncer.c · region fsync

Two threads sharing a struct is where the book's C tooling gains a sanitizer. ThreadSanitizer watches every access from every thread and reports two that touch the same memory without a lock or an atomic between them. It cannot run together with AddressSanitizer, so the build has a target of its own. make verify-c-tsan rebuilds every snapshot that calls pthread_create and runs the tests again:

$ make verify-c-tsan
## C (TSan) code/c/ch11
== c ch11: 207/207 passed

Thread safety of the C library#

POSIX requires every function in the standard to be thread-safe "except for the following functions". The list is short but has old friends on it. strtok keeps its place in a static. localtime and strerror return pointers to one shared buffer. getenv and rand share state. Each has a safe form with _r on the end, and the syncer uses perror, which is on the safe side. C11 standardised threads in <threads.h>, with thrd_create and mtx_t. But the header is optional and macOS does not provide it, so kv uses the POSIX names that every Unix has.

Write kv_aof_load. Open the file read-only, and return 0 when it does not exist, because a missing file is an empty store. Read it in chunks into a kv_buf. After each chunk, run kv_parse in a loop. Execute each complete command with kv_exec into a reply buffer that nobody reads. Count the commands. Bytes left over at the end are a truncated last command. Report them and drop them.

long kv_aof_load(const char *path, kv_store *store) {
    int fd = open(path, O_RDONLY);
    if (fd < 0) {
        return errno == ENOENT ? 0 : -1;

Stuck?Show the full listing
long kv_aof_load(const char *path, kv_store *store) {
    int fd = open(path, O_RDONLY);
    if (fd < 0) {
        return errno == ENOENT ? 0 : -1; /* no file yet is an empty store, not an error */
    }
    kv_buf in = {0};
    kv_buf out = {0}; /* the replies, which nobody reads */
    char tmp[65536];
    long applied = 0;
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = read(fd, tmp, sizeof tmp);
        if (n < 0 && errno == EINTR) {
            continue;
        }
        if (n <= 0) {
            break;
        }
        if (!kv_buf_append(&in, tmp, (size_t)n)) {
            applied = -1;
            break;
        }
        /* the same parser and the same executor as a live client */
        for (;;) {
            kv_cmd cmd;
            size_t used = 0;
            kv_parse_status st = kv_parse(in.data, in.len, &cmd, &used);
            if (st != KV_PARSE_OK) {
                break;
            }
            kv_exec(&cmd, store, &out);
            out.len = 0;
            kv_buf_consume(&in, used);
            applied++;
        }
    }
    if (in.len > 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "aof: dropped %zu trailing bytes of a truncated command\n", in.len);
    }
    kv_buf_free(&in);
    kv_buf_free(&out);
    close(fd);
    return applied;
}
c/ch11/src/aof.c · region load

The absolute deadline needs a command of its own, PEXPIREAT, which turns a wall-clock time back into a monotonic one for the store. A deadline already in the past deletes the key, which is how an expired key stays expired across a restart:

/* PEXPIREAT key <ms since 1970>: the absolute form that the append-only file uses. The
 * wall-clock deadline is turned into a monotonic one for the store. */
static bool kv_cmd_pexpireat(const kv_cmd *c, kv_store *s, kv_buf *out, int64_t now) {
    long long at;
    if (!kv_parse_int(c->argv[2], c->arglen[2], &at)) {
        return kv_reply_error(out, "ERR value is not an integer or out of range");
    }
    kv_entry *e = kv_store_find(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1], now);
    if (e == NULL) {
        return kv_reply_int(out, 0);
    }
    int64_t left = at - kv_wall_ms();
    if (left <= 0) {
        kv_store_del(s, c->argv[1], c->arglen[1]);
    } else {
        e->expires_at = now + left;
    }
    return kv_reply_int(out, 1);
}
c/ch11/src/cmd.c · region pexpireat

Startup replays the file before it serves the first client, so that no client sees an empty store, and then opens the file for appending. At the other end, the clean stop from chapter 10 joins the thread, forces the last bytes to disk and closes the file:

/* KV_AOF names the file. Replay it first, then open it for appending. */
kv_aof aof = {.fd = -1, .policy = KV_FSYNC_EVERYSEC};
const char *path = getenv("KV_AOF");
if (path != NULL && *path != '\0') {
    kv_fsync_policy policy;
    if (!kv_fsync_policy_parse(getenv("KV_FSYNC"), &policy)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "KV_FSYNC must be always, everysec or no\n");
        return 1;
    }
    long applied = kv_aof_load(path, store);
    if (applied < 0) {
        perror(path);
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(stderr, "kv replayed %ld commands from %s\n", applied, path);
    if (!kv_aof_open(&aof, path, policy)) {
        return 1;
    }
}

⚠️write is not fsync C

After write returns, the bytes are in the kernel, not on the disk. If the process is killed, the kernel still has them and writes them out, which is why the scene lost nothing. If the machine loses power, they are gone. fsync makes the kernel write them now and wait. The Linux manual adds that even then the directory entry for a new file may not have reached the disk. On macOS, fsync itself is not enough, and the section above says what is. Most databases have a paragraph like this one in their source.

🖥fork, the other way to do work in the background

Redis takes its snapshots with fork, which "creates a new process by duplicating the calling process". The child writes the whole dataset to a file while the parent goes on serving. The kernel copies a page only when one of them writes to it. The child "is created with a single thread", the one that called fork. That is why a program with threads must be careful what the child does. Windows has no fork. After completion ports, that is the second reason why Redis on Windows was always a port and never the same program. The server kv uses a thread instead of a process, which is the choice Go and Rust make everywhere.

Go: the same reader, backwards#

The Go log is a struct with a lock, because many goroutines record into it. The policy is parsed from the environment into one of three constants:

// Policy says how often the file is forced to disk. Redis has the same three settings.
type Policy int

const (
	Always   Policy = iota // after every command: slow and safe
	EverySec               // once a second: lose at most a second of writes
	No                     // never: the operating system decides
)

func ParsePolicy(s string) (Policy, error) {
	switch strings.ToLower(s) {
	case "", "everysec":
		return EverySec, nil
	case "always":
		return Always, nil
	case "no":
		return No, nil
	}
	return 0, fmt.Errorf("KV_FSYNC must be always, everysec or no, not %q", s)
}

// Log is the open file. Many goroutines record into it, so it has a lock of its own.
type Log struct {
	mu     sync.Mutex
	f      *os.File
	w      *bufio.Writer
	policy Policy
	dirty  bool
	syncs chan struct{} // a request to the syncer goroutine; room for one, so a second waits for nobody
	done  sync.WaitGroup
}
go/ch11/internal/aof/aof.go · region policy

Recording uses the WriteArrayLen and WriteBulk functions from the protocol package, which were written to answer clients and serve for log records too. The buffer is flushed after every record. The book's own test found the bug that this line fixes, and the gotcha below tells the story:

// Record appends one command. A relative expiry is rewritten as an absolute PEXPIREAT,
// because the file may be replayed much later. The bytes reach the kernel before this
// returns: a policy delays only the fsync, never the write, so a crash of the process
// loses nothing and only a crash of the machine can lose the last second.
func (l *Log) Record(args [][]byte, now time.Time) error {
	l.mu.Lock()
	defer l.mu.Unlock()
	for _, cmd := range rewrite(args, now) {
		if err := resp.WriteArrayLen(l.w, len(cmd)); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		for _, a := range cmd {
			if err := resp.WriteBulk(l.w, a); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}
	}
	if err := l.w.Flush(); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	l.dirty = true
	if l.policy == Always {
		return l.syncLocked()
	}
	return nil
}

// rewrite turns one command into the commands the file stores.
func rewrite(args [][]byte, now time.Time) [][][]byte {
	name := strings.ToUpper(string(args[0]))
	switch {
	case name == "SET" && len(args) == 5:
		n, err := strconv.ParseInt(string(args[4]), 10, 64)
		if err != nil || n <= 0 {
			break
		}
		d := time.Duration(n) * time.Millisecond
		if strings.ToUpper(string(args[3])) == "EX" {
			d = time.Duration(n) * time.Second
		}
		return [][][]byte{args[:3], pexpireat(args[1], now.Add(d))}
	case name == "EXPIRE" && len(args) == 3:
		n, err := strconv.ParseInt(string(args[2]), 10, 64)
		if err != nil {
			break
		}
		if n <= 0 {
			return [][][]byte{{[]byte("DEL"), args[1]}}
		}
		return [][][]byte{pexpireat(args[1], now.Add(time.Duration(n)*time.Second))}
	}
	return [][][]byte{args}
}

func pexpireat(key []byte, at time.Time) [][]byte {
	return [][]byte{[]byte("PEXPIREAT"), key, []byte(strconv.FormatInt(at.UnixMilli(), 10))}
}
go/ch11/internal/aof/aof.go · region record

Go again: a goroutine that waits for the disk#

The Go version of the fsync thread is a goroutine and a channel. It is shorter than the C version by the whole of the mutex and the condition variable. The channel has room for one request. A sender that finds it full is a request nobody needs, because one is already waiting. So the select with a default drops it without blocking. The goroutine ranges over the channel and ends when Close closes it, and the WaitGroup is how Close waits for that:

// syncer runs on a goroutine of its own and calls fsync whenever it is asked, so that no
// client ever waits for the disk while holding the log's lock. The range ends when Close
// closes the channel, and the WaitGroup lets Close wait for that.
func (l *Log) syncer() {
	for range l.syncs {
		if err := l.f.Sync(); err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "aof:", err)
		}
	}
}

// Tick is called once a second. With everysec it flushes the buffer to the kernel and
// asks the syncer for an fsync, without waiting for it. The select with a default never
// blocks: if a request is already waiting in the channel, this one is not needed.
func (l *Log) Tick() {
	l.mu.Lock()
	defer l.mu.Unlock()
	if !l.dirty || l.policy != EverySec {
		return
	}
	if err := l.w.Flush(); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "aof:", err)
		return
	}
	l.dirty = false
	select {
	case l.syncs <- struct{}{}:
	default:
	}
}
go/ch11/internal/aof/aof.go · region syncer

The file is the one shared thing. The os package says that "the methods of File are safe for concurrent use". So a Sync on the goroutine and a Write under the lock may overlap. Go's Sync on macOS makes the same F_FULLFSYNC call as the C version, which is why the always policy measures the same 44 a second. The ticker goroutine from chapter 10 calls Tick once a second and returns when the context is cancelled.

Write Replay. Open the file, and return 0 and no error when it does not exist. Wrap it in a bufio.Reader and call resp.ReadCommand in a loop, handing each command to apply. Stop at io.EOF. Treat io.ErrUnexpectedEOF as a truncated last command, print a line about it, and return what you have.

func Replay(path string, apply func(args [][]byte)) (int, error) {

Stuck?Show the full listing
// Replay reads the file with the same parser a client goes through and hands each
// command to apply. A truncated last command is dropped, as Redis drops it. A missing
// file is an empty store, not an error.
func Replay(path string, apply func(args [][]byte)) (int, error) {
	f, err := os.Open(path)
	if errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) {
		return 0, nil
	}
	if err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}
	defer f.Close()
	r := bufio.NewReaderSize(f, 1<<16)
	n := 0
	for {
		args, err := resp.ReadCommand(r)
		if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
			return n, nil
		}
		if errors.Is(err, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF) {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "aof: dropped a truncated command at the end")
			return n, nil
		}
		if err != nil {
			return n, err
		}
		apply(args)
		n++
	}
}
go/ch11/internal/aof/aof.go · region replay

The command function takes the log as a parameter, and records a write before running it. During replay the log is nil, so nothing is recorded twice. The replies during replay go to a writer over io.Discard. Because the log and the store have different locks, two goroutines can record in one order and run in the other. A replay can then end with a different value for a key that both wrote. The Rust version below closes that gap with one lock:

// Execute runs one command against the store and writes its reply. A write command is
// also recorded in the log, when there is one. During replay the log is nil.
func Execute(args [][]byte, s Storer, log *aof.Log, w *bufio.Writer) error {
	now := time.Now()
	if len(args) == 0 {
		return resp.WriteError(w, "ERR empty command")
	}
	name := strings.ToUpper(string(args[0]))
	cmd, ok := commands[name]
	if !ok {
		shown := string(args[0])
		if len(shown) > 40 {
			shown = shown[:40]
		}
		return resp.WriteError(w, "ERR unknown command '"+shown+"'")
	}
	if n := len(args); (cmd.arity < 0 && n < -cmd.arity) || (cmd.arity > 0 && n != cmd.arity) {
		return arity(w, strings.ToLower(name))
	}
	if log != nil && aof.IsWrite(name) {
		if err := log.Record(args, now); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}
	return cmd.run(args, s, w, now)
}
go/ch11/internal/cmd/cmd.go · region execute
// KV_AOF names the file. Replay it first, with no log, then open it for appending.
var log *aof.Log
if path := os.Getenv("KV_AOF"); path != "" {
	policy, err := aof.ParsePolicy(os.Getenv("KV_FSYNC"))
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	sink := bufio.NewWriter(io.Discard)
	n, err := aof.Replay(path, func(args [][]byte) { cmd.Execute(args, s, nil, sink) })
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "aof:", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "kv replayed %d commands from %s\n", n, path)
	if log, err = aof.Open(path, policy); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	go func() {
		tick := time.NewTicker(time.Second)
		defer tick.Stop()
		for {
			select {
			case <-ctx.Done():
				return
			case <-tick.C:
				log.Tick()
			}
		}
	}()
}
go/ch11/cmd/kv/main.go · region startup
⚠️A buffered writer and a kill Go

The first Go version lost every write on restart, and the test caught it. The log used a bufio.Writer, as every Go file writer does, and flushed it once a second from the ticker. The test stops the server with a signal, which runs no Go code. So the bytes still in the buffer never reached the kernel. The C version had no such bug, because it has no buffer between the record and write. The fix is the Flush after every record. A policy decides when to fsync. It must never decide when to write.

Rust: the store and the log under one lock#

The Rust log is a struct around a BufWriter<File>, and it has no lock of its own. Instead the store and the log live in one struct, Db, and the one lock from chapter 9 now guards both. A command and its record happen together, and no other command can come between them:

/// Everything a command may touch. One Mutex around this struct means a command and its
/// record in the log happen together, with no other command in between.
pub struct Db {
    pub store: MapStore,
    pub aof: Option<Aof>,
}

Record first, so that a command the file holds is one the server accepted. Use a let chain, which the 2024 edition allows, one if with two conditions joined by &&.

pub fn execute(&mut self, args: &Command, w: &mut impl Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    // your code here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
impl Db {
    /// Record a write command, then run it. Recording comes first, so that a command
    /// the file holds is one that was accepted, and a crash between the two loses a
    /// reply and never a write.
    pub fn execute(&mut self, args: &Command, w: &mut impl Write) -> io::Result<()> {
        if let Some(log) = self.aof.as_mut()
            && args.first().is_some_and(|name| aof::is_write(name))
        {
            log.record(args, aof::wall_ms())?;
        }
        crate::cmd::execute(args, &mut self.store, w)
    }
}
rust/ch11/src/db.rs · region execute

Recording mirrors the C version. The flush after each record is the same fix as in Go. The first Rust version had the same bug, and the same test found it:

/// Append one command. A relative expiry is rewritten as an absolute PEXPIREAT,
/// because the file may be replayed much later. The bytes reach the kernel before this
/// returns: a policy delays only the fsync, never the write, so a crash of the process
/// loses nothing and only a crash of the machine can lose the last second.
pub fn record(&mut self, args: &Command<'_>, now_ms: i64) -> io::Result<()> {
    for cmd in rewrite(args, now_ms) {
        resp::write_array_len(&mut self.file, cmd.len())?;
        for a in &cmd {
            resp::write_bulk(&mut self.file, a)?;
        }
    }
    self.file.flush()?;
    self.dirty = true;
    if self.policy == Policy::Always {
        self.sync()?;
    }
    Ok(())
}

/// Flush the buffer and force the file to disk, on the calling thread. The always
/// policy does this after every record, and main does it once, last of all.
pub fn sync(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
    self.file.flush()?;
    if mem::replace(&mut self.dirty, false) && self.policy != Policy::No {
        self.file.get_ref().sync_all()?;
    }
    Ok(())
}
rust/ch11/src/aof.rs · region record

Rust again: a scoped thread on a channel#

The Rust fsync thread needs the file and nothing else, so the log gives it a second handle. The standard library says a cloned File "shares the same underlying file handle", and an fsync through either forces what was written through both. The other method is the once-a-second question, and it uses mem::replace, which puts a new value in a place and returns the old one. Its cousin mem::take puts the default there instead, and mem::swap exchanges two places. All three exist because Rust will not let you move a value out of a &mut and leave a hole:

impl Aof {
    /// A second handle to the same file, for the thread that waits for the disk. An
    /// fsync through either handle forces everything written through both.
    pub fn handle(&self) -> io::Result<File> {
        self.file.get_ref().try_clone()
    }

    /// Once a second, with everysec: flush the buffer to the kernel and say whether an
    /// fsync is owed. `mem::replace` reads the flag and clears it in one expression.
    pub fn owes_sync(&mut self) -> io::Result<bool> {
        self.file.flush()?;
        Ok(self.policy == Policy::EverySec && mem::replace(&mut self.dirty, false))
    }
}
rust/ch11/src/aof.rs · region handle

The thread lives in the scope from chapter 10, beside the sweeper and the clients. It owns the handle and the receiving end of an mpsc channel, and it does one thing for each message. The sweeper owns the sending end. When the sweeper returns at shutdown, the sender is dropped and the channel reports that it is disconnected. The for loop ends, and the scope joins the thread. No flag and no stop message:

// The thread that waits for the disk. It receives a request on the channel,
// calls fsync through its own handle, and never touches the lock. The loop ends
// when every sender is dropped, which happens when the sweeper returns.
let (sync_tx, sync_rx) = mpsc::channel::<()>();
if let Some(file) = sync_file {
    s.spawn(move || {
        for () in sync_rx {
            if let Err(e) = file.sync_all() {
                eprintln!("aof: {e}");
            }
        }
    });
}
rust/ch11/src/main.rs · region syncer
// every tenth tick, once a second, the everysec policy flushes the log and
// asks the syncer for an fsync, without waiting for it
if tick.is_multiple_of(10) {
    match db.aof.as_mut().map(Aof::owes_sync) {
        Some(Ok(true)) => {
            let _ = sync_tx.send(());
        }
        Some(Err(e)) => eprintln!("aof: {e}"),
        _ => {}
    }
}
rust/ch11/src/main.rs · region sync

The tokio version cannot spawn a thread that blocks, and fsync blocks. This is the case chapter 9 promised spawn_blocking for. The call runs on a thread tokio keeps for exactly that, and the sweeper task goes on at once. The handle is in an Arc, because each blocking call needs its own owner:

// fsync blocks, and a task must not. spawn_blocking runs the call on
// a thread kept for exactly that, and the task goes on at once.
if owed && let Some(file) = sync_file.clone() {
    tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || {
        if let Err(e) = file.sync_all() {
            eprintln!("aof: {e}");
        }
    });
}
rust/ch11/src/bin/kv_async.rs · region blocking

Replay reads the file in chunks into the same kind of buffer the server reads a socket into. The same parse takes whole commands out of it. The parser does not know whether it is reading a socket or a file, and the replies go into io::sink():

/// Replay the file into the store, through the same parser a client goes through, from
/// the same kind of buffer. A truncated last command is dropped, as Redis drops it. A
/// missing file is an empty store.
pub fn replay(path: &Path, store: &mut MapStore) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let mut file = match File::open(path) {
        Ok(f) => f,
        Err(e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::NotFound => return Ok(0),
        Err(e) => return Err(e),
    };
    let mut sink = io::sink();
    let mut buf: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();
    let mut chunk = vec![0u8; 1 << 16];
    let mut n = 0;
    loop {
        let got = file.read(&mut chunk)?;
        if got == 0 {
            if !buf.is_empty() {
                eprintln!("aof: dropped a truncated command at the end");
            }
            return Ok(n);
        }
        buf.extend_from_slice(&chunk[..got]);
        let mut used = 0;
        while let Parsed::Done(args, len) = resp::parse(&buf[used..])? {
            crate::cmd::execute(&args, store, &mut sink)?;
            n += 1;
            used += len;
        }
        buf.drain(..used);
    }
}
rust/ch11/src/aof.rs · region replay
⚠️Drop does not run when the process is killed Rust

The log has a Drop that syncs the file, and a signal never calls it. Drop runs when a value goes out of scope in a program that is still running. A process ended by kill -9, by the test runner, or by a power cut runs no more Rust code. So the Drop is a courtesy for a clean exit. The clean stop from chapter 10 does the same sync on purpose, last of all. The flush after every record is what the durability of the log rests on, exactly as in Go. Rust's ownership rules say nothing about this. The operating system does.

One thread, three ways#

The same thread was written three times in this chapter, and the three versions are a fair picture of the three languages with threads. The C version is a struct, a mutex, a condition variable and an atomic. A comment on each field says which rule guards it, and a sanitizer checks the comments. The Go version is a channel, and the channel is both the message and the lock. The Rust version is a channel too. The compiler checked that the handle could cross to the thread, and that the thread could not outlive the scope.

The fsync threadCGoRust
Starting itpthread_create with a function and a void *wg.Gos.spawn inside the scope
Waiting for workpthread_cond_wait in a whilefor range chfor () in rx
Asking for worklock, flag, signal, unlocka send, dropped when one is waitinga send
Telling it to stopa second flag under the same lockclose(ch)drop the sender
Waiting for it to endpthread_joinwg.Waitthe end of the scope
A forgotten lockundefined behaviour, found by TSan if the test provokes ita data race, found by the detector if the test provokes itdoes not compile

What a crash takes#

Three kinds of failure, and three policies, make a small table that is worth learning. Every version of kv behaves the same way, because all three call the same kernel.

After a crash ofCGoRust
The process, with any policynothing lost, the kernel has every recordthe samethe same
The machine, policy alwaysnothing lostthe samethe same
The machine, policy everysecup to one second of writes lostthe samethe same
The machine, policy nowhatever the kernel had not written, usually secondsthe samethe same
A truncated last recorddropped at replaythe samethe same

The price of always is the scene's number, and it is why Redis defaults to everysec. On the author's machine, with the disk really flushed, the C server answered 43 SET commands a second with one client. With fifty clients it answered 44, because the disk is the whole cost. With everysec it answered 14,700 from one client and 47,700 from fifty. The no policy was no faster, because one fsync a second on a thread of its own costs the clients nothing. The scene's file held 59,694 commands in 2,686,230 bytes, 45 bytes a command, which is the cost of a format a person can read. And a kill -9 never cut a record in half, because each record is one write call and the kernel either has it or does not. Only the machine's death can leave a truncated last record, and all three versions drop it at replay, as Redis does.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
Writing the fileOKStrongStrongC encodes into a buffer and calls write. Go and Rust reuse the protocol writers and flush.
ReplayStrongStrongStrongAll three reuse the parser from chapter 4 unchanged, which is the point of a log in RESP.
A crash of the processStrongOKOKC writes straight through. Go and Rust needed a flush the book's test had to find.
The clock on diskOKStrongOKC converts between two clocks itself, while Go's time.Time holds both and Rust converts with a helper.
Log and store togetherStrongOKStrongOne C thread needs no lock, Go takes two locks, and Rust takes one around both.
The fsync threadWeakStrongStrongC needs a mutex, a condition variable, an atomic and a sanitizer. Go needs a channel, and Rust a channel the compiler checks.
Reaching the disk on macOSOKStrongStrongC must know about F_FULLFSYNC itself. Both standard libraries know.
Carry forward
  • write and fsync. write passes bytes to the kernel, which survives a dead process. fsync waits for the disk, which survives a dead machine. On this disk that is 43 a second.
  • Condition variable. A place a thread sleeps until another signals it, always inside a while, because a wait may return for no reason.
  • A thread's channel. In Go and Rust the channel is the message and the lock. Closing it, or dropping the last sender, is how the thread learns to stop.

Testing and fuzzing#

Quality and shipping · Chapter 12· 27 min read· 417 lines of code
▶Scene

Take the chapter 4 parser and remove the one check that compares a length field with the room it has. Give the result to a fuzzer, with a single valid request as its only hint:

$ make fuzz-trusting
INFO: seed corpus: files: 1 min: 22b max: 22b total: 22b rss: 35Mb
==15==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x5030005a29d0
WRITE of size 41 at 0x5030005a29d0 thread T0
    #1 0x556e366fc450 in trusting_parse /w/bugs/trusting_parser.c:77:9
0x5030005a29d0 is located 0 bytes after 32-byte region
elapsed 2 s
$ od -c crash-8c6f20f4728eeea01d638af72038b7d1c045481f | head -1
0000000   *   2  \r  \n   $   4   1  \r  \n   E  \0  \0  \0  \0   (  \0

Two seconds. The fuzzer turned $4 into $41, padded the argument to match, and wrote nine bytes past a thirty-two byte buffer. No unit test in this book thought of that input, and no person would have.

Every chapter so far was checked by one script that talks to kv through redis-cli. This chapter adds the tests that live beside the code, in each language's own runner, and the tools that find what tests cannot. A fuzzer throws millions of inputs at the parser. A sanitizer or a race detector watches the program run. The chapter is about what each language can prove, and when.

The protocol tests in tests/protocol/ are the same for all three servers, and that is their value. They do not say which function is wrong, and they only send what a person thought to write. The parser from chapter 4 has five ways to fail on bad input, and the script tries one. A unit test can try all five, and a fuzzer can try five million things nobody thought of.

The toolsCGoRust
A unit testa main you write, with a CHECK macroa TestXxx function in a _test.go filea #[test] function in a mod tests
Running themmake test, a target you writego test ./...cargo test
