What the book runsthe tests under ASan and UBSan, and TSan for the threadsgo vet, go test -racecargo test, clippy -D warnings
📜Why C needs tools the other two do not

C has no test runner in its standard library, and no way to find a bad pointer at run time. Both gaps were filled from outside. Valgrind, released by Julian Seward in 2002, runs a program on a simulated processor and watches every memory access. The program runs twenty to thirty times slower. AddressSanitizer, from Google in 2012, puts the checks into the compiled code instead, at about twice the cost. clang and gcc both carry it. Go and Rust were designed after both tools existed and built the answers in. Go's runtime can watch for races and its test tool can fuzz. Rust's compiler refuses the programs that the sanitizer would have caught. The C tools remain the reason that C is still written at all.

C: a runner you write, and a sanitizer that watches#

A C test is a program. The runner for kv is thirty lines. A counter, and a macro that prints the file and the line of a failed check and carries on. One assertion is checked by the compiler instead of the test. _Static_assert takes a constant expression, and if it is false "a compile-time error occurs and the compiler must display message". A test suite that assumes a limit should fail to build when the limit changes, not fail at run time:

static int failed = 0;
static int passed = 0;

/* Report a failure with its location, and carry on to the next check. */
#define CHECK(cond)                                                                                \
    do {                                                                                           \
        if (cond) {                                                                                \
            passed++;                                                                              \
        } else {                                                                                   \
            failed++;                                                                              \
            fprintf(stderr, "%s:%d: check failed: %s\n", __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond);               \
        }                                                                                          \
    } while (0)

/* The tests assume a request may carry at least four arguments. The compiler checks it,
 * so a smaller limit fails to build instead of failing at run time. */
_Static_assert(KV_MAX_ARGS >= 4, "the tests use requests of up to four arguments");

The tests for the parser cover the three answers from chapter 4, and the inline form. The one that matters most is the second. It cuts a valid request at every byte and checks that the parser says "incomplete" and never "bad". The event loop depends on exactly that:

Exercise 12.1CEvery prefix is incomplete

Write test_parse_incomplete_at_every_cut. Take a valid request, and for every length from 0 to one less than the whole, call kv_parse on that prefix. Each call must return KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE. A single KV_PARSE_BAD would make the server drop a client in the middle of a slow request.

static void test_parse_incomplete_at_every_cut(void) {
    const char *req = "*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n";
    /* your loop here */
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
static void test_parse_complete(void) {
    const char *req = "*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n";
    kv_cmd cmd;
    size_t used = 0;
    CHECK(kv_parse(req, strlen(req), &cmd, &used) == KV_PARSE_OK);
    CHECK(used == strlen(req));
    CHECK(cmd.argc == 2);
    CHECK(cmd.arglen[0] == 4 && memcmp(cmd.argv[0], "ECHO", 4) == 0);
    CHECK(cmd.arglen[1] == 2 && memcmp(cmd.argv[1], "hi", 2) == 0);
}

static void test_parse_incomplete_at_every_cut(void) {
    /* every prefix of a valid request is incomplete, never bad */
    const char *req = "*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n";
    for (size_t n = 0; n < strlen(req); n++) {
        kv_cmd cmd;
        size_t used = 0;
        CHECK(kv_parse(req, n, &cmd, &used) == KV_PARSE_INCOMPLETE);
    }
}

static void test_parse_bad(void) {
    const char *bad[] = {"*x\r\n", "*1\r\n#4\r\nECHO\r\n", "*1\r\n$4\r\nECHOXX",
                         "*1\r\n$99999999\r\n", "*100\r\n"};
    for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof bad / sizeof bad[0]; i++) {
        kv_cmd cmd;
        size_t used = 0;
        CHECK(kv_parse(bad[i], strlen(bad[i]), &cmd, &used) == KV_PARSE_BAD);
    }
}

static void test_parse_inline(void) {
    const char *req = "  SET  a   b\r\n";
    kv_cmd cmd;
    size_t used = 0;
    CHECK(kv_parse(req, strlen(req), &cmd, &used) == KV_PARSE_OK);
    CHECK(cmd.argc == 3);
    CHECK(cmd.arglen[2] == 1 && cmd.argv[2][0] == 'b');
    CHECK(used == strlen(req));
}
c/ch12/tests/test_resp.c · region parse

The list of tests is written once, as an X-macro, the trick from chapter 5's command table. Each use of the list gives X a new meaning. Here it makes a table of names and function pointers, and main walks the table. A name on the command line runs one test, and a new test is one line:

/* The list of tests, written once. Each use of the list defines X to mean something
 * different: a declaration, an entry in a table, or a call. Adding a test is one line
 * here, and nothing else to keep in step. */
#define KV_TESTS                                                                                   \
    X(parse_complete)                                                                              \
    X(parse_incomplete_at_every_cut)                                                               \
    X(parse_bad)                                                                                   \
    X(parse_inline)                                                                                \
    X(parse_int)                                                                                   \
    X(glob)

static const struct {
    const char *name;
    void (*run)(void);
} tests[] = {
#define X(name) {#name, test_##name},
    KV_TESTS
#undef X
};

/* Run every test, or only those whose name contains the argument: ./test_resp parse */
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    const char *only = argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "";
    int ran = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof tests / sizeof tests[0]; i++) {
        if (strstr(tests[i].name, only) == NULL) {
            continue;
        }
        int before = failed;
        tests[i].run();
        printf("%s %s\n", failed == before ? "ok  " : "FAIL", tests[i].name);
        ran++;
    }
    printf("%d tests, %d checks passed, %d failed\n", ran, passed, failed);
    return failed == 0 ? 0 : 1;
}

The Makefile gains a test target. It compiles the test file with every source file except main.c, all under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and runs the result. The sanitizers are the point. A test that passes under them has also proved that it read no freed memory and overflowed no integer on the way:

# The unit tests: every source under src/ except main.c, plus the test file, compiled
# together under the sanitizers. make test fails when a check fails.

test: build/test_resp
	./build/test_resp

build/test_resp: tests/test_resp.c $(SRC) | build
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -fsanitize=address,undefined -o $@ tests/test_resp.c $(filter-out src/main.c,$(SRC))

To see what the sanitizer does when there is something to find, the snapshot includes the bug from the chapter 4 gotcha, on purpose. It keeps a pointer into a buffer, grows the buffer, and reads through the pointer:

int main(void) {
    kv_buf b = {0};
    kv_buf_append(&b, "GET key\r\n", 9);
    const char *key = b.data + 4; /* points at "key", inside the buffer */
    char filler[2048];
    memset(filler, 'x', sizeof filler);
    kv_buf_append(&b, filler, sizeof filler); /* the buffer grows, and may move */
    printf("%.3s\n", key);                    /* reads through the old pointer */
    kv_buf_free(&b);
    return 0;
}

The report names the line that read the freed memory, the line that freed it, and the realloc inside kv_buf_append that did the freeing. Without the sanitizer the program prints key most of the time, because the old bytes are usually still there. That is the whole problem with undefined behaviour. A debugger session#

The third way to see the same bug is to watch it happen. A debugger stops the program at a line and shows what the variables hold. Build the bug without optimisation and with debug information, and give gdb a script of commands. The session below stops before the buffer grows, prints the buffer's address and the pointer into it, steps one line, and prints them again:

$ cc -O0 -g -o use_after_free bugs/use_after_free.c src/buf.c
$ gdb -q -batch -x session.gdb ./use_after_free
Breakpoint 1, main () at bugs/use_after_free.c:15
15	    kv_buf_append(&b, filler, sizeof filler); /* the buffer grows, and may move */
$1 = 0x7ffff7f55020 "GET key\r\n"
$2 = 0x7ffff7f55024 "key\r\n"
16	    printf("%.3s\n", key);                    /* reads through the old pointer */
$3 = 0x7ffff7f51030 "GET key\r\n", 'x' <repeats 191 times>...
$4 = 0x7ffff7f55024 <error: Cannot access memory at address 0x7ffff7f55024>
$5 = 4096

One next, and the buffer's data moved from one address to another while key kept the old one. The debugger cannot even read it now. On macOS the debugger is lldb, with the same commands in a different dialect. The book recorded this session in a Linux container, because gdb is what the container had. A session like this takes a minute, and it is the right tool when a sanitizer says what happened and you want to see why.

The same snapshot holds a second bug on purpose, for the sanitizer chapter 11 introduced. Two threads add to one counter with no lock, which is the simplest data race there is:

static long counter = 0;

static void *add(void *arg) {
    (void)arg;
    for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
        counter++; /* a read, an add and a write, and another thread between them */
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main(void) {
    pthread_t a, b;
    pthread_create(&a, NULL, add, NULL);
    pthread_create(&b, NULL, add, NULL);
    pthread_join(a, NULL);
    pthread_join(b, NULL);
    printf("%ld\n", counter); /* 200000 if nothing went wrong, which something did */
    return 0;
}

$ make race
WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=28355)
  Write of size 8 at 0x00010c76e000 by thread T2:
    #0 add race.c:12
  Previous write of size 8 at 0x00010c76e000 by thread T1:
    #0 add race.c:12
  Location is global 'counter' at 0x00010c76e000
SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race race.c:12 in add
200000

The count came out right, at 200,000, and the race was reported anyway. That is the difference between a detector and a test. The test checks the answer, which was correct by luck. ThreadSanitizer "is a tool that detects data races", and it saw two threads write the same eight bytes with nothing between them, whatever the answer. The clang documentation puts its cost at "about 5x-15x" in time. That is why the book runs it on its own target, make verify-c-tsan, rather than on every build.

A fuzzer is the last tool, and the scene showed what it does. The one that comes with clang is libFuzzer, "an in-process, coverage-guided, evolutionary fuzzing engine". It calls one function of yours millions of times with inputs it mutates. It watches which branches each input reaches, so that it can mutate the interesting ones further. The target for kv feeds the input through the parser and the executor, as the server would:

int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t *data, size_t size) {
    kv_store store = {0};
    kv_buf out = {0};
    const char *p = (const char *)data;
    size_t len = size;
    /* run every complete command in the input, as the server would */
    for (;;) {
        kv_cmd cmd;
        size_t used = 0;
        if (kv_parse(p, len, &cmd, &used) != KV_PARSE_OK) {
            break;
        }
        kv_exec(&cmd, &store, &out);
        p += used;
        len -= used;
    }
    kv_buf_free(&out);
    kv_store_free(&store);
    return 0;
}
c/ch12/fuzz/fuzz_parse.c · region target

The scene's target is the same shape, pointed at the parser that trusts its length field. The parser is the chapter 4 one with a single line missing, and the line is the one the chapter 4 gotcha was about:

/* One request, with the arguments copied out. The bulk length is trusted: nothing
 * checks it against the room in the argument. A length of 40 writes 40 bytes into 32,
 * and the attacker chooses the 8 that land on whatever the heap keeps next. */
int trusting_parse(const char *data, size_t len, trusting_cmd *cmd) {
    const char *end = data + len;
    const char *p = data;
    const char *eol = find_eol(p, end);
    if (eol == NULL || *p != '*') {
        return -1;
    }
    long n;
    if (!parse_number(p + 1, eol, &n) || n > TRUSTING_MAX_ARGS) {
        return -1;
    }
    p = eol + 1;
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (p >= end || *p != '$' || (eol = find_eol(p, end)) == NULL) {
            return -1;
        }
        long blen;
        if (!parse_number(p + 1, eol, &blen)) {
            return -1;
        }
        p = eol + 1;
        if (end - p < blen + 2) {
            return -1;
        }
        memcpy(cmd->argv[i], p, (size_t)blen); /* the missing check was here */
        cmd->arglen[i] = (size_t)blen;
        p += blen + 2;
    }
    cmd->argc = (size_t)n;
    return 0;
}
c/ch12/bugs/trusting_parser.c · region bug

Two things made the two seconds possible. Each argument's buffer is a heap allocation of its own, so AddressSanitizer sees the first byte past it. And the fuzzer started from one valid request, so it did not have to discover what a request looks like. Without the seed, and with the arguments inside one struct, the same fuzzer ran twenty-two million inputs in a minute and found nothing. A fuzzer is only as good as the signal it gets, and a seed corpus and a sanitizer are most of that signal.

🖥Apple's clang has no libFuzzer

The clang that comes with Xcode cannot link a fuzzer. The error is library 'libclang_rt.fuzzer_osx.a' not found. The fuzz targets of the Makefile run in a Linux container instead, with the one-line docker run in their comment. The clang 19 in the container links them without complaint. Against the real kv parser the fuzzer found nothing. That is the usual result after the unit tests have done their work, and no reason to skip it.

✅Run the tests under the sanitizers, every time C

A C test suite without sanitizers checks the answers and nothing else. With -fsanitize=address,undefined it also checks every memory access and every arithmetic operation the tests perform. The cost is about twice the run time, which for a test suite is nothing. kv's make test always builds with them, and so should yours. The one sanitizer that cannot join them is ThreadSanitizer, which needs a build of its own.

Go: the runner is in the box, and so is the fuzzer#

Go tests live in files that end in _test.go, in the same package as the code, and go test finds them by name. The parser test is a table, which is the Go shape for "the same check on many inputs". Each row is a subtest, so that a failure names the case. Three calls in it are the rest of the testing package. t.Run "runs f as a subtest of t called name". t.Parallel "signals that this test is to be run in parallel with (and only with) other parallel tests". The rows share nothing, so they may. And the comparison moved into a helper that calls t.Helper, so that a failure reports the row's line and not the helper's:

func TestReadCommand(t *testing.T) {
	cases := []struct {
		name  string
		input string
		want  []string
		err   error
	}{
		{"array", "*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n", []string{"ECHO", "hi"}, nil},
		{"inline", "  SET  a   b\r\n", []string{"SET", "a", "b"}, nil},
		{"bare LF", "PING\n", []string{"PING"}, nil},
		{"empty value", "*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$1\r\nk\r\n$0\r\n\r\n", []string{"SET", "k", ""}, nil},
		{"closed", "", nil, io.EOF},
		{"cut short", "*2\r\n$4\r\nEC", nil, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF},
		{"not a number", "*x\r\n", nil, ErrProtocol},
		{"wrong marker", "*1\r\n#4\r\nECHO\r\n", nil, ErrProtocol},
		{"too many", "*100\r\n", nil, ErrProtocol},
	}
	for _, c := range cases {
		t.Run(c.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			t.Parallel() // the cases share nothing, so they may run at once
			got, err := ReadCommand(bufio.NewReader(strings.NewReader(c.input)))
			if !errors.Is(err, c.err) {
				t.Fatalf("err = %v, want %v", err, c.err)
			}
			expectArgs(t, got, c.want)
		})
	}
}

// expectArgs compares the parsed arguments with the expected strings. t.Helper makes a
// failure report the caller's line, not this one.
func expectArgs(t *testing.T, got [][]byte, want []string) {
	t.Helper()
	if len(got) != len(want) {
		t.Fatalf("got %q, want %q", got, want)
	}
	for i := range got {
		if string(got[i]) != want[i] {
			t.Fatalf("arg %d = %q, want %q", i, got[i], want[i])
		}
	}
}

Exercise 12.2GoFuzz the parser

Write FuzzReadCommand. Add three seed inputs with f.Add. Then call f.Fuzz with a function that parses the input and returns on an error. When the parse succeeds, write the arguments back out with the protocol writers, parse them again, and fail the test if anything changed. That round trip is a property the parser must keep for every input, and it is the kind of check a fuzzer is good at.

func FuzzReadCommand(f *testing.F) {
	f.Add([]byte("*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n"))
	f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, data []byte) {
		// your code here

Stuck?Show the full listing
// FuzzReadCommand lets the fuzzer mutate the input. Whatever it sends, the parser must
// not panic, and a request it accepts must survive a round trip through the writers.
func FuzzReadCommand(f *testing.F) {
	f.Add([]byte("*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n"))
	f.Add([]byte("PING\r\n"))
	f.Add([]byte("*1\r\n$3\r\nGET\r\n"))
	f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, data []byte) {
		args, err := ReadCommand(bufio.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(data)))
		if err != nil {
			return
		}
		var buf bytes.Buffer
		w := bufio.NewWriter(&buf)
		WriteArrayLen(w, len(args))
		for _, a := range args {
			WriteBulk(w, a)
		}
		w.Flush()
		again, err := ReadCommand(bufio.NewReader(&buf))
		if err != nil {
			t.Fatalf("round trip failed: %v", err)
		}
		if len(again) != len(args) {
			t.Fatalf("round trip changed the argument count")
		}
		for i := range args {
			if !bytes.Equal(again[i], args[i]) {
				t.Fatalf("round trip changed argument %d", i)
			}
		}
	})
}

The fuzzer ran half a million inputs in ten seconds. Had one failed, Go would have written it to testdata/fuzz/FuzzReadCommand/. From then on go test would run it with the seeds, as a regression test, until the bug was fixed. The race detector from chapter 9 is the other built-in tool, and it is worth seeing what it prints. A scratch program that runs the chapter 5 INCR from two goroutines with no lock prints this under the detector:

$ go run -race .
WARNING: DATA RACE
Write at 0x00c000186000 by goroutine 7:

Previous read at 0x00c000186000 by goroutine 6:

errors.Join#

One Go change in this chapter is not a test but a thing tests find. The log's Close from chapter 11 must sync the file and then close it, and either may fail. Returning the first error would skip the close. errors.Join "returns an error that wraps the given errors. Any nil error values are discarded". It "returns nil if every value in errs is nil". So both calls run, and the caller hears about both. errors.Is and errors.As from chapter 4 look inside a joined error as they look inside a wrapped one:

// The file is closed even when the sync failed, and the caller hears about both.
// errors.Join drops the nils, so with no error at all it returns nil.
return errors.Join(sync, l.f.Close())
go/ch12/internal/aof/aof.go · region join
⚠️A detector is not a proof Go

The race detector and the fuzzer report what they saw, not what exists. A race on a path the test never ran is not reported. An input the fuzzer never generated is not tried. Both tools are excellent and both are statistical. That is why kv runs the race detector in make verify on every change and keeps the fuzz corpus. The number of things seen then keeps growing. The next section shows the other kind of tool.

Rust: the compiler already ran, and the tools check the rest#

Rust has three places for a test, and kv now uses all three. The first is the file under test, in a module marked #[cfg(test)]. The attribute "tells Rust to compile and run the test code only when you run cargo test, not when you run cargo build". A helper in that module is compiled only for tests too, which is where a function that turns a typed line into a reply belongs:

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use crate::store::MapStore;

    /// A command typed as one inline line, run against the store, and its reply as
    /// text. The helper is compiled only for tests, like the module around it.
    fn run(store: &mut MapStore, line: &str) -> String {
        let args: Command = line.split(' ').map(str::as_bytes).collect();
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        execute(&args, store, &mut out).unwrap();
        String::from_utf8(out).unwrap()
    }

    #[test]
    fn incr_counts_from_nothing() {
        let mut store = MapStore::new();
        assert_eq!(run(&mut store, "INCR n"), ":1\r\n");
        assert_eq!(run(&mut store, "INCR n"), ":2\r\n");
        assert_eq!(run(&mut store, "GET n"), "$1\r\n2\r\n");
    }

    #[test]
    fn an_expiry_in_the_past_deletes_the_key() {
        let mut store = MapStore::new();
        run(&mut store, "SET k v");
        assert_eq!(run(&mut store, "EXPIRE k 0"), ":1\r\n");
        assert_eq!(run(&mut store, "EXISTS k"), ":0\r\n");
    }
}
rust/ch12/src/cmd.rs · region test

The second place is the documentation. A code block in a doc comment is a test, because "rustdoc supports executing your documentation examples as tests", and cargo test runs them. The example in the comment on parse is the one a reader of the docs sees. It cannot go stale, because a stale example stops the build:

/// One request from the front of `buf`: an array of bulk strings such as
/// `*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n`, or one inline line of words. The returned
/// `Command` borrows `buf`, which the signature says with the elided lifetime: one
/// reference in, so the one reference out lives as long as it.
///
/// A code block in a doc comment is a test. `cargo test` compiles and runs it, and
/// `cargo doc` shows it, so an example that stops being true stops the build:
///
/// ```
/// use kv::resp::{Parsed, parse};
/// let Ok(Parsed::Done(args, used)) = parse(b"*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n") else {
///     unreachable!("a whole request")
/// };
/// assert_eq!(args, [&b"ECHO"[..], b"hi"]);
/// assert_eq!(used, 22);
/// assert!(matches!(parse(b"*2\r\n$4\r\nEC"), Ok(Parsed::Incomplete)));
/// ```
pub fn parse(buf: &[u8]) -> Result<Parsed<'_>> {
    let Some((line, mut used)) = take_line(buf, 0) else {
        return Ok(Parsed::Incomplete);
    };
    if line.first() != Some(&b'*') {
        let words = line.split(|b| *b == b' ').filter(|w| !w.is_empty());
        return Ok(Parsed::Done(words.collect(), used));
    }
    let n = parse_len(&line[1..], b'*')?;
    if n > MAX_ARGS {
        return Err(KvError::Protocol(b'*'));
    }
    let mut args = Vec::with_capacity(n);
    for _ in 0..n {
        let Some((line, start)) = take_line(buf, used) else {
            return Ok(Parsed::Incomplete);
        };
        if line.first() != Some(&b'$') {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(line.first().copied().unwrap_or(b'\n')));
        }
        let size = parse_len(&line[1..], b'$')?;
        if size > MAX_BULK {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(b'$'));
        }
        let end = start + size;
        if buf.len() < end + 2 {
            return Ok(Parsed::Incomplete);
        }
        if &buf[end..end + 2] != b"\r\n" {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(buf[end]));
        }
        args.push(&buf[start..end]);
        used = end + 2;
    }
    Ok(Parsed::Done(args, used))
}

/// The line that starts at `from`, without its ending, and where the next line starts.
/// A bare LF is accepted as well as CRLF, so that a command typed into nc works.
fn take_line(buf: &[u8], from: usize) -> Option<(&[u8], usize)> {
    let rest = &buf[from..];
    let nl = rest.iter().position(|b| *b == b'\n')?;
    let line = rest[..nl].strip_suffix(b"\r").unwrap_or(&rest[..nl]);
    Some((line, from + nl + 1))
}

fn parse_len(digits: &[u8], type_byte: u8) -> Result<usize> {
    std::str::from_utf8(digits)
        .ok()
        .and_then(|s| s.parse().ok())
        .ok_or(KvError::Protocol(type_byte))
}
rust/ch12/src/resp.rs · region parse

The third place is the tests/ directory next to src/. Each file there is an integration test. "Cargo will compile each of the files as an individual crate", and a crate of its own sees only what the library makes pub. That is the point. An integration test cannot reach into private functions, so it tests the crate as a user would. The one in kv runs a request through the parser and the executor, the way the server does:

/// One request through the parser and the executor, as the server runs it, and the
/// reply bytes. A helper that every test in the file shares is an ordinary function.
fn round_trip(store: &mut MapStore, request: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    match resp::parse(request) {
        Ok(Parsed::Done(args, used)) => {
            assert_eq!(used, request.len(), "the whole request is used");
            cmd::execute(&args, store, &mut out).expect("a Vec never fails to write");
        }
        other => panic!("not a whole request: {other:?}"),
    }
    out
}

        round_trip(&mut store, b"*2\r\n$3\r\nGET\r\n$1\r\nk\r\n"),

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    /// The parser works on bytes already in memory, so a test needs no socket.
    fn parse_one(input: &[u8]) -> Result<Parsed<'_>> {
        parse(input)
    }

    fn args_of(input: &[u8]) -> Vec<Vec<u8>> {
        match parse_one(input).unwrap() {
            Parsed::Done(args, used) => {
                assert_eq!(used, input.len());
                args.iter().map(|a| a.to_vec()).collect()
            }
            Parsed::Incomplete => panic!("incomplete"),
        }
    }

    #[test]

        assert_eq!(
            args_of(b"*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n$2\r\nhi\r\n"),
            vec![b"ECHO".to_vec(), b"hi".to_vec()]
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn an_inline_line_and_a_bare_lf() {
        let got = args_of(b"  SET  a   b\n");
        assert_eq!(got.len(), 3);
        assert_eq!(got[2], b"b");
    }

    #[test]
    fn nothing_yet_is_incomplete() {
        for cut in [&b""[..], b"*2\r\n$4\r\nEC", b"*2\r\n$4\r\nECHO\r\n"] {
            assert!(matches!(parse_one(cut).unwrap(), Parsed::Incomplete));
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn bad_bytes_are_a_protocol_error() {
        for bad in [&b"*x\r\n"[..], b"*1\r\n#4\r\nECHO\r\n", b"*100\r\n"] {
            assert!(matches!(parse_one(bad).unwrap_err(), KvError::Protocol(_)));
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_request_survives_a_round_trip() {
        let args = vec![
            b"SET".to_vec(),
            b"k".to_vec(),
            b"a value\r\nwith a line".to_vec(),
        ];
        let mut bytes = Vec::new();
        write_array_len(&mut bytes, args.len()).unwrap();
        for a in &args {
            write_bulk(&mut bytes, a).unwrap();
        }
        assert_eq!(args_of(&bytes), args);

rust/ch12/src/resp.rs · region test

cargo test, and what comes after the dashes#

cargo test runs every unit test, every integration test and every doc test, in that order, each set in a binary of its own. --lib runs only the unit tests, --test roundtrip only that integration file, and --doc only the documentation. A name after the command is a filter, so cargo test incr runs the tests with incr in their name. Everything after a lone -- goes to the test binary rather than to cargo. Two are worth knowing. -- --no-capture shows what a test prints, which the harness hides unless the test fails. -- --test-threads 1 runs the tests one at a time, because Rust runs them in parallel by default and Go only when asked.

Fuzzing in Rust is cargo-fuzz, which the fuzzing book calls "the recommended tool for fuzz testing Rust code". It drives the same libFuzzer that C used, through a crate called libfuzzer-sys, and it needs the nightly toolchain. The targets live in a small crate of their own under fuzz/, and the target for kv is the C one in Rust:

fuzz_target!(|data: &[u8]| {
    let mut input = data;
    let mut store = kv::store::MapStore::new();
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    // run every complete command in the input, as the server would
    while let Ok(kv::resp::Parsed::Done(args, used)) = kv::resp::parse(input) {
        let _ = kv::cmd::execute(&args, &mut store, &mut out);
        input = &input[used..];
    }
});
rust/ch12/fuzz/fuzz_targets/parse.rs · region target
$ cargo install cargo-fuzz
$ cargo +nightly fuzz run parse -- -max_total_time=20
#343809	DONE   cov: 335 ft: 1611 corp: 356/36Kb exec/s: 16371
Done 343809 runs in 21 second(s)

The last tool is Miri, an interpreter that runs a Rust program slowly and checks every memory access against the rules. Its README calls it "an Undefined Behavior detection tool for Rust", and it finds the same things AddressSanitizer finds in C. The server kv has no unsafe code of its own, so Miri has nothing to find until chapter 15. It still runs:

$ rustup +nightly component add miri
$ cargo +nightly miri test --lib
test result: ok. 12 passed; 0 failed; finished in 92.81s

Ninety seconds for tests that take a hundredth of a second natively. That is the cost of checking rules at run time that the compiler could not check at compile time. Safe Rust avoids that cost by having the compiler check them first.

⚠️Two toolchains, and a crate inside a crate Rust

cargo-fuzz and Miri both need nightly, and the fuzz crate must stay out of the main one. The nightly toolchain is a second compiler installed beside the stable one, chosen per command with +nightly. The fuzz/ directory is a separate package with an empty [workspace] table. The main Cargo.toml has one too. So a cargo command in one directory never reads the files of the other. Forget the one in fuzz/ and the first error names a workspace you did not know you had.

Fuzzing, three ways, one engine#

All three fuzzers in this chapter are coverage-guided. They watch which branches an input reaches and mutate the inputs that reach new ones. That is why a fuzzer finds the corner cases of a parser within seconds. Two of the three fuzzers are the same engine. The engine called libFuzzer is what clang links into the C target and what libfuzzer-sys links into the Rust one. Go wrote its own, with the same design, and built it into go test. The rates on the author's machine were 17,000 inputs a second for Rust and 50,000 for Go. The small C target in a container ran at 350,000. None found a bug in kv's parser. The unit tests had already covered the cases a fuzzer finds first, which is the order the book recommends. The fuzzer's own case is the one in the scene, the input that nobody writes down.

What finds what#

The bugCGoRust
Reading freed memoryASan at run time, if a test reaches itcannot be writtencannot be written
A data raceThreadSanitizer, in its own build-race at run time, if a test reaches itthe compiler, always
Integer overflowUBSan at run timewraps, by the language definitionpanics in a debug build, wraps in release
A panic or crash on bad inputa sanitizer, or a core dumpthe fuzzer, in go testthe fuzzer, on nightly
A wrong answeryour testsyour testsyour tests

The table is the chapter in four lines. C finds its bugs with tools that watch the program run, which means a test must reach the bug. Go has two such tools built in, and a language definition that removes the undefined cases. Rust removes two whole rows at compile time, and uses the same run-time tools as C for what remains. The last row is the same for all three, and it is where most bugs live.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
A test runnerWeakStrongStrongC has none, so you write one. Go and Rust have one in the box, with no setup.
Where a test may liveWeakOKStrongC has the file you write, and Go the package and an Example. Rust has the module, the docs and a directory for outsiders.
FuzzingOKStrongOKlibFuzzer is one flag on Linux and a container on a Mac, Go has it built in, and Rust needs nightly and a second crate.
Memory errorsOKStrongStrongC finds them at run time with ASan or Valgrind. Go and Rust cannot write them in safe code.
Data racesOKOKStrongC and Go find the races a test provokes, with a sanitizer or the detector. Rust refuses them at compile time.
Undefined behaviourWeakStrongOKC has it everywhere and UBSan finds some. Go has almost none, a data race being the exception, and Rust confines it to unsafe, where Miri checks it.
Speed of the toolsStrongStrongWeakASan costs two times and the race detector two to twenty, while Miri costs nine thousand.
Carry forward
  • A detector sees what ran. A sanitizer, the race detector and a fuzzer report the bugs a test reached. The compiler's refusal is the only kind of proof.
  • Seed and signal. A fuzzer needs a valid input to start from and a sanitizer to tell it when it has won. With both, two seconds. Without, twenty-two million runs for nothing.
  • Three homes for a Rust test. The cfg(test) module sees everything, the doc comment is read by users, and the tests directory sees only what is pub.
Next

One request through the three parsers, ten million times each. Go takes three times as long as Rust and nine times as long as C. Chapter 13 finds out why, and whether it matters.

Benchmarking and profiling#

Quality and shipping · Chapter 13· 24 min read· 235 lines of code
▶Scene

Time the same request through the three parsers, ten million times each. Each language has its own way to say "run this loop and divide", and the chapter shows all three. The answers, on the author's machine:

C, kv_parse            56 ns      0 allocations
Rust, parse           179 ns      1 allocation
Go, ReadCommand       532 ns      9 allocations, 184 bytes

Go is three times slower than Rust and nine times slower than C, on the one piece of kv that is pure computation. The chapter finds out why, finds out whether it matters, and halves it. Then it turns to the servers, where a Rust number is the one that is wrong.

The book has quoted numbers since chapter 6. This chapter shows how to take one that means something. It also shows how to find where the time goes when the number is worse than you expected. It benchmarks and profiles all four servers, and follows two bad results from a profile to a fix. Measurement is the only argument that ends a discussion about speed.

Chapter 9 reported that the four servers answer about 70,000 to 100,000 requests a second from fifty clients. That number is true and nearly useless, because it measures a round trip on the loopback interface more than it measures kv. The Redis documentation says so in its own words. When the client and the server share a machine, "the CPU is the limiting factor with redis-benchmark". By default the tool "does not use pipelining or any parallelism at all". A benchmark is a question, and a question has to be chosen.

MeasuringCGoRust
The load generatorredis-benchmarkthe samethe same
A micro-benchmarka loop and the clockgo test -benchan example binary, or criterion
Counting allocationsnone to count-benchmema global allocator that counts
What the compiler decided-O0 to -O3, measured-gcflags=-mthe release profile, LTO
A CPU profilesample on macOS, perf on Linuxruntime/pprof, then go tool pprofsample or perf, with symbols kept in the release build
Memory knobsnone: you free itGOGC and GOMEMLIMITnone: you drop it
The surprisenonenine allocations a requesta wall at 200,000 requests a second with pipelining
The fixnone neededfive allocations, from a free list the reader already hada read lock, after four experiments that failed

Taking a number#

Every number in this chapter comes from one command shape. Fifty connections, four client threads so that the client is not the bottleneck, two hundred thousand requests, and two settings of the pipeline. A pipeline of 16 means each connection sends sixteen commands before it waits for a reply. The documentation calls pipelining "a feature often exploited by real world applications". It changes what is measured. Without it, the number is mostly the cost of a round trip. With it, the number is mostly the cost of the server:

$ redis-benchmark -p 6380 -c 50 -n 200000 --threads 4 -t set,get -q          # one at a time
$ redis-benchmark -p 6380 -c 50 -n 200000 --threads 4 -t set,get -q -P 16    # sixteen at a time
                         no pipeline              pipeline of 16
                         SET       GET            SET       GET
C, poll, one thread      88,700    79,900         796,800   800,000
Go, goroutines           88,700    88,700         800,000   800,000
Rust, threads            99,950    88,700         159,700   199,400
Rust, tokio              99,950    99,850         160,000   199,800

The left half says the four servers are the same, within noise, because the left half measures the loopback. The right half says something is wrong with the two Rust servers. Both stop at a fifth or a quarter of what C and Go reach. The second half of the chapter is about that column, and the tools that explain it. First, the shape of a single measurement. The full output of the benchmark, without -q, gives a distribution and not one number:

Summary:
  throughput summary: 79617.83 requests per second
  latency summary (msec):
          avg       min       p50       p95       p99       max
        0.540     0.064     0.487     0.919     1.319     5.103

The median request took half a millisecond. One in a hundred took more than 1.3 milliseconds, and the slowest took five. A server is judged by the p99 column more often than by the average, because the average hides the requests that a user notices.

📜Flame graphs, and what a profile is

A profiler interrupts a program many times a second and writes down what it was doing. The result is a list of stacks with a count against each, and the count says where the time went. In 2011 Brendan Gregg drew those stacks as a picture he called a flame graph. He describes it as "a visualization of hierarchical data that I created to visualize stack traces of profiled software". Each box is a function, and its width is the share of samples that passed through it. The boxes above it are the functions it called. The x axis "is not the passage of time". Every profiler in this chapter produces the same kind of data, and every one of them can draw that picture. The chapter reads the lists instead, because a list fits in a book.

C: a clock, a loop and five flags#

A server profile answers "where does the time go". A micro-benchmark answers "how long does this function take", which is a different question with a different tool. Go has one built in, and Rust has one on the nightly toolchain. C has a clock, which is enough:

Exercise 13.1CTime the parser

Write a benchmark for kv_parse. Build one SET request as a string and read the monotonic clock, with kv_now_ms from chapter 10. Parse the request ten million times in a loop. Read the clock again, and print the nanoseconds for one parse. Count the successful parses and print the count too, so that the compiler cannot remove the loop as unused work. The Makefile target bench builds it with the release flags and no sanitizer.

int main(void) {
    const char *req = "*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$16\r\nkey:000000001234\r\n$3\r\nxxx\r\n";
    /* your code here */
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
int main(void) {
    const char *req = "*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$16\r\nkey:000000001234\r\n$3\r\nxxx\r\n";
    size_t len = strlen(req);
    long runs = 10 * 1000 * 1000;
    kv_cmd cmd;
    size_t used = 0;
    long ok = 0;
    int64_t start = kv_now_ms();
    for (long i = 0; i < runs; i++) {
        ok += kv_parse(req, len, &cmd, &used) == KV_PARSE_OK;
    }
    int64_t elapsed = kv_now_ms() - start;
    /* ok is printed so that the compiler cannot remove the loop as unused work */
    printf("%ld parses in %lld ms: %.1f ns each (%ld ok)\n", runs, (long long)elapsed,
           elapsed * 1e6 / (double)runs, ok);
    return 0;
}
c/ch13/bench/bench_parse.c · region bench

The optimisation levels, measured#

The one number that changes a C benchmark most is a compiler flag. The book has built with -O2 since chapter 2, and the Makefile has a target that builds the same benchmark at every level. The gcc manual describes -O0 as "Reduce compilation time and make debugging produce the expected results. This is the default." At -O2 the compiler "performs nearly all supported optimizations that do not involve a space-speed tradeoff". -O3 adds the ones that do, such as unrolling loops. -Os optimises for size:

$ make bench-levels
-O0  10000000 parses in 998 ms: 99.8 ns each
-O1  10000000 parses in 560 ms: 56.0 ns each
-O2  10000000 parses in 586 ms: 58.6 ns each
-O3  10000000 parses in 551 ms: 55.1 ns each
-Os  10000000 parses in 622 ms: 62.2 ns each

The whole of the gain is between -O0 and -O1, and the rest is noise. That is the usual shape. A parser is small functions and short loops, and the first level already inlines the small functions, such as kv_find_eol, into their one caller. The keyword inline would ask for the same thing by name. But its intent "is to serve as a hint", and "the compilers can (and usually do) ignore presence or absence of the inline specifier". At -O1 and above the compiler has already made that decision from the size of the function, and kv has no inline anywhere. A second keyword makes a promise rather than a request. restrict on a pointer parameter says that nothing else reaches the memory it points to, so the compiler may reorder loads and stores freely. The benchmark below adds two arrays with and without it:

/* Without restrict, the compiler must allow for dst and src overlapping, so each store
 * may change the next load, and the loop is kept in order or guarded by a check. With
 * the promise, the loop may add eight or sixteen numbers in one instruction. */
static void add_plain(int32_t *dst, const int32_t *src, size_t n) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        dst[i] += src[i];
    }
}

static void add_restrict(int32_t *restrict dst, const int32_t *restrict src, size_t n) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        dst[i] += src[i];
    }
}
c/ch13/bench/bench_copy.c · region copy
$ make bench-copy
plain    62 ms for 100000 passes over 4096 ints
restrict 62 ms for 100000 passes over 4096 ints (100% of the time, sum 1677312000000)

No difference, and the reason is worth more than a difference would have been. clang vectorises both loops. For the plain one it adds a run-time check that the arrays do not overlap, and takes the fast path when they do not. They never do. The promise bought nothing that the compiler could not check itself. A broken promise is undefined behaviour, as the C reference says in its own words. The lesson is the chapter's. A keyword that is supposed to make code faster is a hypothesis, and the benchmark is the experiment.

A sampler and a short answer#

macOS ships a sampling profiler called sample. Given a process and a number of seconds, it writes every stack it saw. It adds a summary sorted by the function at the top of the stack. The C server was sampled for five seconds while the benchmark ran:

$ sample $(pgrep kv) 5 -file kv.sample
$ grep -A12 "Sort by top of stack" kv.sample
        read   (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)        1741
        write  (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)        1561
        poll   (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)         427
        _platform_memmove                           67
        kv_server_run  (in kv)                      31
        kv_parse  (in kv)                           17
        strncasecmp_l                               16
        kv_exec  (in kv)                            13

Three system calls hold ninety percent of the samples. The parser and the command code together hold one percent. The C server is not spending its time in C. It is spending it in the kernel, moving bytes in and out of sockets, and no change to kv_parse would be visible in the benchmark. That is the most common result of profiling a server, and the most useful, because it stops you from optimising the wrong thing. On Linux the same question is asked with perf record, which the manual describes as "Run a command and record its profile into perf.data". It is answered with perf report.

✅Measure before you optimise, and measure after C

A profile is cheap and a guess is expensive. The sampler above took five seconds to run and ten seconds to read, and it closed a question that could have cost a day. The second half of the rule matters as much. Every change made for speed is measured again with the same command. A change that does not move the number is reverted, however clever it was.

Go: nine allocations, and the flag that names them#

The Go benchmark is a function in a test file, and the testing package runs it. Functions "of the form func BenchmarkXxx(*testing.B) are considered benchmarks". b.Loop runs the body for as long as the package needs to get a stable number. The flag -benchmem adds two columns that the scene's number came from:

// BenchmarkReadCommand times the parser on one SET request. go test -bench runs the loop
// for as long as it needs to get a stable number. The reader is reused, so that the
// number is the parser and not the cost of a 4 KB buffer per request.
func BenchmarkReadCommand(b *testing.B) {
	req := []byte("*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$16\r\nkey:000000001234\r\n$3\r\nxxx\r\n")
	r := bufio.NewReader(nil)
	for b.Loop() {
		r.Reset(bytes.NewReader(req))
		if _, err := ReadCommand(r); err != nil {
			b.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
}
go/ch13/internal/resp/bench_test.go · region bench
$ go test -run xxx -bench ReadCommand -benchmem ./internal/resp/
BenchmarkReadCommand-12    	 2267204	       532.2 ns/op	     184 B/op	       9 allocs/op

Escape analysis#

Nine allocations for a request with three arguments. Go decides for each value whether it may live on the goroutine's stack, which is free, or must go on the heap. There the garbage collector (GC) will find it later. The guide to the collector says a value escapes to the heap when "the Go compiler cannot determine its lifetime". The compiler will say which, for every line, with one flag. The manual describes -m as "Print optimization decisions. Higher values or repetition produce more detail":

$ go build -gcflags=-m ./internal/resp/ 2>&1 | grep "escapes to heap"
internal/resp/resp.go:54:14: make([][]byte, 0, n) escapes to heap
internal/resp/resp.go:67:14: make([]byte, size + 2) escapes to heap
internal/resp/resp.go:77:16: append escapes to heap

Those three are the arguments and the slice that holds them, four allocations the parser must make, because its caller keeps them. The other five were a surprise. bufio.Reader.ReadBytes returns a fresh slice for each line, four lines in this request, and strconv.Atoi wants a string, which the conversion from bytes allocates. Both values are dead by the next line of the parser. The reader has a second method, ReadSlice, which returns a view into the reader's own buffer, valid until the next read. That is exactly as long as the parser needs it. The number is parsed from the bytes without a string:

// readLine returns one line without its line ending. ReadSlice hands back a view into
// the reader's own buffer, valid until the next read, so no allocation is made for a
// line. Chapter 13 measured the difference. A line longer than the buffer is an error,
// which for a length field it should be.
func readLine(r *bufio.Reader) ([]byte, error) {
	line, err := r.ReadSlice('\n')
	if err != nil {
		if err == io.EOF && len(line) > 0 {
			return nil, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF
		}
		if err == bufio.ErrBufferFull {
			return nil, protoErr(line[0])
		}
		return nil, err
	}
	line = bytes.TrimSuffix(line, []byte("\n"))
	return bytes.TrimSuffix(line, []byte("\r")), nil
}

// atoi parses a non-negative decimal from bytes without making a string of them, which
// strconv.Atoi would need and the compiler would allocate.
func atoi(b []byte) (int, bool) {
	if len(b) == 0 || len(b) > 18 {
		return 0, false
	}
	n := 0
	for _, c := range b {
		if c < '0' || c > '9' {
			return 0, false
		}
		n = n*10 + int(c-'0')
	}
	return n, true
}
go/ch13/internal/resp/resp.go · region readline
$ go test -run xxx -bench ReadCommand -benchmem ./internal/resp/
BenchmarkReadCommand-12    	 3196206	       369.9 ns/op	     162 B/op	       5 allocs/op

From 532 to 370 nanoseconds, and from nine allocations to five, for a change of fifteen lines that the flag pointed at. The five that remain are the ones the caller needs, plus the error values that are never made on the happy path. The Go parser is still twice as slow as the Rust one, which allocates once. It is six times slower than the C one, which allocates nothing. Each of those is a design, not a flaw. Go copies so that the arguments are safe to keep. The rest of the gap is the collector's accounting on every make, which is the price of not writing free.

GOGC, GOMEMLIMIT and the Pool#

The collector has two knobs, both environment variables, and both are worth one experiment. "The GOGC variable sets the initial garbage collection target percentage", and "the default is GOGC=100". A collection runs when the heap has grown by that percentage since the last one. The guide puts the trade in one sentence. "Doubling GOGC will double heap memory overheads and roughly halve GC CPU cost." The second knob is a ceiling. "The GOMEMLIMIT variable sets a soft memory limit for the runtime", and with GOGC=off the collector runs only when the limit is near. The server was run under each setting with the pipelined SET benchmark, and the collections counted with GODEBUG=gctrace=1:

setting                      SET a second   collections   resident memory
GOGC=100 (the default)       796,800        11            10 MB
GOGC=25                      800,000        41             8 MB
GOGC=400                     800,000         2            21 MB
GOGC=off GOMEMLIMIT=32MiB    800,000         1            26 MB

The throughput did not move, because this server allocates little and the collector is not where its time goes. The memory did, in the direction the guide says. A server that must fit in a container with a fixed memory should set the limit. The guide recommends it when "the Go program is the only program with access to some set of resources". sync.Pool, from chapter 9, is the third tool. It is "a set of temporary objects that may be individually saved and retrieved", so that a buffer is reused instead of collected. The five remaining allocations are not worth one. A pool pays when the object is large and the rate is high. The reader's 4 KB buffer is the one object in kv that fits, and it lives for the whole connection already.

The profiler is a package#

Go's profiler is in the standard library. The package runtime/pprof "writes runtime profiling data in the format expected by the pprof visualization tool", and starting it is one call. The chapter 13 server starts a CPU profile when an environment variable names a file, and the clean stop from chapter 10 ends it:

Exercise 13.2GoProfile on request

At the start of main, if KV_CPUPROFILE names a file, create the file and call pprof.StartCPUProfile. Then arrange for the profile to be stopped and the file closed when main returns. That is after the clean stop has waited for every client. Two defer calls do it, in the order that runs last first. Without the stop, the profile file stays empty.

if path := os.Getenv("KV_CPUPROFILE"); path != "" {
	// your code here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
// KV_CPUPROFILE names a file. The profile runs until the server is told to stop, with
// Ctrl-C or kill, so that a benchmark can be profiled from start to end.
if path := os.Getenv("KV_CPUPROFILE"); path != "" {
	f, err := os.Create(path)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	if err := pprof.StartCPUProfile(f); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	defer f.Close()
	defer pprof.StopCPUProfile()
}

$ KV_CPUPROFILE=cpu.prof ./kv &

$ kill -INT %1
$ go tool pprof -top kv cpu.prof
Duration: 4.40s, Total samples = 11.61s (263.58%)
      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
     6.51s 56.07% 56.07%      6.51s 56.07%  syscall.rawsyscalln
     1.89s 16.28% 72.35%      1.89s 16.28%  runtime.pthread_cond_wait
     1.20s 10.34% 82.69%      1.20s 10.34%  runtime.kevent
     0.82s  7.06% 89.75%      0.82s  7.06%  runtime.pthread_cond_signal
     0.01s 0.086% 97.59%      3.66s 31.52%  internal/poll.(*FD).Read
     0.01s 0.086% 97.67%      2.88s 24.81%  internal/poll.(*FD).Write

The total is 263 percent, because the profile adds up the time of every thread, and the server used almost three cores. More than half of that time was in system calls. A tenth was in kevent, which is the Go runtime asking the kernel which sockets are ready. Most of the rest was in the scheduler, parking and waking threads. The cum column says a third of all time was spent somewhere under Read. Again, the code that kv wrote is not in the list, and the nine allocations that the micro-benchmark found are invisible at the server's scale. Both measurements are true. The server one says which to act on.

Rust: one allocation, a profile, four experiments, and a lock#

Stable Rust has no benchmark runner in the box. The one most projects use is criterion, "a statistics-driven micro-benchmarking tool". It runs under cargo bench and compares each run with the last. The server kv keeps to the standard library, and its benchmark is an example binary with the C loop in it. It adds one thing the C version could not. A program may name its own allocator, with "a static item whose type implements the GlobalAlloc trait", and this one counts:

/// Every allocation in the program goes through the global allocator, and a program may
/// name its own. This one counts the calls and passes them on to the system allocator.
struct Counting;

static ALLOCS: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);

// SAFETY: every call is passed through to System unchanged, which is itself a correct
// allocator, and the counter has no effect on the memory handed back.
unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for Counting {
    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
        ALLOCS.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        unsafe { System.alloc(layout) }
    }

    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, layout: Layout) {
        unsafe { System.dealloc(ptr, layout) }
    }
}

#[global_allocator]
static GLOBAL: Counting = Counting;
rust/ch13/examples/bench_parse.rs · region counting
fn main() {
    let req: &[u8] = b"*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$16\r\nkey:000000001234\r\n$3\r\nxxx\r\n";
    let runs = 10_000_000u32;
    let mut ok = 0u32;
    let before = ALLOCS.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
    let start = Instant::now();
    for _ in 0..runs {
        // the parser takes a slice and copies nothing, so no allocation is made per argument
        ok += u32::from(matches!(
            kv::resp::parse(req),
            Ok(kv::resp::Parsed::Done(..))
        ));
    }
    let elapsed = start.elapsed();
    let allocs = ALLOCS.load(Ordering::Relaxed) - before;
    println!(
        "{runs} parses in {} ms: {:.1} ns each ({ok} ok), {} allocations a parse",
        elapsed.as_millis(),
        elapsed.as_nanos() as f64 / f64::from(runs),
        allocs / u64::from(runs)
    );
}
rust/ch13/examples/bench_parse.rs · region bench

The release profile#

The counter says one allocation a parse, the Vec that holds the borrowed arguments. The time depends on the profile. The dev profile of Cargo has no optimisation and full debug information. The release profile is opt-level = 3. The same example, both ways, and then with two settings the release profile leaves off by default. lto = "fat", link-time optimisation (LTO), optimises across every crate at once. codegen-units = 1 gives the compiler the whole crate in one piece, at the cost of a slower build:

cargo run --example bench_parse                        1460.9 ns   (dev: opt-level 0)
cargo run --release --example bench_parse               179.0 ns   (release: opt-level 3)
  with lto = "fat" and codegen-units = 1                149.2 ns
  with #[inline(never)] on the two helpers              185.2 ns

Eight times between the two profiles, which is why a Rust benchmark run without --release measures nothing. The last line is the Rust form of the C inline experiment. The attribute #[inline] "suggests whether a copy of the attributed function's code should be placed in the caller". The reference says that "in every form the attribute is a hint". Forbidding it on the two helpers cost three percent, which is what the compiler's own decision was worth, and kv does not write the attribute. The release build keeps line information when Cargo.toml says so, which costs nothing at run time and lets a profiler name inlined functions:

# Keep function names in the release build, so a profiler can show them. The code is
# as fast as without this; only the binary is larger.
[profile.release]
debug = 1
rust/ch13/Cargo.toml · region profile

The Rust servers stop at 200,000 requests a second with pipelining, and the first question is where the time goes. The sampler names Rust functions, and its summary for the thread server under load is this:

__recvfrom          (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)    67711
__accept            (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)     1411
__semwait_signal    (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)     1409
__sendto            (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)     1252
__psynch_mutexwait  (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)      689
core::slice::memchr::memchr_aligned  (in kv)         256
kv::cmd::execute    (in kv)                           25
kv::resp::read_line (in kv)                           24
⚠️A wall-clock sampler counts sleeping threads Rust

Sixty-seven thousand samples in recvfrom are not CPU time. The sampler records every thread on every tick, and the thread server has fifty threads that spend most of their lives blocked in a read. The C server has one thread, so its list was honest. The Rust list is dominated by waiting. The lines that describe work are lower down. The one that matters is __psynch_mutexwait, which is a thread waiting for a mutex that another thread holds. On Linux, perf samples CPU time by default and does not have this problem.

One line of a profile is a hypothesis, not an answer. The author tested it with experiments, each a few minutes, and the table is the record:

experiment                                      SET        GET      conclusion
one client, pipeline 16                                  201,000   the client limits one connection
50 clients, GET only / SET only                 200,000    253,000   the count of clients changes nothing
parking_lot's user-space mutex                  200,000    199,800   not the kind of mutex
TCP_NODELAY on the socket                       159,700    199,200   not Nagle's algorithm
one socket handle instead of try_clone          199,600    199,400   not the clone
each thread with a private store, no lock       800,000    796,800   the lock

The last line is not a server anyone would ship, because the threads no longer share data, but it answers the question. Without the shared lock the Rust server is as fast as the C one. With it, every command from every thread passes through one mutex. A contended mutex on macOS is a pthread mutex, which passes the lock from one thread to the next through the kernel. The Rust standard library uses a futex on Linux and the pthread mutex on other Unix systems. The same server in a Linux container reached 398,000. Go has the same lock around its store and reaches 800,000. The comment above the Go mutex explains why. A waiting goroutine is parked on a semaphore of the runtime. In what the comment calls "starvation mode", ownership passes "from the unlocking goroutine to the waiter at the front of the queue". The kernel is not involved.

The first fix was to shrink what the lock covers. The command code now returns the reply as a value, and the server writes it after the lock is released:

/// A reply as a value, so that a command can be run under a lock and written after
/// the lock is released. Formatting and the write to the socket cost more than the
/// store operation itself, and neither needs the store.
pub enum Reply {
    Simple(&'static str),
    Error(String),
    Bulk(Vec<u8>),
    Int(i64),
    Nil,
    Array(Vec<Reply>),
}

pub fn write_reply(w: &mut (impl Write + ?Sized), reply: &Reply) -> io::Result<()> {
    match reply {
        Reply::Simple(s) => write_simple(w, s),
        Reply::Error(s) => write_error(w, s),
        Reply::Bulk(b) => write_bulk(w, b),
        Reply::Int(n) => write_int(w, *n),
        Reply::Nil => write_nil(w),
        Reply::Array(items) => {
            write_array_len(w, items.len())?;
            items.iter().try_for_each(|item| write_reply(w, item))
        }
    }
}
rust/ch13/src/resp.rs · region reply

It made no difference. Both servers stayed at 200,000, because the cost was the handoff and not the hold. The change stays, because formatting under a lock is a habit worth losing, and because the second fix needed it. The second fix is the reader-writer lock chapter 9 promised. Reads of the store take a shared lock that any number of threads may hold together. Writes take the exclusive one:

Exercise 13.3RustThe read-only commands

Write execute_read. It takes the arguments by reference and the store by shared reference. It returns Some(reply) for the commands that only read the store, and None for anything else. The table of commands says which is which, with Run::Read and Run::Write, so the function is a lookup and a call.

pub fn execute_read(args: &Command, store: &dyn Store) -> Option<Reply> {
    // your code here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/// The reply of a command that only reads the store, or `None` when the command writes
/// and the caller must take the exclusive lock and call `execute`.
pub fn execute_read(args: &Command, store: &dyn Store) -> Option<Reply> {
    match lookup(args) {
        Ok(Entry {
            run: Run::Read(f), ..
        }) => Some(f(args, store, Instant::now())),
        Ok(_) => None,
        Err(reply) => Some(reply),
    }
}
rust/ch13/src/cmd.rs · region execute-read

The serving loop tries the shared lock first and takes the exclusive one only for a write:

// A read takes the shared lock, which many threads hold at once. A
// write takes the exclusive one. Either way the lock is released
// before the reply is formatted or written.
let reply = {
    let db = db.read().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
    db.execute_read(&args)
};
let reply = match reply {
    Some(reply) => reply,
    None => {
        let mut db = db.write().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
        db.execute(&args)?
    }
};
resp::write_reply(&mut writer, &reply)?;

                         SET       GET            SET       GET
Rust, threads, before    99,950    88,700         159,700   199,400
Rust, threads, after     99,800    99,850         264,900   796,800
Rust, tokio, after       99,850    99,255         199,600   800,000

Reads are fixed. GET with pipelining went from 200,000 to 800,000, the C and Go figure, because fifty readers no longer queue. Writes are not fixed, because fifty writers still do, and 265,000 is where the pthread handoff leaves them. The next step would be to split the store into shards with a lock each, so that writers to different keys never meet. That is what every fast Rust store does, and what kv does not need. The chapter stops here, with a number that is honest about what was fixed and what was not.

The method#

The two halves of the chapter are the same method. A benchmark gave a number that looked wrong. A tool gave one line to suspect, the escape flag in Go and a profile in Rust. Each experiment changed one thing and measured again with the same command. The Go fix was kept because it moved the number. The first Rust fix was kept and measured, found to do nothing, and said so. The second was measured, found to fix half the problem, and said so. The C flags were measured and found to be noise, and said so. Nothing in that sequence needed a particular language. The same steps find the same kind of answer in all three, with their own tools. The "golden rule" of the benchmark documentation applies to all of it. "Only compare apples and apples."

🖥Profilers by platform

On macOS, sample needs nothing installed, and Instruments, started from the command line with xctrace record, gives a time profile with a graphical viewer. Both are macOS tools and do not run on Linux. There, perf is the tool for C and Rust, and its output feeds the flame graph scripts directly. Go's pprof works everywhere Go does, because the profiler is inside the runtime and not in the operating system. On Windows, Visual Studio has a CPU profiler for native code, and pprof again covers Go.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
A micro-benchmarkOKStrongOKC has a clock and a loop, and Go has go test -bench with allocation counts. Rust needs an example binary or a crate.
Seeing what the compiler didOKStrongOKGo prints its decisions for every line. C and Rust measure each flag, profile and attribute yourself.
A profiler in the boxOKStrongOKC and Rust use the operating system's profiler. Go carries its own, and it works the same everywhere.
Reading the profileStrongOKWeakOne C thread gives an honest list and Go needs the cum column, while the fifty Rust threads drown the list in waiting.
The cost of memoryStrongOKStrongC and Rust allocate what the code says. Go allocates what escapes, and a flag has to tell you which.
A fast serverStrongStrongOKC and Go reach 800,000 with pipelining. Rust needs a read lock to match on reads and stays behind on writes.
Why it was slowOKStrongWeakThe Go runtime hides lock handoff from the kernel. Rust's standard mutex is the platform's, and macOS makes it expensive.
Honest numbersStrongStrongStrongredis-benchmark and the same command shape treat all three alike.
Carry forward
  • Two questions, two tools. A micro-benchmark says how long a function takes. A profile says where a server's time goes. The parser was nine times slower in Go and one percent of the server in all three.
  • Escape analysis. Go puts a value on the heap when it cannot prove its lifetime, and -gcflags=-m names each one. Four of nine allocations were the caller's, and five were the parser's habits.
  • A flag is a hypothesis. -O3, inline, restrict, LTO and #[inline] each moved the number by a few percent or not at all. The benchmark decides, not the keyword.

Shipping#

Quality and shipping · Chapter 14· 24 min read· 254 lines of code
▶Scene

Build the C server on a current Linux, copy the binary to a Linux that is six years older, and run it:

$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w gcc:14 sh -c 'ldd --version | head -1; gcc -O2 -pthread -o kv src/*.c'
ldd (Debian GLIBC 2.41-12+deb13u4) 2.41
$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w debian:buster sh -c 'ldd --version | head -1; ./kv'
ldd (Debian GLIBC 2.28-10+deb10u3) 2.28
./kv: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.34' not found (required by ./kv)

Nothing in kv changed between the two machines. The C library did, and the binary carries a note that names the version it was built against. This chapter is about that note, and about everything else a program has to settle before it leaves the machine it was written on.

kv works on the machine it was written on. This chapter builds it for other machines, Linux on two kinds of processor and Windows, from a Mac. It gives each server the options, the configuration and the version a shipped program needs. It covers linking, cross-compilation, the three operating systems, and what the newest C standard changes.

To ship a program, three questions need answers. What does the binary carry with it, and what does it expect to find on the target machine? Which machines is it built for, and from where? And how does a user get a particular version, know which one they have, and tell it where to listen? Each language has settled answers. They differ enough that the same questions produce three different make dist targets.

ShippingCGoRust

What a binary carries#

Chapter 2 showed what the three hello programs linked, and the picture has not changed. A C program calls the C library for everything and links it dynamically by default. The binary then holds a note that says "find libc.so.6 on this machine", and the scene showed the rest of the note. Each function it uses is tagged with the library version that introduced it. A library too old for the tag refuses to load the program. On Linux, a Go program with CGO_ENABLED=0 makes its system calls itself and links nothing. On macOS it still links libSystem, as chapter 2 showed. A Rust program carries its own standard library and still calls the C library for the system. So it links libc.so.6 as the C one does, with the same note.

The old answer was to build on the oldest system you support. The newer answer is to link statically against musl, a small C library written for this. The binary then carries its own copy and asks for nothing. Go made that the default. The other two can choose it.

📜Why static binaries came back

Shared libraries exist to save memory and disk. One copy of the C library serves every program on the machine, which mattered when memory was small and expensive. The cost was that a program depended on the exact library that was there. A program moved to another machine often met a different one. Containers reversed the trade. A container image holds one program, so there is nothing to share, and a binary that needs nothing can run in an empty image. Go chose to link nothing from the start, and the choice fit the container world that arrived a few years later.

C: zig as the cross-compiler#

Cross-compiling C has always been possible and has rarely been pleasant. The compiler must be built for the target, and so must the C library and its headers. Those pieces must be found and told about each other. The Zig project changed that. The project overview says that Zig "is also a C compiler" and carries a C library for 97 targets. As a result, "Zig builds for all supported targets independently of the host", with "no separate cross toolchain". One download, and zig cc -target names the machine:

Exercise 14.1CBuild for two kinds of Linux

Write the dist target. Loop over two targets, x86_64-linux-musl and aarch64-linux-musl. For each, run zig cc over every source file with the usual flags and three more. -target names the machine, -static puts the C library inside the binary, and -s strips the symbols. Name each output after its target under dist/.

ZIG ?= zig
TARGETS := x86_64-linux-musl aarch64-linux-musl

dist: $(SRC)
	mkdir -p dist
	# your loop here
Stuck?Show the full listing
# Cross-compile with zig cc, which carries a C compiler, a linker and the C libraries of
# every target in one download. -static with musl gives a binary that needs no libc file,
# and -s strips the symbols, which is most of the size.
ZIG ?= zig
TARGETS := x86_64-linux-musl aarch64-linux-musl

dist: $(SRC)
	mkdir -p dist
	for t in $(TARGETS); do \
	  $(ZIG) cc -target $$t -static -s -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -o dist/kv-$$t $(SRC) || exit 1; \
	done
	ls -l dist

$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD/dist":/dist redis:8 bash -c \

The second command ran the arm64 binary under emulation on an Intel machine, which is slow and is enough to prove the build. Both answered, and both ran without a file from the system. The scene's binary would have answered on the old Debian too, had it been built this way.

C again: options, and a function that does not come back#

A shipped server is started by a script or a service manager, which passes options. The environment variables kv has used since chapter 3 are not enough. The same standard gives C one function for the job. getopt "parses the command-line arguments", from a string that lists the option letters, and a letter followed by a colon "requires an argument". It returns the letters one at a time, leaves an argument in optarg, and "returns -1" when the options are done:

/* The settings, from the command line first and the environment second. */
typedef struct {
    int port;
    const char *aof;   /* NULL for no persistence */
    const char *fsync; /* NULL for the default */
    const char *hash;  /* "fnv" for the unseeded hash */
} kv_options;

static const char USAGE[] = "usage: kv [-p port] [-a file] [-f always|everysec|no]\n"
                            "  -p port   the port to listen on (KV_PORT), 6380 by default\n"
                            "  -a file   append every write to this file (KV_AOF)\n"
                            "  -f policy how often to fsync the file (KV_FSYNC)\n";

/* getopt walks argv for the options in its string. A letter followed by a colon takes an
 * argument, which getopt leaves in optarg. It returns -1 when the options are done, and
 * optind then says where the rest of the arguments start. */
static kv_options kv_options_parse(int argc, char **argv) {
    const char *port = getenv("KV_PORT");
    kv_options o = {
        .port = port && *port ? atoi(port) : 6380,
        .aof = getenv("KV_AOF"),
        .fsync = getenv("KV_FSYNC"),
        .hash = getenv("KV_HASH"),
    };
    int c;
    while ((c = getopt(argc, argv, "p:a:f:h")) != -1) {
        switch (c) {
        case 'p':
            o.port = atoi(optarg);
            break;
        case 'a':
            o.aof = optarg;
            break;
        case 'f':
            o.fsync = optarg;
            break;
        case 'h':
            fputs(USAGE, stdout);
            exit(0);
        default: /* getopt has already printed which option it did not know */
            die("%s", USAGE);
        }
    }
    if (optind < argc) {
        die("kv: unexpected argument '%s'", argv[optind]);
    }
    if (o.port <= 0 || o.port > 65535) {
        die("kv: not a port: %d", o.port);
    }
    if (o.aof != NULL && *o.aof == '\0') {
        o.aof = NULL;
    }
    return o;
}
c/ch14/src/main.c · region options

The function that reports a bad option is the one to look at. It never returns, and it says so with _Noreturn. That is the C11 specifier that "specifies that the function does not return to its point of invocation". The compiler then knows that the code after a call to die is unreachable, and the reader knows it too. C23 deprecates the keyword for the attribute [[noreturn]], and the section below says why. The other word on the line is older than both. __attribute__ is a GNU extension, outside the standard but shared by gcc and clang. The format attribute says a function takes printf-style "arguments that should be type-checked against a format string". So a wrong %d in a call to die is an error at compile time, as it is for printf itself:

/* Print a message the way printf would, and exit. _Noreturn tells the compiler, and
 * the reader, that nothing follows a call. The attribute is a GNU extension that gcc
 * and clang share, outside the standard: it checks the arguments against the format
 * string at compile time, as the compiler does for printf itself. */
__attribute__((format(printf, 1, 2))) _Noreturn static void die(const char *fmt, ...) {
    va_list ap;
    va_start(ap, fmt);
    vfprintf(stderr, fmt, ap);
    va_end(ap);
    fputc('\n', stderr);
    exit(2);
}
c/ch14/src/main.c · region die
⚠️One source tree, one platform C

The C version of kv does not build for Windows. It uses poll, kqueue or epoll and the socket calls of POSIX, the Portable Operating System Interface. Chapter 9 explained that Windows wants a different loop. A C program that must run on both keeps two versions of the networking code behind one header. It chooses between them with #ifdef _WIN32, as chapter 9 chose a poller. kv does not, and says so. The other two languages carry that #ifdef inside their standard libraries, which is the whole difference in the next two sections.

C17 against C23#

Every C file in this book is built with -std=c17, because every compiler the book names accepts it. The newer standard, ISO/IEC 9899:2024, is in clang 17 and gcc 14, and the snapshot has a tour of it in one file. Most of the list is C catching up with the other two languages, feature by feature. nullptr is a null with a type of its own, so that it cannot be passed where an integer is wanted. constexpr is a constant the compiler evaluates, for the places a #define was used. typeof and auto take a type from an expression, as the other two languages do. Attributes in double brackets replace __attribute__ for the common cases. The booleans are keywords without a header. #embed puts the bytes of a file into an array at compile time, which Go does with go:embed and Rust with include_bytes!:

/* nullptr has a type of its own, so it cannot be mistaken for an int, as 0 or NULL can */
static const char *first_or(const char *s, const char *fallback) {
    return s != nullptr ? s : fallback;
}

/* [[nodiscard]] makes the compiler warn when a caller ignores the result */
[[nodiscard]] static int parse_digit(char c) {
    return c >= '0' && c <= '9' ? c - '0' : -1;
}

/* #embed pastes the bytes of a file into an array at compile time */
static const unsigned char banner[] = {
#embed "banner.txt"
};

int main(void) {
    /* constexpr: a true compile-time constant, usable where a #define was needed before */
    constexpr int limit = 64;
    /* typeof and auto: the type comes from the expression, as in the other two languages */
    typeof(limit) half = limit / 2;
    auto digit = parse_digit('7');
    /* binary literals and digit separators */
    unsigned mask = 0b1111'0000;
    /* true and false are keywords, and bool needs no header */
    bool ok = digit == 7;
    static_assert(limit > 0); /* no message needed any more */
    printf("%s %d %d %u %d %.*s", first_or(nullptr, "default"), half, digit, mask, ok,
           (int)sizeof banner, banner);
    return 0;
}
c/ch14/extras/c23.c · region c23
$ make c23
default 32 7 240 1 kv, three languages

The standard also removes something. A function defined the way Kernighan and Ritchie wrote them in 1978, with the parameter types on separate lines, is no longer C. That is the first removal of a feature from the language in its history. The server kv stays on C17 for now. The one line that would change is the _Noreturn above.

Go: two variables#

Go cross-compiles by design. The compiler is one program that contains the code generators for every target. The standard library is compiled for the target as part of the build. go help environment describes the two variables. GOOS is "The operating system for which to compile code", and GOARCH is "The architecture, or processor, for which to compile code". A third, CGO_ENABLED, says "Whether the cgo command is supported", and setting it to 0 keeps the C library out:

Exercise 14.2GoBuild for four targets

Write a dist target. Loop over the four targets below. Split each into the two variables, add .exe for Windows, and set CGO_ENABLED=0. Build with -ldflags="-s -w", which drops the symbol table and the debugging information.
