Stuck?Show the full listing
# Cross-compile by setting two variables. CGO_ENABLED=0 keeps the binary free of the C
# library, so that it runs on any Linux of the right architecture, and in a scratch
# container. -s -w drop the symbol table and debug information, which halves the size.
TARGETS := linux/amd64 linux/arm64 windows/amd64 darwin/arm64

dist:
	mkdir -p dist
	for t in $(TARGETS); do \
	  os=$${t%/*}; arch=$${t#*/}; ext=""; [ $$os = windows ] && ext=.exe; \
	  CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$$os GOARCH=$$arch go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/kv-$$os-$$arch$$ext ./cmd/kv || exit 1; \
	done
	ls -l dist

✅Turn cgo off unless you need it Go

A Go program that imports a package which uses cgo links the C library and loses the freedom to run anywhere. The usual sources are the net package's name resolver and the os/user package, both of which have pure Go paths that CGO_ENABLED=0 selects. Build with it off, and turn it on only for a package that has no other way, which chapter 15 shows.

Go again: flags, a file, a log and a version#

The Go server reads its settings in three layers, each over the last. The environment comes first, for the test runner. A JSON file comes second, if a flag names one. The flags on the command line come last. The flag package "implements command-line flag parsing". Each call such as flag.StringVar registers a flag with its default and its help text. flag.Parse reads the arguments, and -h prints the help that the package wrote from those calls. The file is read with encoding/json, which "parses the JSON-encoded data and stores the result in the value pointed to by v". The tag on each field of the struct "gives the name of the field" in the file. A field must be exported to be filled:

// config is every setting the server takes. The json tags name the keys in a config
// file, and the same struct is filled from the environment and the flags.
type config struct {
	Port  string `json:"port"`
	AOF   string `json:"aof"`
	Fsync string `json:"fsync"`
}

func env(name, fallback string) string {
	if v := os.Getenv(name); v != "" {
		return v
	}
	return fallback
}

// loadConfig reads the settings in order: the environment, then a JSON file if -config
// names one, then the flags given on the command line, each layer over the last.
func loadConfig() config {
	cfg := config{Port: env("KV_PORT", "6380"), AOF: os.Getenv("KV_AOF"), Fsync: os.Getenv("KV_FSYNC")}
	file := flag.String("config", "", "a JSON file with port, aof and fsync")
	flag.StringVar(&cfg.Port, "port", cfg.Port, "the port to listen on")
	flag.StringVar(&cfg.AOF, "aof", cfg.AOF, "append every write to this file")
	flag.StringVar(&cfg.Fsync, "fsync", cfg.Fsync, "how often to fsync the file: always, everysec or no")
	showVersion := flag.Bool("version", false, "print the version and exit")
	flag.Parse()
	if *showVersion {
		fmt.Print(version)
		os.Exit(0)
	}
	if *file != "" {
		data, err := os.ReadFile(*file)
		if err == nil {
			err = json.Unmarshal(data, &cfg)
		}
		if err != nil {
			slog.Error("config", "file", *file, "err", err)
			os.Exit(2)
		}
		// a flag given on the command line still wins over the file
		flag.Visit(func(f *flag.Flag) {
			switch f.Name {
			case "port":
				cfg.Port = f.Value.String()
			case "aof":
				cfg.AOF = f.Value.String()
			case "fsync":
				cfg.Fsync = f.Value.String()
			}
		})
	}
	return cfg
}

The lines it printed come from the fourth piece, log/slog. It "provides structured logging, in which log records include a message, a severity level" and key-value pairs. The text handler writes key=value. The JSON handler, "whose output is line-delimited JSON", is one line to switch to, for a collector that wants fields and not sentences. The version in the first line is the fifth piece, and it took two directives:

// go generate runs the command in the directive and writes version.txt, which is checked
// in. go:embed then compiles the file's contents into the binary as a string, so that a
// shipped kv can say which commit it is.
//
//go:generate sh -c "git describe --always --dirty > version.txt"
//go:embed version.txt
var version string
go/ch14/cmd/kv/main.go · region version

go generate "runs commands described by directives within existing files". The manual is firm that it "is never run automatically by go build, go test, and so on. It must be run explicitly". So the generated file is checked in. go:embed then does what the C23 #embed does. The embed package "provides access to files embedded in the running Go program". The files are read "from the package directory or subdirectories at compile time", into a string, a byte slice or a file system.

📰Go 1.22 changes the meaning of a loop, 2024

For thirteen years, a goroutine started inside a Go loop saw the loop's last value, not its own. The variable was "created once and updated by each iteration", so every closure captured the same one. The bug was so common that go vet had a check for it, and it reached production often enough that the Go team changed the language. In Go 1.22, "each iteration of the loop creates new variables, to avoid accidental sharing bugs". A change to what existing code means is the thing a language with a compatibility promise cannot do, and Go found a way. The new meaning applies "only in packages contained in modules that declare go 1.22 or later in their go.mod files". The line go 1.27 in kv's module is a shipping decision, then, and not only a minimum. It says which language the code was written in. The preview ran for four months before the release and produced "zero reports of any problems in production code".

Rust: a target, a linker, and zig again#

Rust is in between. The compiler can produce code for any target, and rustup target add fetches the standard library for one. The rustup book is precise about what that gives you. "rustup target add only installs the Rust standard library for a given target", and "There are typically other tools necessary to cross-compile, particularly a linker". The linker, and the C library it links against, are the C problem again. The common answer is the same tool as in C. cargo-zigbuild describes itself as "Compile Cargo project with zig as linker for easier cross compiling":

Exercise 14.3RustA profile for shipping, and three targets

Add a dist profile to Cargo.toml that inherits from release, turns debugging information off, and strips the symbols. Then write a dist target in a Makefile. It runs cargo zigbuild --profile dist for each of the three targets below and copies each binary under dist/. Each target must first be added with rustup target add.

x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
x86_64-pc-windows-gnu

The profile comes first.

# Cross-compile with cargo-zigbuild, which lets zig link for the target. Each target is
# a rustup component: rustup target add <triple>. The musl target is static. The dist
# profile in Cargo.toml strips the symbols that the release profile keeps for profiling.
TARGETS := x86_64-unknown-linux-musl aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu x86_64-pc-windows-gnu

dist:
	mkdir -p dist
	for t in $(TARGETS); do \
	  cargo zigbuild --profile dist -q --target $$t || exit 1; \
	  cp target/$$t/dist/kv dist/kv-$$t 2>/dev/null || cp target/$$t/dist/kv.exe dist/kv-$$t.exe; \
	done
	ls -l dist

The musl binary is static and the gnu one is not. In the arm64 container, ldd lists three shared libraries for it, starting with libc.so.6. That is the note from the first section, and it ran because the container had them. The musl one ran because it needed nothing. The chapter 13 profile setting, debug = 1, is why a separate profile exists. It keeps symbols for the profiler, and a shipped binary does not want them. Stripping took the musl build from 7.3 megabytes to 521 kilobytes.

⚠️A warning from a linker you did not choose Rust

The gnu target prints a warning on every build. It reads warning: linker stderr: ignoring deprecated linker optimization setting "1", under the lint linker_messages. It comes from zig's linker, which is being driven with a flag meant for another, and the binary is fine. Cross-compiling in Rust means rustup, cargo and the linker cooperating. A message from one of them that the others do not understand is the normal cost of that.

Options from the standard library, and the crate everyone uses#

The Rust standard library gives a program its arguments and nothing more. std::env::args "returns the arguments that this program was started with", as an iterator, and "the first element is traditionally the path of the executable". Everything after that is a loop with a match. The server kv writes it itself, because the book has one dependency and will not add a second for this. The function that reports a bad option returns !, the never type, which is what _Noreturn is in C with the compiler's full attention. A call to it can stand where a value is expected, because no value will ever be needed:

/// Every setting the server takes, from the environment first and the command line
/// second. The standard library gives an iterator over the arguments and nothing else.
/// Most Rust programs reach the same result with the clap crate, which writes the
/// parser and the help text from a struct like this one.
struct Options {
    port: u16,
    aof: Option<String>,
    fsync: String,
}

const USAGE: &str = "usage: kv [-p port] [-a file] [-f always|everysec|no]
  -p port   the port to listen on (KV_PORT), 6380 by default
  -a file   append every write to this file (KV_AOF)
  -f policy how often to fsync the file (KV_FSYNC)";

fn env(name: &str) -> Option<String> {
    std::env::var(name).ok().filter(|v| !v.is_empty())
}

/// A usage error is reported and the process ends with status 2, as getopt programs do.
/// The return type `!` is Rust's _Noreturn: this function never comes back.
fn usage_error(msg: &str) -> ! {
    eprintln!("kv: {msg}\n{USAGE}");
    std::process::exit(2)
}

fn options() -> Options {
    let mut o = Options {
        port: 6380,
        aof: env("KV_AOF"),
        fsync: env("KV_FSYNC").unwrap_or_default(),
    };
    let mut port = env("KV_PORT").unwrap_or_else(|| "6380".to_string());
    let mut args = std::env::args().skip(1);
    while let Some(flag) = args.next() {
        let mut value = || {
            args.next()
                .unwrap_or_else(|| usage_error(&format!("{flag} needs a value")))
        };
        match flag.as_str() {
            "-p" => port = value(),
            "-a" => o.aof = Some(value()).filter(|v| !v.is_empty()),
            "-f" => o.fsync = value(),
            "-h" => {
                println!("{USAGE}");
                std::process::exit(0)
            }
            other => usage_error(&format!("unknown option '{other}'")),
        }
    }
    o.port = match port.parse() {
        Ok(port) => port,
        Err(_) => usage_error(&format!("not a port: {port}")),
    };
    o
}
rust/ch14/src/main.rs · region options

Most Rust programs do not write this loop. They add clap, "Command Line Argument Parser for Rust", and put a #[derive(Parser)] on a struct like Options. The parser, the help text and --version are written for them. A config file goes the same way, through the serde crate. It derives the reading of JSON or TOML into a struct, as the Go package does with tags. Both crates are in nearly every shipped Rust program, and the standard library has no such thing. Go put the same two things in its standard library, which is the same decision made in opposite directions. The version needs no crate at all. Cargo sets CARGO_PKG_VERSION from Cargo.toml at build time, and env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION") puts it in the binary.

Three sizes, three reasons#

                      Linux x86_64, stripped    what is inside
C, musl, static              44,824 bytes       kv, and the parts of musl it calls
Rust, musl, static          521,024 bytes       kv, the Rust standard library, and musl
Go, CGO_ENABLED=0         2,556,064 bytes       kv, and the Go runtime with its collector

The C binary is small because C has no runtime and the linker keeps only what is referenced. The Rust binary is ten times larger, because its standard library is inside and is itself written in Rust, with formatting, collections and the allocator. The Go binary is fifty times larger, because the garbage collector, the scheduler and the network poller are inside. They are there whether a program uses them or not. None of the three sizes is a problem for a server. All three are a fact a reader should know before choosing a language for a device with a megabyte of flash.

The three operating systems, in one place#

The platform boxes in earlier chapters each covered one difference. Set together, they are the list of what a program must know when it leaves its first machine. The last three rows are how each language says "this code is for that system". The book used all three in chapters 9 and 10.

The differenceCGoRust
Readiness and completionpoll and kqueue on macOS, epoll on Linux, completion ports on Windowsthe runtime hides itthe runtime hides it
Socketsone API from BSD, with Winsock variants on Windowshiddenhidden
Threads and lockspthreads, or Windows threadshiddenhidden, but the mutex differs underneath
The C librarylibc.so.6, libSystem, or the Windows C runtimenot usedused through a thin layer
Line endings and paths\n and /, or \r\n and \path/filepath and runtime.GOOSstd::path and cfg!(windows)
Choosing code per system#ifdef __linux__, from macros the compiler predefines//go:build unix on the first line, or _linux.go in the name#[cfg(unix)] or #[cfg(target_os = "linux")] on an item
The unit it choosesa region of a file, or a whole file that compiles to nothinga whole file, alwaysone item: a function, a module, a statement
Where it shows in kvthe pollers, the fsync call, every #includeinternal/syssys.rs, and the mutex in chapter 13

The last row is the honest one. The Go version of kv has one file that knows which operating system it runs on, and so does the Rust version. The Rust one still ran twice as fast on Linux as on macOS under contention, because the standard mutex is a different object on each. Hiding a platform is not the same as making it disappear.

Versions and releases#

A version is a promise about change, and the three ecosystems make the promise the same way, with three numbers. Semantic versioning, which Go modules and cargo both read, gives each number a meaning. Increase the "MAJOR version when you make incompatible API changes". Increase the "MINOR version when you add functionality in a backward compatible manner". Increase the "PATCH version when you make backward compatible bug fixes". kv's Rust crate has carried a version in Cargo.toml since chapter 2. Its Go module carries one as a Git tag, which go install reads, and the binary now carries the commit. Its C version carries one wherever you choose to write it.

How a user gets the program differs more. A Go program with a public module path is installed with go install path@version, which fetches and builds it. Or it is shipped as the one binary this chapter made. A Rust program is installed with cargo install from crates.io or a Git URL, or shipped as a binary. A C program is shipped as source, and becomes a package when a distribution packages it, or as a binary built as above. Redis ships as source and as distribution packages, and that is the C norm. The one binary with nothing to install is the Go norm, and increasingly the Rust one.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
Cross-compilingOKStrongOKC needs zig and gets a small static binary. Go needs two variables, and Rust needs a target, a linker and zig.
Static linkingOKStrongOKC and Rust choose musl. Go links nothing by default.
Binary sizeStrongWeakOK45 KB, 2.5 MB and 521 KB for the same server.
Options and configOKStrongOKC has getopt and nothing for a file, and Go has flag, json and slog in the box. Rust has the arguments and a crate for the rest.
WindowsWeakStrongStrongThe C code is Unix-only. Go and Rust build for Windows unchanged.
Knowing the platformWeakStrongOKC sees every difference and Go hides all of them. Rust hides most and leaks one through the mutex.
A releaseWeakStrongStrongC has no mechanism. Go and Rust read a tag or a version field and install from a path.
Carry forward
  • The note in the binary. A dynamic binary names the C library version it needs, and an older machine refuses it. A static musl binary, or a Go binary, carries everything and asks for nothing.
  • Three ways to choose code per system. C uses the preprocessor and macros the compiler predefines. Go uses a constraint on a whole file. Rust uses an attribute on one item.
  • A function that never returns. C says _Noreturn or [[noreturn]] and the compiler trusts it. Rust says ! and the compiler knows it. Go has os.Exit and no way to say so.

Talking to C#

Quality and shipping · Chapter 15· 24 min read· 264 lines of code
▶Scene

Take the chapter 6 pattern matcher, which Go and C both have. Time the Go version against the C version called through cgo, on the same input, from the same benchmark:

$ go test -run xxx -bench Glob -benchmem ./internal/cmatch/
BenchmarkGlobGo-12     	49871018	        24.75 ns/op	       0 B/op	       0 allocs/op
BenchmarkGlobCgo-12    	15145387	        76.56 ns/op	       0 B/op	       0 allocs/op

The C function does the same work in the same number of instructions, and the call takes three times as long. The difference is the border, and the chapter is about what stands on it. The Rust call to the same function costs nothing, and the chapter says why.

Every operating system, database driver and codec exposes a C interface, so Go and Rust both have a door to C. This chapter builds a small C library from kv and calls it from Go through cgo and from Rust through an extern block. It passes a struct and a union across, where the layout of memory is the interface. Then it calls Rust from C.

The hash and the pattern matcher from chapter 6 are the library. They are small, they take bytes and a length, and they allocate nothing, which makes them the easiest kind of C to call from anywhere. The same two functions are already written in Go and Rust, so each call can be checked against a native version, and timed against it.

Talking to CCGoRust
Declaring a C functiona headera C comment before import "C"an unsafe extern "C" block
Passing bytesa pointer and a size_tunsafe.Pointer and C.size_tas_ptr() and len()
A struct across the borderits layout, by the rules of the ABIC.struct_name, laid out as C did#[repr(C)], laid out as C did
A union across the bordera tag and the same bytesa byte array, read with unsafea union, read with unsafe
Who compiles the C fileyou, with makethe go tool, from the package directorybuild.rs, with the cc crate
A trivial call costsnothingabout three times a Go callthe same as a C call
Being called from Cthe normal case//export#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub unsafe extern "C"
What it does to the buildnothingneeds a C compiler and cgo onneeds a C compiler for the C part

The border is a C function#

A compiled function has a name, a place in memory, and a convention for where its arguments and its result go. That convention is the application binary interface (ABI), and the C one is the one every operating system defines and documents. A Go or Rust function has its own. A caller in either language cannot reach a C function without agreeing to the C convention for that one call. The Rust book puts it in one sentence. "The "C" part defines which application binary interface (ABI) the external function uses".

The border has a second property. Nothing on it is checked. The C compiler trusts the header, Go trusts the comment above import "C", and Rust trusts the extern block. A wrong type in any of them compiles and misbehaves at run time. That is why the library below is written to make the declarations hard to get wrong.

📜Why everything speaks C

Unix was written in C, and its system calls were given C wrappers. So the first interface every other language had to reach was a C one. Every operating system since has kept the habit, and so has every library that wants to be used from more than one language. Go got its door early. The Go blog described cgo in March 2011, a year before Go 1, with C as a "pseudo-package" for "C's name space". Rust had extern blocks before 1.0, and the 2024 edition made them say unsafe, because that is what they always were. In October 2022 the border was crossed in the other direction at the largest scale there is. Linus Torvalds accepted the Rust for Linux work into the kernel, released as Linux 6.1, and the first drivers written in Rust followed in 6.8. A kernel is C that calls everything, and it now calls Rust.

C: a library that is easy to call#

A C library is a header and an archive. The header is the only thing the other side reads, so its shape decides how pleasant the border is. The rules are short. Take a pointer and a length, never a C string, because Go and Rust bytes have no terminating zero. Return an int, not a bool, because every language agrees on what a C int is. Allocate nothing, so that no one has to ask which side frees it.

# The hash and the matcher as a static library, for chapter 15. ar bundles object files
# into an archive that a linker can search; this is what every C library is.
lib: build/libkvmatch.a

build/libkvmatch.a: lib/kvmatch.c lib/kvmatch.h | build

A struct and a union on the border#

Two more functions pass something larger than a number. One fills a struct with both answers at once. The other fills a tagged union, the shape chapter 8 used for a value of several kinds. On the border, the shape of a struct is not a detail of the compiler. It is the interface. Every C compiler lays out a struct by the same rule, the one the ABI writes down. Each field sits at the first offset after the previous one that its alignment allows. The struct's size is rounded up to its own alignment. A uint8_t followed by a uint64_t is therefore sixteen bytes, with seven of them padding:

/* Both answers in one call. The struct is part of the interface, and so is its layout:
 * the one-byte flag is followed by seven bytes of padding, so that the hash sits at an
 * offset of 8, and every caller on every side of the border must agree. */
typedef struct kvmatch_stats {
    uint8_t matched; /* 0 or 1 */
    uint64_t hash;   /* of the key */
} kvmatch_stats;

void kvmatch_glob_stats(const char *pat, size_t plen, const char *key, size_t klen,
                        kvmatch_stats *out);

/* A number parsed from bytes. A union holds the integer or the double in the same eight
 * bytes, and the tag is the only record of which one is there. */
enum { KVMATCH_NONE = 0, KVMATCH_INT = 1, KVMATCH_FLOAT = 2 };

typedef struct kvmatch_number {
    int kind; /* KVMATCH_INT or KVMATCH_FLOAT, or KVMATCH_NONE for not a number */
    union {
        int64_t i;
        double f;
    } as;
} kvmatch_number;

/* Parse up to 63 bytes as a decimal integer or, with a point, a double. Returns the kind. */
int kvmatch_parse_number(const char *s, size_t n, kvmatch_number *out);
c/ch15/lib/kvmatch.h · region layout

The C reference defines the alignment requirement as "the number of bytes between successive addresses at which objects of this type can be allocated". offsetof gives the offset of a field "from the beginning of an object of specified type", padding included. A small program asks the compiler for all of the numbers. The Go and Rust tests below assert the same ones:

int main(void) {
    printf("kvmatch_stats:  size %zu, alignment %zu, matched at %zu, hash at %zu\n",
           sizeof(kvmatch_stats), alignof(kvmatch_stats), offsetof(kvmatch_stats, matched),
           offsetof(kvmatch_stats, hash));
    printf("kvmatch_number: size %zu, alignment %zu, kind at %zu, as at %zu, as is %zu bytes\n",
           sizeof(kvmatch_number), alignof(kvmatch_number), offsetof(kvmatch_number, kind),
           offsetof(kvmatch_number, as), sizeof(((kvmatch_number *)0)->as));
    return 0;
}

$ make layout
kvmatch_stats:  size 16, alignment 8, matched at 0, hash at 8
kvmatch_number: size 16, alignment 8, kind at 0, as at 8, as is 8 bytes

Four kilobytes, and the C side is done. C has no door to build, because C is the door. The rest of the chapter is the other two languages arriving at it.

Go: cgo#

cgo is part of the go tool. A Go file that has import "C" is a cgo file. The comment directly above that import is the preamble. The documentation says it "is used as a header when compiling the C parts of the package". Every C name in the preamble appears in Go under the C prefix, so C.size_t is the C type and C.kvmatch_glob is the function. Any .c file in the package directory is compiled with the system C compiler and linked in, which is why kvmatch.c sits beside cmatch.go.

Stuck?Show the full listing
/*
#include "kvmatch.h"
*/
import "C"

import "unsafe"

// Glob reports whether key matches the pattern, by calling the C function. The slices
// are passed as a pointer and a length, and C must not keep the pointer: after the call
// returns, the garbage collector may free the bytes, or move them if they live on a stack.
func Glob(pat, key []byte) bool {
	return C.kvmatch_glob(cstr(pat), C.size_t(len(pat)), cstr(key), C.size_t(len(key))) != 0
}

// Hash returns the FNV-1a hash of b, from the C code.
func Hash(b []byte) uint64 {
	return uint64(C.kvmatch_hash(cstr(b), C.size_t(len(b))))
}

// cstr gives C a pointer to the first byte of a slice, or a pointer to a static byte for
// an empty slice, because unsafe.SliceData of an empty slice may be nil and C must not
// receive nil for a length of zero.
func cstr(b []byte) *C.char {
	if len(b) == 0 {
		return (*C.char)(unsafe.Pointer(&empty))
	}
	return (*C.char)(unsafe.Pointer(unsafe.SliceData(b)))
}

var empty byte
go/ch15/internal/cmatch/cmatch.go · region cgo

The pointer is the delicate part, because Go has a garbage collector and C does not know about it. The cgo documentation gives the rule. "All Go pointers passed to C must point to pinned Go memory". A pointer passed as a function argument has "the memory they point to implicitly pinned for the duration of the call". After that, "C code may not keep a copy of a Go pointer after the call returns". kvmatch_glob reads and returns, so it obeys without trying. A C library that keeps a buffer after the call needs runtime.Pinner, or a copy made with C.CBytes. The copy is freed with C.free, in the C way.

The struct and the union come across under their C names, with the prefix the documentation describes. "To access a struct, union, or enum type directly, prefix it with struct_, union_, or enum_". Go lays the struct out as the C compiler did, padding and all. The test asks the unsafe package for the numbers. The union is the odd one. Go has no unions, so "C's union types are represented as a Go byte array with the same length". The value is read out of those bytes with a conversion that the tag chooses:

// cStats is the C struct, under its cgo name. Go lays it out exactly as the C compiler
// did, padding included, because the bytes cross the border as they are. The type stays
// private: only a cgo file can see the fields of a C struct.
type cStats = C.struct_kvmatch_stats

// Layout asks the Go compiler what it decided about the C struct, with the questions
// sizeof, offsetof and alignof answer in C. The offset is pointer arithmetic, because
// unsafe.Offsetof does not accept a field of a type that cgo generated.
func Layout() (size, hashOffset, align uintptr) {
	var s cStats
	at := uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&s.hash)) - uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&s))
	return unsafe.Sizeof(s), at, unsafe.Alignof(s)
}

// GlobStats fills the C struct through a pointer to a Go value, which the cgo rules
// allow because the struct holds no Go pointers, and takes the two answers out of it.
func GlobStats(pat, key []byte) (matched bool, hash uint64) {
	var out cStats
	C.kvmatch_glob_stats(cstr(pat), C.size_t(len(pat)), cstr(key), C.size_t(len(key)), &out)
	return out.matched != 0, uint64(out.hash)
}

// Number is the parsed value, as Go would rather have it: an interface holding an int64
// or a float64, instead of the C union and its tag.
type Number any

// ParseNumber calls the C parser. cgo represents the union as a byte array of its size,
// so the value is read out of those bytes with an unsafe conversion, chosen by the tag.
func ParseNumber(b []byte) Number {
	var n C.kvmatch_number
	switch C.kvmatch_parse_number(cstr(b), C.size_t(len(b)), &n) {
	case C.KVMATCH_INT:
		return int64(*(*C.int64_t)(unsafe.Pointer(&n.as)))
	case C.KVMATCH_FLOAT:
		return float64(*(*C.double)(unsafe.Pointer(&n.as)))
	}
	return nil
}
go/ch15/internal/cmatch/cmatch.go · region layout
// The layout Go sees must be the layout C wrote: a one-byte flag, seven bytes of
// padding, and the hash at offset 8. Layout asks the compiler through unsafe.
func TestLayoutAgreesWithC(t *testing.T) {
	if size, at, align := Layout(); size != 16 || at != 8 || align != 8 {
		t.Fatalf("size %d, hash at %d, align %d", size, at, align)
	}
	matched, hash := GlobStats([]byte("user:*"), []byte("user:1"))
	if !matched || hash != store.Fnv1a([]byte("user:1")) {
		t.Fatalf("GlobStats = %v, %d", matched, hash)
	}
	if n, ok := ParseNumber([]byte("42")).(int64); !ok || n != 42 {
		t.Fatalf("42 parsed as %v", ParseNumber([]byte("42")))
	}
	if f, ok := ParseNumber([]byte("4.5")).(float64); !ok || f != 4.5 {
		t.Fatalf("4.5 parsed as %v", ParseNumber([]byte("4.5")))
	}
	if ParseNumber([]byte("x")) != nil {
		t.Fatal("x is not a number")
	}
}
go/ch15/internal/cmatch/cmatch_test.go · region layout-test

// The price of the border: the same match, in Go and through cgo.
var sink bool

func BenchmarkGlobGo(b *testing.B) {
	pat, key := []byte("user:*"), []byte("user:1")
	for b.Loop() {

func BenchmarkGlobCgo(b *testing.B) {

go/ch15/internal/cmatch/cmatch_test.go · region bench

The C function does the same work as the Go one and takes three times as long. The difference, about fifty nanoseconds, is the crossing. A goroutine runs on a small stack that can grow, and C expects a large fixed one. So the runtime switches stacks on the way in and back on the way out. It also tells the scheduler that this goroutine is away. Fifty nanoseconds is nothing for a call that then decodes a video frame. It is everything for a call made once per byte.

⚠️One cgo import changes the whole binary Go

A program that imports a cgo package cannot be built with CGO_ENABLED=0. The chapter 14 dist target still works here, because the kv server does not import cmatch. The moment it did, the build would need a C compiler for every target, and a cross-compiler for the foreign ones. The binary would then link the C library. The one-file freedom of chapter 14 is paid for with the rule that the program contains no C.

✅Keep the C in one package Go

Put every cgo call in one small package with a Go interface. Pass a pointer and a length, nothing that holds a Go pointer, and keep the calls coarse. One call that processes a buffer costs the same crossing as one call that processes a byte. Check the standard library first. The net resolver and os/user both have a pure Go path, and most of what a program needs from C already has one.

Rust: extern and unsafe#

Rust has no separate tool. An extern "C" block declares functions that live somewhere else, in Rust syntax with C types. The 2024 edition requires the word unsafe in front of it. The edition guide explains why. "It is the responsibility of the author of the extern block to ensure that the signatures are correct". A wrong one "may result in undefined behavior". The compiler checks that the Rust side of each call matches the declaration. It cannot check that the declaration matches the C.

Exercise 15.3RustDeclare, then wrap

Declare both functions in an unsafe extern "C" block. Use *const u8 for the pointers and usize for the lengths. The C int is std::ffi::c_int. Then write safe glob(pat: &[u8], key: &[u8]) -> bool and hash(bytes: &[u8]) -> u64 around them, each with a SAFETY comment that says why the call is sound.

unsafe extern "C" {
    // your declarations here
}

pub fn glob(pat: &[u8], key: &[u8]) -> bool {
    // your code here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
// What the C header declares, in Rust spelling. The compiler takes these on trust: a
// wrong type here is undefined behaviour, which is why the block is unsafe to call.
unsafe extern "C" {
    fn kvmatch_hash(s: *const u8, n: usize) -> u64;
    fn kvmatch_glob(pat: *const u8, plen: usize, key: *const u8, klen: usize) -> c_int;
    fn kvmatch_glob_stats(
        pat: *const u8,
        plen: usize,
        key: *const u8,

rust/ch15/src/cmatch.rs · region extern
/// Does the key match the pattern? The C function reads `plen` bytes from `pat` and
/// `klen` from `key` and keeps neither pointer, so a slice is safe to pass for the
/// duration of the call.
pub fn glob(pat: &[u8], key: &[u8]) -> bool {
    // SAFETY: both pointers come from live slices and the lengths are their lengths;
    // the C code does not write through them and does not keep them.
    unsafe { kvmatch_glob(pat.as_ptr(), pat.len(), key.as_ptr(), key.len()) != 0 }
}

/// FNV-1a, from the C code.
pub fn hash(bytes: &[u8]) -> u64 {
    // SAFETY: as above, a live slice and its length.
    unsafe { kvmatch_hash(bytes.as_ptr(), bytes.len()) }
}
rust/ch15/src/cmatch.rs · region safe

The five powers, and the pointer they are for#

The wrapper is the whole idea of unsafe in Rust. The Rust book lists five things that only an unsafe block may do. Dereference a raw pointer. Call an unsafe function or method. Access or modify a mutable static variable. Implement an unsafe trait. Access fields of a union. A call into C is the second, and the block around it is a boundary, not a switch. Inside it, the borrow checker still runs and every other rule still holds. Only the five powers are added, and the SAFETY comment records the argument that they were used correctly. Everything that calls glob is ordinary safe Rust and cannot break the rule the comment states.

The first power is about the type that chapter 10's lifetimes never touched. A raw pointer, *const T or *mut T, is a reference with the checks removed. The book says raw pointers "are allowed to ignore the borrowing rules" and "aren't guaranteed to point to valid memory". They "are allowed to be null" and "don't implement any automatic cleanup". Making one is safe, which is what as_ptr does. Reading through one is the first of the five powers. The only place kv does it is on the way back from C, in the exported function below.

The struct is declared again in Rust, with one attribute. A plain Rust struct has no promised layout. The reference says the order of the fields "does not have to be the same as the order in which the fields are specified". #[repr(C)] gives it C's rule instead, field by field in declaration order, so that the bytes mean the same on both sides. The union is a union, a type Rust has for exactly this case. Reading a field of it is the fifth power, "because Rust can't guarantee the type of the data currently being stored in the union instance". The tag the C code set is the argument that the read is sound:

/// The C struct, declared again in Rust. `repr(C)` makes the compiler lay it out as C
/// would, fields in order with C's padding, instead of reordering them as it may for a
/// plain Rust struct. The test below checks the numbers against the C ones.
#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Default)]
pub struct Stats {
    pub matched: u8,
    pub hash: u64,
}

/// The C union: eight bytes that are an integer or a double. Reading a field of a union
/// is unsafe, because the compiler cannot know which one was last written.
#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
union NumberBits {
    i: i64,
    f: f64,
}

#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct CNumber {
    kind: c_int,
    as_: NumberBits,
}

/// What the parser found, as a Rust enum: the tag and the bytes become one value that
/// a match must take apart, and no wrong field can be read.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub enum Number {
    Int(i64),
    Float(f64),
}

pub fn glob_stats(pat: &[u8], key: &[u8]) -> Stats {
    let mut out = Stats::default();
    // SAFETY: live slices and their lengths, and `out` is a valid Stats the C code fills.
    unsafe { kvmatch_glob_stats(pat.as_ptr(), pat.len(), key.as_ptr(), key.len(), &mut out) };
    out
}

pub fn parse_number(bytes: &[u8]) -> Option<Number> {
    let mut n = CNumber {
        kind: 0,
        as_: NumberBits { i: 0 },
    };
    // SAFETY: a live slice and its length, and `n` is a valid CNumber the C code fills.
    // The union field read below is chosen by the tag the C code set, which is the
    // whole contract of a tagged union.
    unsafe {
        match kvmatch_parse_number(bytes.as_ptr(), bytes.len(), &mut n) {
            1 => Some(Number::Int(n.as_.i)),
            2 => Some(Number::Float(n.as_.f)),
            _ => None,
        }
    }
}
rust/ch15/src/cmatch.rs · region layout

The test asks for the same numbers that the C program printed, with size_of, align_of and offset_of!. The three agree, as they must. A program that declares a C struct itself does this for every struct. That is why most Rust projects with a large C library do not declare them at all. They run bindgen, which "automatically generates Rust FFI bindings to C and C++ libraries". FFI is the foreign function interface. It reads the header, writes the repr(C) structs and the extern blocks, and runs from a build script like the one below.

Someone must compile the C file. A build script does, before the crate compiles, using the cc crate, which finds the system compiler and links the result into the crate:

// A build script runs before the crate compiles. This one compiles the C library with
// the cc crate, which finds the system C compiler and links the result into the crate.
fn main() {
    cc::Build::new()
        .file("../../c/ch15/lib/kvmatch.c")
        .include("../../c/ch15/lib")
        .warnings(true)
        .compile("kvmatch");
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=../../c/ch15/lib/kvmatch.c");
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=../../c/ch15/lib/kvmatch.h");
}
rust/ch15/build.rs · region build
# The build script needs a C compiler driver; cc finds the system one.
[build-dependencies]
cc = "1"

# Besides the Rust library, produce a static library a C program can link: libkv.a.
[lib]
crate-type = ["lib", "staticlib"]
rust/ch15/Cargo.toml · region ffi
$ cargo test -q cmatch
running 4 tests
....
test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed

A crossing from Rust to C costs what a C to C call costs. Rust threads use the system stack, and the Rust ABI differs from the C one only in what the compiler is free to choose. So the compiler emits a plain call. The benchmark that the Go section needed does not have a result to show here, because there is no difference to measure.

⚠️miri stops at the border Rust

cargo miri test cannot run a test that calls into C. The tool interprets Rust and knows nothing about the compiled C code, so it reports an unsupported foreign function and stops. It can still check the Rust side of the border. The test for the exported function below passes under miri, because the raw pointers it builds slices from come from Rust. Test the C side with the C tools from chapter 12 and the Rust side with miri. No tool sees both at once.

📰actix-web, 2020

In January 2020 the most used Rust web framework was taken down by its author for a weekend, over the word unsafe. Sergey Davidoff had published an analysis of the framework's internals. He found code that "violates memory safety" by giving out "multiple mutable references to the same data". He wrote that the maintainers "have refused to investigate it". The discussion that followed on Reddit was large and unkind. The maintainer, Nikolay Kim, wrote "I am done with open source" and threatened to "make [Actix] repos private and then delete them". He restored them within days, writing that "a lot of people depend on actix". He passed the project to a new leader, under whom it continues. The Register noted at the time that "there is extensive use of unsafe code in Actix, leading to debate about what should be fixed". The lesson is not about one maintainer. A Rust project is safe exactly to the extent of its unsafe blocks, and the word draws reviewers the way an open port draws scanners. Every such block in kv has a SAFETY comment that states the argument, which is the habit the dispute was about.

The other way: C calls Rust#

Rust can also be the library. A function marked extern "C" uses the C convention, and #[unsafe(no_mangle)] keeps its name as written, so that a C linker can find it. The function below is the chapter 6 matcher behind a C signature:

/// The other direction: a Rust function with a C name and a C signature, for a C program
/// to call. It is the Rust matcher from chapter 6. `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]` keeps the name
/// as written, and `extern "C"` uses the C calling convention.
///
/// # Safety
/// `pat` must point to `plen` readable bytes and `key` to `klen`, as a C caller would
/// promise in a comment. Rust cannot check it, and a wrong length here is the same bug
/// it would be in C.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn kv_rust_glob(
    pat: *const u8,
    plen: usize,
    key: *const u8,
    klen: usize,
) -> c_int {
    if pat.is_null() || key.is_null() {
        return 0;
    }
    // SAFETY: the contract above, which the caller accepted by calling an unsafe function.
    let (pat, key) = unsafe {
        (
            std::slice::from_raw_parts(pat, plen),
            std::slice::from_raw_parts(key, klen),
        )
    };
    c_int::from(crate::store::glob(pat, key))
}
rust/ch15/src/cmatch.rs · region export

It is marked unsafe because calling it is unsafe. The caller promises the lengths, and nothing checks the promise. That is the contract every C function has always had, now written in the signature instead of in a comment. With crate-type = ["lib", "staticlib"] in Cargo.toml, cargo also produces libkv.a, and a C program links it like any archive:

/* The declaration a header would hold. Rust exported this name with #[unsafe(no_mangle)]. */
int kv_rust_glob(const char *pat, size_t plen, const char *key, size_t klen);

int main(void) {
    const char *pat = "user:*";
    const char *key = "user:1";
    int ok = kv_rust_glob(pat, strlen(pat), key, strlen(key));
    printf("kv_rust_glob(\"%s\", \"%s\") = %d\n", pat, key, ok);
    return ok ? 0 : 1;
}
c/ch15/from_rust/main.c · region call
# A C program calling Rust: build the Rust crate as a static library, then link it like
# any other. The flags after -lkv are what the Rust standard library needs from the
# system on each platform.
RUST := ../../rust/ch15
from-rust: build/from_rust
	./build/from_rust

build/from_rust: from_rust/main.c | build
	cargo build --release -q --manifest-path $(RUST)/Cargo.toml
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ from_rust/main.c -L$(RUST)/target/release -lkv $(RUST_LIBS)

# What the Rust standard library needs from the system. On Linux, set RUST_LIBS to the
# list that `cargo rustc --release -- --print native-static-libs` prints.
ifeq ($(shell uname),Darwin)
RUST_LIBS ?= -framework CoreFoundation
endif
c/ch15/Makefile · region from-rust
$ make from-rust
cargo build --release -q --manifest-path ../../rust/ch15/Cargo.toml
cc ... -o build/from_rust from_rust/main.c -L../../rust/ch15/target/release -lkv -framework CoreFoundation
./build/from_rust
kv_rust_glob("user:*", "user:1") = 1
$ ls -l ../../rust/ch15/target/release/libkv.a build/from_rust
-rw-r--r--  19629264 libkv.a
-rwxr-xr-x   1498400 build/from_rust

The archive is nineteen megabytes because it holds the whole crate, tokio included. The C program is 1.5 megabytes, because the linker kept only what one matcher needs. That is still the Rust runtime and its allocator. The -framework CoreFoundation at the end is what the Rust standard library asks of macOS. On Linux the list is different and longer, and cargo rustc --release -- --print native-static-libs prints it. The Rust side knows nothing of this. The C side, as always, must.

Go can be called from C as well, with a //export comment and -buildmode=c-archive. But the archive carries the Go runtime, which starts its scheduler and collector inside the host program. It is done, and it is rarely a comfortable fit. The Rust case has no runtime to start. That is why Rust libraries are the ones you find inside C programs, Python packages and browsers, and now inside the kernel.

What a crossing costs#

The cost of the borderCGoRust
Per callnothingabout 50 nanoseconds and a stack switchnothing
Memory rulesyours, as everpin for the call, copy to keepthe borrow checker stops at the border
A structlaid out by the ABIlaid out by the ABI, fields under their C nameslaid out by the ABI, with repr(C)
A uniona tag you must honourbytes you must converta field read that needs unsafe
What the compiler checksthe header, against the bodythe preamble, against the Go sidethe extern block, against the Rust side
What nothing checksthe header, against the callerthe preamble, against the Cthe extern block, against the C
Tools that crossthe sanitizersthe race detector does notmiri does not
The buildmakea C compiler, per targeta C compiler, per target, for the C part

The row that matters most is the one that nothing checks. In all three languages the declaration is a promise. The chapter 6 tests, run on both sides of the border, are the only thing that keeps it. That is the C way of working, and at the border, every language works the C way.

Verdict##

TopicCGoRustWhy
Calling CStrongOKStrongGo pays a stack switch per call and loses static builds. C and Rust pay nothing per call.
Being called from CStrongWeakStrongA Go archive carries a runtime that must start. A Rust archive is a plain library.
Safety at the borderWeakOKOKC checks nothing anywhere. Go and Rust check their own side and trust the declaration.
A struct on the borderStrongOKStrongC owns the rule. Go follows it under C names, and Rust follows it with repr(C) and can assert the numbers.
A union on the borderOKWeakOKC reads the field the tag names. Go converts the bytes itself, and Rust names the field and marks the read unsafe.
Making the rules visibleWeakOKStrongC has comments and Go has a documented pointer rule. Rust puts unsafe in the signature.
Build cost of C codeStrongWeakOKGo needs cgo on for every target. Rust needs the cc crate and a compiler for the C part only.
Carry forward
  • The border is a C function. A name, a pointer, a length and an int, laid out by the ABI. The declaration on each side is a promise that no compiler checks.
  • Layout is the interface. A struct's offsets, padding and size are fixed by the ABI. C, Go and Rust compute the same sixteen bytes, and repr(C) is how Rust promises to.
  • Five powers. An unsafe block adds raw pointer reads, unsafe calls, mutable statics, unsafe traits and union fields, and nothing else. The SAFETY comment is the argument that they were used correctly.
Next

Fifteen chapters, one server three times over, and a scorecard with more rows than any one language wins. Chapter 16 adds them up, and says which language to pick for what.

The verdict#

The verdict · Chapter 16· 18 min read

Thirteen chapters each ended with a small scorecard. This chapter gathers every row into one table, reads what the pattern says about each language, and turns it into advice. When to choose C, when Go, when Rust, and when the right answer is a language this book did not cover.

One warning before the table. The rows score one project, a key-value server, built by one person who had to learn each language's way as they went. A different project moves rows. A device with sixty-four kilobytes of memory has no row for a garbage collector, because it cannot afford one. A web service has no row for binary size, because it does not care. Read the table as evidence about this kind of program, not as a ranking of languages.

The scorecard#

TopicCGoRustWhy
02  Toolchains and hello, three times
InstallingOKStrongStrongA C compiler is one system command away on macOS and Linux. Go and Rust are one download each, on every platform.
BuildingWeakStrongStrongC has no build tool, only a convention. Go and Rust each have one tool that every project uses.
Seeing what you madeStrongOKOKC shows every step from preprocessor to linker. Go and Rust hide the steps, which is usually what you want.
Binary sizeStrongWeakOK8 KB for C, 2.5 MB for Go because the runtime is inside, 415 KB for Rust.
Running elsewhereWeakStrongOKThe C binary needs the right C library on the target, the Go binary needs nothing, and Rust is in between.
03  Echo server
Opening a portWeakStrongStrongC needs four calls, a struct and an option. Go and Rust need one call that sets the option for you.
Closing it againWeakOKStrongC needs a cleanup label and Go needs a defer you must write, but Rust closes at the end of scope by itself.
The echo loopWeakStrongStrongC needs the short-write loop and the EINTR retry. Both standard libraries contain them.
A lost errorWeakWeakOKC and Go let a return value drop. Rust warns, and with the book's flags refuses.
Seeing what happensStrongOKOKThe C version shows every system call. The other two hide them, which is what you want on most days.
WindowsWeakStrongStrongThe C code needs Winsock changes. Go and Rust build unchanged.
What you must learn firstStrongOKWeakC is the calls themselves. Rust asks for Result, ?, ownership and try_clone before an echo works.
04  Speaking RESP
Reading bytesWeakStrongStrongC has stdio, which blocks, so kv grows its own buffer. Both standard libraries have one.
Holding the argumentsStrongOKOKThe C parser copies nothing. Go and Rust copy each argument once, which is simpler and almost never matters.
Saying "not RESP"OKOKStrongC and Go use a value by convention. Rust uses a kind the compiler knows about and a match the compiler checks.
Saying "the client left"OKWeakStrongGo reuses an error value for a non-error. Rust has Option for exactly this.
Passing an error upWeakWeakStrongC and Go repeat the check at every call. Rust writes one character.
Binary valuesStrongStrongOKC and Go treat all bytes alike. Rust makes you choose between String and Vec<u8>, and the wrong choice rejects real data.
An error with detailsWeakOKStrongC has an enum and a fixed buffer, and Go has a type found by searching a chain. Rust has an enum variant the compiler matches.
05  GET and SET
A key is bytesOKStrongOKC carries a length beside every pointer, Go has []byte and string, and Rust makes you pick Vec<u8> because String rejects binary data.
Copying and owningWeakStrongStrongC copies and comments, Go lets the collector own everything, and Rust moves and checks.
Parsing a numberWeakOKOKC needs a careful parser to avoid undefined behaviour. The other two accept forms Redis rejects.
OverflowWeakOKStrongC must check before it adds and Go checks against a constant, while Rust has checked_add built in.
A missing caseWeakWeakStrongAn enum match in Rust must be complete. In C and Go, a new error kind can be forgotten at a call site.
Reading the codeOKStrongOKThe Go store is the shortest. The Rust signatures say more and take longer to read.
A table of commandsOKStrongOKC needs an X-macro and a function pointer type, and Go has a map of funcs. Rust needs dyn Write and a macro for the rows.
Text against bytesWeakOKStrongC has no text type at all, and Go has rune helpers. Rust makes a str keep its promise and a Vec<u8> make none.
06  Your own hash table
Writing the tableWeakStrongOKC needs an owner comment on every pointer and three cleanup paths, Go is the shortest, and Rust argues about borrows in set.
Freeing memoryWeakStrongStrongC must free in three places that agree. Go and Rust free for you, in different ways.
Freeing on timeStrongWeakStrongC and Rust free on the line that removes an entry. Go frees at the next collection.
Testing itWeakStrongStrongC has no test runner in the box. go test and cargo test are built in.
Shipping unused codeWeakOKStrongC warns only for static functions and Go ignores unused functions, while Rust reports each one.
Needing to write oneStrongWeakWeakIn C the table is the store. In Go and Rust it is an exercise, because the map is built in.
Writing it once for any typeWeakOKStrongC has void pointers, macros and _Generic, each with a hole. Go has type parameters since 2022, and Rust has bounds the compiler checks at the impl.
Seeing where a value livesStrongOKStrongC says it in every line, and Rust says it in the types. Go decides for you and shows its decision with a flag.
07  Modules, packages and dependencies
Splitting codeWeakStrongOKC needs guards, prefixes and a Makefile that tracks headers, while Go needs a folder and Rust a mod line that is easy to forget.
Hiding a nameOKStrongStrongC has static, for functions only. Go and Rust hide by default or by a letter.
Adding a dependencyWeakOKStrongC has three competing ways and no default, while Go and Rust each have one command, and Rust also has one registry.
Having too manyStrongStrongWeakC and Go programs stay small by cost and by a wide standard library. Rust programs grow dozens of crates.
Keeping one styleOKStrongStrongclang-format needs a config everyone agrees on. gofmt and rustfmt need nothing.
Finding mistakesWeakOKStrongclang-tidy must be installed. go vet is built in. clippy is built in and has 800 checks.
Swapping an implementationOKStrongStrongC has a struct of function pointers that nobody checks. Go has implicit interfaces, and Rust has checked traits with two kinds of dispatch.
Hiding a structStrongStrongStrongC has the opaque type, and Go and Rust have unexported fields. All three keep the map out of reach.
08  Data types
A value of several kindsWeakOKStrongC has a tag nothing checks, and Go has a type switch nothing checks. Rust has a match the compiler checks.
Adding a kind laterOKWeakStrongC warns at each switch with no default, and Go falls to default in silence. Rust refuses to build until every match knows.
A list, a hash, a setWeakStrongStrongC writes each, or nests the table. Go and Rust have them in the standard library.
Walking a collectionWeakOKStrongC needs a callback and a context struct, and Go has range over a function. Rust has adaptors that compose.
Scanning by cursorStrongOKOKC and the hand-written table scan buckets. The Go map sorts, and the Rust map counts from the start.
Reading the codeWeakStrongOKThirteen C commands need a helper each, and Go reads like prose. Rust reads well once match and let else are familiar.
09  Many clients
Serving many clientsWeakStrongOKC needs 200 lines of event loop and three pollers, Go one keyword, and Rust an Arc, a Mutex and a clone per thread.
Using every coreWeakStrongStrongThe C loop is one thread by design. Go and Rust spread clients over every core.
A forgotten lockn/aWeakStrongGo compiles it and the detector may catch it. Rust refuses to compile it.
Platform codeOKStrongStrongC needs a file per poller under ifdef. Go and Rust need one guarded function, and their runtimes hide the pollers.
Memory for a clientStrongStrongOKC sizes two buffers and a goroutine is a few kilobytes, while a Rust thread is 2 MiB until tokio fixes that at the cost of a dependency.
Reading the codeWeakStrongOKThe C loop is subtle and the Go version is the chapter 7 code, while the tokio version is a second copy of the parser.
WindowsWeakStrongStrongThe C loop reports readiness and Windows reports completion. Both runtimes hide that.
10  Expiry
A deadlineOKStrongStrongC uses zero to mean none, which the comments must say. Go's zero Time and Rust's Option say it in the type.
The clockOKStrongStrongC picks the clock by name, while Go carries both in one value and Rust gives each a type.
Lazy expiryStrongOKOKC deletes on find. Go and Rust must leave it to the sweep because of the read lock or the borrow.
The sweepStrongStrongWeakC has a cursor and Go a random sample. Rust's retain walks the whole map.
A client that hangs upWeakStrongStrongC dies unless one line ignores SIGPIPE. Both runtimes turn it into an error.
Stopping cleanlyOKStrongOKC needs a handler, a pipe and a rule about what a handler may do. Go needs a context, and Rust the C library or tokio.
A bug in one commandWeakStrongOKC corrupts or crashes, and Go recovers per connection. Rust panics per thread, and the scope reports it.
The parser's argumentsOKOKStrongC borrows by comment, Go copies and caps the capacity, Rust borrows by lifetime and the compiler checks it.
Testing timeWeakStrongStrongGo and Rust tests pass a clock in. The C store has no test runner yet.
11  Persistence
Writing the fileOKStrongStrongC encodes into a buffer and calls write. Go and Rust reuse the protocol writers and flush.
ReplayStrongStrongStrongAll three reuse the parser from chapter 4 unchanged, which is the point of a log in RESP.
A crash of the processStrongOKOKC writes straight through. Go and Rust needed a flush the book's test had to find.
The clock on diskOKStrongOKC converts between two clocks itself, while Go's time.Time holds both and Rust converts with a helper.
Log and store togetherStrongOKStrongOne C thread needs no lock, Go takes two locks, and Rust takes one around both.
The fsync threadWeakStrongStrongC needs a mutex, a condition variable, an atomic and a sanitizer. Go needs a channel, and Rust a channel the compiler checks.
Reaching the disk on macOSOKStrongStrongC must know about F_FULLFSYNC itself. Both standard libraries know.
12  Testing and fuzzing
A test runnerWeakStrongStrongC has none, so you write one. Go and Rust have one in the box, with no setup.
Where a test may liveWeakOKStrongC has the file you write, and Go the package and an Example. Rust has the module, the docs and a directory for outsiders.
FuzzingOKStrongOKlibFuzzer is one flag on Linux and a container on a Mac, Go has it built in, and Rust needs nightly and a second crate.
Memory errorsOKStrongStrongC finds them at run time with ASan or Valgrind. Go and Rust cannot write them in safe code.
Data racesOKOKStrongC and Go find the races a test provokes, with a sanitizer or the detector. Rust refuses them at compile time.
Undefined behaviourWeakStrongOKC has it everywhere and UBSan finds some. Go has almost none, a data race being the exception, and Rust confines it to unsafe, where Miri checks it.
Speed of the toolsStrongStrongWeakASan costs two times and the race detector two to twenty, while Miri costs nine thousand.
13  Benchmarking and profiling
A micro-benchmarkOKStrongOKC has a clock and a loop, and Go has go test -bench with allocation counts. Rust needs an example binary or a crate.
Seeing what the compiler didOKStrongOKGo prints its decisions for every line. C and Rust measure each flag, profile and attribute yourself.
A profiler in the boxOKStrongOKC and Rust use the operating system's profiler. Go carries its own, and it works the same everywhere.
Reading the profileStrongOKWeakOne C thread gives an honest list and Go needs the cum column, while the fifty Rust threads drown the list in waiting.
The cost of memoryStrongOKStrongC and Rust allocate what the code says. Go allocates what escapes, and a flag has to tell you which.
A fast serverStrongStrongOKC and Go reach 800,000 with pipelining. Rust needs a read lock to match on reads and stays behind on writes.
Why it was slowOKStrongWeakThe Go runtime hides lock handoff from the kernel. Rust's standard mutex is the platform's, and macOS makes it expensive.
Honest numbersStrongStrongStrongredis-benchmark and the same command shape treat all three alike.

Cross-compilingOKStrongOKC needs zig and gets a small static binary. Go needs two variables, and Rust needs a target, a linker and zig.
Static linkingOKStrongOKC and Rust choose musl. Go links nothing by default.
Binary sizeStrongWeakOK45 KB, 2.5 MB and 521 KB for the same server.
Options and configOKStrongOKC has getopt and nothing for a file, and Go has flag, json and slog in the box. Rust has the arguments and a crate for the rest.
WindowsWeakStrongStrongThe C code is Unix-only. Go and Rust build for Windows unchanged.
Knowing the platformWeakStrongOKC sees every difference and Go hides all of them. Rust hides most and leaks one through the mutex.
A releaseWeakStrongStrongC has no mechanism. Go and Rust read a tag or a version field and install from a path.
15  Talking to C
Calling CStrongOKStrongGo pays a stack switch per call and loses static builds. C and Rust pay nothing per call.
Being called from CStrongWeakStrongA Go archive carries a runtime that must start. A Rust archive is a plain library.
Safety at the borderWeakOKOKC checks nothing anywhere. Go and Rust check their own side and trust the declaration.
A struct on the borderStrongOKStrongC owns the rule. Go follows it under C names, and Rust follows it with repr(C) and can assert the numbers.
A union on the borderOKWeakOKC reads the field the tag names. Go converts the bytes itself, and Rust names the field and marks the read unsafe.
Making the rules visibleWeakOKStrongC has comments and Go has a documented pointer rule. Rust puts unsafe in the signature.
Build cost of C codeStrongWeakOKGo needs cgo on for every target. Rust needs the cc crate and a compiler for the C part only.

One hundred and one rows. C was strong in 28, ok in 29 and weak in 43. Go was strong in 58, ok in 30 and weak in 13. Rust was strong in 57, ok in 37 and weak in 7. One row for C had no mark, because a forgotten lock cannot happen on one thread. The thorough edition added rows for abstraction, generics, sum types and iteration in chapters 7 and 8. It added rows for signals, background work, platform code and the structs on the border in the chapters after. Those sums are less interesting than where the marks fall, because each language's weak rows belong to one or two families.

C: the price of seeing everything#

Almost every weak row for C is the same row. Memory that must be freed by the right code at the right time. An error that must be checked by the next line or is lost. A platform difference that the program must know about, because nothing stands between it and the operating system. A value of several kinds that is a tag and a union the compiler never checks against each other. A lock, a condition variable and an atomic that a comment, not a type, says how to use. Those are not five weaknesses. They are one property, that C hides nothing, seen from five sides.

The same property fills C's strong rows. The binary was forty-five kilobytes. The profile read like the source, because the source is what ran. The sanitizers found the use-after-free in chapter 12 in a second, because they watch the real memory operations. And at the border in chapter 15, C was not a language calling another. It was the border. Every other language's door is shaped like a C function, and that will not change in your career.

Choose C when the program must be small, or must run where no runtime fits. Choose it when the program is itself the thing other languages will call, or when the platform is the subject. An operating system, a C library, a device driver, a codec, an interpreter that other languages embed. Choose it knowing that the compiler checks types and nothing else. The chapter 12 tools are not optional in C. They are the part of the compiler that was left out.

Go: the server language#

Go's strong rows cluster around the task this book set. A server that talks to many clients, in one word, go, with a runtime that schedules them across every core. A test runner, a fuzzer, a race detector and a profiler in the box, with no decision to make about any of them. A channel that is both the message and the lock, which made the fsync thread of chapter 11 the shortest of its three versions. One command to build for any machine, and a binary that needs nothing. The chapter 9 server was the shortest of the four. It was also the one that used every core without a line of code written for the purpose.

Go's weak rows are the cost of the runtime and the cost of simplicity. The binary is 2.5 megabytes before the program starts. Calling C costs a stack switch and the one-file freedom. The language has no way to say that a function can fail except a second return value. Chapter 3 showed what happens when the caller ignores it. The forgotten lock in chapter 9 compiled and ran, and only the race detector, run on purpose, said anything. A value of several kinds is an interface and a type switch, and the compiler does not say when a case is missing. The parser allocated nine times a request until a flag said where. What lives on the heap is the compiler's decision and not the programmer's. Go trusts the programmer to check every error and every lock. It gives better tools than C for finding the ones they missed, and no more protection at compile time.

Choose Go when the program is a network service, a command-line tool, or anything a team must read, build and deploy with the least effort. Choose it when the people who will maintain it are many, or new, or both. Go has one way to do most things, and the formatter enforces it. Do not choose it for a library that C or Python will embed, or for a device with a megabyte of flash. Do not choose it when correctness depends on the compiler catching a race.

Rust: the compiler as the reviewer#

Rust is strong in the rows that were weak for C. The hash table freed itself. The lost error could not be lost, because a Result that is dropped is a warning and a ? is a line. The forgotten lock did not compile. The data race did not compile. The value of several kinds was an enum, and a match that forgot a kind did not compile either. The parser that borrowed its arguments from the buffer could not outlive it, because a lifetime said so. At the border in chapter 15, the unsafe block was a labelled boundary with a written argument, not a mood. Rust is what C would be if the compiler checked the comments.

Rust's weak rows are the cost of that checking, and one surprise. The compiler is slower. A clean release build of chapter 15 took 19 seconds in Rust, 8 in Go and 1 in C. The chapter 12 tools took the longest to run. The chapter 13 profile was the hardest to read, because the sampler counted fifty sleeping threads and buried the one line that mattered. The mutex in chapter 13 was a different object on macOS and on Linux, and the standard library did not say so. And in chapter 6, writing a hash table was harder than in Go, and harder than the rest of Rust had been. A structure that owns its entries and lends references to them is exactly what the borrow checker was built to question. That one is a real cost. Rust is at its most awkward when writing the data structures it is best at using.

Choose Rust when the program must be fast and must be correct. Choose it when the people who will run it are not the people who wrote it. A database engine, a proxy, a parser for untrusted input, a command-line tool that must never crash. A library that will be embedded in C, in Python or in a browser. Choose it knowing that the first month is spent arguing with the compiler, and that the argument is the point. Do not choose it for a program that will be rewritten next quarter, or for a team that has no time to learn it. A half-learned Rust is slower to write than Go, and a program full of unwrap() crashes when Go would have returned an error.

When the answer is none of them#

This book chose a server so that all three languages would be in their element. Many programs are not servers. A script that runs once, a report, a prototype that exists to be thrown away. A program whose whole cost is the time of the person writing it. For those, a language with a garbage collector, a large library and no build step is the right choice. That it runs many times slower than C does not appear in any row that matters. Python, JavaScript, Ruby and their relatives exist for this, and a systems programmer who refuses them is choosing the wrong tool out of pride.

The honest version of the question is not "which language is best". It is "what does this program need to be true, and which compiler will check it". C checks the types. Go checks the types and watches the running program. Rust checks the types, the lifetimes and the sharing. Each check has a price in time and in freedom, and the right language is the one whose price buys a guarantee the program needs.

What this book did not do#

A list, so that the scorecard is read with it. No chapter ran a Windows binary, so every Windows row rests on documentation and a file command. The Rust chapters used tokio and did not compare it with another runtime. The C server ran kqueue and epoll but never completion ports, because the book has no Windows machine. ThreadSanitizer ran the C tests on Linux only, because on macOS it defers a signal handler for ever. The garbage collector was measured by its count of collections and its memory, not by its pauses, because kv never allocated enough to show one. No chapter sharded the Rust store, so its write number in chapter 13 stayed where the mutex left it. And the three appendices teach the long tail of each language in two sentences each, which is a reminder and not a lesson. Each of those would change a row or add one.

Where to go from here#

kv is small enough to understand and large enough to extend. The next features, in rough order of difficulty, are more data types, replication to a second server, and a cluster that shares keys by hash. Each is a chapter this book did not write. Each is a chance to learn whether the scorecard above survives contact with a harder problem. Pick the language whose weak rows worried you least and build the feature. Then build it again in the language whose weak rows worried you most. The second build is where the learning is.

Next

If you chose Rust, Part V goes further. It starts by counting the allocations of one HGETALL on the chapter 15 server. There are two thousand and two of them, and every one is a copy of bytes the store already holds.
