Ownership from the machine up#

Rust from first principles · Chapter 17· 18 min read· 97 lines of code
▶Scene

Copy examples/allocs.rs from code/rust/ch17 into your chapter 15 crate. It fills a hash with a thousand fields of a hundred bytes each. Then it runs one HGETALL and counts the calls to the allocator, with the counting allocator of chapter 13:

$ cd code/rust/ch15
$ cp ../ch17/examples/allocs.rs examples/
$ cargo run -q --release --example allocs
HGETALL of 1000 fields: 125007 bytes of reply, 2002 allocations, 174007 bytes allocated

The reply is 125 kilobytes. To send it, the server asked the allocator for 174 kilobytes, in two thousand and two pieces. Every one of those pieces was a copy of bytes the store already held.

Part V is for readers who chose Rust. In each chapter you build one mechanism of the language yourself, inside kv. You check it, and then you meet the library version. This chapter removes the two thousand copies. On the way it shows what a move is in memory, why a borrow cannot outlive a lock, and what variance and for<'a> mean.

Chapters 5 to 15 used ownership as a set of rules that the compiler enforces. You moved a value, borrowed it, or cloned it when the compiler refused. That is enough to build a server. It is not enough to read the source of a library such as tokio, where every type is designed around these rules. This chapter goes one level down, to the bytes, and builds the rules up again from there.

The scene is the reason to go down. A command in kv returns a Reply, and the server writes it after the lock is released. A reply has to survive the release, so it owns its bytes. Each bulk string in it is a Vec<u8>, copied out of the store. One HGETALL of a thousand fields makes two thousand vectors, and one more for the array that holds them.

A move copies three words#

Start with the cheapest thing in the scene, the move of a reply from the command to the writer. What does a move cost? A Vec<u8> is three machine words. They are a pointer to the heap, a capacity and a length. Moving the vector copies those three words. The heap block does not move, and nothing is allocated:

let v: Vec<u8> = vec![b'x'; 1000];
let heap = v.as_ptr();
assert_eq!(std::mem::size_of_val(&v), 3 * std::mem::size_of::<usize>());
let w = v; // 24 bytes copied, 1000 bytes untouched
assert_eq!(w.as_ptr(), heap);

After the copy, two places hold the same pointer. If both were usable, both would free the block, which is the double free of chapter 6. So the compiler forgets the source. Any use of v after the move is error E0382, "borrow of moved value". That is the whole of a move. It is a copy of the bytes of the value, and a rule that the old name is dead.

A Copy type is one whose bytes are the whole value. The standard library says that copying such a value "is always a simple bit-wise copy". An integer, a bool and a shared reference are Copy. The source stays usable, because there is nothing for two owners to free twice. A type that owns a heap block cannot be Copy. The documentation says that a type that implements Drop "is managing some resource besides its own size_of::<T> bytes".

Clone is the other kind of duplicate. It runs code that you or a derive wrote, and for a vector that code allocates a new block and copies every byte into it. That is the line the scene crossed two thousand times. The reply held a Vec, the store held a Vec, and the only way to get one from the other was a clone.

⚠️A derive cannot make an owner Copy Rust

#[derive(Clone, Copy)] on a struct with a Vec field is error E0204. The derive checks that every field is Copy, and a vector is not. The fix is never to force it. A value that owns memory has one owner, and a second copy of its bytes would be a second owner.

A reply that borrows, by hand#

The copies exist because the reply owns its bytes. A reply that borrows them would need none. The store already holds the field names and values. The request buffer already holds the argument of ECHO. A reply could point at those bytes and send them where they lie.

A borrowed slice is a &'a [u8], and the reply needs a lifetime to say how long it borrows. Some replies still make new bytes, such as the cursor that SCAN returns as text. So a bulk string must be borrowed sometimes and owned sometimes. The standard library has a type for exactly that. Cow is "a clone-on-write smart pointer" that "can enclose and provide immutable access to borrowed data".

Exercise 17.1RustA reply with a lifetime

Give Reply a lifetime parameter 'a. Change Bulk to hold a Cow<'a, [u8]>, and the array to hold Reply<'a> items. write_reply takes any reply, so its lifetime can be '_. The function that builds an array of bulk strings borrows each slice with Cow::Borrowed and copies nothing.

pub enum Reply<'a> {
    Simple(&'static str),
    Error(String),
    Bulk(/* your type here */),
    Int(i64),
    Nil,
    Array(/* your type here */),
}

fn bulks<'a>(items: impl Iterator<Item = &'a [u8]>) -> Reply<'a> {
    // your code here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/// A reply as a value. A bulk string borrows the bytes it sends, from the store or from
/// the request, for as long as `'a`, so a read reply copies nothing until it is
/// formatted. `Cow` is "borrowed or owned": a reply made of new bytes, such as a SCAN
/// cursor, owns them, and the type is the same either way.
pub enum Reply<'a> {
    Simple(&'static str),
    Error(String),
    Bulk(Cow<'a, [u8]>),
    Int(i64),
    Nil,
    Array(Vec<Reply<'a>>),
}

pub fn write_reply(w: &mut (impl Write + ?Sized), reply: &Reply<'_>) -> io::Result<()> {
    match reply {
        Reply::Simple(s) => write_simple(w, s),
        Reply::Error(s) => write_error(w, s),
        Reply::Bulk(b) => write_bulk(w, b),
        Reply::Int(n) => write_int(w, *n),
        Reply::Nil => write_nil(w),
        Reply::Array(items) => {
            write_array_len(w, items.len())?;
            items.iter().try_for_each(|item| write_reply(w, item))
        }
    }
}
rust/ch17/src/resp.rs · region reply

Now every command that reads the store can lend its bytes. GET becomes Reply::Bulk(Cow::Borrowed(val)) where it was Reply::Bulk(val.to_vec()). The cursor of SCAN is the one reply that uses Cow::Owned, because those bytes did not exist before the command.

Then build the server, and read the first error with care. It is the chapter in one message:

error[E0597]: `db` does not live long enough
   --> src/main.rs:100:25
    |
 98 |                     let reply = {
    |                         ----- borrow later stored here
 99 |                         let db = db.read().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
    |                             -- binding `db` declared here
100 |                         db.execute_read(&args)
    |                         ^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
101 |                     };
    |                     - `db` dropped here while still borrowed

Why the reply cannot outlive the lock#

The name db on line 99 is not the store. It is the guard that read() returns. A guard is a value whose Drop releases the lock. The store is reachable only through the guard, so a borrow of the store is a borrow of the guard. The block ends on line 101, the guard is dropped there, and the lock is released. The reply would then point into a store that another thread may now change.

When is a value dropped? The Reference answers it in two rules. Variables "are dropped in reverse order of declaration". The fields of a struct "are dropped in declaration order". A lock guard follows the first rule, so the guard dies at the end of its block. The old code moved an owned reply out of the block, so nothing borrowed the guard. The new reply borrows, so it must be used up before the block ends.

So the server formats the reply into bytes inside the block. It writes into a Vec<u8> named out, which is memory and not the socket. Formatting copies each byte once, into out. The write to the socket comes after the guard is gone, so the lock is still never held during network input and output:

Exercise 17.2RustFormat under the lock, write after it

In serve, keep a buffer out next to the request buffer. Inside the block that holds the read guard, call execute_read. If it gives a reply, format it into out before the block ends. If it gives None, take the write lock and do the same with execute. After both blocks, write out to the client and clear it.

let done = {
    let db = db.read().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
    // your code here: format the reply into `out`, while `db` is alive
};
if !done {
    // your code here: the same, under the write lock
}
writer.write_all(&out)?;
out.clear();
Stuck?Show the full listing
// The reply borrows from the store, so it cannot outlive the lock
// guard. It is formatted into `out`, a buffer in memory, while the
// lock is held. The write to the socket, the slow part, comes after
// the guard is dropped. A read takes the shared lock, which many
// threads hold at once; a write takes the exclusive one.
let done = {
    let db = db.read().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
    match db.execute_read(&args) {
        Some(reply) => {
            resp::write_reply(&mut out, &reply)?;
            true
        }
        None => false,
    }
};
if !done {
    let mut db = db.write().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
    let reply = db.execute(&args)?;
    resp::write_reply(&mut out, &reply)?;
}
writer.write_all(&out)?;
out.clear();
rust/ch17/src/main.rs · region format-under-lock
✅Formatting under the lock has a price Rust

The lock is now held while the reply is formatted. Before this chapter, the lock covered only the store operation. Now it also covers the copy of each byte into out. For a reply of a few hundred bytes that is less work than the two thousand allocations it replaces. For a reply of many megabytes, a writer waits for the whole copy. A server with huge values copies each one once into a shared buffer with a count of owners, as the bytes crate does. Another way is to split the reply into pieces. kv keeps the simple version and the measurement that justifies it.

The order of drops is visible in a small test. Two locals and a struct with two fields each push their name into a log when they are dropped. The struct goes first, because it was declared last. Inside it, the fields go in the order they were written:

let log = RefCell::new(Vec::new());
{
    let _a = Loud("local a", &log);
    let _b = Loud("local b", &log);
    let _p = Pair { first: Loud("field first", &log), second: Loud("field second", &log) };
}
assert_eq!(*log.borrow(), ["field first", "field second", "local b", "local a"]);

Shared or mutable is a promise about memory#

The read guard lends the store to many threads at once, through shared references. The write guard lends it to one thread, through a mutable reference. That is the rule from chapter 5, any number of readers or one writer. Down at the bytes, it is a promise that the compiler and the optimiser rely on.

The Reference states the promise for a mutable reference. A &mut T "must point to memory that is not read or written by any pointer not derived from the reference". No other reference may point there either. So while a &mut is live, nothing else can see the memory change. The compiler may keep a value in a register, or reorder two writes, because no other code can observe the difference.

A shared reference makes the mirror promise. The memory behind a &T does not change while the reference is live. That is why the read replies can borrow from the store at all. Each borrowed slice is valid for as long as the read guard lives, and no writer can run while it does.

The Reference words the shared promise with one exception. The memory behind a &T "is not mutated while they are live (except for data inside an UnsafeCell<U>)". That exception is how a lock works. Both read() and write() take a shared reference to the lock. Yet the guard of write() gives a mutable reference to the store. Inside the RwLock the store sits in an UnsafeCell, and the lock's own code proves that only one writer gets through. Every type that changes behind a shared reference, from Cell to Mutex, is built on that one cell. Chapter 20 builds a type on it yourself.

One lifetime for two borrows#

Look at the signature that execute_read now has:

/// Everything a command may touch. One Mutex around this struct means a command and its
/// record in the log happen together, with no other command in between.
pub struct Db {
    pub store: MapStore,
    pub aof: Option<Aof>,
}

impl Db {
    /// A read-only command, run under a shared lock. `None` means it writes, and the
    /// caller must take the exclusive lock and call `execute`. The reply borrows from
    /// the store and from the request, so `'a` is the shorter of the two: a `Command`
    /// of a longer-lived buffer is accepted as a `Command<'a>`, because a borrow may
    /// always be treated as shorter than it is.
    pub fn execute_read<'a>(&'a self, args: &Command<'a>) -> Option<Reply<'a>> {
        crate::cmd::execute_read(args, &self.store)
    }

    /// Record a write command, then run it, and return the reply for the caller to
    /// format before it releases the lock. Recording comes first, so that a command the
    /// file holds is one that was accepted.
    pub fn execute<'a>(&'a mut self, args: &Command<'a>) -> io::Result<Reply<'a>> {
        if let Some(log) = self.aof.as_mut()
            && args.first().is_some_and(|name| aof::is_write(name))
        {
            log.record(args, aof::wall_ms())?;
        }
        Ok(crate::cmd::execute(args, &mut self.store))
    }
}
rust/ch17/src/db.rs · region db

One name, 'a, appears three times. The store lives as long as the guard. The request lives as long as the read buffer. Those are two different regions of the program. How can one name cover both?

The answer is that a shared borrow can always be treated as shorter than it is. A &'long [u8] works anywhere a &'short [u8] is asked for, because a reference that is valid for longer is valid for less. The compiler picks 'a as the region where both borrows are valid, and shortens each one to fit. The name for this is variance. The Reference lists &'a T as "covariant" in 'a. A longer lifetime is a subtype of a shorter one, and a reference follows its lifetime in the same direction.

A mutable reference is different, and the difference is a safety rule. The Reference lists &'a mut T as "invariant" in T. Suppose a function receives a &mut &'static [u8]. If the compiler let it be treated as a &mut &'short [u8], the function could store a short borrow into it. The caller would then hold a "static" reference to memory that is about to be freed:

fn store<'a>(slot: &mut &'a [u8], value: &'a [u8]) {
    *slot = value;
}
let mut forever: &'static [u8] = b"static bytes";
{
    let local = vec![1u8, 2, 3];
    store(&mut forever, &local); // rejected: forever would point into local
}
println!("{forever:?}");

The compiler refuses with E0597. Its note says that the type annotation "requires that local is borrowed for 'static". Invariance is the reason. It cannot shorten the 'static inside the mutable reference, so it demands that local live for ever, which it cannot.

A table of functions for every lifetime#

The command table is an array of function pointers, one per command. Try the old type for a read first, and leave the lifetime for the compiler to fill in:

type Read = fn(&Command, &dyn Store, Instant) -> Reply;

This is error E0106, "missing lifetime specifier". The compiler fills in an elided lifetime by fixed rules. The Reference says each elided input lifetime "becomes a distinct lifetime parameter". An output lifetime is filled only "if there is exactly one lifetime used in the parameters". This type has two references and a Command that borrows, so the reply's lifetime is ambiguous.

Naming it needs a new piece of syntax. A function in the table must work for whatever lifetime each call brings. The table cannot fix one 'a for every call, because each request has its own buffer. The type says "for all choices of 'a":

Exercise 17.3RustThe command table for every lifetime

Change Run::Read so that a read function may return a reply that borrows from the request and the store, for any lifetime. Write functions keep returning a reply that borrows nothing, so their type is Reply<'static>. Then give get, hgetall and the other readers that lend bytes a lifetime parameter of their own.

enum Run {
    Read(/* your type here */),
    Write(fn(&Command, &mut dyn Store, Instant) -> Reply<'static>),
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/// A command either reads the store or writes it. A read takes `&dyn Store`, so many
/// threads can run reads at once under a read lock; a write takes `&mut dyn Store` and
/// the exclusive lock. The table says which is which, so the server need not know.
///
/// A read's reply may borrow from the request and from the store, so its type names one
/// lifetime `'a` for all three. `for<'a>` says the function works for every `'a` the
/// caller picks, which is what a table of functions needs: each call has its own.
/// A write's reply borrows nothing, because the exclusive lock is released before the
/// reply is written.
enum Run {
    Read(for<'a> fn(&Command<'a>, &'a dyn Store, Instant) -> Reply<'a>),
    Write(fn(&Command, &mut dyn Store, Instant) -> Reply<'static>),
}

struct Entry {
    name: &'static [u8],
    run: Run,
    arity: i32,
}

macro_rules! commands {
    ($($name:literal => $kind:ident($run:ident), $arity:expr;)*) => {
        const COMMANDS: &[Entry] = &[$(Entry { name: $name, run: Run::$kind($run), arity: $arity }),*];
    };
}

commands! {
    b"PING" => Read(ping), -1;
    b"ECHO" => Read(echo), 2;
    b"SET" => Write(set), -3;
    b"GET" => Read(get), 2;
    b"DEL" => Write(del), -2;
    b"EXISTS" => Read(exists), -2;
    b"INCR" => Write(incr), 2;
    b"APPEND" => Write(append), 3;
    b"STRLEN" => Read(strlen), 2;
    b"GETRANGE" => Read(getrange), 4;
    b"LPUSH" => Write(lpush), -3;
    b"RPUSH" => Write(rpush), -3;
    b"LLEN" => Read(llen), 2;
    b"LRANGE" => Read(lrange), 4;
    b"HSET" => Write(hset), -4;
    b"HGET" => Read(hget), 3;
    b"HGETALL" => Read(hgetall), 2;
    b"SADD" => Write(sadd), -3;
    b"SISMEMBER" => Read(sismember), 3;
    b"SMEMBERS" => Read(smembers), 2;
    b"TYPE" => Read(type_cmd), 2;
    b"SCAN" => Read(scan), -2;
    b"EXPIRE" => Write(expire), 3;
    b"PEXPIREAT" => Write(pexpireat), 3;
    b"TTL" => Read(ttl), 2;
    b"DBSIZE" => Read(dbsize), 1;
    b"KEYS" => Read(keys), 2;
    b"COMMAND" => Read(command), -1;
}
rust/ch17/src/cmd.rs · region table

The Rustonomicon reads for<'a> as "for all choices of 'a". It "produces an infinite list" of types that the function must satisfy, one for each lifetime. This is a higher-ranked type. A bound on a closure that takes a reference has the same form, such as F: for<'a> Fn(&'a [u8]). The compiler usually writes it for you. A function pointer in a table is one of the places where you must write it yourself.

A reader that returns Reply<'static>, such as STRLEN, still fits Run::Read. A 'static reply may be used as a reply of any shorter lifetime, because the return type of a function pointer is covariant. Variance again. Only the functions that lend bytes needed a new signature.

'static is a bound on a type#

The write functions return Reply<'static>. That does not mean the reply lives until the program ends. It means the reply holds no borrow that could end. An Int or a Simple borrows nothing, so it is 'static and is freed at the end of its block like any other value.

The same reading explains std::thread::spawn. Its closure must be 'static. The documentation gives the reason, that "threads can outlive the lifetime they have been created in". A closure that borrows a local fails with E0373. Chapter 9 used thread::scope instead, which proves that every thread ends before the scope does. The scope lets the threads borrow the store, with no Arc and no 'static.

A String is 'static in this sense, and so is a Vec<u8>. Both own everything they hold. So T: 'static is a bound that an owned value meets, and a &'static str is a reference to bytes that do last for ever. They share a name and mean two different things.

Check it#

Run the scene again, against this chapter's crate:

$ cd code/rust/ch17
$ cargo run -q --release --example allocs
HGETALL of 1000 fields: 125007 bytes of reply, 2 allocations, 64007 bytes allocated

Two allocations remain. One is the vector of two thousand replies inside the array, 64,000 bytes for two thousand replies of 32 bytes each. The other is seven bytes. The command lookup copies the name HGETALL in capitals to compare it. Chapter 21 removes that copy too. The 110,000 bytes of copied fields are gone.

Behaviour has not changed, and three checks say so. The protocol tests drive both servers through redis-cli:

$ tests/run.sh rust ch17
== rust ch17: 207/207 passed
$ KV_RUST_BIN=kv_async tests/run.sh rust ch17
== rust ch17: 207/207 passed

Every counter-example in this chapter is a doc test in src/lessons.rs. A compile_fail block passes only when the compiler rejects it, with the error code the chapter names. So cargo test --doc checks that each error happens.

The last check is miri, an interpreter for Rust that reports undefined behaviour. This chapter adds no unsafe, so miri should find nothing. It runs every unit test of the library, slowly:

$ cargo +nightly miri test -q --lib
test result: ok. 13 passed; 0 failed; 3 ignored

The three ignored tests call the C library of chapter 15. A call into C goes through the foreign function interface, or FFI. The miri interpreter runs only Rust. Its documentation says the program "has no access to most platform-specific APIs or FFI". So those tests carry #[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)]. Chapter 21 returns to miri, with code that it does reject.

The real one: Cow, Deref and Bytes#

The hand-built piece was one type and a change of order. The type was Cow, which the standard library already had, so the real version is close to what you wrote. Two things about it are worth knowing.

First, write_bulk takes a &[u8], and the reply hands it a &Cow<[u8]>. Nobody wrote a conversion. Cow implements Deref, and the compiler "will silently insert calls to Deref::deref" until the types match. This is deref coercion, the same rule that turns a &String into a &str. The documentation warns not to implement Deref for a type whose methods "are likely to collide" with the target's. A smart pointer is the case it was made for.

Second, a borrowing reply ties the reply to the lock. That is why the reply is formatted under the lock. A server that wants to keep values after the lock is released, without copying, needs shared ownership instead of a borrow. The bytes crate, which tokio uses, gives a Bytes type that counts its owners. A clone of Bytes adds one to a count and copies nothing. Chapter 20 is about that count, and you build one yourself there.

Lending bytes without a copyCGoRust
A view of bytesa pointer and a length, which the programmer keeps valida slice, which keeps its array alivea &[u8], which may not outlive the owner
Borrowed or owneda flag in the struct, checked by handalways shared, the collector frees itCow, checked by the type
Reply after the lockcopy, or document who frees itthe slice keeps the old array alivethe compiler rejects the borrow, so format first
A table of handlersfunction pointers with a void * contexta map of funcs, with closuresfor<'a> fn, one type for every lifetime

C has the cheapest version and the most dangerous one. A pointer and a length cost nothing, and nothing stops the store from freeing them while the reply is being written. Go has the safest version with the least control. A slice keeps its array alive, so a reply may outlive the lock, and the old bytes stay in memory until the collector runs. Rust is safer than C and gives more control than Go. The borrow costs nothing, as in C, and the compiler proves that the store outlives it.

Carry forward
  • A move copies the bytes of the value. For a Vec that is three words, and the old name is dead, so the heap block keeps one owner.
  • A borrow cannot outlive its guard. Locals drop in reverse order of declaration, so a reply that borrows the store is formatted before the lock guard drops.
  • Variance and for<'a>. A shared borrow may be treated as shorter, so one lifetime covers two borrows. A for<'a> type works for every lifetime.
Next

scan still collects a page of keys into a vector. Give the trait a method that returns an iterator instead, and every &mut dyn Store in kv stops compiling. Chapter 18 opens the trait object to see why.

Traits all the way down#

Rust from first principles · Chapter 18· 18 min read· 91 lines of code
▶Scene

Chapter 17 left KEYS collecting every key into a vector before the reply copies them into a second one. An iterator would avoid the first vector. Add one method to the Store trait in your chapter 17 crate, implement it for MapStore, and build:

$ grep -n keys_iter src/store.rs
81:    fn keys_iter(&self, now: Instant) -> impl Iterator<Item = &[u8]>;
$ cargo build 2>&1 | grep -c '^error'
50
$ cargo build 2>&1 | head -3
error[E0038]: the trait `Store` is not dyn compatible
  --> src/cmd.rs:21:39
   |

One new method, and fifty errors. None of them is in the method. They are in every line of cmd.rs that names dyn Store.

A trait object is two pointers, and one of them points to a table of functions. This chapter builds that table yourself, then uses it to explain which traits can be objects. On the way kv gets a sealed trait, a family of standard traits, and an iterator that lends out its own buffer.

Chapter 7 introduced dyn Store as a pointer that "carries a second pointer to a table of the type's methods". It also stated a rule without its reason. A trait with a generic method cannot be a dyn. The scene broke a rule of the same family. To know what the rule protects, you have to see the table.

A trait object is two words#

Start with sizes, because they are facts the compiler reports. A reference to a MapStore is one machine word, an address. A reference to a dyn Store is two:

assert_eq!(size_of::<&MapStore>(), size_of::<usize>());
assert_eq!(size_of::<&dyn Store>(), 2 * size_of::<usize>());
assert_eq!(size_of::<Box<dyn Store>>(), 2 * size_of::<usize>());

The first word is the address of the value. The second is the address of a vtable, a table in static memory with one function pointer for each method of the trait. The compiler makes one table for each pair of a type and a trait, such as MapStore as a Store. A call through &dyn Store loads the function from the table and calls it with the first word. A pointer of two words like this is called a fat pointer. A slice reference is the other common one, an address and a length.

A vtable, by hand#

You can write the same thing in plain Rust. The table is a struct of function pointers. The object is a pointer whose type has been forgotten, next to a reference to the table:

Exercise 18.1RustThe table and the object

Write StoreVTable with two entries, len and has. Each takes a *const (), a pointer to something of unknown type. Write StoreRef<'a> with the data pointer, a &'static StoreVTable, and a PhantomData<&'a ()> so that the type remembers the borrow. Mark the entries unsafe fn. Only a caller that passes a pointer of the right type may call them.

struct StoreVTable {
    len: /* your type here */,
    has: /* your type here */,
}

struct StoreRef<'a> {

Stuck?Show the full listing
/// One entry per method. Each takes the forgotten pointer and casts it back to the
/// type it was made from. Only the code that built the table knows that type, so the
/// entries are `unsafe fn`: a caller must pass a pointer of the right type.
struct StoreVTable {
    len: unsafe fn(*const ()) -> usize,
    has: unsafe fn(*const (), &[u8], Instant) -> bool,
}

/// A reference to some store, of a type nobody here can name. Two words, as a
/// `&dyn Store` is. `PhantomData` keeps the borrow of the store in the type, because a
/// raw pointer carries no lifetime of its own.
struct StoreRef<'a> {
    data: *const (),
    vtable: &'static StoreVTable,
    _borrow: PhantomData<&'a ()>,
}
rust/ch18/examples/vtable.rs · region vtable

The table for a type S is a constant, so it sits in static memory once, as the compiler's tables do. Each entry casts the forgotten pointer back to *const S and calls the real method. The constructor is the only place that knows S. It takes a &S, keeps its address, and picks the table for S. That pairing is the proof that every cast is correct, which is what each // SAFETY: comment says:

Exercise 18.2RustOne table per type

Put the table in an associated constant of a generic struct Tables<S>, so that each type S gets its own. Write StoreRef::new, which takes a &'a S. Then write the two methods, which call through the table. Compare the result with the compiler's version.

impl<S: Store> Tables<S> {
    const VTABLE: StoreVTable = StoreVTable {
        // your code here: cast `data` back to *const S and call the method

Stuck?Show the full listing
/// One table per type `S`, in static memory, as the compiler makes them.
struct Tables<S>(PhantomData<S>);

impl<S: Store> Tables<S> {
    const VTABLE: StoreVTable = StoreVTable {
        // SAFETY: the caller passes a pointer made from a `&S` in `StoreRef::new`.
        len: |data| unsafe { (*(data as *const S)).len() },
        // SAFETY: as above.
        has: |data, key, now| unsafe { (*(data as *const S)).value(key, now).is_some() },
    };
}

impl<'a> StoreRef<'a> {
    /// The only way to make a `StoreRef`, so the pointer and the table always agree.
    fn new<S: Store>(store: &'a S) -> Self {
        StoreRef {
            data: store as *const S as *const (),
            vtable: &Tables::<S>::VTABLE,
            _borrow: PhantomData,
        }
    }

    fn len(&self) -> usize {
        // SAFETY: `new` built the table for the type that `data` points to, and `'a`
        // keeps that value alive.
        unsafe { (self.vtable.len)(self.data) }
    }

    fn has(&self, key: &[u8], now: Instant) -> bool {
        // SAFETY: as in `len`.
        unsafe { (self.vtable.has)(self.data, key, now) }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut store = MapStore::new();
    store.set(b"k".to_vec(), b"v".to_vec());
    let by_hand = StoreRef::new(&store);
    let by_compiler: &dyn Store = &store;
    println!(
        "by hand: {} bytes, len {}, has k {}",
        size_of_val(&by_hand),
        by_hand.len(),
        by_hand.has(b"k", Instant::now())
    );
    println!(
        "by the compiler: {} bytes, len {}, has k {}",
        size_of::<&dyn Store>(),
        by_compiler.len(),
        by_compiler.value(b"k", Instant::now()).is_some()
    );
}

$ cargo run -q --example vtable
by hand: 16 bytes, len 1, has k true
by the compiler: 16 bytes, len 1, has k true

Sixteen bytes each, and the same answers. The difference is that the compiler writes and checks the casts, so &dyn Store needs no unsafe. Your version needs it in three places, and a wrong table would be undefined behaviour with no error at all.

What a vtable cannot hold#

Now the scene makes sense. keys_iter returned impl Iterator, which means "some iterator type, chosen by the implementation". For MapStore it is a filter over a hash map's iterator. Another store would choose another type. A vtable has one slot for keys_iter, and a slot is a function pointer with one signature. No single signature can return a different type for each store.

The Reference calls a trait that a vtable can serve dyn compatible. The older term, used in chapter 7 and in many books, is "object safe". A method can be called through the vtable only if it has no type parameters, "although lifetime parameters are allowed". It must also not use Self "except in the type of the receiver". A generic method fails because it has one body per type argument, an unbounded number. A method that returns Self fails because the caller does not know the size of Self.

The way out keeps the trait dyn compatible and moves the variation into an argument. Instead of returning an iterator, the store calls a closure once per key. A closure behind &mut dyn FnMut is itself a trait object, so the signature is the same for every store. This is the shape of kv_store_each in the C version of chapter 7. A function pointer and a context pointer are, together, a dyn FnMut written out:

Exercise 18.3RustA callback the vtable can hold

Replace the two methods that return vectors with each_key and scan_each. Each takes f: &mut dyn FnMut(&'a [u8]). The lifetime 'a is that of &'a self, so each key may borrow from the store. Then rewrite KEYS to push a reply for each matching key into a vector made with with_capacity.

fn each_key<'a>(&'a self, now: Instant, f: &mut dyn FnMut(&'a [u8]));
Stuck?Show the full listing
fn each_key<'a>(&'a self, now: Instant, f: &mut dyn FnMut(&'a [u8])) {
    for (k, e) in &self.map {
        if !e.expired(now) {
            f(k);
        }
    }
}

fn scan_each<'a>(
    &'a self,
    cursor: usize,
    count: usize,
    now: Instant,
    f: &mut dyn FnMut(&'a [u8]),
) -> usize {
    let mut rest = self.map.iter().skip(cursor);
    for (k, e) in rest.by_ref().take(count) {
        if !e.expired(now) {
            f(k);
        }
    }
    if rest.next().is_some() {
        cursor + count
    } else {
        0
    }
}
rust/ch18/src/store.rs · region each
fn keys<'a>(args: &Command<'a>, store: &'a dyn Store, now: Instant) -> Reply<'a> {
    // the store's length bounds the number of keys, so the vector never grows
    let mut keys = Vec::with_capacity(store.len());
    store.keys_with(now, |k| {
        if glob(args[1], k) {
            keys.push(Reply::from(k));
        }
    });
    Reply::Array(keys)
}
rust/ch18/src/cmd.rs · region keys
⚠️A callback cannot stop early Rust

The store decides when each_key ends, not the caller. An iterator is lazy. A caller that wants the first match stops calling next, and no more work is done. A closure has no way to say "stop" unless the method's signature gives it one, for example by returning a bool or a ControlFlow. SCAN does not need it, because the store counts the page itself. A command that wanted the first key matching a pattern would pay for a walk over the whole store. That is the price of keeping Store dyn compatible.

A &mut dyn FnMut is not pleasant to pass. A second trait can give every store a generic method that wraps the closure. Generic methods cannot go in the vtable, but they can go in a trait that is never used as an object. A blanket implementation then gives that trait to every type that implements Store:

/// Generic methods, which the vtable of `dyn Store` cannot hold, live in a second trait.
/// The blanket impl gives them to every store, and `?Sized` includes `dyn Store`
/// itself. Each body calls only the dispatchable methods, so it works through a vtable.
pub trait StoreExt: Store {
    /// `each_key` with any closure, passed as a `&mut dyn FnMut` for the store.
    fn keys_with<'a, F: FnMut(&'a [u8])>(&'a self, now: Instant, mut f: F) {
        self.each_key(now, &mut f);
    }

    /// `scan_each` with any closure.
    fn scan_with<'a, F: FnMut(&'a [u8])>(
        &'a self,
        cursor: usize,
        count: usize,
        now: Instant,
        mut f: F,
    ) -> usize {
        self.scan_each(cursor, count, now, &mut f)
    }
}

impl<S: Store + ?Sized> StoreExt for S {}
rust/ch18/src/store.rs · region ext

The bound S: Store + ?Sized includes dyn Store itself. So a command that holds a &dyn Store can call keys_with and pass a plain closure. The generic body is compiled for dyn Store and calls each_key through the vtable. You get static dispatch where the type is known and dynamic dispatch where it is not, from one method.

There is a shorter way to the same place, inside the trait itself. A method with the bound where Self: Sized is left out of the vtable. The Reference calls it "explicitly non-dispatchable". The trait stays dyn compatible, and the method exists only on concrete types. The cost is that a dyn Store cannot call it at all. The extension trait has no such gap, which is why kv uses it.

What each kind of dispatch costs#

A call through a vtable is an indirect call. The processor loads an address from the table and jumps to it. The compiler cannot see which function that will be, so it cannot inline it or optimise across it. For a command that takes microseconds, one indirect call is noise. For a method called once per byte, it can be most of the cost.

A generic function has the opposite cost. The compiler writes one copy of it for each type it is used with, which is monomorphisation. Each copy calls the methods directly and can inline them. The price is compile time and the size of the binary, which grow with every type. keys_with pays it once per closure type. Each closure is its own type, so each call site gets its own small copy, which then calls each_key through the vtable.

Static dispatch is not better than dynamic dispatch in general, and the reverse is not true either. A table of commands needs one type for many functions, so it needs dyn. A hot inner loop wants the compiler to see everything, so it wants generics. Rust lets you choose for each call, and the type in the signature says which choice was made.

The standard traits are a family#

Every reply constructor in chapter 17 spelled out Reply::Bulk(Cow::Borrowed(..)). The standard library has a trait for "this type can be made from that one", and the rest of the library is written against it. Implement From, and the compiler gives you Into in the other direction:

/// `From` is the standard way to say "this type can be made from that one", and `Into`
/// comes with it for free. A borrowed slice becomes a bulk string that borrows, an owned
/// vector one that owns, and an integer an integer reply.
impl<'a> From<&'a [u8]> for Reply<'a> {
    fn from(b: &'a [u8]) -> Self {
        Reply::Bulk(Cow::Borrowed(b))
    }
}

impl From<Vec<u8>> for Reply<'_> {
    fn from(b: Vec<u8>) -> Self {
        Reply::Bulk(Cow::Owned(b))
    }
}

impl From<i64> for Reply<'_> {
    fn from(n: i64) -> Self {
        Reply::Int(n)
    }
}
rust/ch18/src/resp.rs · region from

The call sites now read Reply::from(val), and a function that takes impl Into<Reply> accepts a slice, a vector or an integer. Chapter 4's ? operator works on the same idea. It calls From to turn one error type into another.

Borrow is the member of the family that makes lookups cheap. A HashMap<Vec<u8>, _> can be searched with a &[u8]. The reason is that a Vec<u8> borrows as a [u8]. The hand-written table of chapter 6 asked for a &K, so a search for a slice had to build a vector first. The documentation states the promise that makes the borrowed form safe to search with. Eq, Ord and Hash "must be equivalent for borrowed and owned values". A key and its borrowed form must land in the same bucket.

AsRef looks similar, and the difference is that promise. An AsRef<[u8]> is a cheap view as bytes, with nothing said about equality or hashing. The table uses AsRef to hash and Borrow to compare, and the bound asks for both. A type whose bytes and whose equality disagreed would satisfy AsRef and break Borrow's promise. The table would then fail to find its own keys:

Change the three lookups on Table to take a &Q, where K: Borrow<Q>. Mark Q as ?Sized, so that [u8] qualifies. Hash key.as_ref(), and compare with e.key.borrow() == key. Then implement Index, so that table[key] works.

pub fn get<Q>(&self, key: &Q) -> Option<&V>
where
    K: Borrow<Q>,
    Q: AsRef<[u8]> + PartialEq + ?Sized,

    // your code here

Stuck?Show the full listing
/// A lookup takes any `Q` that the key can be borrowed as. A table of `Vec<u8>`
/// keys can then be searched with a `&[u8]`, with no vector made for the search.
/// `Borrow` promises that `Q` hashes and compares as the key does, and the table's
/// bound adds the same view as bytes, so the bucket is the same.
pub fn get_mut<Q>(&mut self, key: &Q) -> Option<&mut V>
where
    K: Borrow<Q>,
    Q: AsRef<[u8]> + PartialEq + ?Sized,
{
    if self.buckets.is_empty() {
        return None;
    }
    let i = self.bucket(key.as_ref());
    self.buckets[i]
        .iter_mut()
        .find(|e| e.key.borrow() == key)
        .map(|e| &mut e.val)
}

/// The value under key, made with `make` when the key is new. Written as a search
/// for the position first, because a borrow from `get_mut` would block the push.
pub fn insert_with(&mut self, key: K, make: fn() -> V) -> &mut V {
    if self.buckets.is_empty() {
        self.buckets.resize_with(16, Vec::new);
    }
    let mut i = self.index(&key);
    if let Some(j) = self.buckets[i].iter().position(|e| e.key == key) {
        return &mut self.buckets[i][j].val;
    }
    if self.len >= self.buckets.len() {
        self.grow();
        i = self.index(&key);
    }
    self.buckets[i].push(Entry { key, val: make() });
    self.len += 1;
    &mut self.buckets[i].last_mut().expect("just pushed").val
}

pub fn get<Q>(&self, key: &Q) -> Option<&V>
where
    K: Borrow<Q>,
    Q: AsRef<[u8]> + PartialEq + ?Sized,
{
    if self.buckets.is_empty() {
        return None;
    }
    let chain = &self.buckets[self.bucket(key.as_ref())];
    chain.iter().find(|e| e.key.borrow() == key).map(|e| &e.val)
}

/// `table[key]`, as for a HashMap: an operator is a trait, and `Index` is the one for
/// square brackets. A missing key panics, as indexing out of range does, so the server
/// uses `get`, and `[]` is for code that knows the key is there.
impl<K, V, Q> Index<&Q> for Table<K, V>
where
    K: AsRef<[u8]> + PartialEq + Borrow<Q>,
    Q: AsRef<[u8]> + PartialEq + ?Sized,
{
    type Output = V;

    fn index(&self, key: &Q) -> &V {
        self.get(key).expect("no entry for the key")
    }
}
rust/ch18/src/table.rs · region index

Index is an operator. Every operator in Rust is a trait. The plus sign is Add, a double equals sign is PartialEq, and square brackets are Index. A missing key panics, as an index out of range does. So the server keeps get, and the brackets are for code that knows the key is there, such as a test.

Blanket impls and the orphan rule#

The blanket impl<S: Store + ?Sized> StoreExt for S covers types that do not exist yet. What stops two crates from implementing the same trait for the same type in two ways? Rust answers with coherence. For any trait and type there is at most one implementation, everywhere.

Two rules enforce it. The first is the orphan rule. An implementation "is only allowed if either the trait or at least one of the types in the implementation is defined in the current crate". So kv may not implement Display for Vec<u8>, which is error E0117. The overlap rule forbids two implementations that could apply to one type. Take a blanket implementation for every type that is Debug. A second one for u8 is error E0119, because u8 is Debug too.

The price is a familiar annoyance. You cannot add a standard trait to a standard type. The usual answer is a newtype, a struct of one field that kv owns, such as struct Key(Vec<u8>). The benefit is that adding a dependency can never change which implementation your code calls.

Sealing a public trait#

This chapter added two required methods to Store. Suppose a user of the kv library had written their own store. Their code would have stopped compiling. For a published crate, a new required method on a public trait is a breaking change.

The Rust API guidelines name a pattern for traits that "are only meant to be implemented within the crate that defines them". The trait gets a supertrait that lives in a private module. Code outside the crate cannot name it, so it cannot implement it. The guidelines put the guarantee in one sentence. "The empty private Sealed supertrait cannot be named by downstream crates":

/// A trait in a private module. Code outside the crate cannot name it, so it cannot
/// implement it, and so it cannot implement `Store` either.
mod private {
    pub trait Sealed {}
    impl Sealed for super::MapStore {}
}
rust/ch18/src/store.rs · region sealed

Outside the crate, impl kv::store::Store for Mine is now error E0277, because Mine does not implement Sealed. Everyone can still call the trait's methods and hold a dyn Store. Only the crate can add an implementation, and so only the crate decides when a new method is safe to add.

An iterator that lends its buffer#

The read loop of every server so far kept a buffer, a count of used bytes, and a loop that called parse on the rest. Each parsed Command borrows the buffer. Could that be an iterator, so that the loop says what it means?

Try it, and the type of Iterator::Item stops you. Item is one type for the whole iteration. A Command<'a> borrows the iterator's own buffer, and that borrow is new at each call to next. An ordinary iterator's items may be kept after the next call, so its items cannot borrow from it.

A generic associated type lets an associated type take a lifetime parameter. type Item<'a> is a different type for each borrow, and next returns the one for the borrow it was given. The feature became stable in Rust 1.65. The Rust blog's announcement used this very case. It "allows the next function to return an item that borrows from self". The pattern is called a lending iterator:

Exercise 18.5RustA lending iterator over requests

Write a trait Lend with type Item<'a> where Self: 'a and fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item<'_>>. Write Requests, which owns the buffer and the count of used bytes. Its push drops the used bytes and appends a read. Its next parses one request and returns it borrowed. Then change both servers' read loops to while let Some(args) = requests.next().

pub trait Lend {
    type Item<'a>
    where
        Self: 'a;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item<'_>>;
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/// An iterator whose items borrow from the iterator itself. `Iterator::Item` is one type
/// for the whole iteration, so it cannot name a borrow of `self` that is new at each
/// call. A generic associated type can: `Item<'a>` is a different type for each `'a`,
/// and `next` returns the one for the borrow it was given. The price is that a lender
/// works with `while let`, not `for`, and each item must be gone before the next call.
pub trait Lend {
    type Item<'a>
    where
        Self: 'a;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item<'_>>;
}

/// The requests in a client's read buffer. Each `next` parses one whole request, whose
/// arguments borrow the buffer. `push` adds the bytes of a read, after it has dropped
/// the requests that were used. Nothing is copied out of the buffer.
#[derive(Default)]
pub struct Requests {
    buf: Vec<u8>,
    used: usize,
}

impl Requests {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self::default()
    }

    /// Forget the requests already parsed and append new bytes. No request can still
    /// borrow the buffer, because `push` takes `&mut self`.
    pub fn push(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<()> {
        self.buf.drain(..self.used);
        self.used = 0;
        self.buf.extend_from_slice(bytes);
        if self.buf.len() > MAX_REQUEST {
            return Err(KvError::Protocol(b'*')); // a request that never ends
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl Lend for Requests {
    type Item<'a> = Result<Command<'a>>;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Result<Command<'_>>> {
        match parse(&self.buf[self.used..]) {
            Ok(Parsed::Done(args, n)) => {
                self.used += n;
                Some(Ok(args))
            }
            Ok(Parsed::Incomplete) => None,
            Err(e) => Some(Err(e)),
        }
    }
}

// `while let`, not `for`: each request borrows `requests`, and the borrow ends
// at the bottom of the loop, before `next` is called again.
while let Some(args) = requests.next() {

The loop is a while let and not a for, and the compiler insists. for args in requests is error E0277, because Requests is not an Iterator. That is the honest answer. A for loop may keep each item, and a lender's item must be gone before the next one exists.

Why is Lend not a method on Store? A trait with a generic associated type is not dyn compatible, and kv's commands need dyn Store. A GAT belongs where the type is known at compile time, as the read loop's is.

Check it#

The allocation example of chapter 17 now also runs a KEYS over a thousand keys. Against the chapter 17 crate and this one:

$ cd code/rust/ch17 && cargo run -q --release --example allocs | grep KEYS
KEYS of 1000 keys: 17007 bytes of reply, 11 allocations, 64708 bytes allocated
$ cd ../ch18 && cargo run -q --release --example allocs | grep KEYS
KEYS of 1000 keys: 17007 bytes of reply, 2 allocations, 32036 bytes allocated

The callback alone took it from eleven to ten. The vector of replies still grew by doubling, nine times. Reserving store.len() places, which bounds the number of keys, took it to two. The measurement mattered more than the design here, which is a reason to keep measuring.

Both servers pass all 207 protocol tests. Every rule this chapter states is a doc test in src/lessons.rs. They cover dyn compatibility (E0038), sealing (E0277), the orphan rule (E0117), overlap (E0119) and the for loop over a lender (E0277). On a nightly toolchain, rustdoc also checks that each error has the code the chapter names.

The hand-built vtable uses raw pointers, so it runs under miri too. miri reports nothing, which is evidence and not proof. It checks only the paths that the run takes:

$ cargo +nightly miri run -q --example vtable
by hand: 16 bytes, len 1, has k true
by the compiler: 16 bytes, len 1, has k true

The real ones#

The compiler's vtable holds more than your two entries. It also holds the size and alignment of the value and the function that drops it, so a Box<dyn Store> can free what it holds. The layout of the table is not a stable interface. That is why your StoreRef cannot be turned into a &dyn Store by a cast.

The lending iterator has no standard trait. The pattern appears in crates under names such as LendingIterator, and in the standard library as plain methods. BufRead::read_line fills a buffer that the caller owns, which avoids the question. The language may one day let for loops use lenders. Until then, a while let loop is the idiom.

Dispatch through a tableCGoRust
A call through an interfacea struct of function pointers, filled by handan interface value of two words, a type and a pointera fat pointer of two words, the data and a vtable
Who builds the tablethe programmer, for each typethe compiler and the runtimethe compiler, one per type and trait
Visiting every keya function pointer and a void * contexta callback, or an iter.Seqa &mut dyn FnMut, so the trait stays dyn compatible
Who may implement itanyone who fills the structany type with the methods, in any packagethe orphan rule decides, and a sealed trait allows only its crate

The C version is the vtable with nothing hidden. Every pointer and every cast is visible, and nothing checks them. Go hides the table and checks the types when it builds an interface value. A Go interface is satisfied by any type with the right methods, so the table is the only contract. Rust hides the table and also decides at compile time which traits can have one. It decides who may implement a trait, and which implementation a call reaches. That is more rules than Go has, and each rule is one less question at run time.

Carry forward
  • A trait object is a fat pointer. It holds the address of the value and of a vtable, one table of function pointers for each type and trait.
  • Dyn compatible means the vtable can serve it. A generic method or an impl Trait return has no single signature, so it goes in an extension trait or takes a callback.
  • Traits control who may implement them. Coherence allows one implementation per type, and a sealed trait allows only its own crate, so its methods can grow.

The tokio server formats each reply under the lock and writes it after. Move one write inside the lock, and tokio::spawn refuses the whole task. Chapter 19 builds a future, a waker and an executor yourself, to see what the compiler saw.

Futures by hand#

Rust from first principles · Chapter 19· 20 min read· 203 lines of code
▶Scene

The tokio server of chapter 18 formats a reply while it holds the read lock. It writes the reply to the client after the lock is released. Move the write up, inside the block that holds the guard, so that each read reply goes out at once. Then build:

$ cargo build -q --bin kv_async
error: future cannot be sent between threads safely
   --> src/bin/kv_async.rs:171:9
    |
171 | /         tokio::spawn(async move {
    | |__________^ future created by async block is not `Send`
    |
note: future is not `Send` as this value is used across an await
 50 |                 let db = db.read().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
    |                     -- has type `std::sync::RwLockReadGuard<'_, Db>` which is not `Send`
 54 |                         stream.write_all(&out).await?;
    |                                                ^^^^^ await occurs here, with `db` maybe used later

The error is on tokio::spawn, a hundred lines from the change. It talks about a type that nobody wrote, a "future created by async block".

The compiler turned that async block into a type, and the lock guard became a field of it. This chapter shows what that type is. You write a future, a waker, an executor and a reactor yourself, and kv runs on them. Then Pin, Send futures and cancellation are each one fact about that type.

Chapter 9 used async and await as a way to serve many clients with few threads. The rules came with the tool. A task must not block. A task given to tokio::spawn must be Send. A guard must not live across an await. Each rule has a reason, and every reason is in the code that the compiler writes for an async block. So this chapter writes that code itself.

A future is a value that waits#

The standard library defines a future in one sentence. "A future is a value that might not have finished computing yet." The trait has one method:

pub trait Future {
    type Output;
    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>;
}

poll asks the future to make progress. It returns Poll::Ready with the result, or Poll::Pending if the result is not there yet. Nothing else calls a future. It has no thread of its own and runs only inside poll. So a future that nobody polls does nothing at all:

let ran = Cell::new(false);
let fut = async { ran.set(true) };
drop(fut);
assert!(!ran.get());

Who polls it again after Pending? The documentation describes a contract. When a future is not ready, poll "stores a clone of the Waker copied from the current Context". The waker "is then woken once the future can make progress". A waker is a handle that tells an executor to poll a task again. A future that returns Pending without arranging a wake is never polled again.

An async block is a state machine#

What does the compiler make of an async block? It makes an enum. Each variant is one place where the block can be waiting, and holds every local that is still needed after that place. poll runs from the current variant to the next await, then stores the new variant and returns Pending. The std::pin documentation names this directly. It speaks of "the state machines generated by the compiler to implement Future for async fns".

Here is that enum written out, for async { sleep(d).await; a + b }. It has a state before the sleep, a state during it, and a state after the result is returned:

enum AddLater {
    Start { a: u32, b: u32, d: Duration },
    Waiting { a: u32, b: u32, sleep: Sleep },
    Done,
}

impl Future for AddLater {
    type Output = u32;
    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<u32> {
        loop {
            match &mut *self {
                AddLater::Start { a, b, d } => {
                    let (a, b, sleep) = (*a, *b, sleep(*d));
                    *self = AddLater::Waiting { a, b, sleep };
                }
                AddLater::Waiting { a, b, sleep } => match Pin::new(sleep).poll(cx) {
                    Poll::Pending => return Poll::Pending,
                    Poll::Ready(()) => {
                        let sum = *a + *b;
                        *self = AddLater::Done;
                        return Poll::Ready(sum);
                    }
                },
                AddLater::Done => panic!("polled after it returned Ready"),
            }
        }
    }
}

Now read the scene again. In the tokio server, the guard db is a local that is still alive at the await on write_all. So the guard is a field of one of the variants. The future's type contains a RwLockReadGuard. The compiler's note says that the "future is not Send as this value is used across an await".

Why a spawned future must be Send#

tokio::spawn takes F: Future + Send + 'static. Its documentation gives the reason. "The spawned task may execute on the current thread, or it may be sent to a different thread to be executed". Tokio moves a task to an idle thread between two polls. Moving the task moves the future, and the future holds every local that lives across an await. So every one of those locals must be Send.

A standard RwLockReadGuard is not Send. The operating system's lock must be released by the thread that took it, and a guard that moved could be dropped on another thread. The fix is the one chapter 17 made for its own reason. Format the reply while the guard is alive, end the block, and await the write after it. The guard is then not a field of any variant.

The same rule explains why an Rc cannot cross an await in a tokio task, and why it can if it is dropped first. The doc tests in src/lessons.rs show both. The future is Send exactly when no variant holds anything that is not.

A future, a waker and an executor, by hand#

Now build each part yourself, and put kv on top of it. The pieces are small. A future that waits for a moment in time. A waker that puts a task back on a queue. An executor that polls whatever is on the queue. A reactor that sleeps until a socket or a timer is ready, and then wakes the right task. They go in a module kv::fp, for first principles.

Start with the future, because it is the contract in its smallest form. Sleep asks the clock. If the moment has not come, it gives its waker to the reactor and says Pending:

    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()> {

Stuck?Show the full listing
/// Ready at a moment in time. Each poll asks the clock. If the moment has not come, it
/// gives its waker to the reactor, which wakes the task when the moment comes, and
/// says `Pending`. A future that says `Pending` without arranging a wake is never
/// polled again.
pub struct Sleep {
    at: Instant,
}

pub fn sleep(d: Duration) -> Sleep {
    Sleep {
        at: Instant::now() + d,
    }
}

impl Future for Sleep {
    type Output = ();

    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()> {
        if Instant::now() >= self.at {
            return Poll::Ready(());
        }
        exec::wake_at(self.at, cx.waker().clone());
        Poll::Pending
    }
}

A waker is a Waker value, and the standard library builds one from any type that implements the Wake trait. The documentation calls Wake "a memory-safe and ergonomic alternative to constructing a RawWaker". You wrap your type in an Arc and call Waker::from. This executor's waker holds the task's number and the ready queue, and waking pushes the number:

/// A task, as the executor keeps it: the future, boxed and pinned so that it never moves
/// again, and the waker that puts its number back on the ready queue. The executor runs
/// on one thread, so the future need not be `Send`.
type Task = (Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()>>>, Waker);

/// What a waker does: put the task's number on the queue. `Wake` turns an `Arc` of this
/// into a `Waker` with no `unsafe` code. The queue is behind a `Mutex` because a waker
/// is `Send` and may be called from any thread, although this executor's wakers are only
/// called from its own.
struct TaskWaker {
    id: usize,
    ready: Arc<Mutex<VecDeque<usize>>>,
}

impl Wake for TaskWaker {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) {
        self.wake_by_ref();
    }

    fn wake_by_ref(self: &Arc<Self>) {
        self.ready
            .lock()
            .unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())
            .push_back(self.id);
    }
}
rust/ch19/src/fp/exec.rs · region waker

The executor keeps every task in a vector of slots. A task is a boxed future and its waker. To run a task, it takes the task out of its slot. It polls the task with a Context made from its waker, and puts it back if it is still pending. The task comes out of the slot first for a practical reason. While it runs, it may spawn tasks or register wakers, and those borrow other parts of the executor:

/// Poll one task. It is taken out of its slot first, so that while it runs it may
/// spawn tasks or register wakers, which borrow other fields. A woken task that has
/// already finished has an empty slot, and the wake is ignored.
fn run(&self, id: usize) {
    let Some(Some((mut fut, waker))) = self.tasks.borrow_mut().get_mut(id).map(Option::take)
    else {
        return;
    };
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
    match fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
        Poll::Pending => self.tasks.borrow_mut()[id] = Some((fut, waker)),
        Poll::Ready(()) => self.free.borrow_mut().push(id),
    }
}
rust/ch19/src/fp/exec.rs · region run

How does Sleep find the reactor to give its waker to? It has no field that points there. Real runtimes answer with a thread-local, a value that each thread has its own copy of. block_on marks the runtime as running on this thread. The three functions that register a waker or a task use the runtime of the thread they are called on:

/// Called by a future that is about to return `Pending` on a socket: wake this waker
/// when `fd` is ready to read, or to write. One entry per descriptor and direction, so
/// a future that is polled twice replaces its waker instead of adding a second one.
pub fn wake_on(fd: i32, write: bool, waker: Waker) {
    with_running(|rt| {
        let mut io = rt.io.borrow_mut();
        match io.iter_mut().find(|(f, w, _)| *f == fd && *w == write) {
            Some(entry) => entry.2 = waker,
            None => io.push((fd, write, waker)),
        }
    });
}

/// Called by a future that is about to return `Pending` on the clock.
pub fn wake_at(at: Instant, waker: Waker) {
    with_running(|rt| rt.timers.borrow_mut().push((at, waker)));
}

/// Start a task. It runs when the executor next looks at its queue, and it ends when
/// its future returns, or when `block_on` returns, which drops it where it stands.
pub fn spawn(fut: impl Future<Output = ()> + 'static) {
    with_running(|rt| rt.spawned.borrow_mut().push(Box::pin(fut)));
}

The reactor is the part that waits. When no task is ready, it collects every socket that a future is waiting on and calls poll(2). The timeout is the nearest deadline of a timer. When poll returns, it wakes each task whose socket is ready and each timer whose moment has passed. This is the loop of the C server of chapter 9, with wakers where the C version had callbacks:

Exercise 19.3RustThe reactor

Write wait. Compute the timeout from the nearest timer. Take the list of sockets and build a sys::Wait for each one. Call sys::poll, wake the entries that are ready, and keep the others. Then wake every timer that is due. If there is no socket and no timer, nothing can ever wake a task, so panic with a message that says so.

fn wait(&self) {
    let now = Instant::now();
    let timeout = /* the nearest deadline, or None */;
    // your code here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/// Nothing is ready: sleep until a socket is ready or the nearest deadline comes, and
/// wake whatever that was. This is the reactor. With no socket to watch, a plain sleep
/// does the same job, and miri can run it, where it cannot run `poll`.
fn wait(&self) {
    let now = Instant::now();
    let timeout = self
        .timers
        .borrow()
        .iter()
        .map(|(at, _)| at.saturating_duration_since(now))
        .min();
    let io = std::mem::take(&mut *self.io.borrow_mut());
    assert!(
        !io.is_empty() || timeout.is_some(),
        "every task is waiting, and nothing can wake one"
    );
    if io.is_empty() {
        std::thread::sleep(timeout.unwrap_or_default());
    } else {
        let waits: Vec<sys::Wait> = io
            .iter()
            .map(|(fd, write, _)| sys::Wait {
                fd: *fd,
                write: *write,
            })
            .collect();
        let ready = sys::poll(&waits, timeout).expect("poll failed");
        let mut keep = self.io.borrow_mut();
        for (entry, ready) in io.into_iter().zip(ready) {
            if ready {
                entry.2.wake();
            } else {
                keep.push(entry);
            }
        }
    }
    let now = Instant::now();
    self.timers.borrow_mut().retain(|(at, waker)| {
        let due = *at <= now;
        if due {
            waker.wake_by_ref();
        }
        !due
    });
}
rust/ch19/src/fp/exec.rs · region wait
/// One descriptor to wait on, for reading or for writing.
#[cfg(unix)]
pub struct Wait {
    pub fd: i32,
    pub write: bool,
}

/// Sleep until at least one descriptor is ready, or until `timeout` passes, and say which
/// are ready. This is the system call under every event loop on Unix, the one the C
/// server of chapter 9 runs as kqueue or epoll. `poll` is older and slower with many
/// descriptors, and it is the same on macOS and Linux.
#[cfg(unix)]
pub fn poll(waits: &[Wait], timeout: Option<std::time::Duration>) -> std::io::Result<Vec<bool>> {
    let mut fds: Vec<libc::pollfd> = waits
        .iter()
        .map(|w| libc::pollfd {
            fd: w.fd,
            events: if w.write { libc::POLLOUT } else { libc::POLLIN },
            revents: 0,
        })
        .collect();
    // round up, so that a deadline 0.4 ms away does not become a busy loop of 0 ms polls
    let ms = timeout.map_or(-1, |d| {
        d.as_micros().div_ceil(1000).min(i32::MAX as u128) as i32
    });
    // SAFETY: `fds` is a valid array of `fds.len()` pollfd structs, which poll reads, and
    // of which it writes only the `revents` fields.
    let rc = unsafe { libc::poll(fds.as_mut_ptr(), fds.len() as libc::nfds_t, ms) };
    if rc < 0 {
        let e = std::io::Error::last_os_error();
        if e.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::Interrupted {
            return Ok(vec![false; fds.len()]); // a signal arrived: nothing is ready
        }
        return Err(e);
    }
    Ok(fds.iter().map(|p| p.revents != 0).collect())
}
rust/ch19/src/sys.rs · region poll
⚠️Pending with no waker hangs for ever Rust

A future that returns Pending and registers nothing is never polled again. Nothing reports the mistake. The task stays in its slot and the client waits. A real runtime cannot tell this from a client that is quiet. This reactor can tell in one case. Suppose every task is waiting, and the reactor has no socket and no timer to watch. Then it panics with "every task is waiting, and nothing can wake one". With even one quiet socket in the list, it waits instead, as tokio would. The rule to keep is simple to state. Every Pending passes a waker to something that will call it.

Sockets become futures in the same way as the clock. The socket is set to non-blocking, so a read that has no data returns the error WouldBlock at once. The future turns that error into a registration and Pending. std::future::poll_fn makes a future from a closure, which saves writing a struct for each operation:

pub struct Stream(TcpStream);

impl Stream {
    pub async fn read(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        poll_fn(|cx| match self.0.read(buf) {
            Err(e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock => {
                exec::wake_on(self.0.as_raw_fd(), false, cx.waker().clone());
                Poll::Pending
            }
            other => Poll::Ready(other),
        })
        .await
    }

    /// Write every byte, a piece at a time, waiting whenever the socket's buffer is full.
    pub async fn write_all(&mut self, mut buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
        while !buf.is_empty() {
            let n = poll_fn(|cx| match self.0.write(buf) {
                Err(e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock => {
                    exec::wake_on(self.0.as_raw_fd(), true, cx.waker().clone());
                    Poll::Pending
                }
                other => Poll::Ready(other),
            })
            .await?;
            if n == 0 {
                return Err(io::ErrorKind::WriteZero.into());
            }
            buf = &buf[n..];
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

Last, block_on ties the parts together. It polls the main future, adopts newly spawned tasks, runs every task on the ready queue, and calls the reactor when the queue is empty. When the main future returns, every other task is dropped:

Exercise 19.4Rustblock_on

Write block_on. Pin the main future on the stack with pin!, and give it a waker with a number that no task uses. Loop. Poll main when it has been woken, and break with its result when it is ready. Run the ready queue. Call the reactor when nothing is ready. After the loop, take every task out of the runtime and drop it.

pub fn block_on<F: Future>(main: F) -> F::Output {
