Stuck?Show the full listing
/// Run `main` to completion on this thread, with every task it spawns. When `main`
/// returns, the tasks still running are dropped: that is how they are cancelled.
pub fn block_on<F: Future>(main: F) -> F::Output {
    RT.with(|rt| assert!(!rt.running.replace(true), "block_on inside block_on"));
    let mut main = pin!(main);
    let ready = RT.with(|rt| Arc::clone(&rt.ready));
    let main_waker = Waker::from(Arc::new(TaskWaker { id: MAIN, ready }));
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&main_waker);
    let mut main_ready = true;
    let out = RT.with(|rt| {
        loop {
            if main_ready {
                main_ready = false;
                if let Poll::Ready(out) = main.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
                    break out;
                }
            }
            rt.adopt();
            while let Some(id) = rt.next_ready() {
                if id == MAIN {
                    main_ready = true;
                } else {
                    rt.run(id);
                }
                rt.adopt();
            }
            if !main_ready {
                rt.wait();
            }
        }
    });
    // cancel: every task left is dropped here, outside any borrow of the runtime
    let (tasks, spawned) = RT.with(|rt| {
        rt.io.borrow_mut().clear();
        rt.timers.borrow_mut().clear();
        rt.free.borrow_mut().clear();
        rt.ready.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner()).clear();
        (
            std::mem::take(&mut *rt.tasks.borrow_mut()),
            std::mem::take(&mut *rt.spawned.borrow_mut()),
        )
    });
    drop((tasks, spawned));
    RT.with(|rt| rt.running.set(false));
    out
}
rust/ch19/src/fp/exec.rs · region block-on

That is a complete executor. kv can run on it. The new binary kv_mini has the same read loop as the tokio server. It has one difference that the single thread allows. No task ever moves to another thread, so nothing needs to be Send. The store is an Rc<RefCell<Db>>, with no lock:

/// The same loop as the tokio version. One thread runs every task, so the store is
/// an `Rc<RefCell<Db>>`, with no lock: a borrow is a check of a counter, and nothing
/// else can run while a task holds it, because a task runs until its next await.
async fn serve(mut stream: Stream, db: Rc<RefCell<Db>>) -> resp::Result<()> {
    let mut requests = Requests::new();
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    let mut chunk = [0u8; 4096];
    loop {
        let n = stream.read(&mut chunk).await?;
        if n == 0 {
            return Ok(());
        }
        requests.push(&chunk[..n])?;
        while let Some(args) = requests.next() {
            let args = match args {
                Ok(args) => args,
                Err(e @ KvError::Protocol(_)) => {
                    resp::write_error(&mut out, "ERR Protocol error")?;
                    stream.write_all(&out).await?;
                    return Err(e);
                }
                Err(e) => return Err(e),
            };
            // the borrow ends at the end of this block, before any await
            let mut db = db.borrow_mut();
            let reply = db.execute(&args)?;
            resp::write_reply(&mut out, &reply)?;
        }
        if !out.is_empty() {
            stream.write_all(&out).await?;
            out.clear();
        }
    }
}
rust/ch19/src/bin/kv_mini.rs · region serve

Is the RefCell safe without a lock? A task runs until its next await, and no other task runs in between. The borrow ends at the end of the block, before the write_all is awaited. If it did not end there, the next task's borrow_mut would panic. That panic is the single-threaded form of the scene's compile error.

Why a future must not move#

Look at the first await in serve, stream.read(&mut chunk). The buffer chunk is a local that lives across the await, so it is a field of the future. The read future borrows it, and the read future is a field of the same future while it waits. So the future holds a pointer into itself.

What happens if such a future moves after its first poll? The std::pin documentation says that "the pointer will still point to the old address where the value was located". The next poll would read the client's bytes into memory that is no longer the buffer. A future that borrows from itself must stay in one place from its first poll until it is dropped.

Pin is that promise in the type system. A Pin<&mut F> is a mutable reference that cannot be used to move F. A pinned value, in the documentation's words, "is guaranteed to remain located at the same place in memory" until its drop is called. That is why poll takes self: Pin<&mut Self>. Whoever polls a future has promised not to move it again.

The executor keeps that promise in two ways. Each task is a Pin<Box<dyn Future>>. The future lives on the heap, and moving the box moves only the pointer. The main future is pinned on the stack of block_on with pin!, which shadows it so that it cannot be named and moved again.

Most types have no pointer into themselves. They implement the auto trait Unpin, which "cancels the restrictive effects of Pin". Sleep holds only an Instant, so it is Unpin. So Pin::new can pin it from a plain mutable reference. That is what the hand-written state machine above does. An async block that borrows its own local across an await is not Unpin. A function that asks for F: Unpin rejects it with E0277, and accepts it once it is inside Box::pin.

Dropping a future cancels it#

When block_on returns, the client tasks are still waiting in their reads. They are dropped. Their code after the await never runs, and their locals are dropped as at the end of any scope. A test shows both halves. A task with a guard in it waits sixty seconds, and main returns after one millisecond:

/// A task still waiting when main returns is dropped. Its code after the await
/// never runs, and its locals are dropped, as at the end of any scope.
#[test]
fn a_task_left_waiting_is_cancelled_by_drop() {
    struct Guard(Rc<Cell<bool>>);
    impl Drop for Guard {
        fn drop(&mut self) {
            self.0.set(true);
        }
    }
    let finished = Rc::new(Cell::new(false));
    let dropped = Rc::new(Cell::new(false));
    block_on({
        let (finished, dropped) = (Rc::clone(&finished), Rc::clone(&dropped));
        async move {
            spawn(async move {
                let _guard = Guard(dropped);
                sleep(Duration::from_secs(60)).await;
                finished.set(true);
            });
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(1)).await;
        }
    });
    assert!(!finished.get(), "the code after the await never ran");
    assert!(dropped.get(), "the task's locals were dropped");
}
rust/ch19/src/fp/exec.rs · region cancel

This is the whole of cancellation in Rust's async model. A future runs only when it is polled, so a future that is no longer polled has stopped. Dropping it frees what it holds. Nothing has to be flagged or caught. tokio::select! uses the same rule. It polls several futures, and when one is ready, it drops the others.

The danger is in the word "where". A future is dropped wherever it last waited, which may be in the middle of a job. Tokio's documentation defines a cancellation safe future as one where "it must be a no-op to drop that future and recreate it". It lists AsyncWriteExt::write_all as one that is not. A select! that drops a half-finished write_all has sent part of a reply, and no code knows how much. In kv, the losing branch of each select! is either the whole client or the stop signal, never a single write.

Blocking inside async#

An executor runs one task at a time on each of its threads. A task that blocks the thread, on a disk or a long computation, stops every other task on that thread. Tokio's documentation puts it plainly. Blocking "may prevent the executor from driving other futures forward". spawn_blocking "runs the provided closure on a thread dedicated to blocking operations", and the tokio server already sends its once-a-second fsync there. kv_mini gives the same job to a plain thread and a channel.

Moving the call is not always enough. With KV_FSYNC=always, the log calls fsync after every write, while the write lock is held. Under a benchmark of writes, a PING from redis-cli --latency took 1,824 milliseconds on the tokio server. It also took 1,127 milliseconds on the threaded server. The task did not block the executor. It held a lock that the PING needed. A blocking call under a lock blocks everyone who needs the lock, on any runtime. That is a design problem, and no executor can solve it.

Check it#

The protocol tests drive kv_mini as they drive the other two servers. They include fifty clients at once from redis-benchmark, and a restart that replays the log. They also send a SIGTERM that must end the process with status 0:

$ tests/run.sh rust ch19 --bin kv_mini
== rust ch19: build
== rust ch19: 207/207 passed

Four unit tests check the executor itself. One checks that a sleep ends and the main value comes back. One checks that two tasks wait at the same time. The test does not measure a time, which would depend on the machine. A 30 millisecond task starts first and a 10 millisecond task second, and the test checks that the short one finishes first. One checks cancellation by drop, and one that a Sleep polled outside block_on panics with "no fp runtime".

miri runs all four, because the reactor uses a plain sleep when no socket is waiting. The first version of the concurrency test asserted that it took less than 55 milliseconds. It passed natively and failed under miri, which interprets every instruction and is much slower. The order-based test passes in both places, and checks the same thing.

The real one: tokio#

Tokio has the same parts, built for production. Its scheduler runs one queue per thread, and an idle thread takes tasks from a busy one. That is why its tasks must be Send. Its reactor uses the best event queue of each system rather than poll. Its timers are designed for millions of deadlines. Its wakers are built on RawWaker, a pointer and a table of four functions. The four are clone, wake, wake by reference, and drop. That is the hand-built vtable of chapter 18 again, and building one needs unsafe for the same reason.

Tokio also finds its reactor through a thread-local. Run its sleep on the executor you wrote, and it panics:

$ cat examples/tokio_sleep_on_fp.rs
fn main() {
    kv::fp::exec::block_on(tokio::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(1)));
}
$ cargo run -q --example tokio_sleep_on_fp
thread 'main' panicked at examples/tokio_sleep_on_fp.rs:2:28:
there is no reactor running, must be called from the context of a Tokio 1.x runtime

Your Sleep fails in the same way inside tokio. A future can be woken only by the reactor it registered with. This is why async libraries name their runtime, and why a crate written for one runtime may not run on another.

Waiting for many clientsCGoRust
What waitsa loop around kqueue or epoll, written by handthe runtime's scheduler, hiddena reactor inside the executor, in a library
The state between two readsa struct per client, kept by the loopthe goroutine's own stacka future, an enum the compiler writes
A blocking callstops the loop and every clientthe runtime parks the goroutine and starts a threadstops the executor thread, unless sent to spawn_blocking
Cancelling a joba flag that the loop checksa context that the code must checkdrop the future, wherever it waits

C makes you write the state machine. Each client's progress is a struct, and the loop decides what to do next with it. Go hides the state machine inside the runtime. Each goroutine has a stack, a blocking call parks it, and the code reads as if it were sequential. Rust writes the state machine for you, as a type. That type is why the rules on Send, Pin and guards exist, and also why a Rust future costs no stack of its own. A thousand waiting clients cost a thousand enums.

Carry forward
  • A future is a state machine. Each await is a variant, and each local that lives across one is a field, which decides whether the future is Send.
  • A waker brings a future back. A future that returns Pending has given its waker to a reactor, which wakes it when a socket or a timer is ready.
  • Pin and cancellation come from the type. A future that borrows itself must not move once polled, and a future that is dropped stops where it last waited.
Next

The tokio server shares its store through an Arc. Swap it for an Rc, and the server no longer compiles. The two types differ by one machine instruction. Chapter 20 writes that instruction yourself.

Shared state from atoms#

Rust from first principles · Chapter 20· 17 min read· 71 lines of code
▶Scene

The tokio server of chapter 19 shares its store between tasks with an Arc. The single-threaded server shares it with an Rc. Both count their owners. In the tokio server, change the Arc around the store to an Rc and build:

$ cargo build -q --bin kv_async
error: future cannot be sent between threads safely
   --> src/bin/kv_async.rs:131:5
    |
131 | /     tokio::spawn(async move {
    = help: within `{async block@src/bin/kv_async.rs:131:18: 131:28}`, the trait `Send` is
            not implemented for `Rc<std::sync::RwLock<Db>>`
note: required by a bound in `tokio::spawn`

Two types with the same job, the same methods and the same size. The compiler lets one cross threads and refuses the other.

The difference between Rc and Arc is one kind of instruction, an atomic one. This chapter builds an Arc and a channel yourself, on atomics, a lock and a condition variable. Then two tools test them. loom tries every order in which the threads could run, and miri watches for data races.

Chapters 9 to 15 shared state with the standard library's types. You put the store in an Arc<RwLock<Db>> or lent it through a scope, and the compiler checked the rest. Two marker traits did most of that checking, Send and Sync. This chapter writes a type that the compiler cannot check, because it holds a raw pointer. You then promise its safety yourself, and test the promise.

Why a counter needs an atomic#

An Rc keeps a count of its owners next to the value. A clone adds one to it. A drop subtracts one and frees the value when the count reaches zero. The count is a plain integer, and "add one" is three steps for the processor. It loads the count, adds, and stores the result.

Now let two threads clone at the same moment. Both load 1. Both store 2. There are three owners, and the count says two. Two drops later the value is freed, and the third owner points at freed memory. That is why Rc is not Send. Its documentation in chapter 6 called it single-threaded. The scene is the compiler holding you to it.

An atomic operation does all three steps as one, so no other thread can see a half-done state. AtomicUsize::fetch_add loads, adds and stores in one instruction, and returns the old value. Two threads that call it at once get 1 and 2, and the count ends at 3. That one change turns an Rc into an Arc. The rest of this chapter is about a second question, which is harder. When one thread writes to memory, when does another thread see the write?

When a write becomes visible#

A processor does not run your instructions in the order you wrote them. The compiler may reorder them too. Both may reorder reads and writes, and keep values in registers or caches, as long as a single thread cannot tell. A second thread can tell. It may see a flag set before it sees the value that the flag announces.

Rust does not define its own rules for this. The Rustonomicon says that Rust inherits "the memory model for atomics from C++20". Each atomic operation takes an Ordering, which says what other memory it puts in order. The standard library defines four that this chapter uses:

  • Relaxed puts nothing else in order. The operation itself is atomic, and that is all.
  • Release, on a store, makes "all previous operations become ordered before any load of this value with Acquire".
  • Acquire, on a load that sees a Release store, makes "all subsequent operations become ordered after that store".
  • SeqCst adds that "all threads see all sequentially consistent operations in the same order".

Release and acquire are a pair. Thread A writes a value, then stores a flag with Release. Thread B loads the flag with Acquire and sees it set. The Rustonomicon describes the result in one sentence. "Causality is established." Everything A did before the release happens before everything B does after the acquire:

When Relaxed is enough#

The threaded server has used an atomic since chapter 10, with Relaxed. The stop thread sets stopping to true, and the accept loop reads it after each connection. Why is no stronger ordering needed? The flag publishes nothing. No thread reads other memory because the flag was set. The accept loop only breaks, and the scope then joins every thread, and a join is itself a synchronization. So the flag needs only to be atomic, so that a read never sees half a write. That is what Relaxed gives.

The rule to keep is a question. Does any thread read other memory because of what this atomic says? If not, Relaxed is correct. If so, the store that announces must be a Release and the load that hears must be an Acquire.

⚠️SeqCst everywhere is not a fix Rust

Making every ordering SeqCst does not make wrong code right. It adds one total order of the SeqCst operations, and it is slower on some processors. It does nothing for a design whose steps can interleave badly. A check of a count followed by a separate decrement is wrong under every ordering, because another thread can run between the two steps. The fix is one atomic step, such as fetch_sub or compare_exchange, and then the weakest ordering whose reason you can state.

Every lock and every channel is built on this pair. Unlocking a mutex is a release. Locking it is an acquire. That is why data written under a lock is visible to the next thread that takes the lock. It is also why you have never had to think about orderings until now.

An Arc, by hand#

The Arc you build keeps the count and the value together in one heap allocation. The handle is a pointer to it. The pointer is raw, a NonNull. Many handles point to the same place, and none of them is the only owner, as a Box would be:

Exercise 20.1RustThe shared allocation and its handle

Write Inner<T> with an AtomicUsize count and the value. Write Arc<T> with a NonNull<Inner<T>> and a PhantomData<Inner<T>>. In new, box an Inner with a count of 1 and keep the pointer with Box::leak. Implement Deref so that *arc reaches the value.

struct Inner<T> {
    count: AtomicUsize,
    data: T,
}

pub struct Arc<T> {
    // your fields here
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
/// The count and the value live together on the heap, in one allocation.
struct Inner<T> {
    count: AtomicUsize,
    data: T,
}

/// A pointer to the shared allocation. The pointer is raw, so the compiler knows nothing
/// about what it points to. `PhantomData<Inner<T>>` tells it: an `Arc<T>` owns an
/// `Inner<T>`, so dropping one may drop a `T`. Drop check uses that, and so does
/// variance: `Arc<&'static str>` may be used as an `Arc<&'a str>`, as a `Box` may.
pub struct Arc<T> {
    ptr: NonNull<Inner<T>>,
    _owns: PhantomData<Inner<T>>,
}
rust/ch20/src/fp/arc.rs · region arc
impl<T> Arc<T> {
    pub fn new(data: T) -> Self {
        let inner = Box::new(Inner {
            count: AtomicUsize::new(1),
            data,
        });
        Arc {
            ptr: NonNull::from(Box::leak(inner)),
            _owns: PhantomData,
        }
    }

    fn inner(&self) -> &Inner<T> {
        // SAFETY: the allocation lives while any clone does, and `self` is one.
        unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() }
    }

    /// The number of clones now. Another thread may change it at once, so it is a hint.
    pub fn count(this: &Self) -> usize {
        this.inner().count.load(Ordering::Relaxed)
    }
}

impl<T> Deref for Arc<T> {
    type Target = T;

    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
        &self.inner().data
    }
}
rust/ch20/src/fp/arc.rs · region new

Why the PhantomData? A raw pointer says nothing about ownership. To the compiler, an Arc<T> with only a NonNull in it does not own a T, so dropping it could not drop one. That matters to drop check, the analysis that decides whether a value's Drop might use a borrow that has already ended. The standard library describes the field as marking a type that acts "as though it stores a value of type T". It also says that this "has effects on the Rust compiler’s drop check analysis". The marker also decides variance. The Reference lists PhantomData<T> as covariant in T, as a box is. So an Arc of a 'static borrow may be used where an Arc of a shorter borrow is wanted. The marker costs nothing at run time. It is zero-sized.

Clone adds one to the count. Relaxed is enough here, and the reason is precise. The new handle is made from a handle that is alive, so the count is at least one before and after. The clone publishes no other memory to any thread:

impl<T> Clone for Arc<T> {
    /// One more owner. `Relaxed` is enough: the new clone was made from a live one, so the
    /// count is at least one before and after, and no other memory is published here.
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        let old = self.inner().count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        // a count that wraps would free the value while clones remain; std aborts too
        if old > isize::MAX as usize {
            std::process::abort();
        }
        Arc {
            ptr: self.ptr,
            _owns: PhantomData,
        }
    }
}
rust/ch20/src/fp/arc.rs · region clone

Why abort, and not panic? A count that passed the largest value would wrap to zero. The next drop would then free a value that a billion handles still point to. A panic can be caught, and the program would go on with a wrong count. Aborting ends the process before any handle can use the freed memory. The standard Arc makes the same choice. The case needs about nine quintillion clones, which a program reaches only by leaking them in a loop.

Drop is where the orderings matter. Each owner subtracts one. The owner that takes the count from 1 to 0 frees the value. Every other owner may have read the value shortly before its own drop, on its own thread. All of those reads must happen before the free:

Exercise 20.2RustThe last owner frees the value

In drop, call fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release). If the old value was not 1, return. Otherwise call fence(Ordering::Acquire), then rebuild the Box with Box::from_raw and drop it. Write a // SAFETY: comment that says why no other handle can still use the value.

impl<T> Drop for Arc<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // your code here
    }
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
impl<T> Drop for Arc<T> {
    /// One less owner. The decrement is `Release`: everything this thread did with the
    /// value happens before it. The last owner's `Acquire` fence then sees all of it,
    /// from every thread, before the value is dropped and the memory freed.
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        #[cfg(not(feature = "planted-relaxed-drop"))]
        {
            if self.inner().count.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) != 1 {
                return;
            }
            fence(Ordering::Acquire);
        }
        // The bug chapter 20 plants for loom to find: no ordering at all.
        #[cfg(feature = "planted-relaxed-drop")]
        if self.inner().count.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Relaxed) != 1 {
            return;
        }
        // SAFETY: the count was 1, so this is the last owner and no other clone exists to
        // read the value. The pointer came from `Box::leak` in `new`.
        drop(unsafe { Box::from_raw(self.ptr.as_ptr()) });
    }
}
rust/ch20/src/fp/arc.rs · region drop

The Release on every decrement puts each thread's earlier reads of the value before its decrement. The Acquire fence on the last owner's thread puts the free after every decrement it saw. Together they give the order that the standard library's own source asks for. Its comment cites the Boost documentation. Every access to the object in one thread must "happen before deleting the object in a different thread". The standard Arc uses the same fetch_sub(1, Release) followed by an Acquire fence.

Send and Sync are promises#

A struct whose fields are all Send is Send, and the compiler works this out by itself. The standard library declares both traits as unsafe auto trait. "Auto" means the compiler implements them from the fields. A raw pointer is not Send and not Sync, because the compiler cannot see what it gives access to. So your Arc is not Send or Sync until you say so. Saying so is unsafe impl, because the compiler takes your word for it:

// SAFETY: an Arc hands out `&T` to every thread that holds a clone, so `T` must be `Sync`.
// The last clone to be dropped drops the `T`, on whichever thread that is, so `T` must be
// `Send`. The count itself is atomic. These are the bounds `std::sync::Arc` has.
unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for Arc<T> {}
// SAFETY: sharing an `&Arc<T>` lets another thread clone it, which needs the same bounds.
unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for Arc<T> {}
rust/ch20/src/fp/arc.rs · region send-sync

Each bound has a reason. Every thread that holds a clone can get a &T, so T must be Sync. The documentation gives the exact rule. A type is Sync "if and only if" a shared reference to it is Send. The last clone may be dropped on any thread, and it drops the T there, so T must be Send. Leave out Sync, and an Arc<Cell<u32>> could cross threads. Two threads would then write the same Cell with no lock, and the compiler would believe your impl. A doc test in src/lessons.rs checks that such an Arc is refused.

A channel, by hand#

The log's sync thread of chapter 11 waits on a channel. Each request to sync is a message. The thread sleeps until one arrives, and stops when every sender is gone. Build that channel on the Arc, a Mutex and a Condvar. A condition variable is a value that a thread can sleep on until another thread notifies it:

Exercise 20.3RustSend, and wait to receive

Share a Mutex<State<T>> and a Condvar through your Arc. The state holds a queue and a count of senders. send pushes under the lock and calls notify_one. recv pops under the lock. When the queue is empty it returns None if there are no senders, and otherwise waits on the condition variable, in a loop. The last sender's Drop notifies the receiver.

pub fn recv(&self) -> Option<T> {
    let mut state = self.0.state.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
    loop {
        // your code here
    }
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
struct State<T> {
    queue: VecDeque<T>,
    senders: usize,
}

/// What both ends share: the queue and the count of senders, behind one lock, and a
/// condition variable that the receiver sleeps on.
struct Shared<T> {
    state: Mutex<State<T>>,
    ready: Condvar,
}

pub struct Sender<T>(Arc<Shared<T>>);
pub struct Receiver<T>(Arc<Shared<T>>);

/// No `unsafe impl` is needed here. `Arc<Shared<T>>` is `Send` and `Sync` when
/// `Shared<T>` is, and a `Mutex<State<T>>` is both when `T` is `Send`. The compiler works
/// it out from the fields; only the type with the raw pointer had to promise.
pub fn channel<T>() -> (Sender<T>, Receiver<T>) {
    let shared = Arc::new(Shared {
        state: Mutex::new(State {
            queue: VecDeque::new(),
            senders: 1,
        }),
        ready: Condvar::new(),
    });
    (Sender(shared.clone()), Receiver(shared))
}
rust/ch20/src/fp/channel.rs · region channel
impl<T> Sender<T> {
    pub fn send(&self, value: T) {
        let mut state = self.0.state.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
        state.queue.push_back(value);
        drop(state);
        self.0.ready.notify_one();
    }
}

impl<T> Clone for Sender<T> {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        self.0
            .state
            .lock()
            .unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())
            .senders += 1;
        Sender(self.0.clone())
    }
}

/// The last sender wakes the receiver, so that it can see there is nothing more to wait for.
impl<T> Drop for Sender<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        let mut state = self.0.state.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
        state.senders -= 1;
        let last = state.senders == 0;
        drop(state);
        if last {
            self.0.ready.notify_one();
        }
    }
}
rust/ch20/src/fp/channel.rs · region send
impl<T> Receiver<T> {
    /// The next value, waiting for one if the queue is empty. `None` once the queue is
    /// empty and every sender is gone. The loop is there because a condition variable may
    /// wake a thread when nothing has changed.
    pub fn recv(&self) -> Option<T> {
        let mut state = self.0.state.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
        loop {
            if let Some(v) = state.queue.pop_front() {
                return Some(v);
            }
            if state.senders == 0 {
                return None;
            }
            state = self.0.ready.wait(state).unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
        }
    }
}

/// So that `for x in receiver` works, as it does for `std::sync::mpsc`.
impl<T> Iterator for Receiver<T> {
    type Item = T;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        self.recv()
    }
}
rust/ch20/src/fp/channel.rs · region recv

Every lock() in kv is followed by unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner()), and the channel keeps that habit. A standard Mutex is poisoned when a thread panics while it holds the lock. Every later lock() then returns an error that carries the guard. The data may be half updated, and the error makes the next thread decide. The state of kv here is a queue and a count, which a panic cannot leave half written. So kv takes the guard out of the error and goes on. A program whose data could be torn would stop instead.

The wait is in a loop because a condition variable may wake a thread when nothing has changed. The loop checks the state again after every wake. The channel needs no unsafe impl. It is built from your Arc around a shared struct. That Arc is Send and Sync when the struct is. A Mutex of a queue is both when T is Send. Only the type with the raw pointer had to promise anything.

The servers now use both. kv and kv_mini send their requests to sync the log through the hand-built channel. kv_async shares its store and its log file through the hand-built Arc, across tokio's threads. The scene's error does not return, because your Arc made the same promise as the standard one.

Check it#

An ordinary test runs the threads in one order, whichever the machine picks that time. A wrong ordering may pass a million runs and fail on another processor. Two tools look further. The first is loom, which "runs a test many times, permuting the possible concurrent executions of that test under the C11 memory model". It replaces the atomics and locks with its own, so the module fp::sync picks loom's types when the crate is built with --cfg kv_loom.

The model is the drop of the Arc itself. A value is shared by two threads. Each reads it and drops its handle. The value's Drop writes to it, through loom's UnsafeCell, which records every access:

/// A value that loom watches. Every thread reads it through loom's `UnsafeCell`, and its
/// `Drop` writes it. If a read on one thread does not happen before the write on another,
/// loom reports a data race: the drop could free memory that is still being read.
struct Probe(UnsafeCell<u32>);

impl Probe {
    fn read(&self) -> u32 {
        // SAFETY: loom checks that no write can run at the same time as this read.
        self.0.with(|p| unsafe { *p })
    }
}

impl Drop for Probe {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // SAFETY: as above, for the write.
        self.0.with_mut(|p| unsafe { *p = 0 });
    }
}
rust/ch20/tests/loom.rs · region probe

To prove that the tool can find a bug, plant one. The cargo feature planted-relaxed-drop makes the decrement Relaxed and removes the fence. Run the models with and without it:

$ RUSTFLAGS="--cfg kv_loom" cargo test -q --release --test loom
test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed
$ RUSTFLAGS="--cfg kv_loom" cargo test -q --release --test loom --features planted-relaxed-drop
arc_drop_happens_after_every_read --- FAILED
Causality violation: Concurrent read and write accesses to `UnsafeCell`.

loom found an order in which one thread's read and the other thread's drop are not ordered. On a machine, that order means freeing memory that is still being read. The loom README suggests a switch named loom. This crate uses kv_loom, because the tokio crate reads a switch named loom for its own tests. The same flag would change how tokio is built.

miri finds the same bug in a different way. It runs the program with real threads and a detector that reports any two unordered accesses to the same memory. The first test of the Arc passed under miri with the bug planted, on all 64 seeds of -Zmiri-many-seeds=0..64. That test joins its threads before main drops the last handle, and the join orders everything. The bug was there, and the test's shape hid it. A second test lets either thread drop last:

$ cargo +nightly miri test -q --lib --features planted-relaxed-drop either_thread
error: Undefined Behavior: Data race detected between (1) retag read on thread ... and
(2) retag write of type `fp::arc::Inner<std::vec::Vec<u32>>` on thread `unnamed-2`

With the bug, that test fails on the default run and on 11 of the 64 seeds. With the correct orderings, all 64 seeds pass. Both tools found the bug. The loom run found it by trying every order of a small model. The miri run found it once a test let the bad order happen. No tool can find a bug that the tests never set up.

Chapter 12 ran the C server under ThreadSanitizer, which watches a compiled program for unordered accesses as it runs. The go test -race detector does the same for Go. The miri interpreter is the same kind of tool for Rust, and it shares their limit. It sees only the runs that happen. The loom crate is a different kind of tool. It runs a small model many times, once for each order that the memory model allows. It is too slow for a whole server. It is also the only one of these tools that can say that every order of a model was checked. A model of three threads and a few operations is within its reach, and that is where the orderings of a hand-built type live.

The server is the last check. All three binaries pass the 207 protocol tests, with the hand-built channel and Arc in place.

The real ones#

std::sync::Arc has the same core, and more around it. It has weak references, which do not keep the value alive and so break cycles. A tree whose children point back to their parent needs them, or no node is ever freed. It holds unsized values, such as Arc<str> and Arc<dyn Trait>. make_mut clones the value only if another owner exists. Its clone aborts the process if the count would overflow, as yours does.

std::sync::mpsc is a channel built with lock-free techniques taken from the crossbeam crate, not a mutex around a queue. It has bounded queues, timeouts and a non-blocking try_recv. Your channel is slower, and you know every line of it. For the log's sync thread, which receives one message a second, the difference cannot be measured.

Sharing a value between threadsCGoRust
Counting ownersby hand, with a C11 atomic_fetch_addnot needed, the collector frees the valueArc, an atomic count, or Rc on one thread
Memory orderingmemory_order_*, the same modelsync/atomic is sequentially consistentOrdering, the C++20 model
Who may cross threadsanything, and nothing checksanything, and the race detector checks at run timeonly Send types, checked at compile time
Testing the orderingsThreadSanitizer, on the runs that happengo test -race, on the runs that happenloom on every order of a model, and miri on the runs that happen

C has the same memory model, with nothing to stop a mistake. ThreadSanitizer finds a race only on a run where it happens. Go chose a simpler model. Its atomics are sequentially consistent, and the garbage collector means nobody has to count owners at all. Rust has the full model and a compiler that refuses to send a type across threads unless the type promises it may go. The promise is only as good as its unsafe impl. That is why a tool like loom exists for Rust, to test the few lines where the compiler takes your word.

Carry forward
  • An atomic is one indivisible step. fetch_add loads, adds and stores at once, which is the only difference in kind between Arc and Rc.
  • Release and acquire order memory. A load with Acquire that sees a store with Release also sees everything before the store. Locks and the last drop of an Arc work this way.
  • Send and Sync are promises. The compiler derives them from the fields, and a raw pointer needs an unsafe impl, which loom and miri can test and the compiler cannot.

Unsafe and macros, soundly#

Rust from first principles · Chapter 21· 20 min read· 182 lines of code
▶Scene

The command lookup copies every command name into a new vector, in capitals, to compare it with the table. In your chapter 20 crate, change lookup to uppercase the name where it lies, through a pointer, and compare that:

$ grep -n -A3 'as_ptr() as \*mut' src/cmd.rs
73:    let p = name.as_ptr() as *mut u8;
74-    for i in 0..name.len() {
75-        unsafe { (*p.add(i)).make_ascii_uppercase() };
76-    }
$ tests/run.sh rust ch20
== rust ch20: 207/207 passed
$ cargo test -q
error: test failed, to rerun pass `--lib`
  process didn't exit successfully: ... (signal: 10, SIGBUS: access to undefined memory)

The server passes every protocol test. The unit tests die with a bus error, and the message does not say where.

The last chapter is about the code the compiler takes on trust. It names the five things unsafe allows, and the rule of soundness that every unsafe block must keep. It builds a reply buffer on uninitialised memory yourself. Then it builds a derive macro, which is code that writes code.

Chapters 13, 15, 18 and 20 each used unsafe for one job. The jobs were a counting allocator, a call into C, a vtable and a reference count. Each block had a // SAFETY: comment, and each was right. The scene shows what wrong looks like. The code compiles with no warning, the server works, and a test crashes for a reason that the crash does not give. This chapter gives the reason, and a tool that finds it.

What unsafe allows#

An unsafe block does not turn off the borrow checker or the type checker. The Rustonomicon lists everything it allows, and then says "That's it." There are five:

  • Dereference raw pointers. kv does it in the reply buffer of this chapter.
  • Call unsafe functions, "including C functions, compiler intrinsics, and the raw allocator". The server calls poll and the signal functions in sys.rs. The buffer calls copy_nonoverlapping.
  • Implement unsafe traits. The hand-built Arc of chapter 20 implements Send and Sync.
  • Access or modify mutable statics. kv has none, and the doc tests show why. Since the 2024 edition, even a shared reference to a static mut is error "creating a shared reference to mutable static". An atomic does the same job without unsafe.
  • Access fields of unions. The parser of chapter 15 reads the i or f field of a C union, chosen by the tag that C set.

Each power is a place where the compiler cannot check a rule, so you must. The rules themselves do not change. They are listed in the Reference under "Behavior considered undefined", and the list "is not exhaustive". Breaking one is undefined behaviour. The compiler may assume it never happens, and the program may then do anything at all.

Sound means no caller can break it#

An unsafe block is correct only if it keeps the rules for every possible input. That property has a name. A function is sound if no safe code that calls it, in any way, can cause undefined behaviour. The scene's lookup is unsound. Nothing in its signature says that the name must be in writable memory, and nothing could. A safe caller that passes a byte literal crashes the program.

Soundness is a property of a module, not of a block. The usual shape is a type with a private field and an invariant, a fact about that field that every method keeps true. The unsafe blocks inside rely on the invariant. Safe code outside cannot touch the field, so it cannot break the invariant. The comment on each block then says which fact it relies on. That is what a // SAFETY: comment is for, and since chapter 20 clippy refuses an unsafe block without one.

✅How to write a SAFETY comment Rust

Name the fact, and say where it comes from. "This is safe" says nothing. A useful comment names the condition that the operation needs, such as "the pointer is in bounds". It then says why that condition holds here, such as "the check two lines above" or "the invariant of the type". A reviewer can then check the comment against the code. If you cannot write the second half, the block is not yet sound.

The 2024 edition marks more of it#

The edition that kv uses moved three things behind the keyword. Each was a place where a program could cause undefined behaviour without writing unsafe. First, an extern block must now be written unsafe extern. A plain one is error "extern blocks must be unsafe". The block declares functions whose types the compiler cannot check, so the declaration itself is a promise.

Second, attributes that can break the program must say so. #[no_mangle] gives a function a global name that could clash with another, so it is now #[unsafe(no_mangle)]. Without the wrapper, it is error "unsafe attribute used without unsafe". Chapter 15 exports a function to C this way.

Third, the body of an unsafe fn is no longer one large unsafe block. A dereference inside it needs its own block, or the compiler warns with E0133. An unsafe fn states that its caller must keep a contract. The block inside states which operation relies on it. When the contract and the operation are kept apart, each // SAFETY: comment sits next to the one line it explains. A reviewer then reads them together.

The rule the scene broke#

Two things went wrong in the scene, and they are different. The unit tests send requests that are byte literals, such as b"*1\r\n$4\r\nPING\r\n". A literal lives in read-only memory, so the first write through the pointer stopped the process with a bus error. The server's requests live in a heap buffer, which is writable. So the server appeared to work.

It did not work. It broke a rule that the processor does not check. The Reference states it for shared references. A &T "must point to memory that is not mutated while they are live (except for data inside an UnsafeCell<U>)". The name in lookup is a &[u8]. The pointer was made from it, so writing through the pointer mutates memory behind a live shared reference. The compiler may assume that this never happens. It may, for example, keep a byte that it read before the write and use it again after.

miri checks this rule. It tracks, for every pointer, which reference it was derived from and what that reference allows. Its default model is called Stacked Borrows. The test a_request_in_a_heap_buffer_is_only_read, in this chapter's cmd.rs, sends a request from a heap vector, as the server does. Natively it passes. Copy it into the chapter 20 crate with the scene's change, and run it under miri:

error: Undefined Behavior: trying to retag from <155889> for SharedReadWrite permission at
alloc52860[0x8], but that tag only grants SharedReadOnly permission for this location
  --> src/cmd.rs:75:18
75 |         unsafe { (*p.add(i)).make_ascii_uppercase() };

A pointer made from a shared reference has read-only permission, and the write asked for more. The miri README describes a second model, Tree Borrows, as "even more experimental", and -Zmiri-tree-borrows turns it on. Tree Borrows allows some patterns that Stacked Borrows rejects. It rejects this one too, with "write access through <152337> ... is forbidden".

The fix needs no unsafe at all. The lookup does not need the name in capitals. It needs to compare without case, and the standard library has a method for that:

// compare without case, byte by byte: no copy of the name, and no write to the
// request, whose bytes the command only borrows
let Some(entry) = Cmd::TABLE
    .iter()
    .find(|e| e.name.eq_ignore_ascii_case(name))
else {
    let shown = String::from_utf8_lossy(&name[..name.len().min(40)]);
    return Err(Reply::Error(format!("ERR unknown command '{shown}'")));
};
rust/ch21/src/cmd.rs · region lookup

eq_ignore_ascii_case compares byte by byte, with no copy and no write. The measurement of chapter 17 now drops to one allocation for a HGETALL. The seven bytes that remained were the copy of its name. The first answer to "can I make this faster with unsafe?" is to look for the safe method that already does it.

Memory that was never written#

Every reply goes into a Vec<u8>. Underneath, a vector is a block of memory and a count of the bytes written so far. The bytes past the count have never been written. What may a program do with them?

Not read them. The Reference says that an integer "must be initialized, i.e., must not be obtained from uninitialized memory". The documentation of MaybeUninit adds a warning. It is "undefined behavior to have uninitialized data in a variable even if that variable has an integer type". A u8 can hold any bit pattern. An uninitialised u8 is not one of them. The compiler may treat it as a value that changes each time it is read.

MaybeUninit<T> is a type that may hold a T or nothing. The documentation calls it "a wrapper type to construct uninitialized instances of T". Writing to one is always allowed. Reading one as a T is unsafe, and correct only if a T was written there.

A reply buffer, by hand#

Build the core of a vector yourself, for bytes. A block of MaybeUninit<u8> and a count are the whole state. The invariant is one sentence. The first len bytes are initialised, and nothing reads the rest:

Exercise 21.1RustThe block and its invariant

Write WriteBuf with a private Box<[MaybeUninit<u8>]> and a private len. Make with_capacity with Box::new_uninit_slice, which allocates and writes nothing. State the invariant in the doc comment, because every unsafe block will rely on it.

pub struct WriteBuf {
    // your fields here
}

/// The bytes `[0, len)` of `block` are initialised. The bytes from `len` on are not, and
/// nothing may read them. Every method keeps that true, and that is the whole proof that
/// the `unsafe` blocks below are sound: no safe call can make one of them wrong.
pub struct WriteBuf {
    block: Box<[MaybeUninit<u8>]>,
    len: usize,
}
rust/ch21/src/fp/buf.rs · region buf

Two methods need unsafe. push_slice copies new bytes in after len, through a raw pointer, then adds to len. as_slice returns the first len bytes as a &[u8]. Each block's comment names the fact it relies on. The copy relies on the capacity check above it. The slice relies on the invariant:

Exercise 21.2RustPush and read back

Write push_slice. If the bytes do not fit, grow first. Then copy them with copy_nonoverlapping to the address block.as_mut_ptr().add(len), cast to a byte pointer. Add their count to the length. Write as_slice with slice::from_raw_parts over the first len bytes. Implement io::Write, so that write_reply can format into the buffer.

pub fn push_slice(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) {
    if self.block.len() - self.len < bytes.len() {
        self.grow(self.len + bytes.len());
    }
    // your code here, with a SAFETY comment
}
Stuck?Show the full listing
impl WriteBuf {
    pub fn with_capacity(cap: usize) -> Self {
        WriteBuf {
            // a block of uninitialised bytes: nothing is written, so nothing is zeroed
            block: Box::new_uninit_slice(cap),
            len: 0,
        }
    }

    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
        self.len
    }

    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.len == 0
    }

    /// Forget the bytes. They stay in memory, and count as uninitialised again.
    pub fn clear(&mut self) {
        self.len = 0;
    }

    /// Append bytes, growing the block to twice its size, or more, if they do not fit.
    /// The copy goes through a raw pointer, with no bounds check: the check above it is
    /// the only thing between this code and a write past the end of the block.
    pub fn push_slice(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) {
        #[cfg(not(feature = "planted-off-by-one"))]
        let short = self.block.len() - self.len < bytes.len();
        // The bug chapter 21 plants for miri to find: one byte too few is still "fits".
        #[cfg(feature = "planted-off-by-one")]
        let short = self.block.len() - self.len + 1 < bytes.len();
        if short {
            self.grow(self.len + bytes.len());
        }
        // SAFETY: the check above makes `len + bytes.len() <= capacity`, so the
        // destination is in bounds. A `u8` has the layout of a `MaybeUninit<u8>`. The
        // regions cannot overlap: `bytes` is a shared borrow, and the block is borrowed
        // mutably here.
        unsafe {
            let dst = self.block.as_mut_ptr().add(self.len).cast::<u8>();
            std::ptr::copy_nonoverlapping(bytes.as_ptr(), dst, bytes.len());
        }
        self.len += bytes.len();
    }

    /// The bytes written so far.
    pub fn as_slice(&self) -> &[u8] {
        // SAFETY: the first `len` bytes are initialised (the invariant above), and the
        // slice borrows `self`, so no push can change them while it lives.
        unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(self.block.as_ptr().cast::<u8>(), self.len) }
    }

    /// A bigger block, with the written bytes moved into it. Safe code throughout: the
    /// new block starts uninitialised, and the copy goes through `push_slice`'s logic.
    fn grow(&mut self, need: usize) {
        let cap = need.max(self.block.len() * 2);
        let mut bigger = WriteBuf::with_capacity(cap);
        bigger.push_slice(self.as_slice());
        *self = bigger;
    }
}

/// So that `write_reply` and `write!` can format into it, as into a `Vec<u8>`.
impl io::Write for WriteBuf {
    fn write(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        self.push_slice(bytes);
        Ok(bytes.len())
    }

    fn flush(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
        Ok(())
    }
}
rust/ch21/src/fp/buf.rs · region methods

Is it sound? The fields are private, so only these methods change them. Each method keeps the invariant, and grow uses no unsafe of its own. A safe caller can push, clear and read in any order and never reach an uninitialised byte. The three servers now format every reply into a WriteBuf, and pass the 207 protocol tests.

Check it#

The capacity check is the one line between this code and a write past the end of the block. To see what that line protects, plant a bug in it. The feature planted-off-by-one lets a push through when it is one byte too long.

Run natively, the bug gives two different answers. A test that fills a block of eight bytes with nine passes, because the ninth byte lands in memory that the allocator keeps spare. A test that starts with a capacity of zero dies with SIGSEGV. Under miri, both tests fail, at the same line, with the same explanation:

error: Undefined Behavior: memory access failed: attempting to access 2 bytes, but got
alloc56461+0x7 which is only 1 byte from the end of the allocation
  --> src/fp/buf.rs:59:13
59 |             std::ptr::copy_nonoverlapping(bytes.as_ptr(), dst, bytes.len());

Many real bugs in C have this shape, a write one byte past the end that passes its tests. The miri interpreter reports it on its first run. It also runs the whole library, with the correct buffer, under both models:

$ cargo +nightly miri test -q --lib
test result: ok. 25 passed; 0 failed; 3 ignored
$ MIRIFLAGS="-Zmiri-tree-borrows" cargo +nightly miri test -q --lib
test result: ok. 25 passed; 0 failed; 3 ignored

A clean run under miri is evidence, not proof. miri checks the paths that the tests take, and no others. That is why the buffer has a test that lands exactly on the end of the block. It is the path where an off-by-one lives.

Let a tool write the extern block#

Chapter 15 declared the functions of the C library itself, from kvmatch.h. A wrong type there is undefined behaviour. No tool sees it, because the compiler takes an extern block on trust. The bindgen tool reads the C header with libclang, the C compiler as a library, and writes the block for you. This is the block that chapter 15 wrote:

// wrong type here is undefined behaviour, which is why the block is unsafe to call.

    fn kvmatch_hash(s: *const u8, n: usize) -> u64;
    fn kvmatch_glob(pat: *const u8, plen: usize, key: *const u8, klen: usize) -> c_int;
    fn kvmatch_glob_stats(
        pat: *const u8,
        plen: usize,
        key: *const u8,
        klen: usize,
        out: *mut Stats,
    );
    fn kvmatch_parse_number(s: *const u8, n: usize, out: *mut CNumber) -> c_int;
}

The generated code is longer and more literal. A const char * becomes *const c_char, where the hand-written version chose *const u8. The anonymous union gets the name kvmatch_number__bindgen_ty_1. Both are correct, and only one of them can drift from the header. Projects with large C interfaces run bindgen in build.rs, so that the bindings are made again from the header at every build.

The price is a dependency on libclang. Without it, the tool stops with the message "Unable to find libclang". Its advice is to "set the LIBCLANG_PATH environment variable". The four functions of kv stay as chapter 15 wrote them. The generated file is kept in bindgen/, for comparison.

A derive, by hand#

Since chapter 5, the command table has been a macro_rules! invocation. A declarative macro matches token patterns and fills in a template. It cannot compute a name from another name, and it cannot report an error at the place that caused it. A procedural macro can, because it is a Rust function that the compiler runs.

The Reference states the contract. A derive is "a pub function ... with a type of fn(TokenStream) -> TokenStream". It must be defined "in the root of a crate with the crate type of proc-macro". So the derive lives in a crate of its own, kv-macros. The compiler builds it for its own machine, loads it, and calls it on the item that the derive is attached to.

The item is an enum with one variant per command. An attribute on each variant says whether the command reads or writes, and how many words it takes. The derive writes the table:

/// The commands, one variant each, and the table that `#[derive(Commands)]` writes from
/// them: `Cmd::TABLE`. The name of a command is its variant's name in capitals, and the
/// function that runs it has the variant's name in lower case. The enum exists to carry
/// the attributes, and its values are never made.
#[allow(dead_code)]
#[derive(Commands)]
enum Cmd {
    #[cmd(read, arity = -1)]

    #[cmd(read, arity = 2)]
    Echo,
    #[cmd(write, arity = -3)]

Tokens are hard to work with directly, so two crates do the parsing and the printing. The syn crate is "a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree". The derive's entry point parses the input, builds the table, and turns any error into a compile_error!:

/// What one `#[cmd(...)]` attribute says.
struct Command {
    write: bool,
    arity: i32,
    run: Ident,
}

impl Command {
    fn parse(v: &syn::Variant) -> syn::Result<Self> {
        if !matches!(v.fields, syn::Fields::Unit) {
            return Err(Error::new_spanned(
                &v.fields,
                "a command variant holds no data",
            ));
        }
        let Some(attr) = v.attrs.iter().find(|a| a.path().is_ident("cmd")) else {
            return Err(Error::new_spanned(
                &v.ident,
                "every command needs #[cmd(read | write, arity = N)]",
            ));
        };
        let (mut kind, mut arity, mut run) = (None, None, None);
        attr.parse_nested_meta(|meta| {
            if meta.path.is_ident("read") || meta.path.is_ident("write") {
                if kind.is_some() {
                    return Err(meta.error("say read or write, once"));
                }
                kind = Some(meta.path.is_ident("write"));
            } else if meta.path.is_ident("arity") {
                let value = meta.value()?;
                let negative = value.parse::<Option<Token![-]>>()?.is_some();
                let n: i32 = value.parse::<LitInt>()?.base10_parse()?;
                arity = Some(if negative { -n } else { n });
            } else if meta.path.is_ident("run") {
                run = Some(meta.value()?.parse::<Ident>()?);
            } else {
                return Err(meta.error("expected read, write, arity or run"));
            }
            Ok(())
        })?;
        let Some(write) = kind else {
            return Err(Error::new_spanned(
                attr,
                "say whether the command is read or write",
            ));
        };
        let Some(arity) = arity else {
            return Err(Error::new_spanned(attr, "give the command an arity"));
        };
        let run = run
            .unwrap_or_else(|| Ident::new(&v.ident.to_string().to_lowercase(), Span::call_site()));
        Ok(Command { write, arity, run })
    }
}

Exercise 21.4RustWrite the table

Write table. For each variant, make the name with LitByteStr::new from the variant's name in capitals. Choose the kind of run, and emit one Entry with quote!. Interpolate the rows with #(#rows),* into impl #ty { const TABLE: ... }. Then write the entry point with #[proc_macro_derive(Commands, attributes(cmd))].

rows.push(quote! {
    Entry { name: #name, run: Run::#kind(#run), arity: #arity }
});
Stuck?Show the full listing
fn table(input: &DeriveInput) -> syn::Result<proc_macro2::TokenStream> {
    let Data::Enum(data) = &input.data else {
        return Err(Error::new_spanned(
            &input.ident,
            "Commands can be derived only for an enum",
        ));
    };
    let mut rows = Vec::new();
    for v in &data.variants {
        let cmd = Command::parse(v)?;
        let name = syn::LitByteStr::new(
            v.ident.to_string().to_uppercase().as_bytes(),
            v.ident.span(),
        );
        let run = &cmd.run;
        let kind = if cmd.write {
            quote!(Write)
        } else {
            quote!(Read)
        };
        let arity = cmd.arity;
        rows.push(quote! {
            Entry { name: #name, run: Run::#kind(#run), arity: #arity }
        });
    }
    let ty = &input.ident;
    Ok(quote! {
        impl #ty {
            const TABLE: &'static [Entry] = &[#(#rows),*];
        }
    })
}
rust/ch21/kv-macros/src/lib.rs · region table
/// Each variant is one command. Its name in capitals is the command's name, and the
/// function that runs it has the variant's name in lower case, unless `run = ...` names
/// another. `read` or `write` says which lock it needs, and `arity` how many words it
/// takes, negative for "at least".
///
/// ```text
/// #[derive(Commands)]
/// enum Cmd {
///     #[cmd(read, arity = 2)] Get,
///     #[cmd(write, arity = -3)] Set,
///     #[cmd(read, arity = 2, run = type_cmd)] Type,
/// }
/// ```
///
/// becomes `impl Cmd { const TABLE: &'static [Entry] = &[...]; }`, with one `Entry` per
/// variant. `Entry` and `Run` are found where the derive is used.
#[proc_macro_derive(Commands, attributes(cmd))]
pub fn derive_commands(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    match table(&input) {
        Ok(tokens) => tokens.into(),
        // an error becomes a compile_error! at the span it names, so the message points
        // at the variant or the attribute that is wrong, in the user's own file
        Err(e) => e.to_compile_error().into(),
    }
}
rust/ch21/kv-macros/src/lib.rs · region derive

The error spans are the part a declarative macro cannot match. Leave the attribute off one variant, and the error points at that variant, in your file:

error: every command needs #[cmd(read | write, arity = N)]
 --> examples/derive_error.rs:8:5
  |
8 |     Echo,
  |     ^^^^

The price is compile time. In a clean debug build of kv, which takes 22.9 seconds, syn alone takes 5.1 seconds. Only tokio takes longer, at 8.4. With proc-macro2, quote and their build scripts, the macro adds about 10 seconds of compiler work, part of it in parallel with tokio. A table of 28 commands does not need that. A derive earns its cost when many types use it. The Serialize derive of the serde crate is the common example. The table of kv uses one here only because this chapter teaches it.

The real ones#

Vec<u8> is your WriteBuf with a generic element type, a zero-capacity case that allocates nothing, and decades of review behind it. Its spare_capacity_mut method gives the uninitialised part as a slice of MaybeUninit. That is the safe form of what you wrote in this chapter. The bytes crate's BytesMut adds a buffer that can be split into shared, counted pieces, as chapter 17 mentioned. For kv, Vec<u8> was always enough. The hand-built buffer exists to show what is inside.

Most crates need no unsafe at all, and can say so. The crate attribute #![forbid(unsafe_code)] makes every unsafe block in the crate an error, and no inner attribute can allow it again. The derive crate kv-macros carries it, because a function from tokens to tokens has no reason to touch raw memory. The main crate of kv cannot carry it. It calls C, waits in poll, and holds the hand-built types of Part V. Its unsafe sits in a few named modules, and each block has a comment that a reviewer can check. A reader of a new crate can search for the word unsafe and find every place that needs that review.

The procedural macro you are most likely to meet is a derive from a crate such as serde, thiserror or clap. Each reads a type and writes the impl that you would otherwise write. You now know what happens when one runs. A function in another crate receives your type as tokens, and its output is compiled as if you had typed it.

Code the compiler does not checkCGoRust
Raw memoryevery pointer, everywherethe unsafe package, and cgoraw pointers, inside unsafe blocks only
Finding undefined behavioursanitizers, on the runs that happenthe race detector, and few other kinds existmiri, on the runs that happen, and soundness by design
Generated declarations for Cthe header is the declarationcgo reads the headerbindgen writes an extern block from the header
Code that writes codethe preprocessor, text in and text outgo generate, a program run before the buildmacro_rules!, and procedural macros on tokens

In C, all memory is raw, so a buffer like WriteBuf is ordinary code, and an off-by-one in it is an ordinary bug. Go keeps raw memory behind the unsafe package, and most Go programs never import it. Rust keeps it behind a keyword that marks each place, and asks for a safe interface around each one. The marked places are few, so a tool like miri and a reviewer can check them closely. The rest of the program then depends on a few lines that someone has checked.

Carry forward
  • Unsafe allows five things. It allows raw pointers, unsafe calls, unsafe traits, mutable statics and union fields, and every rule of the language still holds.
  • Sound means no safe caller can break it. A private field and an invariant, kept by every method, make the unsafe blocks inside correct for any use.
  • A procedural macro is a function on tokens. One crate parses the item and another writes the output. Its errors point at the code that caused them.
Next

Part V ends here, and so does the book's teaching. Appendix E lists every Rust concept in a line or two, with a link to where kv uses it. The last section of the verdict lists what to build next.

A thread and a shared counter#

C
static int count;
static pthread_mutex_t mu = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
void *work(void *arg) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&mu);
    count++;
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&mu);
    return NULL;
}
pthread_t t;
pthread_create(&t, NULL, work, NULL);
pthread_join(t, NULL);

var count int

	mu.Lock()
	count++
	mu.Unlock()
})

Rust
let count = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));
let c = Arc::clone(&count);
let t = thread::spawn(move || {
    *c.lock().unwrap() += 1;
    // unlocked here, when the guard drops
});
t.join().unwrap();

Handing work to another thread#

C

let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
thread::scope(|s| {
    s.spawn(move || for j in rx { work(j) });  // ends when tx is dropped

    drop(tx);
});

Appendix B: Glossary#

Appendices · Appendix B· 6 min read

The terms the book uses, each with the section that explains it. The first use of a term in each chapter links here.

TermMeaningSee
ABIApplication binary interface. The convention for how a compiled function receives its arguments and returns its result.The border is a C function
AddressSanitizerA compiler mode that watches every memory access and reports a use after free or an access outside a block.C: a runner you write, and a sanitizer that watches
AOFAppend-only file. kv's log of every write, replayed at start to rebuild the store.C: a file descriptor, a write, and a thread for the fsync
asyncRust code that pauses at an await point instead of blocking a thread, run by a runtime such as tokio.Rust once more: tasks on tokio
atomicAn operation on a shared variable that no other thread can see half done, with a memory order that says what else it promises.C again: the second thread
borrow checkerThe part of the Rust compiler that tracks who may read or change a value and for how long.Rust: a value has one owner
build constraintThe comment on the first line of a Go file, //go:build, that says which systems or settings the file is for.Go's platform files: a line at the top
bulk stringThe RESP form of a byte string. A dollar sign, a length, a line break, the bytes, a line break.C: a buffer, a parser and three answers
cfgThe Rust attribute, #[cfg(...)], that keeps an item out of the build on every system or setting it does not name.Rust's platform code: an attribute on the item
cgoThe part of the go tool that lets Go code call C and be called from it.Go: cgo
chainingA hash table design where each bucket holds a linked list of the entries that hash to it.C: an array of chains, and every pointer accounted for
channelA queue that goroutines or threads send values through, which in Go and Rust is also the lock.Go again: fifty workers and three channels
clippyThe Rust linter. It reports patterns that compile but are slower, longer or riskier than they need to be.One style, enforced by a tool
closureA function literal that captures variables from the scope around it.Go: two kinds of string, and a copy between them
condition variableA place a thread sleeps until another thread signals it, always inside a loop that checks the condition again.C again: the second thread
contextThe Go value that carries a cancellation, a deadline and request values down a chain of calls.context in one paragraph
crateA Rust package. A library crate, a binary crate, or both, described by Cargo.toml.Rust: a module is a file you must announce
cross-compilingBuilding on one machine a binary that runs on another kind of machine.C: zig as the cross-compiler
cursorA number the client sends back so that the server can continue a walk where it stopped.C: a tag and a union
data raceTwo threads touching the same memory at the same time, one of them writing, with no lock between them.Go: one word, and one lock
deadlineThe moment a key expires, stored with the key as a reading of the monotonic clock.C: a deadline on the entry, and a sweep with a cursor
dynamic linkingLinking where the binary holds only the name of a library and finds it on the machine at start.What a binary carries
epollThe Linux call that waits for many sockets at once. kqueue on macOS and completion ports on Windows do the same job.C: one thread, and a poller to say who is ready
escape analysisThe Go compiler's decision, for each value, whether it may live on the stack or must go on the heap.Escape analysis
event loopOne thread that asks which sockets are ready and serves each in turn.C: one thread, and a poller to say who is ready
executorThe part of an async runtime that polls the tasks whose wakers have been called, one at a time on each thread.A future, a waker and an executor, by hand
extern blockThe Rust declaration of functions that live in another language, marked unsafe since the 2024 edition.Rust: extern and unsafe
fat pointerA pointer of two words, the address and one more fact, such as a slice's length or a trait object's vtable.A trait object is two words
file descriptorThe small integer a Unix system gives a program for an open file or socket.C: four calls, and a way to clean up
flame graphA picture of a profile in which each box is a function and its width is the share of samples through it.Taking a number
fsyncThe system call that makes the operating system write a file's bytes to the disk before it returns.What a crash takes
fuzzingTesting with generated inputs that a tool mutates toward the paths it has not yet run.Fuzzing, three ways, one engine
garbage collectorThe part of the Go runtime that finds memory nothing points to and frees it.Go: the same table, with nothing to free
genericA function or type written once for many types, with type parameters that the compiler fills in.Go: the same table, with nothing to free
goroutineA function the Go runtime runs on its own small stack, a few kilobytes, scheduled over the real threads.Go: one word, and one lock
goroutine leakA goroutine that waits for a message or a reply that never comes, and lives until the process ends.Go again: fifty workers and three channels
happens-beforeThe order the memory model guarantees between two operations, made by a Release store that an Acquire load sees.When a write becomes visible
hash tableAn array of buckets, with a hash of the key choosing the bucket. The store under GET and SET.C: an array of chains, and every pointer accounted for
headerA C file of declarations, included by every file that uses them.C: headers, static, and a Makefile that knows about both
header guardThe #ifndef at the top of a header that stops it being read twice.C: headers, static, and a Makefile that knows about both
interfaceA Go type that names methods, satisfied by any type that has them, without being told.Go: a folder is a package, and a capital letter is an export
iteratorA value with a next method that yields one item at a time, which adaptors wrap and nothing runs until asked.Rust: an enum with data in each variant
lazy expiryChecking a key's deadline when the key is read, and deleting it then.C: a deadline on the entry, and a sweep with a cursor
lending iteratorAn iterator whose items borrow from the iterator itself, which needs a generic associated type.An iterator that lends its buffer
libcThe C standard library, which also wraps the system calls. glibc and musl are two of them.What a binary carries
libFuzzerThe in-process, coverage-guided fuzzing engine in clang, which cargo-fuzz drives for Rust.C: a runner you write, and a sanitizer that watches
lifetimeThe name, written 'a, that says how long a reference in a type is valid, which the compiler checks and never extends.Lifetimes, in the one place kv needs them
linkerThe tool that joins compiled files and libraries into one binary.What a binary is
miriAn interpreter for Rust that checks unsafe code for undefined behaviour while it runs.Rust: the compiler already ran, and the tools check the rest
moduleIn Go, a set of packages with a version. In Rust, a file or block of code with its own names.Go: a folder is a package, and a capital letter is an export
monotonic clockA clock that only goes forward, unaffected by the user changing the time.C: a deadline on the entry, and a sweep with a cursor
muslA small C library for Linux that is designed to be linked statically.What a binary carries
mutexA lock. One thread holds it at a time, and the others wait.Go: one word, and one lock
ownershipThe Rust rule that every value has one owner, and is freed when the owner goes away.Rust: a value has one owner
packageIn Go, a folder of files that share a name. In Rust, a crate with a Cargo.toml.Go: a folder is a package, and a capital letter is an export
pipeliningSending many commands before reading any reply, so that the network wait is paid once.Taking a number
pollThe portable call that waits until one of a set of sockets is ready.C: one thread, and a poller to say who is ready
pollerThe loop's question to the kernel, which socket is ready, asked with poll, kqueue or epoll.C again: poll, kqueue and epoll behind one header
procedural macroA Rust function that the compiler runs on tokens at compile time, such as a derive, which writes code.A derive, by hand
profileA record of where a running program spent its time, taken by sampling the stack.C: a clock, a loop and five flags
race detectorThe Go tool, go test -race, that watches memory access and reports a data race it sees.Go: the runner is in the box, and so is the fuzzer
raw pointerA Rust pointer, *const T or *mut T, with the borrow checker's guarantees removed, which only an unsafe block may read through.The five powers, and the pointer they are for
reactorThe part of an async runtime that waits for sockets and timers, and calls the waker of each one that is ready.A future, a waker and an executor, by hand
regionA marked part of a listing that the book pulls in by name, so the text and the code cannot drift.The code
repr(C)The Rust attribute that lays a struct or union out as a C compiler would, so that the bytes mean the same on both sides.The five powers, and the pointer they are for
RESPThe Redis serialization protocol. Arrays of bulk strings in, and simple strings, errors, integers, bulk strings or nil out.C: a buffer, a parser and three answers
ResultThe Rust type that is either a value or an error, and must be looked at.Rust: a Result at every step
sanitizerA compiler mode that adds checks for memory errors, undefined behaviour or data races.C: a runner you write, and a sanitizer that watches
scoped threadA Rust thread spawned inside thread::scope, which may borrow local data because the scope joins it before returning.Rust again: the load generator with scoped threads
self-pipe trickA signal handler that writes one byte into a pipe the event loop waits on, so that a signal becomes an event.C: a signal, a flag and a pipe
semantic versioningThree numbers, major, minor and patch, that say what kind of change a release holds.Versions and releases
Send and SyncThe two Rust marker traits that say a value may move to another thread, or be shared between threads, derived by the compiler.Send and Sync
soundnessThe property of a safe API that no safe caller can cause undefined behaviour through it, in any way.Sound means no caller can break it
static linkingLinking where the binary carries its libraries inside and needs nothing from the machine.What a binary carries
sum typeA value that is one of several kinds, with a tag that says which. A tagged union in C, an interface in Go, an enum in Rust.C: a tag and a union
sweepThe background pass that deletes expired keys nobody has asked for.C: a deadline on the entry, and a sweep with a cursor
tokioThe Rust async runtime that the book's second Rust server runs on.Rust once more: tasks on tokio
trait objectA value of unknown concrete type behind dyn Trait, called through a table of function pointers at run time.Rust: a module is a file you must announce
type switchThe Go switch on the dynamic type inside an interface value, one case per type.Go: any, and a switch on the type
undefined behaviourA C or unsafe Rust operation the standard does not define, after which the compiler may do anything.C: a runner you write, and a sanitizer that watches
unionA C or Rust type whose fields share the same bytes, so that only one is meaningful at a time.A struct and a union on the border
unsafeThe Rust keyword that marks a block where the five extra powers are allowed, and the author takes responsibility.Rust: extern and unsafe
varianceThe rule for when a type with one lifetime may be used where another is wanted, such as a long borrow for a short one.One lifetime for two borrows
vtableA table of function pointers, one per method of a trait, which a trait object points to next to its value.A vtable, by hand
wakerA handle that a pending future gives to a reactor, so that its task is polled again when it can progress.A future is a value that waits
X-macroA list written once as a macro, reused with a different meaning of X for a table, a declaration or a call.C: a runner you write, and a sanitizer that watches
zigA toolchain that includes a C compiler and the C libraries of many targets, used here to cross-compile.C: zig as the cross-compiler
